docs.title: Full Stack Engineering Knowledge Base
docs.text: Welcome to my personal, continuously growing reference for understanding how software works, from network communication and operating systems to user interfaces, data, and production infrastructure.

docs.title: Learning roadmap
docs.text:
The sections are organized to build understanding from foundational systems through application development and deployment:

  1. Networking and Protocols
  2. Frontend Development
  3. Backend Development
  4. Databases
  5. Application Architecture
  6. Servers and Infrastructure
  7. DevOps and Deployment
  8. Operating Systems and Linux
  9. Security and Testing
  10. Rust and Systems Programming

docs.title: How to use these notes
docs.text: Start with a section's overview, then follow its lessons or jump to a topic that answers a specific question. Lessons will focus on clear explanations, practical examples, developer perspectives, terminology, and revision questions. Related concepts will be linked as the notes grow.

docs.title: Networking and Protocols
docs.text:
This section explains how computers communicate and how information travels between a client and a server across the Internet.

Think of a web request as several cooperating layers: a name is resolved to an address, the network carries packets, a transport protocol manages delivery, and an application protocol describes the request and response.

docs.title: One request, several layers
docs.text:
Imagine entering https://example.com/products in a browser. The browser needs the server's address, a route to reach it, a transport for delivery, protection for the connection, and an application protocol to request the page. These jobs are related, but one layer's success does not prove that the next layer is healthy.

What you observe What it tells you What it does not prove DNS returned an address The name was resolved by that resolver That the destination is reachable A TCP connection opened A TCP endpoint accepted that connection That the HTTP request will succeed HTTPS certificate is valid The peer passed certificate checks for the host That the site or its content is trustworthy HTTP returned 200 The response was successful by HTTP semantics That a business operation did what you intended

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the Internet's basic building blocks and addressing.
  • Follow the journey of a request through DNS, transport, and web protocols.
  • Explain how a device joins a local network and finds its next-hop router.
  • Recognize the roles of encryption, persistent connections, and ports.
  • Choose troubleshooting tools based on which network layer may have failed.

docs.title: How protocols appear in real services
docs.text:
Most public websites use the same Internet building blocks. The business may have additional identity checks, security controls, or private connections, but a familiar website URL does not imply a special transport protocol.

Service example Common network path Why these protocols fit Shopping, news, or video website DNS, Wi-Fi or Ethernet, IP, TCP or QUIC, TLS, HTTP; often a CDN HTTP delivers pages and APIs; TLS protects data in transit; a CDN can serve content closer to users Online banking website or app Usually the same DNS, IP, TLS, and HTTPS foundation; may also use MFA and risk checks Standard web protocols interoperate with browsers; authentication, authorization, fraud controls, and payment processing are additional application/system responsibilities Crypto exchange or wallet interface HTTPS for pages and API calls; WebSockets may stream prices; a blockchain network uses its own peer and transaction rules A web interface and a blockchain are different protocol layers; using HTTPS does not mean a blockchain transaction is sent as an ordinary web page Government service portal Usually DNS, IP, TLS, and HTTPS; some internal services may use private networks or additional identity systems Common web standards support public access; identity proofing, accessibility, audit, and policy requirements sit above the basic transport Email service DNS records to locate mail servers; SMTP to send mail; IMAP or POP3 for mailbox access; TLS commonly protects connections Email needs separate protocols for delivery between mail servers and access by a user's mail client Remote server administration IP routing followed by SSH, commonly over TCP port 22 SSH provides an authenticated encrypted terminal and related secure functions; access should be restricted to authorized administrators

These are typical patterns, not guarantees about any particular provider. Financial, cryptocurrency, and government systems may also use private networks, specialized payment or identity systems, or organization-specific controls that are not visible from the public website. Never infer that a service is secure or trustworthy solely because it uses HTTPS.

docs.title: Suggested learning path
docs.text:
1. Begin with Internet Fundamentals, then learn IP addressing.
  2. See how a device joins a network with Ethernet and Wi-Fi, gets configuration through DHCP, and finds a local next hop with ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
  3. Compare TCP and UDP, then learn how ports direct data to applications.
  4. Follow name resolution in DNS, then study TLS and SSL and HTTP and HTTPS. Continue with QUIC and HTTP/3 to understand the modern UDP-based web transport.
  5. Explore other application protocols: WebSockets for interactive communication, Email Protocols for mail, SSH and SFTP for remote access, MQTT for device messaging, and gRPC for service-to-service APIs.
  6. Learn how VPNs and Tunneling connect private networks and why NTP matters to distributed systems.
  7. Use ICMP and Network Diagnostics to understand common troubleshooting signals.

When diagnosing a problem, ask which step failed rather than treating "the Internet is down" as one explanation. A name lookup issue, blocked connection, invalid certificate, and application error have different causes and different tools. A ping response, for example, is not required for an HTTPS service to work.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) helps an IPv4 device find the local link-layer address associated with an IPv4 address on its local network. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP), which is part of ICMPv6, for neighbor and router discovery.

IP addresses guide packets between networks. Ethernet and Wi-Fi frames need link-layer destination addresses for delivery on the current local link. ARP and NDP connect those two jobs.

docs.title: Why do they exist?
docs.text: A device may know the IP address of its default gateway but still need the gateway's local MAC address to send the next frame. Address resolution lets the device deliver an IP packet to the correct next hop without requiring applications to know local hardware addresses.

docs.title: IPv4 ARP
docs.text:
1. A device checks its ARP cache for a recent IP-to-MAC mapping.
  2. If there is no usable mapping and the destination is local, it broadcasts an ARP request on the local network: "Who has this IPv4 address?"
  3. The device using that IPv4 address replies with its MAC address.
  4. The sender stores the mapping temporarily and sends the IP packet inside a frame addressed to that MAC address.

If the destination IP is outside the local subnet, the sender resolves the MAC address of its gateway, not the remote server's MAC address. Routers forward packets one link at a time; the remote server is not on the sender's local Ethernet or Wi-Fi link.

docs.title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
docs.text:
IPv6 does not use ARP. NDP uses ICMPv6 messages and multicast on the local link to discover neighbors and routers. It also supports functions such as address reachability checks and duplicate address detection. IPv6 uses Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages for address resolution.

Feature IPv4 ARP IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Network protocol IPv4-related link operation ICMPv6 Discovery method Local broadcast request and reply Multicast solicitation and advertisement Additional roles Address-to-link mapping Router discovery, reachability checks, and other local-link functions

Both use caches to avoid repeating resolution for every packet. Entries can expire or change as devices and network configurations change.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a laptop opens an online banking site, it resolves the site's name with DNS and determines the destination is outside the home subnet. Before sending the first IP packet, it uses ARP (or IPv6 NDP) to find the local router's link-layer address. The bank's server MAC address is not discovered directly by the laptop.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Application developers rarely send ARP or NDP messages themselves. These protocols matter when diagnosing local-network failures, IP conflicts, stale neighbor entries, or problems reaching a gateway. A failure at this layer can prevent DNS and web requests from working even when the browser is configured correctly.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Windows, arp -a displays IPv4 ARP cache entries. On Linux, ip neigh displays neighbor-cache information for IPv4 and IPv6. Output depends on recent local traffic and is not a list of every device on the Internet.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Address resolution: finding a local link-layer address for an IP neighbor.
  • ARP cache: temporary IPv4-to-MAC mappings maintained by a device.
  • Neighbor cache: IPv6 neighbor information maintained by a device.
  • Default gateway: the router used to reach destinations outside the local subnet.
  • Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement: ICMPv6 messages used by NDP.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Local resolution enables IP to run over local link technologies without applications managing hardware addresses. Because devices accept local network information, network operators should use appropriate link security and monitoring; ARP and NDP are not cryptographic proof of a user's identity.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A laptop normally resolves the gateway's MAC address for a remote website, not the website server's MAC address.
  • ARP is for IPv4; IPv6 uses NDP.
  • A MAC address is not routed end-to-end across the Internet.
  • A cached neighbor entry can become stale and is not proof that the neighbor is currently reachable.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol
  • RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6
  • RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically supplies network configuration to devices. A DHCP server can provide an IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS resolver, and lease duration.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Without automatic configuration, each device would need its network parameters entered manually. DHCP reduces setup work and helps prevent address conflicts by managing address leases centrally.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
A common DHCPv4 exchange is called DORA:

  1. Discover: a new client broadcasts to find DHCP servers.
  2. Offer: a server proposes an address and configuration.
  3. Request: the client asks to use one offered configuration.
  4. Acknowledge: the server confirms the lease and its options.

The client uses the address for a lease period and attempts to renew it before it expires. A lease is temporary ownership of an address, not a permanent identity. If the DHCP server is on another network, a configured DHCP relay can forward the client's messages between networks.

Common configuration includes:

Option Purpose IP address and subnet mask/prefix Identify the client's interface and local subnet Default gateway Provide a next hop for destinations outside the subnet DNS resolver Tell the client where to send name lookups Lease time Set how long the client may use the assigned address

DHCPv6 provides IPv6 configuration services, but IPv6 can also use Router Advertisements and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC). Networks may use these mechanisms together. DHCPv4's DORA exchange is not the exact message sequence for DHCPv6.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a phone joins home Wi-Fi, the router or a separate DHCP server commonly leases it a private IP address and tells it which gateway and DNS resolver to use. The same setup lets a laptop reach a government website or a bank without manually configuring an address for each service.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: DHCP is normally managed by operating systems and network administrators, not web application code. It is still useful to understand when a device gets no address, receives the wrong gateway, or uses an unexpected resolver. Cloud servers often use static or managed addressing rather than a typical home DHCP setup, but automatic configuration concepts remain relevant.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Windows, ipconfig /all shows the DHCP status, lease information, and network settings reported by the operating system. On Linux, ip address and ip route show assigned addresses and routes. These inspect current configuration; they do not change a DHCP server.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Lease: time-limited assignment of an address and configuration.
  • DHCP server: service that provides address configuration.
  • DHCP client: device requesting configuration.
  • Relay agent: forwards DHCP messages when clients and servers are on different IP networks.
  • SLAAC: IPv6 mechanism that lets a device configure an address from router-advertised prefix information.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: DHCP simplifies onboarding and centralized address management. Clients depend on correct server configuration and network reachability; a faulty server can provide unusable settings to many devices.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• DHCP provides local network configuration; it does not provide Internet access by itself.
  • A DHCP address can change when a lease is renewed or a device joins a different network.
  • DNS and DHCP are separate protocols, even when one home router provides both services.
  • IPv6 address configuration may use SLAAC, DHCPv6, or both.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 2131: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
  • RFC 8415: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
  • RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a distributed naming system. It lets people use names such as www.example.com while software looks up records such as an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Numeric addresses are awkward to remember and may change as services move. DNS separates a memorable name from network configuration. It is a hierarchy of independently managed zones, not one central address book.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
A browser or operating system asks a recursive resolver for an answer. The resolver may already have a cached answer. If not, it follows DNS delegation:

  1. A root server points it toward the relevant top-level domain, such as .com.
  2. A top-level domain server points it toward the domain's authoritative servers.
  3. An authoritative server returns the record for the requested name.
  4. The resolver caches the answer for its time-to-live (TTL) and returns it to the client.

The client normally asks a recursive resolver; it usually does not contact root servers directly. DNS commonly uses port 53 over UDP or TCP. Traditional DNS is not encrypted in transit. DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT) encrypt the connection to a resolver, but that resolver can still see the query.

docs.title: Common record types
docs.text:
Record What it stores Example use A IPv4 address Map www.example.com to an IPv4 endpoint AAAA IPv6 address Map a name to an IPv6 endpoint CNAME Another DNS name Make one name an alias of another MX Mail exchange host and priority Route email for a domain TXT Text data Publish domain verification or email policy data NS Name server for a zone Delegate DNS authority CAA Certificate issuance policy Indicate which certificate authorities may issue for a domain

If a record has a TTL of 300 seconds, a resolver may reuse the cached answer for about five minutes. A low TTL can help changes become visible sooner after caches expire, but it does not force resolvers to discard existing cached data immediately.

docs.title: DNS for application domains
docs.text:
When deploying a web application, DNS connects the name users type to the hosting platform or service endpoint. A typical setup might include:

Name and record Example purpose example.com — A or AAAA Point the domain to an IPv4 or IPv6 address when the host provides one www.example.com — CNAME Alias www to a platform-provided hostname api.example.com — CNAME, A, or AAAA Route API traffic to its host, gateway, or load balancer example.com — MX Route email for the domain; unrelated to web hosting Domain verification — TXT Prove domain control to a hosting or identity provider

This is an illustrative design, not a universal deployment recipe. A DNS provider may offer an apex-alias feature for the root domain, and hosting providers specify which targets and record types they support. A DNS CNAME cannot generally coexist with other ordinary records at the same owner name; follow the provider's instructions for the domain apex.

Changing a record changes authoritative DNS data, but resolvers can retain older answers until cached TTLs expire. During a migration, the old and new destinations may both receive traffic for a time. Lowering a TTL well before a planned change can reduce some cache delay, but does not guarantee instantaneous propagation.

DNS selects a destination name or address; it does not configure TLS certificates, application virtual hosts, redirects, or API routing. Those must also be configured at the host, proxy, and application layers.

DNSSEC adds signatures that let a validating resolver check that DNS data matches its signed chain of trust. It does not encrypt DNS queries; DoH and DoT encrypt the connection to the chosen resolver. These technologies address different concerns.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When opening https://www.example.com/, the browser may check local caches before asking a resolver. Once it gets an address, it can attempt a connection to that server. A DNS answer is not proof the server is available. See IP addressing and HTTP and HTTPS.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: TTL and resolver caches mean a DNS change may not appear everywhere immediately. Troubleshoot name resolution separately from routing, firewall, TLS, and application errors. Multiple DNS answers can distribute traffic, but do not by themselves guarantee health-aware routing. For an application, check that the DNS record points to the intended host and that the host is configured to serve the requested domain name.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
On Windows, run nslookup example.com. On Linux or macOS, dig example.com shows a query and answer when dig is installed. Both query a resolver; they do not change DNS records. Another resolver may have a different cached answer.

To inspect selected record types, use dig example.com A, dig example.com AAAA, or dig example.com MX. On Windows, nslookup -type=MX example.com queries MX records. These commands do not reveal every resolver's cache state or prove that the web service is healthy.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Recursive resolver: service that looks up answers for a client and returns a result.
  • Authoritative server: server that publishes records for a DNS zone.
  • Record: typed DNS data, such as A, AAAA, MX, or CNAME.
  • TTL: how long a DNS response may be cached.
  • Delegation: referral from one part of the DNS hierarchy to another.
  • DNSSEC: signatures that support validation of DNS data authenticity and integrity.
  • Cache miss: a lookup for which the resolver does not have a reusable answer.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Delegation lets organizations manage their own domains, and caching helps reduce repeated lookups. Caches can temporarily hold old data, and DNS can fail independently of the website it helps locate.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A DNS response does not prove the server is healthy.
  • Changing a record does not instantly clear every resolver's cache.
  • HTTPS protects the web connection; it does not automatically encrypt a traditional DNS query.
  • DNSSEC does not hide a query; encrypted DNS does not mean the resolver cannot see the name being requested.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): DNS introduces the naming system and the role of DNS records.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 1034, Domain Names—Concepts and Facilities explains DNS design and delegation.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 1035, Domain Names—Implementation and Specification describes DNS messages and basic record handling.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Email relies on several protocols because sending a message between mail servers and accessing a mailbox are different tasks. Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) sends and relays mail. Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) and Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) let a client access messages in a mailbox.

docs.title: Why do they exist?
docs.text: Email must move between independently operated providers while allowing users to read messages from different devices. SMTP supports transfer between mail systems; IMAP is designed for synchronized mailbox access; POP3 provides a simpler download-oriented mailbox model.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A user composes mail in a webmail service or mail application.
  2. The sending client submits the message to its provider, commonly with authenticated SMTP submission.
  3. The sending mail server looks up the recipient domain's DNS MX record and transfers the message to a receiving mail server using SMTP.
  4. The receiving provider applies its policies and stores the message in the recipient's mailbox.
  5. The recipient reads it through webmail or an email client using IMAP, POP3, or a provider-specific interface.
Protocol and common port Role Typical use SMTP relay, TCP 25 Transfer mail between mail servers Server-to-server delivery SMTP submission, TCP 587 Authenticated message submission, commonly with STARTTLS Mail client sends through its provider SMTP submission, TCP 465 Submission with implicit TLS in common deployments Encrypted client-to-provider submission IMAP, TCP 143 / 993 Access and synchronize mailbox 143 may upgrade with STARTTLS; 993 commonly uses implicit TLS POP3, TCP 110 / 995 Retrieve mailbox messages 110 may upgrade with STARTTLS; 995 commonly uses implicit TLS

Port use can vary by provider configuration; verify the provider's published settings. TLS protects the connection between the two endpoints using it, but mail may pass through multiple systems and is not necessarily end-to-end encrypted.

docs.title: Domain and sender checks
docs.text: DNS MX records identify mail exchangers for a domain. Email-domain authentication mechanisms include SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. They help receiving systems evaluate whether mail is authorized and whether signed or aligned domain information is present. They do not prove that every message is truthful or safe.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A government office sends a notification from its mail provider. SMTP moves the message toward the recipient's provider; IMAP may synchronize it to the recipient's phone and laptop. A phishing email can imitate the same visible sender name, so users and mail systems need additional checks beyond recognizing a protocol.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Applications that send mail often call a provider API or submit through an SMTP service. Protect credentials, configure domain authentication, handle delivery failures, and avoid treating "accepted by SMTP" as proof that a person received or read a message. Do not send sensitive information through email without understanding the organization's data-protection requirements.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Inspect the mail settings published by an email provider to identify its SMTP submission and IMAP/POP3 endpoints. Use only a mailbox and provider account you are authorized to access; do not test guessed credentials or third-party mail servers.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Mail user agent (MUA): app or interface a person uses to read or send email.
  • Mail transfer agent (MTA): server software that relays mail.
  • SMTP: protocol for submitting and transferring email.
  • IMAP: protocol for synchronized access to mailbox messages.
  • POP3: protocol for retrieving messages using a simpler download model.
  • MX record: DNS record identifying mail exchangers for a domain.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC: domain-based mechanisms that help receiving systems assess authorization and message-domain alignment.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Open email protocols allow communication across providers and a broad range of clients. Delivery can be delayed, filtered, rejected, or misclassified, and conventional SMTP transport does not guarantee end-to-end confidentiality.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• SMTP sends and relays mail; IMAP and POP3 are for mailbox access.
  • Email is not necessarily private end-to-end just because a client uses TLS.
  • An MX record routes mail; it does not validate the content or safety of a message.
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC reduce some forms of domain abuse but do not make all email trustworthy.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 5321: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
  • RFC 9051: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) Version 4rev2
  • RFC 1939: Post Office Protocol Version 3
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Ethernet and Wi-Fi connect a device to a nearby network. Ethernet usually uses a cable; Wi-Fi uses radio. They carry link-layer frames between devices on the local network. IP then carries packets between networks.

docs.title: Why do they exist?
docs.text: An application needs a way to send data to the next device on its path. Ethernet and Wi-Fi provide local delivery over different physical media while allowing higher-level protocols such as IP, TCP, DNS, and HTTP to work above them.

docs.title: How do they work?
docs.text:
1. A device joins a local network. A wired device connects to an Ethernet switch; a wireless device associates with a Wi-Fi access point.
  2. The network interface sends a frame containing local link information, including source and destination Media Access Control (MAC) addresses.
  3. A switch or access point forwards the frame on the local network.
  4. If the IP destination is outside the local subnet, the frame is addressed to the local router. The router removes the local frame and forwards the IP packet toward another network.
  5. At each link, a new frame is used for that link. The end-to-end IP destination normally remains the same, except where network address translation or other gateways change it.

Ethernet and Wi-Fi are not the same protocol, but both can carry IP traffic. Ethernet defines wired local-network behavior. Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) defines wireless local-network behavior, including how devices share radio airtime. Wi-Fi access points commonly bridge wireless devices onto the same local network as wired devices.

Property Ethernet Wi-Fi Medium Cable, commonly twisted-pair copper or fiber through network equipment Radio Typical connection Network interface to switch or router Device associates to an access point Common trade-off Stable performance and predictable physical connection Mobility and convenient access; performance varies with signal and interference Link protection Depends on the network and configuration WPA2 or WPA3 can protect access to the local wireless network

Link-layer security protects a local wireless connection. It does not replace HTTPS/TLS, which protects a connection across the wider network to a service.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a phone opens a government portal, it first sends traffic over Wi-Fi to the home access point. The access point forwards it toward the router. A banking app on Ethernet follows the same network-layer route from the computer's point of view, even though its local link is wired.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Most application code does not construct Ethernet or Wi-Fi frames directly; the operating system's network stack handles them. Understanding the local link helps distinguish a weak Wi-Fi signal or disconnected cable from a DNS, TLS, or application problem. A browser can fail to reach the Internet even when it is still connected to a local access point.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Windows, ipconfig /all shows network adapters and connection details. On Linux, ip link lists network interfaces. These commands inspect local configuration; they do not prove that a remote website is reachable.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Frame: data unit used for delivery over a local link.
  • MAC address: link-layer address used to deliver frames on a local network; it is not a permanent identity for a person.
  • Switch: device that forwards frames within a local network.
  • Access point: device that connects Wi-Fi clients to a network.
  • SSID: name advertised for a Wi-Fi network.
  • Router: device that forwards IP packets between networks.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Ethernet is often predictable and fast but requires a physical connection. Wi-Fi supports mobility and simpler access but shares radio spectrum and can be affected by walls, distance, interference, and access-point capacity.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Wi-Fi is not the same thing as the Internet; it is one way to join a local network.
  • MAC addresses are used for local frame delivery, not global Internet routing.
  • A strong Wi-Fi signal does not prove that DNS, routing, or the remote service is working.
  • WPA-protected Wi-Fi does not replace HTTPS for protecting web traffic.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• IEEE 802.11 Working Group
  • IEEE 802.3 Ethernet Working Group
  • MDN: How the Web works

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: gRPC is a remote procedure call (RPC) framework for communication between services. It commonly uses HTTP/2 for transport and Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) to define service methods and structured messages. It is often used for service-to-service communication rather than direct human browsing.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Distributed services need an explicit contract for calling operations and exchanging structured data. gRPC can generate client and server code from a service definition, support multiple programming languages, and stream messages in either direction.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Developers define messages and service methods in a .proto schema.
  2. Code generators create typed client and server interfaces for supported languages.
  3. A client calls a generated method; the gRPC library encodes the request, commonly as Protobuf.
  4. The request travels over HTTP/2, typically protected by TLS outside a trusted local development environment.
  5. The server invokes the matching handler and returns a response, status, and optional metadata.

gRPC supports unary calls, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. These describe message-flow patterns; applications still need timeouts, retries appropriate to the operation, authorization, and error handling.

Call type Message flow Example Unary One request, one response Look up a product Server streaming One request, many responses Stream status updates Client streaming Many requests, one response Send a sequence of measurements Bidirectional streaming Both sides send multiple messages Interactive service session

Browser use has additional constraints: browser JavaScript generally uses gRPC-Web or a compatible gateway rather than native gRPC directly, depending on the server and deployment.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A government portal may expose HTTPS APIs to a browser while its internal services use gRPC between an identity service and a case-management service. A bank can use the same pattern inside a controlled service environment. Those are architectural choices, not a special financial or government network protocol.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: gRPC can be a good fit for typed internal APIs and streaming communication between services. Consider client-language support, browser compatibility, observability, schema evolution, and operational tooling. For public browser APIs, ordinary HTTP with JSON may be easier to inspect and integrate.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Read a service's .proto definition and identify its messages, method signatures, and streaming type. In a project you control, use its generated client rather than hand-constructing binary Protobuf data.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• RPC: a programming model that invokes an operation on a remote service.
  • Protocol Buffers: schema-based binary serialization format commonly used with gRPC.
  • Service definition: schema describing gRPC methods and message types.
  • Metadata: request or response information carried outside the main message body.
  • Streaming RPC: RPC where one or both sides send multiple messages.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: gRPC offers generated interfaces, compact structured messages, and streaming patterns. It can be less convenient to inspect manually than JSON APIs and requires compatible tooling, HTTP/2 support, schema management, and browser adaptation in some deployments.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• gRPC is not itself a replacement for IP, TCP, or TLS; it uses lower layers such as HTTP/2 and a transport.
  • Protobuf is a data serialization format, not a network transport.
  • Retries can duplicate a non-idempotent operation unless the API handles that case.
  • gRPC is not automatically more secure than a REST-style HTTP API; security still depends on transport configuration and application authorization.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• gRPC: Core concepts
  • gRPC: Introduction to Protocol Buffers
  • RFC 9113: HTTP/2

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) defines how clients and servers exchange resources. A browser sends a request; a server sends a response. HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS. This builds on DNS, IP addressing, and TCP and UDP.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Clients and servers need shared rules for describing actions, data, and results. HTTP defines methods, headers, status codes, and message semantics so different browsers, servers, and applications can interoperate.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The client connects to the server. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
  2. For HTTPS, TLS protects the connection before HTTP data is exchanged.
  3. The client sends a request with a method, target, headers, and sometimes a body.
  4. The server sends a response with a status code, headers, and sometimes a body.
  5. The client interprets the response and may request related resources.
Method Common use Useful property GET Retrieve a representation Intended to be safe; should not change application state POST Submit data or request processing Often creates or triggers an operation PUT Replace a resource representation Defined as idempotent PATCH Apply a partial modification Meaning depends on the API and patch format DELETE Request resource removal Defined as idempotent HEAD Retrieve response metadata without a body Useful for checking headers OPTIONS Ask about communication options Used for browser CORS preflight in relevant cases

The exact result depends on the server and resource. Status codes also have families: 2xx indicates success, 3xx redirection, 4xx a client-side issue, and 5xx a server-side issue. A 404 means the requested resource was not found; a 200 means the response was successful according to HTTP semantics, not necessarily that the business task succeeded.

docs.title: Read a simple exchange
docs.text:
A request can be represented in a simplified form like this:

GET /products/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
Accept: application/json

The server might return 200 OK, a Content-Type header, and a response body containing the product representation. Real exchanges include more headers, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode messages differently on the wire, but the request/response semantics are familiar.

For a JSON API, the frontend might send:

POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{"productId":"p-42","quantity":1}

Content-Type describes the request body; Accept describes response formats the client can handle. The server must validate the body and authenticate and authorize the operation before changing application state.

docs.title: Headers, authentication, and browser CORS
docs.text:
Common headers include Content-Type, Accept, Authorization, Cache-Control, and Origin. Bearer tokens are commonly sent as Authorization: Bearer ...; treat them as credentials and never put them in URLs.

Browsers use Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) response headers to decide whether frontend JavaScript may read a cross-origin response. For some requests, the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight describing the intended method and headers. The server responds with appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers.

CORS is not authentication, authorization, or a firewall. Other clients are not restricted by browser CORS checks, so the API must verify identity, permissions, and input for every request. Cookie-based authentication needs CSRF protections appropriate to the application. JavaScript-accessible tokens require protection against script injection.

docs.title: Caching and conditional requests
docs.text:
HTTP caching can reduce latency and server work. Cache-Control controls whether and how responses can be stored. ETag and Last-Modified let a client revalidate a cached representation; the server can reply 304 Not Modified when it remains current.

Personalized or sensitive API responses need deliberate cache rules. Check authorization, shared proxy caches, and cache keys so one user's content is not served to another. no-store is useful for some sensitive responses, but cache policy should follow the data and application requirements.

docs.title: HTTP versions and connection reuse
docs.text:
Version Typical transport Developer-relevant point HTTP/1.1 TCP Persistent connections can be reused HTTP/2 TCP Multiplexes request streams over a connection and compresses headers HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP Uses QUIC streams; see QUIC and HTTP/3

Application code generally uses the same HTTP semantics regardless of version. Browsers, servers, proxies, and CDNs negotiate a compatible version.

docs.title: HTTP in a full-stack application
docs.text:
1. The browser requests the frontend document and static assets from a web server or content delivery network.
  2. Frontend JavaScript sends API requests, often using fetch() with JSON.
  3. A reverse proxy or API gateway may terminate TLS, route by host or path, enforce request limits, and forward the request to an application service.
  4. The backend authenticates and authorizes the operation, validates input, runs business logic, and may query databases or other services.
  5. The backend returns a status, headers, and an optional body; the frontend interprets the response and updates the interface.

The browser-to-API call and the backend-to-database query are separate protocol exchanges. HTTP does not define business rules or database transactions.

For frontend code, handle network errors separately from HTTP error responses. fetch() normally resolves with a Response for statuses such as 404 and 500; check response.ok or response.status. A DNS failure, TLS error, timeout, and API validation error need different handling.

Status family Meaning Example 2xx Request succeeded according to the response 200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 204 No Content 3xx Further action such as following a redirect 301 Moved Permanently 4xx Request or authorization problem 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Content, 429 Too Many Requests 5xx Server failed to fulfill a valid request 500 Internal Server Error

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: Opening a product page may issue GET requests for HTML, images, and stylesheets. Submitting an order form may send a POST request with order data. A banking frontend might make a similar HTTPS API call to retrieve account information after sign-in; the API still needs authorization checks on every request, even if the interface hides restricted actions.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Use methods and status codes according to their defined semantics. Safe means a method is not intended to change server state; idempotent means repeating it has the same intended effect as performing it once. Do not automatically retry non-idempotent operations, such as a payment submission, unless the API defines a safe mechanism such as an idempotency key.

HTTP is stateless: each request is interpreted independently, although cookies, tokens, and server-side storage can maintain authenticated sessions. Never put passwords, access tokens, or sensitive data in URLs. Use HTTPS, validate inputs, enforce authorization on the server, and do not assume a successful connection means a successful request.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: curl -i https://example.com/ sends an HTTP request and prints response headers and body. curl -I https://example.com/ sends a HEAD request and prints headers only. These are real requests to the specified public site; use an endpoint you are permitted to query.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Method: the intended action, such as GET or POST.
  • Header: metadata about a request or response.
  • Status code: a numeric summary of the response outcome.
  • Body: optional data sent with a request or response.
  • Idempotent: repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once.
  • Stateless: each request carries the information needed to interpret it; the protocol itself does not require the server to remember earlier requests.
  • Cookie: a small value a browser stores and may send with later requests to a site.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: HTTP is widely supported and extensible. Plain HTTP does not protect data in transit; HTTPS adds TLS protection but cannot make an unsafe application secure by itself.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• HTTPS does not prove a site is honest; it protects a connection to a host.
  • 200 OK does not guarantee that the user's broader task succeeded.
  • HTTP transfers more than HTML, including JSON, images, and media.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): An overview of HTTP introduces requests, responses, and the client-server model.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics defines methods, status codes, fields, and HTTP semantics.
  • Official standards — IETF: HTTP/3, RFC 9114 explains HTTP/3's use of QUIC.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) carries control and diagnostic messages associated with IP. ICMP is not a transport protocol like TCP or UDP, and it does not carry ordinary application requests such as HTTP. IPv6 has ICMPv6, which also supports important local-network functions.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: IP routers and hosts need a way to report certain delivery problems and provide diagnostic signals. ICMP can report that a destination is unreachable, that a packet's time-to-live expired, or that a packet is too large for a path.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
ICMP messages are carried inside IP packets. Common uses include:

Use Example What it can tell you Echo request/reply ping Whether an endpoint responds to this diagnostic exchange Time exceeded traceroute/tracert A hop's packet lifetime expired; a router may send a response Destination unreachable Network or host unreachable message A device reports it cannot deliver the packet for a stated reason Packet Too Big (ICMPv6) Path MTU discovery A sender should reduce packet size for the path

Routers decrease an IP packet's Time to Live (IPv4 TTL) or Hop Limit (IPv6) as it is forwarded. Diagnostic tools can send packets with increasing limits. When a limit reaches zero, a router may return a time-exceeded message, helping the tool infer part of the path. Some routers or firewalls do not return these messages, so a missing hop is not proof that traffic stopped there.

ICMPv6 is more than a ping mechanism: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery relies on it. Blocking all ICMPv6 can therefore break normal IPv6 behavior, including neighbor discovery or path-MTU handling.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A developer may use ping to see whether a server responds to ICMP echo, then use an HTTPS request to test the actual web service. A government portal may block echo requests while continuing to serve pages normally. Likewise, a successful ping to a bank host does not show that login or payment APIs work.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use diagnostics to answer a specific question. ping tests ICMP echo behavior, not DNS, TLS, or HTTP. tracert and traceroute attempt to show responding hops, not necessarily every router or the exact forward and return paths. A complete application check should test the application protocol as well.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
On Windows:

ping example.com
tracert example.com

On Linux, use ping example.com and traceroute example.com or tracepath example.com if installed. Run diagnostics only for systems you are permitted to test. Firewalls and network policies can limit the output.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• ICMP: control and diagnostic messaging for IPv4.
  • ICMPv6: control messaging for IPv6, including messages used by NDP.
  • Echo request/reply: messages used by the common ping diagnostic.
  • TTL/Hop Limit: IP field limiting how many router hops a packet can traverse.
  • Path MTU: largest packet size that can travel across a path without fragmentation at a constrained link.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: ICMP provides useful feedback for network operation and troubleshooting. Its messages may be filtered, rate-limited, or deprioritized, so diagnostics can be incomplete and should not be treated as definitive service health checks.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A failed ping does not prove a website is down.
  • A successful ping does not prove that the web server or application works.
  • traceroute does not guarantee that every hop will reply.
  • ICMP is not the same as TCP or UDP and does not carry HTTP requests.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 792: Internet Control Message Protocol
  • RFC 4443: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6)
  • RFC 8201: Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The Internet is a global system of interconnected networks. Home networks, mobile providers, universities, cloud platforms, and businesses operate their own networks and exchange traffic using shared protocols. The Web is one service that uses the Internet; email, voice calls, games, and file transfer use it too.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Networking lets devices share information and services without requiring one central computer. Standard protocols let equipment and software from different makers communicate. The trade-off is that communication depends on many independently operated networks, so a failure or policy on the path can affect a connection.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
When a browser opens a site, several jobs happen in sequence:

  1. The device joins a local network over Wi-Fi or Ethernet and usually receives its IP address, gateway, and resolver through DHCP or an IPv6 configuration mechanism.
  2. The browser reads the URL and identifies the host name. DNS finds one or more IP addresses for that name.
  3. The device determines whether the destination is local. For a remote destination it sends the packet toward its default gateway, resolving that local next hop with ARP or IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
  4. Routers pass IP packets between networks. A transport such as TCP, or QUIC over UDP, carries data between application endpoints. Ports help identify the destination program.
  5. For HTTPS, TLS protects the connection. HTTP carries the request and response. The network may use ICMP for control and diagnostic messages along the way.

Each layer has a distinct job. A router forwards packets; it does not need to understand the web page. The response can take a different route back.

An application creates data, such as an HTTP request. Lower layers add information needed for delivery: transport data identifies the application endpoint, IP data identifies network endpoints, and the local network technology carries a frame to the next device. At the destination, those layers are interpreted in reverse. This wrapping is called encapsulation.

Networks also have different performance characteristics. Bandwidth is the capacity of a link; throughput is the rate actually achieved; latency is the time a packet takes to travel. A fast link can still feel slow when latency is high or the server takes time to respond.

Term Simple meaning Example effect Bandwidth Maximum link capacity Limits how much data can be sent at once Throughput Measured successful data rate Drops during congestion or loss Latency Time for data to travel Affects interactive actions such as a game move Packet loss Data that fails to reach its destination May trigger recovery or lower-quality media

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: Loading a video page may involve one request for HTML, others for images and scripts, and separate media requests to a content delivery network. The browser coordinates these exchanges while the network carries their packets. An online banking site or a government service portal follows the same basic DNS, IP, transport, TLS, and HTTP layers. Their extra identity checks, application controls, and private service connections are additional requirements, not replacements for the public web protocols.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Layering helps narrow down problems. If DNS returns an address, name lookup worked, but that does not prove the server accepts connections. A connection does not prove the application returned the expected page. Diagnose one step at a time; see DNS, IP addressing, and HTTP and HTTPS. A ping test and an HTTPS request check different protocol behavior.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Windows, run nslookup example.com to inspect name resolution, then ping example.com to try a network diagnostic. To inspect the path on Windows, use tracert example.com; on many Linux systems use traceroute example.com or tracepath example.com. These commands may show incomplete results because some routers do not send diagnostic replies. A blocked ping or missing hop does not prove the website is offline. On Linux or macOS, ping -c 4 example.com sends four echo requests.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Packet: a formatted unit of network data.
  • Router: equipment that forwards packets between networks.
  • Protocol: shared rules for communication.
  • Client/server: roles in which a client requests a service and a server provides it.
  • ISP: an Internet service provider that connects customers to other networks.
  • Latency: time taken for data to travel between endpoints.
  • Throughput: measured rate of successfully transferred data.
  • Encapsulation: adding layer-specific information around data for delivery.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Interconnection enables global services and lets networks be operated independently. The same distributed design means congestion, equipment failures, or filtering along a path can interrupt service.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• The Internet and the Web are not synonyms; the Web is one Internet service.
  • Packets do not necessarily follow one fixed route.
  • An IP address identifies a network endpoint at a point in time, not reliably a person.
  • Bandwidth is not the same as throughput, and neither is the same as latency.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): How the Web works follows a browser request and response in accessible language.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts describes core host communication requirements.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
An Internet Protocol (IP) address labels a network interface so packets can be delivered toward it. IPv4 addresses contain 32 bits and are often written as four decimal numbers, such as 192.0.2.25. IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits and use hexadecimal groups, such as 2001:db8::25.

An address is not a web site name. DNS can resolve a name to one or more IP addresses.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Routers need a destination address to decide where to forward a packet. Prefixes group addresses into networks so routing can use compact rules instead of listing every device separately.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A device sends an IP packet with source and destination addresses.
  2. It checks whether the destination is on its local subnet. If not, it sends the packet to a configured gateway, usually a router.
  3. Routers use routing tables to choose a next hop. The packet may cross several networks before reaching its destination.
  4. IP makes a best-effort delivery attempt. It does not itself guarantee that packets arrive, arrive once, or arrive in order.

A prefix such as 192.168.1.0/24 means the first 24 bits identify the network. That leaves 8 bits for addresses within this IPv4 subnet. In a typical /24 local network, 192.168.1.42 belongs to the range represented by 192.168.1.0/24.

docs.title: Worked prefix example
docs.text:
For 192.168.1.42/24, /24 means the first 24 bits are the network prefix. The corresponding network is 192.168.1.0/24; in a conventional IPv4 subnet, .0 names the network and .255 is its directed broadcast address, leaving .1 through .254 for host addresses. This /24 arithmetic is a learning example, not a rule that every network must use a /24. IPv6 uses prefix lengths too, but has no broadcast address.

Address type Example Typical purpose Private IPv4 192.168.1.42 Internal home or office network Public IPv4 Assigned by a provider or cloud host Globally routed destination Loopback IPv4 127.0.0.1 This same device Loopback IPv6 ::1 This same device IPv6 documentation prefix 2001:db8::/32 Examples in learning material, not public assignment

Private IPv4 ranges are used inside networks and are not globally routed. Network address translation (NAT) commonly lets multiple private devices share a public IPv4 address. IPv6 provides a much larger address space; it does not remove the need for firewalls or all forms of address translation.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: Your laptop may receive 192.168.1.42 from a home router. When it connects to a public web server, the router typically translates the connection so the outside service sees the network's public address rather than that private address.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Do not treat an IP address as a permanent identity. Addresses can change, servers can have several, and NAT can place many users behind one public address. Use DNS names for service discovery and IP tools to diagnose network paths. An address alone does not establish a user's identity.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Windows, ipconfig shows interface addresses and the default gateway. On Linux, ip address lists local addresses and ip route displays routes. These commands inspect local configuration. 127.0.0.1 and ::1 are loopback addresses used to reach the same device.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Interface: a network attachment such as Wi-Fi or Ethernet.
  • Prefix/subnet: a set of addresses sharing a number of leading bits.
  • Gateway: a router used to reach destinations outside the local subnet.
  • Loopback: an address used by a device to communicate with itself.
  • NAT: translation of network addresses, often performed by a router.
  • Network address: the prefix identifying a subnet, such as 192.168.1.0/24.
  • Broadcast: an IPv4 destination used to reach all hosts on a local subnet; IPv6 does not use broadcast.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: IP is scalable and independent of application meaning. Its best-effort delivery means applications need an appropriate transport or recovery strategy. IPv6 offers many more addresses, but real networks still need to interoperate with IPv4 during deployment.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A public IP does not necessarily identify one person or one device.
  • A private address can reach public services through a gateway.
  • IP by itself does not provide reliable, ordered application data; see TCP and UDP.
  • IPv6 is not simply IPv4 written differently; it has a larger address format and different network behaviors.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): IP address introduces the address concept and its role in routing.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 791, Internet Protocol specifies IPv4 packet delivery.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 8200, Internet Protocol, Version 6 specifies IPv6.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 1918, Address Allocation for Private Internets defines the familiar private IPv4 address ranges.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) is a lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol commonly used by devices with limited resources or intermittent network connections. Clients exchange messages through a broker using named topics.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Small sensors and devices may not need a direct connection to every system that consumes their data. A broker separates publishers from subscribers: devices publish readings, and interested consumers subscribe to topics. This reduces tight coupling between device producers and application consumers.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. An MQTT client connects to a broker, commonly over TCP.
  2. A publisher sends a message to a topic, such as building/room-4/temperature.
  3. The broker checks its subscriptions and forwards the message to matching subscribers.
  4. Depending on the Quality of Service (QoS) selected, MQTT provides different delivery acknowledgement behavior.
  5. Clients may reconnect and optionally use retained messages or persistent sessions according to broker and client configuration.
QoS Delivery behavior Trade-off 0 At most once No protocol acknowledgement; a message may be lost 1 At least once Retries may result in duplicates; consumers should handle them 2 Exactly once within the MQTT exchange More protocol work and state

QoS is not the same as a business transaction guarantee. Applications may still need identifiers, idempotency, durable storage, or reconciliation. MQTT over plain TCP commonly uses port 1883; MQTT protected with TLS commonly uses port 8883. Broker deployments can use different ports and access policies.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A building sensor publishes temperature updates to an MQTT broker. A dashboard subscribes to the relevant topic, while an alert service subscribes to a broader set of measurements. A bank or government portal is not usually an MQTT client-facing website, though organizations may use MQTT internally for device telemetry or building systems.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: MQTT is useful when building IoT telemetry and command systems. Design topic names, authentication, authorization, message validation, retention, and offline behavior carefully. TLS protects transport when configured, but clients still need broker permissions that restrict which topics they can publish to or subscribe to.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a development system you control, use an MQTT client and broker to publish a non-sensitive test value to a topic and subscribe to it from another authorized client. Do not publish private device data to a public broker.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Broker: server that receives publications and forwards messages to subscribers.
  • Publisher: client that sends a message to a topic.
  • Subscriber: client that registers interest in topics.
  • Topic: hierarchical name used to route messages.
  • QoS: MQTT delivery level for a message exchange.
  • Retained message: broker-held latest message for a topic, available to a future matching subscriber when configured.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: MQTT has a small messaging model and decouples producers from consumers. It adds a broker dependency and requires careful topic permissions and message handling; delivery level alone does not ensure exactly-once business processing.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• MQTT is not only for tiny devices; it is a messaging protocol often chosen for IoT-style communication.
  • A broker forwarding a message does not prove that the subscriber processed it successfully.
  • QoS 2 does not make an entire application workflow exactly once.
  • MQTT does not provide authorization policy automatically; the broker must be configured to enforce it.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OASIS MQTT Version 5.0 Standard
  • OASIS MQTT Version 3.1.1 Standard

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A network port is a number used by a transport protocol to deliver traffic to an application endpoint. An IP address identifies a network interface; the port helps distinguish services using that address. TCP and UDP have separate port spaces.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: A server can offer several services on one address, and a computer can run many client programs at once. Ports let the operating system match incoming TCP segments or UDP datagrams to the appropriate socket.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
TCP and UDP headers include source and destination ports. A server application binds a socket to a local address and port and listens or waits for datagrams. A client normally uses a temporary ephemeral port as its source port.

A network connection is commonly distinguished by the transport protocol, source address and port, and destination address and port. The same port number can be used simultaneously by TCP and UDP because they are separate transport namespaces.

For example, these values describe an HTTPS connection from a laptop:

Part Example Role Protocol TCP Selects the transport behavior Source address 192.168.1.25 Client's local interface address Source port 53000 Temporary client endpoint Destination address 203.0.113.10 Server network endpoint Destination port 443 HTTPS service endpoint

Together, the protocol and these four values form what is commonly called a five-tuple. Network address translation may rewrite an address or port as traffic passes through a router, then track the mapping so replies can be sent back to the correct internal client.

docs.title: Ports full-stack developers commonly encounter
docs.text:
Port Transport Common service Developer context 22 TCP SSH Authorized remote administration and Git over SSH 53 UDP and TCP DNS Name queries; TCP is also used for some responses and transfers 80 TCP HTTP Unencrypted web endpoint, often redirected to HTTPS 443 TCP and UDP HTTPS / HTTP/3 HTTPS commonly uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP 3000, 5173 TCP Common development servers Examples only; framework and developer configuration determine actual ports 5432 TCP PostgreSQL default Keep database access private and restricted 3306 TCP MySQL default Keep database access private and restricted 6379 TCP Redis default Do not expose an unauthenticated service to untrusted networks

These are conventions and defaults, not guarantees. A service can use a different port, and a port number does not prove which program is listening. Cloud firewalls, host firewalls, containers, proxies, and network policies also affect reachability.

The port range is split into registration categories:

Range IANA category Common description 0–1023 System Ports Well-known service ports 1024–49151 User Ports Registered application services 49152–65535 Dynamic/Private Ports Often used for temporary client ports

Operating systems may use different local ephemeral-port ranges. IANA categories are not a promise that a port is free or safe to expose.

IANA divides the range into System Ports (0–1023), User Ports (1024–49151), and Dynamic/Private Ports (49152–65535). These categories describe registration and allocation practices; they do not guarantee that a port is available or that an application uses its registered number.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A browser might connect from an ephemeral local port such as 53000 to a web server's TCP port 443. The server's reply is addressed back to that client socket. The exact client port is selected by the operating system and can differ for another connection.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Applications bind to a local address and port. A service bound only to loopback is intended for local access; a service bound to a network interface may be reachable from other devices, subject to routing and firewalls. Opening a listener is not the same as making it reachable from the Internet. For local development, a backend can listen only on 127.0.0.1 when it needs to serve the same computer. Binding to 0.0.0.0 listens on all IPv4 interfaces and can expose the service to other devices if the network and firewall permit it. Use the narrowest binding and access rules needed.

In production, a common arrangement exposes HTTP(S) only at a load balancer or reverse proxy and keeps application and database ports on private networks. For example, a public HTTPS listener may forward to an application service, while the database accepts connections only from approved application hosts. Network segmentation complements database credentials and application authorization; it does not replace them.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
On Linux, ss -tuln lists listening TCP and UDP sockets without changing configuration. On Windows, netstat -ano lists connection and listening information with process IDs. These show local state, not whether an external firewall permits access.

For an authorized Windows TCP connectivity check, use Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443. It tests whether a TCP connection to that endpoint could be established; it does not validate TLS, HTTP, or application authorization. For HTTP/3, a TCP-only port test does not test the UDP-based QUIC path.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Listening: a TCP socket waiting for incoming connections.
  • Ephemeral port: temporary port commonly used by a client.
  • Socket: operating-system endpoint for network communication.
  • Binding: associating an application socket with a local address and port.
  • Port range: a range used for specific registration and allocation categories.
  • Five-tuple: transport protocol plus the source and destination addresses and ports that identify a network flow.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Ports let many services share an address and help operating systems route traffic to applications. Misconfigured listeners can expose services; a port number provides no authentication or encryption.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A network port is not a physical connector.
  • Port 443 alone does not guarantee correct TLS.
  • A listening port does not prove that external networks can reach it.
  • TCP port 53 and UDP port 53 are distinct endpoints; DNS can use both.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): Port introduces network ports and their role in communication.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 6335, Internet Assigned Numbers Authority Procedures for the Management of the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry explains port ranges and registration procedures.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Network Time Protocol (NTP) lets computers synchronize their clocks with time sources across a network. Correct time supports useful logs, scheduled jobs, certificate validation, and coordination among distributed services.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Independent device clocks drift. If servers disagree about time, event logs are difficult to compare, scheduled actions can run incorrectly, and time-based security checks may fail. NTP provides a way to estimate and correct clock offset while accounting for network delay.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A client sends a time request to an NTP server, commonly over UDP port 123.
  2. The server responds with timestamps describing the exchange.
  3. The client estimates clock offset and round-trip delay.
  4. The operating system gradually adjusts its clock and may compare several configured sources according to its time-synchronization policy.

Internet time is not perfectly instantaneous. Network delay and asymmetric routes affect measurements. Systems often use a hierarchy of time sources; organizations may operate internal servers for consistency and policy.

Network Time Security (NTS) adds authentication and protection for NTP client-server exchanges. Ordinary NTP without such protection should not be assumed to authenticate its time source.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A government portal's servers, a bank's application logs, and a crypto exchange's monitoring systems need consistent clocks to correlate events. Their business rules and auditing requirements are separate from NTP itself; NTP provides time synchronization, not proof that a transaction occurred. High-precision financial or industrial systems may require specialized timing methods such as Precision Time Protocol (PTP).

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Developers use synchronized time for log correlation, certificate checks, token expiry, distributed tracing, and scheduled work. Prefer server-side time for security-sensitive decisions, and design distributed systems with clock skew in mind. A client's wall-clock time is user-controlled and should not be trusted for authorization.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Windows, w32tm /query /status reports Windows Time status. On Linux, inspect the time synchronization service configured for the distribution, such as timedatectl status where available. These commands inspect local time service state; they do not validate a financial transaction timestamp.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Clock offset: difference between a local clock and a reference clock.
  • Clock drift: gradual divergence between clocks over time.
  • Stratum: a level in an NTP time-source hierarchy; lower stratum does not automatically mean a source is more trustworthy in every respect.
  • NTS: Network Time Security, which adds authentication and protection for NTP exchanges.
  • PTP: Precision Time Protocol, used where tighter synchronization is required than typical Internet NTP provides.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: NTP provides practical clock synchronization across general-purpose networks. It is affected by network conditions and source trust; ordinary NTP should not be treated as a cryptographic timestamp or transaction receipt.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• NTP synchronizes clocks; it does not synchronize application data.
  • A timestamp in a client request is not trustworthy just because servers use NTP.
  • NTP does not guarantee exact zero-offset time.
  • Time synchronization and authentication of a user are unrelated functions.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 5905: Network Time Protocol Version 4
  • RFC 8915: Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol
  • RFC 8573: Message Authentication Code for the Network Time Protocol

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: QUIC is a secure transport protocol that runs over UDP. HTTP/3 is HTTP mapped onto QUIC. Together they provide a modern option for web connections, alongside HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 deployments that commonly use TCP.

docs.title: Why do they exist?
docs.text: With TCP, loss affecting one connection can delay delivery of later bytes in that same ordered stream. HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over a TCP connection, but TCP still delivers one ordered byte stream. QUIC supports independent streams, so loss affecting one stream need not block delivery on every other stream. QUIC also integrates its security handshake and can resume connections efficiently.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A client and server exchange QUIC packets over UDP. Web servers commonly accept HTTP/3 on UDP port 443.
  2. QUIC performs a TLS 1.3-based handshake and derives keys to protect transport and application data. QUIC does not use a separate TLS record layer in the same way as HTTPS over TCP.
  3. HTTP/3 sends request and response data over QUIC streams.
  4. QUIC detects loss, retransmits needed data, and applies congestion control. It provides reliable streams while retaining UDP as its underlying datagram transport.
  5. A connection can use connection identifiers to survive some client address changes, such as moving between Wi-Fi and cellular, when the network and peer permit it.
Stack Typical transport Security Multiplexing behavior HTTP/1.1 TCP TLS for HTTPS Multiple requests can reuse a connection, but request scheduling differs HTTP/2 TCP TLS in typical browser use Multiple HTTP streams share one TCP byte stream HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP TLS 1.3 integrated into QUIC Independent QUIC streams reduce transport-level blocking between streams

QUIC still needs congestion control and can still experience loss, latency, or server overload. HTTP/3 is negotiated when supported; services commonly retain other HTTP versions for compatibility.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A video site or government portal may deliver HTTP/3 to a compatible browser. If a network blocks or degrades UDP, the browser and server may use another available HTTP version. The site still uses familiar HTTP methods and semantics; the transport below HTTP differs.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Application developers normally use browser, server, proxy, and CDN implementations rather than implementing QUIC directly. It is useful to understand HTTP/3 when diagnosing why a service behaves differently over UDP versus TCP, interpreting browser DevTools, or configuring network firewalls and load balancers.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: In browser DevTools, inspect a request's protocol column when available to see whether it used h2 or h3. A protocol label may be absent or hidden depending on the browser and tooling. Compare requests to services you control; do not assume every server enables HTTP/3.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• QUIC: secure, multiplexed transport protocol over UDP.
  • HTTP/3: HTTP semantics and messaging over QUIC.
  • Stream: independent ordered sequence of data within a QUIC connection.
  • Head-of-line blocking: delay where missing data prevents later data from being delivered; QUIC limits cross-stream transport blocking.
  • Connection migration: ability to continue a QUIC connection after certain network address changes.
  • Congestion control: behavior that adjusts sending rate to network conditions.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: QUIC can reduce connection setup delay and avoid TCP-level blocking across independent streams. It introduces a newer transport stack and may be handled differently by middleboxes or networks that restrict UDP. It does not remove the effects of congestion or poor connectivity.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• QUIC uses UDP, but it is not simply unreliable application data; QUIC implements reliability and congestion control.
  • HTTP/3 is not a replacement for HTTP semantics; it changes how HTTP is transported.
  • HTTP/3 still uses TLS-based security.
  • UDP is not automatically faster in every network or workload.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 9000: QUIC Transport
  • RFC 9001: Using TLS to Secure QUIC
  • RFC 9114: HTTP/3
  • MDN: HTTP/3

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol for authenticated, encrypted communication with a remote system. It is commonly used for command-line administration and secure tunneling. SFTP is a file-transfer protocol that runs over an SSH connection; it is not the same protocol as FTP.

docs.title: Why do they exist?
docs.text: Administrators and automated deployment systems need to manage remote servers without sending credentials and commands as readable network data. SSH provides a protected channel and supports multiple authentication methods. SFTP reuses that channel for file operations.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A client connects to an SSH server, commonly on TCP port 22.
  2. The endpoints negotiate algorithms and establish an encrypted session.
  3. The client verifies the server's host key against its trust information, such as a known-hosts entry.
  4. The client authenticates as a user, often with a public/private key pair or another configured method.
  5. The authenticated connection can carry an interactive shell, commands, port forwarding, or an SFTP session, depending on server policy.

Public-key authentication uses a private key kept by the client and a matching public key registered with the server. A private key should remain private and may be protected with a passphrase or an agent. The host key serves a different purpose: it helps the client recognize the server. Do not automatically accept an unexpected host-key change without verifying it through a trusted channel.
