Protocol/tool Purpose Important distinction SSH Secure remote connection and related channels Provides transport protection and authentication mechanisms SFTP File operations over SSH Not FTP wrapped in TLS FTP Older file-transfer protocol Credentials/data protection depends on configuration; plain FTP is not encrypted FTPS FTP secured with TLS Different protocol family and connection behavior from SFTP

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A developer deploys an application to a cloud virtual machine using an authorized SSH account. A bank or government organization may also use SSH for restricted server administration or automated transfers, but their customer-facing websites still commonly use HTTPS. Administrative access should be separated from public website access and limited by policy.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Developers may use SSH for Git operations, deployment, remote debugging, or access to authorized servers. Use managed keys and accounts, verify server identity, and follow the organization's access controls. Prefer a provider's documented deployment workflow when one is available.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
For a server you own or are authorized to administer:

ssh user@server.example
sftp user@server.example

The commands initiate a connection; they do not bypass authentication. Use the actual host and account information supplied by the administrator. Never paste private keys into a repository, chat, or issue.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Host key: key used to identify an SSH server to clients.
  • User key pair: client-held private key and corresponding public key used for authentication.
  • Known-hosts file: client-side record of SSH server host keys.
  • Port forwarding: carrying another connection through an SSH channel when permitted by policy.
  • SFTP: SSH File Transfer Protocol, a file-transfer protocol carried over SSH.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: SSH protects remote administration traffic and supports strong key-based authentication and file transfer. Mismanaged credentials or unverified server keys can undermine trust, and exposed administrative services need careful access control and monitoring.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• SFTP and FTPS are different protocols.
  • A host key identifies the server; a user key authenticates a client user.
  • Encryption does not make an unauthorized login acceptable or safe.
  • Port 22 is common for SSH but a port number alone does not prove what service is running.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 4251: The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture
  • RFC 4253: SSH Transport Layer Protocol
  • OpenSSH Manual Pages
  • OpenSSH: SFTP

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) carry application data between programs using port numbers. Both sit above IP addressing, but they offer different communication models.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: IP forwards packets but does not promise that application data arrives complete or in order. Applications need transport behavior suited to their task: some need an ordered stream, while others need independent messages and can tolerate loss.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
TCP first establishes connection state. A typical opening uses a three-message handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. Once established, sequence numbers and acknowledgements let TCP detect missing data and retransmit it. Flow control helps avoid overwhelming the receiver; congestion control adapts sending to network conditions.

TCP delivers an ordered byte stream, not a sequence of the application's original writes. If a program sends two writes, the receiver may read their bytes in a different grouping.

UDP sends separate datagrams without a TCP-style connection. It provides no transport-level retransmission, ordering, or congestion control. An application protocol can add behavior it needs. For example, QUIC runs over UDP while implementing reliability and congestion control itself.

Property TCP UDP Data model Ordered byte stream Independent datagrams Delivery recovery Acknowledgements and retransmission Not provided by UDP Setup Connection handshake No TCP-style handshake Typical fit Web pages, file transfer, database connections DNS queries, voice, games, or protocols built on UDP

docs.title: Reliable delivery is not the same as fast delivery
docs.text:
TCP retransmits missing bytes and keeps later bytes from being delivered to the application before earlier missing bytes. This provides a useful ordered stream, but waiting for recovery can delay later data. UDP exposes individual datagrams to the application without doing that transport-level recovery. Applications that need reliable UDP-based communication must implement or use a protocol that handles acknowledgements, retransmissions, and congestion control. QUIC is one such protocol and is used by HTTP/3.

TCP's byte-stream behavior also matters when designing a server. A single send call is not guaranteed to match a single receive call. Applications need message framing, such as a length field or delimiter, to identify where their own messages end. UDP preserves datagram boundaries, but a datagram can still be lost or too large for a path.

docs.title: TCP in web applications
docs.text:
Traditional HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 deployments commonly use TCP. A client establishes a TCP connection to a server endpoint, often TCP port 443 for HTTPS, and the HTTP implementation may reuse that connection for multiple requests. Browsers and servers manage connection pools and keep-alive behavior; application code usually does not open one TCP socket per fetch() call.

Connections can fail or become idle while a request is in flight. Backend and proxy clients should use appropriate connect, read, and overall deadlines. Retrying can help with transient failures, but retries should be bounded and must not duplicate non-idempotent operations unless the application has a safe retry mechanism.

WebSockets also commonly begin over TCP before the protocol upgrade; see WebSockets. HTTP/3 is different: it uses QUIC over UDP, which provides its own reliable streams.

HTTP persistent connections let an HTTP implementation reuse a connection for more than one request. TCP keepalive probes are a separate operating-system mechanism that can probe an idle TCP connection. Neither mechanism guarantees that an application server is healthy or that a request will complete; applications still need deadlines and error handling.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A file download normally needs all bytes in order, so TCP's recovery is useful. A live call values timely audio; an old packet that arrives late may be less useful than continuing with newer audio. The calling application still manages its own media and network behavior.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Choose a transport based on required delivery semantics, latency, and the application protocol—not on the claim that UDP is always faster. TCP handles many reliability details, but stream boundaries must be designed at the application layer. UDP provides datagrams, but the application must consider loss, ordering, security, and congestion. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP; see HTTP and HTTPS.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Linux, ss -t -a lists TCP sockets and ss -u -a lists UDP sockets. These commands inspect local socket state. An empty result does not prove a remote service is unreachable; proxies, containers, and firewalls affect what is visible. To test a service you are authorized to reach from Windows, Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443 reports whether a TCP connection could be established; it does not test whether an HTTP page works.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Handshake: opening exchange that establishes protocol state.
  • Byte stream: ordered bytes with no preserved message boundaries.
  • Datagram: a discrete message delivered by UDP.
  • Acknowledgement: a signal used to confirm receipt of data.
  • Congestion control: behavior that adapts sending to network load.
  • Flow control: behavior that helps prevent a sender from overwhelming the receiver.
  • Retransmission: sending data again after it appears to have been lost.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: TCP provides a convenient ordered stream and recovery, but maintains connection state and retransmits lost data. UDP has simple datagram semantics and no TCP-style setup, but leaves important reliability behavior to the application.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• UDP is not inherently insecure or guaranteed to be faster.
  • TCP does not preserve the boundaries of individual writes.
  • UDP does not mean an application cannot be reliable; QUIC is an example of a protocol that builds additional behavior over UDP.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) summarizes TCP's role in network communication.
  • Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): User Datagram Protocol (UDP) introduces UDP datagrams and how they differ from TCP.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol defines TCP behavior.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 768, User Datagram Protocol specifies UDP datagrams and checksums.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Transport Layer Security (TLS) protects data exchanged between endpoints. It is designed to provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS. Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) is the obsolete predecessor; current systems should use modern TLS, not SSL.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Network traffic can cross equipment and networks neither endpoint controls. Without protection, an intermediary could read or alter data, or a client could be tricked into connecting to an impostor. TLS helps protect the connection in transit.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
In a simplified TLS 1.3 connection:

  1. The client offers supported TLS versions and cryptographic parameters.
  2. Client and server exchange key-agreement data and derive shared session keys.
  3. The server presents a certificate. The client checks that it is trusted, valid, and matches the requested host name.
  4. The endpoints confirm the handshake and protect application records with the derived keys.
  5. HTTP data travels inside the protected connection.

Certificates are signed statements that bind a public key to one or more names. A browser checks the certificate chain against trusted certificate authorities and verifies the requested name. Ordinary web browsing typically authenticates the server; client certificates can also be used when mutual authentication is required.

docs.title: Public-key and symmetric cryptography
docs.text:
Public-key cryptography helps establish shared secrets and verify signatures without sending the eventual session key as plain text. After the handshake, TLS uses symmetric session keys to protect application data efficiently. Modern TLS also uses authenticated encryption so the receiver can detect tampering. The protocol and library manage these details; application developers should not invent their own key exchange.

Certificate checking is a chain of specific questions:

  1. Is the certificate within its validity period?
  2. Does it identify the host name the browser requested?
  3. Does its signature chain lead to a certificate authority the client trusts?
  4. Has the client been configured with any additional trust or revocation checks?

Passing these checks means the connection is authenticated according to the client's trust model. It does not certify the site's intent or content.

docs.title: TLS with domains, proxies, and HTTP
docs.text:
One IP address can host multiple HTTPS domains. The client commonly sends the requested hostname using Server Name Indication (SNI) during the TLS handshake so the server or TLS-terminating proxy can select an appropriate certificate. After TLS is established, HTTP also carries the request host name for routing. SNI helps select the TLS identity; it does not replace HTTP host routing or application authorization.

Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) lets the endpoints negotiate an application protocol, such as HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, as part of TLS setup. HTTP/3 uses QUIC and negotiates through QUIC's TLS handshake.

In many deployments, a load balancer or reverse proxy terminates public TLS and then forwards traffic to an application service. The operator must secure and control the proxy-to-service path too. TLS at the public edge does not automatically encrypt every internal hop.

docs.title: Common TLS failures a developer may see
docs.text:
Symptom Possible cause to check Hostname mismatch Certificate does not cover the requested domain or proxy serves the wrong virtual host Expired or not-yet-valid certificate Renewal, deployment, or device clock problem Untrusted issuer Missing or incorrect certificate chain, or an unexpected local trust configuration Certificate works for one domain but not another SNI, certificate selection, or domain configuration problem Secure page reports mixed content Page loads a resource over insecure HTTP Connection fails only on one network Proxy inspection, firewall, unsupported configuration, or network policy; diagnose without disabling certificate validation

Do not make a client ignore certificate errors as a production fix. Verify the domain, certificate chain, server clock, and proxy configuration.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When signing in to an online service, the browser checks the service's certificate, establishes TLS, and sends the login request through the encrypted connection. TLS protects the data in transit but cannot protect a compromised browser or server.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use maintained TLS libraries and secure defaults; do not write custom cryptography or disable certificate checks to silence an error. Keep certificates valid and host names correct. Remember that TLS does not hide all connection metadata, prevent phishing, or make application logic secure. See HTTP and HTTPS and SSL certificates. For full-stack deployments, also check whether TLS terminates at the CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy, or application server, and document how each subsequent hop is protected.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: curl -I https://example.com/ requests a response over TLS. If OpenSSL is installed, openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com displays connection and certificate details. These commands connect to the specified host; do not send credentials or private data in a diagnostic test.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Handshake: initial negotiation and authentication exchange.
  • Certificate: signed information binding a public key to one or more identities.
  • Certificate authority (CA): an issuer trusted to sign certificates.
  • Session key: a temporary symmetric key used to protect data.
  • Integrity: assurance that protected data has not been silently altered.
  • Public key: a key that can be shared and used for operations such as signature verification.
  • Symmetric encryption: encryption that uses a shared secret key for protecting data.
  • Certificate chain: linked certificates used to establish trust from a server certificate to a configured trust anchor.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: TLS reduces eavesdropping and tampering and helps authenticate the server. It requires correct configuration and certificate maintenance. A valid connection cannot protect data after it reaches a compromised endpoint.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• The browser padlock signals a protected connection, not an honest business.
  • SSL is not the current protocol to enable; modern deployments use TLS.
  • Encryption does not prevent phishing, malware, or unsafe application code.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN (beginner-friendly): Transport Layer Security (TLS) explains TLS, certificates, and their role in web security.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 8446, The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3 specifies TLS 1.3 handshakes and record protection.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) creates a logical tunnel across an underlying network. VPN technologies can authenticate endpoints and protect traffic between a device and a VPN gateway, or between two networks. IPsec, WireGuard, and OpenVPN are examples of VPN technologies with different designs and deployment models.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Organizations need to connect remote users or separate offices to internal services over networks they do not fully control. A VPN can provide an authenticated, protected path to a private network without making every internal service directly public.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A VPN client establishes a tunnel to a configured VPN gateway or peer.
  2. The endpoints authenticate and negotiate or use configured cryptographic keys.
  3. The sender places inner network traffic inside an outer tunnel packet.
  4. The tunnel protects the traffic across the underlying network according to its configuration.
  5. The receiving endpoint removes the tunnel wrapper and forwards the inner traffic according to its routing and access policy.

Some VPNs route only selected traffic (split tunneling); others route most or all device traffic through the tunnel. A site-to-site VPN connects networks, while a remote-access VPN connects a user's device to an organization's network.

Type Typical purpose Example Remote access Connect an authorized user device to an organization An employee reaches an internal development or finance service Site-to-site Connect two controlled networks A branch office reaches approved services at a data center Consumer privacy VPN Route traffic through a provider's gateway A user changes the network path visible to public services

These are different use cases. A VPN does not make an untrusted VPN provider trustworthy, and it does not automatically provide end-to-end encryption between an application and its service. HTTPS/TLS is still valuable inside a VPN.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A bank employee may use an organization-managed VPN to reach restricted administrative systems. Customers using the bank's public website commonly connect through HTTPS without needing that employee VPN. Government agencies and cloud teams may use site-to-site tunnels for controlled service connectivity.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Developers may encounter VPNs when accessing development environments, private databases, or company source-control services. A VPN can change routes, DNS resolvers, and the apparent source address, so connection problems may differ between on-VPN and off-VPN use. Follow organizational policy; do not expose private services as a workaround for a VPN issue.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Check the VPN provider's documented client and connection status, then compare the device's routes and DNS settings before and after connecting. On Windows, route print displays routes; on Linux, ip route does. These commands inspect local configuration and do not test whether an internal service grants access.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Tunnel: encapsulated traffic carried through another network.
  • VPN gateway: endpoint that terminates or forwards VPN traffic.
  • Remote-access VPN: tunnel between a user device and an organization.
  • Site-to-site VPN: tunnel connecting networks through their gateways.
  • Split tunneling: sending only selected traffic through the VPN.
  • Encapsulation: wrapping one protocol's packet inside another for transport.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: VPNs can protect traffic to a trusted gateway and provide controlled access to private networks. They add configuration and operational complexity, can change routing and name resolution, and do not remove the need for application-level authentication and TLS.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A VPN does not make every website connection end-to-end encrypted; HTTPS remains important.
  • A VPN hides some network-path information from local observers but moves trust to the VPN operator and endpoint.
  • Connecting to a VPN does not automatically authorize access to every internal service.
  • A VPN is not a substitute for application authentication, authorization, or a firewall.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
  • WireGuard: Conceptual Overview
  • OpenVPN Documentation

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: WebSocket enables two-way communication over a long-lived connection. After the connection is established, either endpoint can send messages without waiting for the other to make a new request. Standard URLs use ws://; wss:// uses TLS.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Ordinary web requests are usually initiated by the client. A page that needs frequent server updates could repeatedly poll, but that adds requests and delays. WebSockets are useful for chat, collaboration, live dashboards, and multiplayer features where both sides need timely updates.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The browser connects to a server and negotiates a WebSocket connection. The classic WebSocket opening uses an HTTP/1.1 upgrade handshake.
  2. If the server accepts, both sides switch to the WebSocket framing protocol.
  3. The client and server send text or binary messages independently.
  4. Either side can close the connection. The application must decide whether and how to reconnect.

WebSocket provides framing, not application meaning. The application still needs a message format, authorization rules, validation, error handling, and resource cleanup. With wss://, TLS protects the connection in transit.

docs.title: Choosing between live-update approaches
docs.text:
Approach How updates arrive Often a good fit Repeated polling Browser asks again at intervals Infrequent updates or simple prototypes Server-Sent Events Server streams one-way text events to browser Live feeds where the browser mainly receives updates WebSocket Both sides send over one long-lived connection Chat, collaboration, and interactive sessions

WebSockets also have control frames, including Ping, Pong, and Close. They help manage the connection, but applications still need a clear policy for stale clients. A heartbeat can detect a connection that appears open but is no longer responsive.

Reconnection should use a bounded delay that grows between attempts, often with random variation (jitter), rather than retrying continuously. After a reconnect, the app may need to authenticate again and request missed updates; the WebSocket protocol itself does not provide durable message history.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A signed-in chat page opens a wss:// connection. When a new message arrives, the server can push it to the browser without waiting for the browser to poll again. The app still needs to decide who may join each conversation.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use WebSockets for ongoing two-way communication. For one-way server updates, polling or Server-Sent Events may be simpler. Account for reconnects, timeouts, load balancing, and authentication. Validate every message and check the browser Origin where appropriate; a secure transport does not replace authorization.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For an application you control, open browser developer tools and inspect the Network panel when its live feature connects. Look for the handshake, connection status, frames, and close reason. This observes traffic without sending test messages to a third-party service.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Handshake: negotiation that opens a WebSocket connection.
  • Frame: protocol unit carrying data or control information.
  • Full-duplex: both endpoints can send independently.
  • Heartbeat: periodic application or protocol check that helps notice a stale connection.
  • Close frame: signal used to end a WebSocket connection.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE): a browser API for receiving a stream of server-to-client events over HTTP.
  • Jitter: a small random variation in retry delays to prevent many clients reconnecting at exactly the same time.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: WebSockets enable server push and two-way messages without repeated HTTP requests. Persistent connections consume resources and require careful handling during restarts, reconnections, and horizontal scaling.

docs.title: WebSockets in a full-stack chat application
docs.text:
1. The browser first authenticates with the application, commonly through an existing session or another documented credential flow.
  2. The browser opens wss:// to the WebSocket endpoint. The server validates the request and its Origin against the application's allowed origins.
  3. The server authenticates the connection and associates it with a user or authorized room. It must still authorize each action; being connected is not permission to read or send every message.
  4. The client and server exchange application messages, often JSON with a message type, identifier, and payload. The server validates size, shape, rate, and authorization before acting.
  5. To deliver a message to clients connected to multiple application instances, deployments commonly publish events through a shared broker or message system. Each instance forwards the event to its own connected clients.

The WebSocket protocol does not define chat rooms, message persistence, read receipts, offline delivery, or exactly-once processing. Store durable messages separately when required, and let reconnecting clients request missed events using an application-level cursor or sequence.

docs.title: Browser authentication considerations
docs.text:
The browser's built-in WebSocket constructor does not provide a general option for setting arbitrary HTTP request headers. Common designs therefore use a secure session cookie during the handshake or an application-defined authentication exchange after the connection opens. If authentication is sent as the first WebSocket message, restrict what an unauthenticated connection can do and close it promptly if authentication fails.

Avoid putting long-lived access tokens in the WebSocket URL: URLs can appear in logs and monitoring systems. If a design uses a short-lived connection ticket in the URL, it should be single-use where practical, narrowly scoped, and protected from logging. Regardless of the credential design, validate the expected Origin for browser clients and authorize each requested room or action.

docs.title: Connection lifecycle and operational details
docs.text:
Concern Developer responsibility Authentication Validate the user during connection setup and handle session expiry or revocation Authorization Check room membership and permissions for each subscription and message Origin Allow only expected web origins when cookie-based authentication is used Heartbeat Detect broken or idle connections; network intermediaries may close quiet connections Reconnect Use bounded backoff with jitter and define how clients recover missed state Scaling Track connection ownership and distribute events across server instances when needed Backpressure Bound queued messages or disconnect slow consumers to avoid unbounded memory growth Deployment Configure proxies and load balancers to support long-lived upgraded connections and sensible idle timeouts Observability Record connection counts, close reasons, message rates, and errors without logging secrets or private message bodies

If authentication uses cookies, browsers may attach those cookies to a WebSocket handshake. Validate Origin and use appropriate cookie and session protections to reduce cross-site WebSocket hijacking risk. Do not assume CORS response rules alone protect WebSockets.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• WebSocket starts with an HTTP-based handshake, then uses WebSocket frames.
  • wss:// protects transport but does not validate application permissions.
  • A persistent connection can still be interrupted by networks or servers.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — MDN: The WebSocket API explains browser-side connections and message events.
  • Official standard — RFC Editor: RFC 6455, The WebSocket Protocol specifies the opening handshake and framing.
  • Official documentation — MDN: Writing WebSocket client applications describes browser connection and event handling.

docs.title: Frontend Development
docs.text:
Frontend development is the work of building the parts of an application people see and interact with. It includes the page structure, visual design, interactive behavior, browser performance, accessibility, and communication with backend services.

The browser is the runtime where a web interface is displayed. It downloads HTML, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, and images; interprets them; and gives the user controls such as links, forms, and buttons. A frontend developer works with these browser capabilities directly and through libraries and frameworks.

docs.title: What this section teaches
docs.text:
You will learn how to:

  • Structure content with semantic HTML and build accessible forms.
  • Style pages with CSS, understand the cascade, and create responsive layouts.
  • Write JavaScript that responds to events and communicates with servers.
  • Use TypeScript to describe program data and make code easier to change.
  • Understand how browsers render pages and use DevTools to investigate them.
  • Build reusable interfaces with React and full-stack web applications with Next.js.

docs.title: How a frontend page comes together
docs.text:
1. A browser requests a URL and receives a document or application response.
  2. HTML describes the content and its structure.
  3. CSS determines how that content is laid out and presented.
  4. JavaScript handles interactions and can request additional data.
  5. The browser renders the result and exposes it to visual, keyboard, and assistive-technology users.

React and Next.js do not replace these foundations. They provide higher-level ways to organize user interfaces, manage rendering, and connect an application to data and routes.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
Follow the expandable subject groups in the navigation. A useful order is:

  1. HTML, to describe meaningful content.
  2. CSS, to control presentation and responsive layout.
  3. JavaScript, to add behavior.
  4. Browser Internals, to understand rendering and investigate pages with DevTools.
  5. TypeScript, to make larger JavaScript codebases easier to reason about.
  6. React, to compose interfaces from components.
  7. Next.js, to build React applications with routing and server features.

You can open any subject from its dropdown when you need a focused reference. Every lesson includes practical examples, important terminology, common misconceptions, revision questions, and official learning resources.

The expanded curriculum includes HTML forms and accessible content; CSS layout, responsive design, positioning, and visual states; JavaScript collections, objects, browser APIs, and asynchronous scheduling; TypeScript configuration, advanced types, and React integration; browser rendering, DevTools, origins, and CORS; React rendering, shared state, refs, and testing; and Next.js routing, server/client boundaries, data, actions, security, and deployment. Some concepts have original diagrams to show how the pieces interact.

docs.title: A first practical exercise
docs.text: Create a small page with a heading, a paragraph, and a button. Use HTML for the content, CSS for spacing and color, and JavaScript to change the message when the button is clicked. Then open the browser's Console and Network panels to inspect the page and its loaded resources.

docs.title: Before moving on
docs.text:
• Which parts of a page are described by HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?
  • What does the browser do with those files?
  • Why should a developer learn browser fundamentals before relying on a framework?

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A browser is more than a window that displays files. It requests resources, interprets HTML and CSS, runs JavaScript, and presents an interactive page. Understanding this process helps explain loading delays, layout changes, and why some code affects responsiveness.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Browsers turn web standards into a consistent interactive experience across devices. Knowing their main responsibilities helps developers build pages that load predictably, work with different input methods, and avoid unnecessary work on the main thread.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: The browser requests a document and related resources. It parses HTML into a DOM and CSS into a CSSOM, combines those inputs to calculate layout, then paints and composites visible content. JavaScript can react to events and may change the DOM or styles, which can require further layout or painting. Browsers perform many tasks concurrently, but some work can delay rendering.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: If a page downloads a large image above the fold, that image may delay the user's perception of loading. If a script repeatedly changes layout-related styles while measuring elements, it can trigger expensive rendering work. Optimizing images and batching updates can improve the experience.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Think about the critical resources needed for the first useful view. Use semantic markup and efficient assets, avoid long main-thread tasks, and measure before optimizing. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript lessons cover the inputs involved. Browser Developer Tools (DevTools) provide direct evidence about page behavior: inspect messages in the Console, requests in Network, saved browser data in Application, and runtime work in Performance.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
To keep an image from causing a large layout shift, reserve its space:

<img src="/images/city.jpg" width="800" height="500" alt="City skyline at dusk">

The dimensions let the browser calculate a space before the image has loaded. The alternative text communicates the image's relevant content.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• DOM: Tree of parsed HTML nodes.
  • CSSOM: Representation of parsed CSS rules.
  • Layout: Calculation of element sizes and positions.
  • Paint: Drawing visual details such as text, borders, and backgrounds.
  • Main thread: A browser execution context that handles many script and UI tasks.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• The browser does not simply display HTML source; it parses and renders it.
  • Every style change does not necessarily trigger every rendering stage, but some changes can require layout or paint.
  • Adding more JavaScript is not always faster than a browser-provided feature.

docs.title: Explore browser tools and rendering
docs.text:
• Page rendering pipeline
  • DevTools overview
  • Console panel
  • Network panel
  • Application panel
  • Performance panel

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Reference: MDN: How browsers work explains parsing, rendering, and the critical rendering path.
  • Reference: MDN: Critical rendering path describes how browsers prioritize resources and build a page for rendering.
  • Review: Browser Internals Interview Questions and Answers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML content is presented: colors, spacing, typography, layout, and adaptation to different screen sizes. Separating styles from content makes pages easier to change and reuse.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: HTML describes content; CSS describes its presentation. This separation lets a site share a design across pages and adapt layouts without rewriting content.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
A CSS rule has a selector and declarations. The browser matches selectors to elements and resolves competing declarations using the cascade, specificity, and inheritance. Selectors can target element types, classes, IDs, and states.

CSS also provides layout algorithms, responsive conditions, custom properties, and functions. A property accepts values with defined syntax; the browser computes the final value after applying the cascade.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A product page may use Grid for desktop columns, a single column on a phone, and a visible focus outline for keyboard users, while keeping the same HTML.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Prefer understandable class names and reusable rules. Test different viewport sizes, keyboard focus, and color contrast. CSS works with HTML, while JavaScript can update classes or styles when interaction requires it.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
/* Flexible columns with a readable minimum width. */
.card-list {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(15rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

.card a:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid royalblue;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

The grid creates suitably sized columns; the focus rule makes keyboard navigation visible.

docs.title: Important CSS topic map
docs.text:
• Syntax, selectors, units, and values
  • Essential CSS properties
  • Cascade and specificity
  • Box model, Flexbox, and Grid
  • Responsive design
  • Positioning and stacking contexts
  • Typography, color, and custom properties
  • Focus, visual states, and motion
  • Transforms and animations
  • CSS architecture and debugging

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Selector: A pattern that identifies which elements a rule affects.
  • Declaration: A property and value, such as color: navy.
  • Cascade: The process for resolving applicable declarations.
  • Responsive design: Layout and styling that adapt to device or viewport needs.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: CSS offers declarative styling and adapts designs without duplicated content. Overly specific selectors and overrides can make the cascade hard to reason about.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• CSS is not only for colors; it also controls layout and responsive behavior.
  • A selector matching an element does not guarantee its rule wins; the cascade determines the final result.
  • Responsive design is not simply shrinking a desktop page.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Reference: MDN CSS explains CSS concepts and documents selectors, properties, and values.
  • Official standard: W3C CSS Snapshot summarizes the current set of CSS specifications and links to modules.
  • Review: CSS Interview Questions and Answers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and meaning of web content. Browsers read elements such as headings, links, forms, and images to build a document people can navigate.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: The web needs a shared way to express documents. HTML provides that vocabulary. Semantic elements communicate purpose to browsers, assistive technologies, and developers. For example, <nav> identifies navigation more clearly than a generic <div>.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: An HTML document is a tree of elements. Tags mark the beginning and end of most elements; attributes provide extra information. The browser parses the source into a Document Object Model (DOM), which scripts and styles can work with. Elements can contain other elements, but they must be nested correctly.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A news story might use <main>, <article>, <h1>, <time>, and <figure> to identify its content and image caption before CSS changes its appearance.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Start with meaningful structure, use headings in order, give images useful alternative text, and associate labels with form controls. Semantic HTML provides useful accessibility behavior without extra scripting. See also CSS, JavaScript, and browser internals.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Project guide</title>
</head>
<body>
<main>
<article>
  <h1>Choosing a first programming project</h1>
  <p>Published <time datetime="2026-03-08">March 8, 2026</time></p>
  <p>Pick a small problem you would enjoy solving.</p>
  <a href="/projects">Explore project ideas</a>
</article>
</main>
</body>
</html>

The datetime value provides a consistent date for software.

docs.title: Learning path and detailed lessons
docs.text:
• Document structure: doctype, html, head, body, metadata, and page landmarks.
  • Elements and global attributes: element syntax, void elements, global attributes, and common attributes.
  • Text and content overview: choose a focused lesson on paragraphs, headings, lists, or inline semantics.
  • Text and paragraphs
  • Headings
  • Lists
  • Inline text semantics
  • Semantic HTML and accessibility: semantic page, text, and interactive elements.
  • Forms overview, then focused lessons on submission, input types, selection controls, and validation.
  • Links and media overview, then focused lessons on links, images, and audio and video.
  • Tables and embedded content overview, followed by lessons on tables and embedded content.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Element: A unit of content, usually represented by opening and closing tags.
  • Attribute: A name-value setting on an element, such as href.
  • DOM: The browser's in-memory tree representation of the document.
  • Semantic markup: Elements selected for their meaning, not merely appearance.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: HTML is widely supported and provides semantic features. It does not define visual design or application logic; CSS and JavaScript usually handle those. Poorly structured markup is difficult to navigate and maintain.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• HTML is not a programming language; it marks up content.
  • A page is not accessible just because it uses HTML; correct semantics and thoughtful labels and alternatives matter.
  • A <div> is not the best default for every piece of content.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official standard: WHATWG HTML Living Standard defines HTML elements, parsing, and browser behavior.
  • Reference: MDN HTML explains core concepts and provides element and attribute guides.
  • Review: HTML Interview Questions and Answers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: JavaScript is a programming language used in browsers and other environments. In a web page it can respond to actions, update the DOM, validate input, and communicate with servers. It adds behavior to the structure described by HTML and the presentation defined by CSS.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: JavaScript lets pages respond to users: a button can open a menu, a form can report missing information, or a page can request data without reloading.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
An engine parses and executes JavaScript. The browser provides APIs such as the DOM and fetch; these are host features, not the language itself. The event loop coordinates queued asynchronous work.

JavaScript is dynamically typed: values have runtime types, while variables can refer to values of different types at different times. It supports functions as values, objects, modules, and asynchronous operations using Promises and async/await.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a user submits a search, code can request and render results. The server must still validate the query; browser checks are not a security boundary.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use small functions and descriptive names, and prefer const unless a value must be reassigned. Handle asynchronous failures and test unusual input. Larger projects may use TypeScript, and React builds user interfaces using JavaScript components.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
const button = document.querySelector("#greeting");

button?.addEventListener("click", () => {
  button.textContent = "Hello, learner!";
});

The browser finds the element and runs the callback on a click. The optional chain avoids calling the listener method if the element is absent; TypeScript or a deliberate null check can make that condition more explicit.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Variable: A named binding for a value.
  • Function: Reusable code that can accept inputs and return a result.
  • Event: A notification of an action or occurrence, such as a click.
  • Promise: An object representing a result that may become available later.
  • DOM: A programmable representation of a web document.
  • Event loop: Host scheduling mechanism that runs queued asynchronous callbacks when JavaScript execution is available.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: JavaScript runs widely and supports small scripts and large applications. Inconsistent conventions, unhandled asynchronous errors, or excessive client-side work can make code harder to maintain or pages slower.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• JavaScript and Java are distinct languages.
  • The browser DOM and fetch are Web APIs, not built-in parts of ECMAScript.
  • Client-side validation cannot replace server-side validation.

docs.title: Explore JavaScript topics
docs.text:
• Values, variables, and functions: primitive types, declarations, operators, and basic functions.
  • Strings and type conversion: string operations, coercion, parsing, and explicit conversion.
  • Operators and control flow: comparisons, conditionals, switch statements, and loops.
  • Control flow and collections: iteration and the core collection types.
  • Arrays and array methods: common methods including forEach, map, filter, reduce, sort, chaining, and two-dimensional arrays.
  • Objects, destructuring, and spread: nested objects, object/array destructuring, rest parameters, and spread.
  • Objects, prototypes, and this
  • Functions and scope: declarations, expressions, arrow functions, parameters, return values, and scope.
  • Closures and classes: closures, constructors, static members, inheritance, super, getters, and setters.
  • Browser input, output, and debugging: common output methods, input dialogs, and console timing.
  • DOM and events overview, followed by focused lessons on DOM navigation and updates and event listeners and forms.
  • Callbacks, timers, and callback hell
  • Promises and async/await
  • Event loop and concurrency
  • JSON and fetching API data
  • Browser APIs and storage
  • Window, document, and cookies
  • Navigator and device APIs: browser language, online hints, permissions, location, media, clipboard, sharing, and other capability APIs.
  • Dates and internationalization
  • Modules and error handling
  • JavaScript Interview Questions and Answers: review core concepts with concise answers and examples.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Reference: MDN JavaScript Guide teaches language features with examples.
  • Official standard: ECMAScript Language Specification defines the JavaScript language itself, rather than browser APIs.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Next.js is an open-source React framework created by Vercel and first released in 2016. It gives React applications conventions and tools for routing, server-side code, rendering, and production builds. Next.js applications still use React; Next.js adds a framework around it.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: React helps build user interfaces, but a production website also needs a routing system, a way to load data, decisions about where pages render, and a deployment strategy. Next.js integrates these concerns so a team can build many kinds of web applications in one project.

docs.title: Next.js compared with React
docs.text:
React by itself Next.js A UI library for building components A framework built on React Does not prescribe a built-in routing system Provides file-system routing Rendering and data-loading choices come from the app and its tools Adds server and static rendering options, with behavior depending on route and configuration Can be used in many environments Provides conventions for web applications and supported deployments

Neither is automatically faster or better for every project. Choose based on the application's needs, the team's familiarity, hosting constraints, and how the user experience should work.

docs.title: What Next.js adds
docs.text:
• File-system routing: folders and special files define URL routes.
  • Rendering choices: pages can use static generation, request-time server rendering, client-side work, or a combination appropriate to the route.
  • Server-side endpoints: Route Handlers can expose HTTP endpoints within the application.
  • Image and metadata tools: the Image component and metadata APIs support image delivery and page descriptions, subject to configuration and hosting.
  • Production tooling: the framework provides build and optimization features, including code splitting, while the actual result depends on how the application is structured.

These features help, but they do not automatically guarantee better SEO, faster pages, or a secure API. Those outcomes still depend on implementation, content, and deployment.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: In the App Router, files inside app define routes and UI boundaries. Server Components are rendered on the server by default; Client Components support browser interactivity and APIs. Next.js supports static and request-time rendering, with behavior depending on version and route configuration.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A product page can render its title and description as server-generated content, while a small client component handles an interactive quantity selector. This keeps the browser work focused on the parts that need it.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Learn React first, then study routes, rendering, and the boundary between server and browser code. Never put secrets in client-side code. Understand TypeScript if the project uses typed components.

The App Router has evolved over several releases. Check the version-specific official documentation before copying a configuration or caching example from an older tutorial.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The current recommended starter command creates a project using the current stable release:

npx create-next-app@latest

In the project directory, start the development server:

cd my-app
npm run dev

By default, the local app is available at http://localhost:3000. To use another port with the standard npm script, pass the argument through:

npm run dev -- --port 3001

The URL is local to your development machine; it is not a public production address.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• React framework: A system built on React that adds application-level conventions and capabilities.
  • App Router: The routing system based on the app directory.
  • Server rendering: Producing page output on the server rather than building the entire initial page in the browser.
  • Static generation: Producing route output ahead of a user request when its data and configuration allow it.
  • Hydration: Connecting browser-side React behavior to server-rendered markup when client interactivity is needed.

docs.title: Advantages and trade-offs
docs.text: Next.js supplies routing, build tooling, and multiple rendering options in an integrated framework. Server/client boundaries and caching introduce additional concepts; teams also need to understand the behavior of the specific framework version they deploy.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Next.js is not a competing UI library; it is built on React.
  • Server rendering does not mean every component runs only on the server.
  • Static generation, server rendering, and client-side rendering are not interchangeable terms.
  • Server rendering does not guarantee a fixed speed improvement. Results depend on the route, server, network, assets, caching, and application code.
  • A "use client" file is not a safe place for secrets.

docs.title: Explore the Next.js topics

  • Rendering strategies overview, then focused lessons on client rendering, static rendering, server rendering, and ISR.

  • Link and Image overview, followed by focused lessons on the Link and Image components.

docs.text:

  • Official docs: Next.js App Router documents the App Router and its features.
  • Review: Next.js Interview Questions and Answers.

docs.title: React
docs.text: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. A React component describes UI for its current inputs; state and events let the interface respond to user actions.

docs.title: What React provides
docs.text:
• Components: reusable functions that describe interface parts.
  • Props: inputs passed from a parent component.
  • State: data that changes and causes the UI to update.
  • JSX: syntax for describing UI in JavaScript source.
  • Hooks: functions such as useState, useEffect, and useContext that connect function components to React capabilities.
  • Rendering and reconciliation: React calculates UI and applies needed updates to the host environment.

React itself does not prescribe a complete application architecture, server-rendering strategy, or built-in router. Frameworks such as Next.js build on React and supply application-level conventions.

docs.title: How a React update works
docs.text:
1. A user event invokes an event handler.
  2. The handler may call a state setter.
  3. React renders the affected component tree using current props and state.
  4. React reconciles the result and commits necessary DOM changes.
  5. Effects synchronize with external systems after commit where appropriate.

Rendering should be pure: do not mutate external state, manipulate the DOM, or make side-effecting requests while calculating the component output.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useState } from "react";

function LikeButton() {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setLikes((current) => current + 1)}>
      Likes: {likes}
    </button>
  );
}

Calling the state setter requests a render with the updated count.

docs.title: React topic map
docs.text:
• Components, JSX, and props
  • State and events
  • Hooks and effects
  • Custom hooks
  • Lists, forms, and UI states
  • Rendering and reconciliation
  • Context and state sharing
  • Refs and performance
  • Suspense and error boundaries
  • Testing React interfaces

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Learn JavaScript first. Keep components focused, use stable list keys, and place state at the nearest common owner that needs it. Learn accessibility and browser behavior alongside React; a framework does not automatically make controls accessible.

  • React is not the same thing as JSX; JSX is commonly used syntax transformed by build tooling.
  • A component render does not mean the browser rebuilds the entire DOM.
  • Effects are for synchronizing with external systems, not a default place for every calculation.
  • State setters schedule updates; they do not synchronously replace the current variable's value.

docs.text:

  • React API reference
  • React Interview Questions and Answers

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text: TypeScript is a programming language and toolchain built on JavaScript. It adds a static type system that checks many relationships between values before the program runs. TypeScript source is transformed to JavaScript for execution; ordinary type annotations do not exist at runtime.

docs.title: Why use it?
docs.text: Types can document a function's contract, improve editor completion, and catch errors during development. They are especially helpful when many components and developers share data structures. They do not prove that a network response or user input is valid.

docs.title: Type inference and annotations
docs.text:
The checker can infer types from values. Add explicit annotations where they clarify a public contract or prevent an ambiguous type.

const siteName = "Engineering Notes"; // inferred string
let visitCount: number = 0;           // explicit annotation

function greet(name: string): string {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

docs.title: Everyday type building blocks
docs.text:
• Primitive types: string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, and undefined.
  • Arrays: string[] or Array<string>.
  • Objects: named properties, including optional properties like nickname?: string.
  • Union: A | B, meaning one of several possibilities.
  • Literal type: an exact value such as "loading" or 200.
  • Tuple: fixed-position values such as [number, string].
  • Function type: parameter and return types, such as (id: string) => boolean.
  • unknown: a value that must be checked before use.
  • never: a value that cannot occur, useful for exhaustive checks.

Prefer unknown to any at uncertain boundaries. any turns off many useful checks.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type LoadState =
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; items: string[] }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

function describe(state: LoadState): string {
  switch (state.status) {
    case "loading":
      return "Loading";
    case "success":
      return `${state.items.length} items`;
    case "error":
      return state.message;
  }
}

The discriminant status lets the checker know which fields are available in each branch.

docs.title: TypeScript and runtime data
docs.text: Types are erased or otherwise do not automatically check arbitrary values at runtime. Validate API responses, browser storage, user input, and other external data. See runtime validation.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
• Types and narrowing
  • Functions, objects, and generics
  • Advanced and utility types
  • Compiler and project configuration
  • TypeScript with React
  • Runtime data validation

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• TypeScript does not replace JavaScript at runtime.
  • A type assertion does not convert or validate the actual value.
  • A type-safe program can still have logic, accessibility, security, and performance bugs.
  • More annotations are not always better; inference is often clear and reliable.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook
  • TypeScript for JavaScript Programmers
  • TypeScript Interview Questions and Answers

docs.title: The Browser Application Panel
docs.text: The Application panel inspects data and web platform features associated with a site. In Chromium-based DevTools, it includes storage, cookies, IndexedDB, cache storage, and service workers.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Persistent browser data can explain why a page remembers a session, shows stale information, or behaves differently after deployment. The panel helps inspect that state while debugging.

docs.title: Important storage types
docs.text:
Storage Typical lifetime and use localStorage String key/value data retained across browser sessions sessionStorage String key/value data scoped to a tab's page session Cookies Small values sent with matching HTTP requests, subject to attributes IndexedDB Structured, larger client-side data Cache Storage Request/response entries commonly managed by service workers

These are not interchangeable. Data can be partitioned or restricted by browser privacy settings, origin, and security attributes.

docs.title: Practical debugging workflow
docs.text: Inspect the relevant storage entry, confirm its origin and expiry, and then reproduce the behavior. Clear site data can help test a first visit, but it deletes state and may sign you out; use it deliberately. Inspect service worker registration and cache contents when an older application build keeps appearing.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Cookies can have security attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite; these have different purposes. JavaScript cannot read an HttpOnly cookie, although browser DevTools can display cookie metadata. Origin is the scheme, host, and port tuple; service worker is a programmable browser worker that can mediate requests and support offline behavior.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• localStorage is not a secure location for secrets.
  • Clearing storage may remove login or offline data.
  • A service worker cache is separate from the ordinary HTTP cache.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools: Application panel
  • MDN: Web Storage API

docs.title: The Browser Console Panel
docs.text: The Console displays JavaScript errors, warnings, and log messages. It can also run expressions in the context of the current page, making it useful for quick investigation.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Errors often include a message, source location, and stack trace. These details help identify where a failure occurred and which sequence of calls led to it.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
• Reproduce the behavior and look for errors at the time it occurs.
  • Expand the stack trace and open the source location.
  • Filter by level or text to focus on relevant messages.
  • Use console.debug, console.info, console.warn, and console.error to communicate the intended diagnostic level.
  • Use console.table() for arrays of similarly shaped objects.
  • Clear or preserve messages when needed; browser options and shortcuts vary.
  • In the Console prompt, inspect page values carefully and avoid changing production data.

The Console API also includes assert, dir, dirxml, trace, nested group methods, count counters, and time timers. See the JavaScript Console API lesson for the method reference and examples. DevTools adds interface features such as filtering, live expressions, source links, and preservation of messages; those controls vary by browser.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 4 },
  { name: "Pen", price: 2 },
];

console.table(products);

In application code, use structured logging that can be removed or controlled for production rather than leaving noisy debug output everywhere.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text:
Read the first useful application frame in a stack trace and inspect the values passed into that function. Stack trace is a record of nested calls; source map connects built code back to original source; exception is an error thrown during execution.

Do not paste commands into a Console unless you understand what they do: Console code runs with the permissions of the page and may access account data.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A warning is not always harmless; understand its source before ignoring it.
  • The Console is not a substitute for automated tests.
  • A runtime error may be caused by data or timing, not only syntax.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools: Console overview
  • Chrome DevTools: Console features reference
  • MDN: Console API

docs.title: Browser DevTools Overview
docs.text: Browser Developer Tools (DevTools) are built-in tools for inspecting a page, its code, network activity, browser storage, and performance. The names and exact features can differ slightly between browsers.

docs.title: Why developers use DevTools
docs.text: The tools show what the browser actually received and executed. This is often more useful than guessing from source code: a request may fail, a CSS rule may be overridden, or a stale service worker may serve an old file.

docs.title: How to open and navigate
docs.text:
In Chrome and Edge, common shortcuts are F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows and Linux, and Cmd+Option+I on macOS. You can also use the browser menu. Right-clicking an element and choosing Inspect opens the Elements panel near that element.

Panel Useful for Elements Inspecting DOM nodes, computed styles, and layout Console Reading errors, warnings, and running small expressions Network Inspecting requests, responses, headers, and timing Application Examining storage, cookies, and service workers Performance Recording runtime activity and diagnosing slow interactions Sources Setting breakpoints and stepping through JavaScript

docs.title: A practical debugging workflow
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the problem and note the page URL and user action.
  2. Check Console for errors and Network for failed or unexpected requests.
  3. Inspect the element or stored data related to the behavior.
  4. Record Performance only when you have a performance question.
  5. Change one thing, repeat the same action, and compare the result.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use a local development environment when possible. DevTools can change page state, disable cache, emulate conditions, and expose private data. A breakpoint pauses execution; computed style is the final style after the cascade; waterfall visualizes request timing.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A clean Console does not prove that the page is correct.
  • DevTools emulation is helpful but does not perfectly reproduce every physical device or network.
  • Do not share screenshots, HAR files, or Console output without checking for tokens and personal data.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools documentation
  • Microsoft Edge DevTools documentation

docs.title: Browser Internals Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review browser behavior and practical use of developer tools. Exact interface names may vary slightly between browsers.

docs.title: 1. What happens after a browser receives HTML?
docs.text: The browser parses HTML into a DOM, processes CSS into style information, calculates layout, paints pixels, and composites layers. Scripts and resource loading can affect this process; browsers optimize and interleave work rather than following one rigid sequence for every page.

docs.title: 2. What is the DOM?
docs.text: The DOM is the browser's object model for a document. JavaScript can query, change, create, and remove nodes through DOM APIs.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between the DOM and CSSOM?
docs.text: The DOM represents document structure and content. The CSS Object Model (CSSOM) represents CSS rules and style information. The browser combines them when calculating how elements should be displayed.

docs.title: 4. What is the browser event loop?
docs.text: It coordinates JavaScript jobs, tasks, microtasks, and rendering opportunities. Promise reactions are microtasks; timers are tasks. Long synchronous work can delay input handling and rendering.

docs.title: 5. How can DevTools help diagnose a failed request?
docs.text: The Network panel shows requests, status codes, timing, headers, payloads, and response information. Check the URL, method, status, console messages, and whether the browser blocked access due to policy or connectivity.

docs.title: 6. What is the same-origin policy?
docs.text: It is a browser security model that restricts how a document or script can interact with resources from a different origin. An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port.

docs.title: 7. What is CORS?
docs.text: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a mechanism by which a server can use HTTP headers to allow selected cross-origin browser requests to be read. CORS is enforced by browsers and is not a replacement for server authentication or authorization.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between cookies and Web Storage?
docs.text: Cookies can be sent automatically with matching HTTP requests and can have server-set security attributes. localStorage and sessionStorage are JavaScript-accessible string storage and are not automatically attached to requests.

docs.title: 9. What is the Console panel used for?
docs.text: It displays logs, warnings, and errors; lets developers run JavaScript in the page context; and can help inspect values. Avoid exposing secrets or sensitive user data in production logs.

docs.title: 10. What can the Application panel help inspect?
docs.text: Depending on the browser, it can inspect storage such as cookies, local/session storage, IndexedDB, cache storage, and service workers. Stored values may be sensitive, so protect user accounts and devices.

docs.title: 11. What is the Performance panel used for?
docs.text: It records runtime activity such as scripting, rendering, layout, and painting over time. It helps locate main-thread work and performance bottlenecks; use representative conditions when profiling.

docs.title: 12. How would you investigate a slow page?
docs.text: Reproduce the slowdown, use Network to inspect resource sizes and timing, then record a Performance trace to locate long tasks, expensive scripts, layout work, or rendering delays. Change one likely cause at a time and measure again.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Browser Internals overview
  • MDN: Critical rendering path
  • MDN: Same-origin policy
  • Chrome DevTools documentation

docs.title: JavaScript Runtime and the Browser Event Loop
docs.text: The browser provides the environment around JavaScript: a JavaScript engine, Web APIs, event handling, rendering, and an event loop that coordinates queued work.

docs.title: Engine, APIs, and scheduling
docs.text: The engine parses and executes JavaScript. The browser exposes APIs such as the DOM, timers, and fetch. Some operations are handled by browser subsystems while JavaScript continues; completion queues callbacks for later execution. JavaScript on the main thread runs a job to completion before a different job can run there.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A long-running JavaScript task can delay input, animation, and rendering. Understanding the runtime helps explain why asynchronous code improves responsiveness but does not make CPU-heavy synchronous work disappear.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Keep main-thread work short. Use a Worker for suitable CPU-intensive work that can be separated from DOM access. Use DevTools Performance recordings to find real long tasks before optimizing.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• The event loop is not a second JavaScript thread that executes callbacks simultaneously.
  • Browser APIs are not part of the ECMAScript language specification.
  • An asynchronous API can still lead to expensive synchronous callback work.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: JavaScript event loop
  • MDN: Web Workers

docs.title: The Browser Network Panel
docs.text: The Network panel records requests made by a page, including documents, scripts, stylesheets, images, fonts, and API calls. It shows what was sent, what came back, and how long each step took.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The panel helps distinguish a frontend bug from a failed request, wrong response, caching issue, or slow dependency. It is also useful for confirming that a form or page is sending the data the developer intended.

docs.title: How to investigate a request
docs.text:
1. Open Network before reproducing the action; enable Preserve log if a navigation would otherwise clear the list.
  2. Filter by request type or search for the endpoint.
  3. Inspect the status, method, URL, and initiator.
  4. Open Headers for request and response headers, Payload for submitted data, and Response or Preview for returned content.
  5. Use the timing details and waterfall to locate waiting or transfer delays.
  6. Retry under a throttled profile only to explore how limited connections affect the page; it is not a replacement for real-user measurements.

docs.title: Status and timing clues
docs.text: A 2xx status usually indicates HTTP success; a 4xx often points to a request or authorization problem, and a 5xx indicates a server-side error. These are clues, not a complete diagnosis: inspect the response body and application behavior too. A cached response may not involve a fresh network transfer.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: An initiator is the script or document that caused a request. TTFB (time to first byte) measures time until response data begins arriving. Waterfall displays request phases over time. Compare the same action before and after a change.

docs.title: Common misconceptions and safety
docs.text:
• A fast server response does not guarantee a fast page if rendering or client-side work is slow.
  • The Network panel shows only what happened during its capture.
  • HAR exports and screenshots may contain cookies, authorization headers, search queries, or personal data. Remove sensitive values before sharing.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools: Network overview
  • Chrome DevTools: Network reference

docs.title: Origins, CORS, and Browser Security
docs.text: Browsers enforce rules that limit how one website can interact with data from another. The same-origin policy and related protections help prevent a page from freely reading private data belonging to another site.

docs.title: What is an origin?
docs.text: An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port. For example, https://shop.example:443 and http://shop.example have different schemes and therefore different origins. A different subdomain or port is also a different origin.

docs.title: Same-origin policy and CORS
docs.text:
The same-origin policy restricts certain cross-origin reads by scripts. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a server-controlled mechanism that allows a server to tell browsers which origins may read selected responses. The browser enforces the response headers; adding a request header in frontend JavaScript cannot grant permission.

Some cross-origin requests trigger a preflight OPTIONS request. Simple requests may be sent without preflight, but the browser can still block JavaScript from reading a response if the CORS policy does not allow it.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Configure CORS on the server that owns the resource. Allow only the origins and methods needed. CORS is not authentication: it does not prevent non-browser clients from calling a public endpoint, and it does not replace authorization or CSRF protections.

Origin is scheme/host/port; preflight asks permission before certain cross-origin requests; credentialed request includes credentials such as cookies under specific browser and server policies.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• CORS is not a frontend setting that can override a server response.
  • A CORS error does not necessarily mean the server never received the request.
  • CORS does not protect an API from all unauthorized access.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Same-origin policy
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

docs.title: The Browser Performance Panel
docs.text: The Performance panel records a timeline of browser activity. It helps investigate slow page loads, delayed interactions, long JavaScript tasks, and unnecessary rendering work.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A page can look correct and still feel slow. A recording helps locate when work happened and which activity occupied the main thread, rather than relying on a guess or a single timing number.

docs.title: A careful profiling workflow
docs.text:
1. Choose one question, such as “Why does opening this menu feel delayed?”
  2. Use a representative page and device or throttling profile.
  3. Start a recording, perform the same interaction, then stop.
  4. Inspect the timeline, main-thread flame chart, network activity, and rendering tracks.
  5. Find long tasks or repeated work, then inspect the relevant source.
  6. Make one change and record again under similar conditions.

The flame chart shows nested work over time. Long tasks are blocks of main-thread work that can delay responsiveness. User Timing marks can annotate application-specific events.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Profile realistic production-like builds as well as local development builds: development tools may add extra work. Check more than one device class, and pair lab recordings with real-user metrics when available. Optimize the largest measured bottleneck rather than chasing small isolated numbers.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A single recording is not proof of performance for every user.
  • Network delay and main-thread delay are different bottlenecks.
  • Improving a synthetic score may not improve the user's actual task.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools: Performance overview
  • web.dev: Learn performance

docs.title: The Browser Rendering Pipeline
docs.text: The rendering pipeline is the work a browser performs to turn downloaded resources into pixels and keep the page updated as it changes.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Understanding the pipeline helps explain blank screens, layout shifts, slow interactions, and why some updates cost more than others. It also helps focus optimization on measured user-visible work.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The browser requests HTML and discovers linked stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts, and other resources.
  2. It parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into style information. These tasks can proceed while resources are still arriving.
  3. It calculates styles and layout: which rules apply, and where elements fit.
  4. It paints visual details and composites layers into the displayed frame.
  5. JavaScript, user input, animations, and new resources can trigger further work.

This is a useful mental model, not a strict sequence for every browser or every update. Browsers optimize and overlap work. Some scripts and stylesheets can delay rendering, depending on how they are loaded.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An image without reserved dimensions may load after the text and push content down, causing layout shift. Declaring its intrinsic dimensions lets the browser reserve space:

<img src="/images/city.jpg" width="800" height="500" alt="City skyline">

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use the Performance panel to record a real interaction before changing code. Layout calculates geometry; paint draws visual content; compositing combines layers; layout shift is unexpected movement of visible content.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Every style change does not cause every rendering stage.
  • The browser does not wait for every resource before showing anything.
  • More JavaScript is not a universal solution to rendering problems.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: How browsers work
  • MDN: Critical rendering path

docs.title: CSS Architecture and Debugging
