docs.text: CSS architecture is how a project organizes styles so that rules remain understandable as the interface grows. Debugging is the process of finding why the browser computed an unexpected result.

docs.title: Keep styles maintainable
docs.text:
• Use clear component or feature class names.
  • Keep selectors as simple as practical.
  • Group related rules and avoid broad global overrides.
  • Use custom properties for shared colors, spacing, and typography.
  • Remove obsolete rules instead of layering new overrides indefinitely.

CSS Modules, utility classes, and naming conventions are different organization strategies; none removes the need to understand the cascade.

docs.title: Debug in the browser
docs.text:
1. Inspect the element in DevTools.
  2. Check the matched rules and identify overridden declarations.
  3. Review computed styles, inherited properties, and the box model.
  4. Toggle one declaration to test a hypothesis.
  5. Inspect the parent layout and containing block if geometry is unexpected.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: Cascade conflict occurs when multiple declarations compete. Computed style is the resolved property value. Specificity is one factor in resolving rules. CSS Module scopes class names through a build-time mechanism, depending on the toolchain.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Increasing selector complexity is not the only way to fix a rule conflict.
  • CSS Modules do not change how layout or properties work.
  • A computed value may come from inheritance or browser defaults, not only the rule closest to the element.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: CSS troubleshooting
  • Chrome DevTools: Inspect and change CSS

docs.title: CSS Box Model and Layout
docs.text: Every rendered element has a box. The box model describes the content area, padding, border, and margin. Layout systems such as Flexbox and Grid arrange these boxes.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Understanding box sizing helps explain unexpected widths and spacing. Layout tools let developers arrange content without fragile positioning hacks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: With the default content-box, declared width applies to the content; padding and border are added outside it. With border-box, the declared width includes content, padding, and border. Flexbox is suited to arranging items along one primary axis; Grid is suited to rows and columns together.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(15rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

auto-fit and minmax() let the grid use available space while respecting a minimum card width.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use normal flow, Flexbox, or Grid for most layouts. Reserve absolute positioning for overlays or elements intentionally removed from normal flow. Padding is inner spacing, margin is outer spacing, and gap spaces items in a layout without adding margins to each child.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Margin is not part of an element's background-painted content box.
  • z-index does not place every element in one global stack; stacking contexts affect ordering.
  • Flexbox and Grid can be combined; they solve related but different layout problems.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: The box model
  • MDN: CSS layout

docs.title: CSS Cascade, Specificity, and Inheritance
docs.text: When multiple CSS declarations can style one property on an element, the cascade determines which value is applied. Selectors identify elements; specificity and other cascade rules help resolve competing declarations.

docs.title: How the cascade decides
docs.text: The browser considers, in order, whether a declaration is relevant, its origin and importance, cascade layer, specificity, scoping proximity where applicable, and source order. A later rule does not automatically win when an earlier declaration has greater precedence.

docs.title: Specificity
docs.text:
As a useful simplified comparison, specificity has three groups:

  1. ID selectors, such as #header.
  2. Class, attribute, and pseudo-class selectors, such as .card, [disabled], and :focus.
  3. Type and pseudo-element selectors, such as button and ::before.

Compare groups left to right, not by adding them into a single number. Universal selectors and combinators do not add specificity. Pseudo-class :where() has zero specificity; :is(), :not(), and :has() use the specificity of their arguments under the selector rules.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text: Some properties, commonly text-related properties such as color and font-family, inherit from an ancestor. Many layout properties do not. inherit, initial, unset, and revert are global keyword values with different reset behavior.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
article p { color: #333; } /* 0 IDs, 0 classes, 2 element selectors */
.notice { color: darkred; } /* 0 IDs, 1 class, 0 element selectors */

<article>
  <p class="notice">The class selector wins in this example.</p>
</article>

The class rule has greater specificity than the two type selectors, assuming the declarations have equal origin, importance, and layer.

docs.title: Cascade layers and !important
docs.text: @layer lets a project establish ordering among groups of author styles. Layer order is considered before selector specificity for normal declarations. Important declarations reverse layer ordering. Use !important sparingly; it can make later maintenance and overrides difficult.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Prefer simple selectors and establish layer or component conventions early. When a style does not appear, inspect matched rules and computed styles in DevTools. Use custom properties for repeated values:

:root { --brand-color: #2457a7; }
.button { background: var(--brand-color); }

Specificity is selector precedence weight; inheritance passes selected values from ancestors; cascade layer groups rules into an explicit order.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• The last declaration does not always win.
  • A class selector does not outrank a declaration with higher origin, importance, or layer precedence.
  • Specificity is not calculated by treating every selector symbol as one point.
  • !important does not fix a confusing stylesheet design.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Cascade
  • MDN: Specificity
  • MDN: Inheritance

docs.title: Essential CSS Properties
docs.text: CSS has many properties. This page is a practical reference to frequently used properties for layout, spacing, typography, color, and interaction. Consult the property reference for exact syntax and browser support.

docs.title: Display and layout
docs.text: Property Common values Purpose display block, inline, inline-block, flex, grid, none Selects the element's layout behavior position static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky Controls positioning behavior inset, top, right, bottom, left lengths or percentages Offsets a positioned element z-index integer or auto Controls stack order within stacking contexts overflow visible, hidden, auto, scroll Controls content outside a box float, clear left, right, none, etc. Primarily wraps text around content; legacy layout use is discouraged

docs.title: Sizing and spacing
docs.text: Property Purpose width, height Set a preferred size min-width, max-width, min-height, max-height Constrain size ranges box-sizing Determines whether declared size includes padding and border margin Outer spacing; supports logical variants such as margin-inline padding Inner spacing border, border-radius Border edges and corner rounding gap, row-gap, column-gap Space between Grid/Flex items

docs.title: Flexbox and Grid
docs.text:
Flexbox: flex-direction, flex-wrap, justify-content, align-items, align-content, flex, flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, and order.

Grid: grid-template-columns, grid-template-rows, grid-template-areas, grid-column, grid-row, place-items, and place-content.

Use the layout lesson for complete examples and how the algorithms differ.

docs.title: Typography and text
docs.text: Property Purpose font-family Typeface list with fallbacks font-size Text size font-weight Stroke weight font-style Such as normal or italic line-height Line box spacing text-align Inline content alignment text-decoration Underlines and other text decoration white-space Wrapping and whitespace handling overflow-wrap Breaks long unbreakable text where needed

docs.title: Color and backgrounds
docs.text: color sets foreground text color. background-color, background-image, background-size, background-position, and background-repeat control backgrounds. opacity affects an element and its descendants; use alpha colors when only the background needs transparency.

docs.title: Interaction and accessibility
docs.text: cursor changes the pointer hint but does not make an element interactive. outline styles a focus indicator; do not remove it without providing a visible alternative. pointer-events controls pointer hit testing, not keyboard access. visibility: hidden hides an element while preserving layout space; display: none removes it from layout and generally from the accessibility tree.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
.lesson-card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 42rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding: clamp(1rem, 3vw, 2rem);
  color: #172334;
  background-color: white;
  border: 1px solid #cbd5e1;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
}

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• opacity affects the whole rendered element, not only its background.
  • z-index behavior depends on the element's layout role and stacking context; it is not one global ordering number.
  • display: none and visibility: hidden have different layout behavior.
  • float is not a substitute for Flexbox or Grid for general application layout.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: CSS reference
  • MDN: Flexbox
  • MDN: CSS Grid

docs.title: CSS Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: Use these questions to review CSS fundamentals and common layout and responsive-design decisions.

docs.title: 1. What is CSS?
docs.text: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) describes how HTML and other document content is presented, including layout, color, typography, and responsive behavior.

docs.title: 2. What is the cascade?
docs.text: The cascade resolves competing declarations by considering origin and importance, cascade layer, specificity, and source order. The exact comparison rules matter when multiple rules match the same property.

docs.title: 3. What is CSS specificity?
docs.text: Specificity is one part of resolving competing selectors. IDs generally outrank classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes, which outrank type selectors. Specificity is compared only after higher-priority cascade factors, such as origin, importance, and layer, are considered.

docs.title: 4. What is inheritance in CSS?
docs.text: Some properties, such as color and font-family, commonly inherit from an element's parent. Others, such as margin and border, do not normally inherit. Consult the property's behavior rather than assuming all styles inherit.

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between a class and an ID selector?
docs.text: A class selector such as .card can match multiple elements and can be combined with other classes. An ID selector such as #main targets the element with that ID and has higher specificity. Classes are usually more reusable for styling.

docs.title: 6. What is the CSS box model?
docs.text: An element's box consists of content, padding, border, and margin. box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border within the declared width and height, which can make sizing easier to reason about.

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between Flexbox and Grid?
docs.text: Flexbox is primarily one-dimensional, arranging items along a row or column. Grid is two-dimensional, controlling rows and columns together. They can be combined in one layout.

docs.title: 8. What does position: absolute position against?
docs.text: An absolutely positioned element is positioned relative to its nearest ancestor that establishes a containing block for absolute positioning, commonly one with a non-static position. If none exists, it uses the initial containing block.

docs.title: 9. What does z-index do?
docs.text: z-index controls stacking order within applicable stacking contexts. Large numbers do not escape their stacking context, so a child may still appear behind content in another context.

docs.title: 10. What is the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden?
docs.text: display: none removes the element from layout. visibility: hidden keeps its layout space while hiding it visually. Accessibility-tree behavior can depend on the element and context; use the appropriate interaction pattern.

docs.title: 11. What is a media query?
docs.text: A media query applies styles when a condition is true, commonly based on viewport width or user preferences such as reduced motion. Use it to adapt the layout to content and available space.

docs.title: 12. What is the difference between px, em, and rem?
docs.text: px is a CSS reference pixel. em is relative to the relevant font size (for many properties, the element's computed font size); rem is relative to the root element's font size. Choose units based on the desired relationship.

docs.title: 13. What are pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements?
docs.text: A pseudo-class such as :hover, :focus-visible, or :checked selects an element in a state. A pseudo-element such as ::before or ::first-line styles a generated or specific part of an element.

docs.title: 14. What are CSS custom properties?
docs.text:
Custom properties store reusable values and can participate in the cascade:

:root { --accent: #3156c9; }
.link { color: var(--accent); }

docs.title: 15. How should motion preferences be respected?
docs.text: Use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to reduce or remove nonessential animation for users who request reduced motion. Keep information and functionality available without animation.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• CSS overview
  • MDN: CSS reference
  • MDN: CSS layout

docs.title: CSS Positioning and Stacking
docs.text: CSS positioning controls how an element participates in document layout and where it is placed. Stacking rules determine which overlapping content is painted on top.

docs.title: Position modes
docs.text:
• static is the normal flow default.
  • relative keeps the element in flow but allows an offset; it can also establish a containing block for positioned descendants.
  • absolute removes the element from normal flow and positions it against a containing block.
  • fixed positions relative to the viewport in common cases.
  • sticky behaves like normal flow until a scroll threshold is reached.

docs.title: Stacking contexts
docs.text: z-index is not one global number line. Certain properties create stacking contexts, which are painted as a group relative to other contexts. A child with a huge z-index cannot necessarily escape a lower parent stacking context.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
.card { position: relative; }
.badge {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: 0.5rem;
  inset-inline-end: 0.5rem;
}

.site-header { position: sticky; inset-block-start: 0; z-index: 10; }

Logical inset properties work with writing direction and avoid hard-coding left/right for every language direction.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Use normal flow and layout systems first; use positioning for overlays, badges, anchored controls, and sticky elements. Inspect ancestors and stacking-context triggers when layering seems wrong.

Containing block is the reference box for positioned coordinates; stacking context is a local painting order; normal flow is the browser's default layout participation.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• position: relative does not remove an element from flow.
  • A higher z-index does not always win across stacking contexts.
  • fixed content can obscure users when zoomed or on small screens.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Position
  • MDN: Stacking context

docs.title: Responsive Design
docs.text: Responsive design lets a page adapt to its content and viewing environment, including narrow phones, tablets, laptops, zoomed text, and wide displays.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: People do not all use the same screen size, orientation, or input method. Responsive layouts preserve readability and useful controls rather than shrinking a desktop design until it becomes cramped.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Start with flexible layouts and intrinsic sizing. Add breakpoints only when the content no longer fits well. Media queries can change layout at a viewport condition; relative units such as %, rem, and vw express relationships rather than fixed device assumptions.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
.page {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
}

.article-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .article-grid {
    grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr;
  }
}

The content stays within a readable maximum width and gains a second column only when enough space is available.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Test real content at multiple widths, zoom levels, and keyboard navigation. Avoid relying on a particular phone model; breakpoints should be chosen where the design needs them. Use responsive images where appropriate, and ensure controls remain easy to operate.

Viewport is the visible page area. Breakpoint is a condition where layout rules change. Mobile-first commonly means starting with the simplest narrow layout, then enhancing it for wider space.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Responsive design is not one special CSS framework or a list of device widths.
  • A layout that fits the viewport can still be hard to read or operate.
  • Media queries complement, but do not replace, flexible layout.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Responsive design
  • web.dev: Responsive web design basics

docs.title: CSS Syntax, Selectors, Units, and Values
docs.text: CSS describes presentation through rules. Each rule has a selector and one or more declarations; a declaration is a property paired with a value.

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
.lesson-card {
  color: #172334;
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ccd5e0;
}

.lesson-card is the selector. color, padding, and border are properties; the text after each colon is its value.

docs.title: Selector types
docs.text:
Selector Example Matches Type p All paragraph elements Class .notice Elements with class notice ID #main The element with ID main Attribute input[required] Required inputs Descendant article p Paragraphs anywhere inside an article Child nav > a Anchors that are direct children of nav Pseudo-class button:hover A button in its hover state Pseudo-element p::first-line A generated/selected part of an element Selector list h1, h2 Both heading types

Use classes for reusable styling. IDs are usually better for unique document identity and fragment navigation than for CSS styling.

docs.title: Values and units
docs.text:
• Unitless values: 0, line-height numbers, opacity values, and some other properties.
  • Absolute lengths: px is a CSS reference pixel, not necessarily one physical display pixel.
  • Relative lengths: rem relates to the root font size; em relates to the current context; % relates to a property's reference dimension.
  • Viewport units: vw, vh, and newer dynamic/small/large viewport variants relate to viewport size; use carefully on mobile.
  • Colors: hex, rgb(), hsl(), named values, and custom properties.
  • Functions: calc(), min(), max(), clamp(), and var().
.reading-column {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 68rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
  font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.3vw, 1.2rem);
}

docs.title: At-rules
docs.text:
At-rules begin with @ and control groups of declarations or CSS behavior:

  • @media applies conditions such as viewport width or user preferences.
  • @supports applies rules if a browser supports a feature.
  • @font-face declares a downloadable typeface.
  • @keyframes defines animation steps.
  • @layer defines cascade layer ordering.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Prefer readable selectors and values that adapt to content. A CSS pixel is a logical measurement and can map to multiple device pixels. A selector matching an element does not guarantee its rule wins; see the cascade lesson.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: CSS syntax
  • MDN: CSS selectors
  • MDN: CSS values and units

docs.title: CSS Transforms and Animations
docs.text: Transforms change how an element is drawn without changing its normal-flow layout position. Transitions interpolate property changes; keyframe animations define named sequences of styles.

docs.title: Transform properties and functions
Transitions
docs.text:
The transition shorthand combines property, duration, timing function, and delay. The longhands are transition-property, transition-duration, transition-timing-function, and transition-delay.

.button {
  background-color: #2457a7;
  transition: background-color 160ms ease;
}

.button:hover {
  background-color: #173c79;
}

Transition only the properties that need a smooth change. Avoid transition: all when it can animate an unintended property.

docs.title: Keyframe animations
docs.text:
@keyframes defines a sequence; animation applies it. Related properties include animation-name, duration, timing-function, delay, iteration-count, direction, fill-mode, and play-state.

@keyframes appear {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(0.5rem); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

.notice {
  animation: appear 180ms ease-out both;
}

docs.title: Accessibility and performance
docs.text:
Respect reduced-motion preferences for nonessential motion:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .notice {
    animation: none;
    transition: none;
  }
}

Motion should communicate change, not obscure it. Prefer animating transform or opacity when appropriate, but profile real pages—compositor behavior and performance depend on the browser and page.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A transform changes drawing, not normal-flow layout.
  • Adding will-change everywhere can use more memory; use it only after evidence of a need.
  • Reduced-motion support is not just disabling every transition; preserve essential state feedback.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Using CSS transitions
  • MDN: CSS animations
  • MDN: prefers-reduced-motion

docs.title: CSS Typography, Colors, and Custom Properties
docs.text: Typography and color strongly affect readability, hierarchy, and brand identity. CSS custom properties let a design reuse values consistently.

docs.title: Typography
docs.text: Choose readable font sizes, line heights, and line lengths. Use a fallback font stack because a preferred font may not be installed or may fail to load. For long text, test at different zoom levels and screen widths.

docs.title: Color and contrast
docs.text: Use color to reinforce meaning, not as the only way to distinguish states. Check text and interface contrast against accessibility guidance. A muted color that looks fine on one display may be difficult to read elsewhere.

docs.title: Custom properties
docs.text:
:root {
  --color-text: #1d2733;
  --color-accent: #2457a7;
  --space-3: 1rem;
}

.notice {
  color: var(--color-text);
  border-inline-start: 0.25rem solid var(--color-accent);
  padding: var(--space-3);
}

Custom properties participate in the cascade and can be overridden on a component or theme root.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use a small, meaningful token set rather than inventing a new value for every element. Fallback font is a substitute when the primary typeface is unavailable; contrast ratio compares perceived luminance; design token is a named reusable design value, often implemented with a custom property.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A named color does not guarantee sufficient contrast.
  • Custom properties are not compile-time constants; they inherit and cascade.
  • A font size that looks comfortable on one monitor may not work at zoom or on a small device.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: CSS custom properties
  • W3C WAI: Contrast minimum

docs.title: CSS Visual States and Motion
docs.text: CSS controls not only the default appearance but also visual states such as hover, keyboard focus, disabled controls, and transitions between states.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Clear visual feedback helps users understand which control is active and what will happen next. Thoughtful motion can explain a change, but unnecessary or fast animation can distract or cause discomfort.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Pseudo-classes such as :hover, :focus-visible, and :disabled match element states. Transitions interpolate supported property changes over time. Animations can define multiple steps, while the prefers-reduced-motion media feature lets a page respect a user's operating-system preference.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
.button {
  background: #2457a7;
  color: white;
  transition: background-color 150ms ease;
}

.button:hover { background: #173c79; }
.button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid orange; outline-offset: 3px; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Do not remove the keyboard focus indicator unless you replace it with an equally clear one. Keep motion short and meaningful. Pseudo-class matches a state; transition interpolates a property change; reduced motion is a user preference that should influence nonessential animation.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Hover is not available on every device and must not be the only feedback.
  • Focus styling is important for keyboard users, not just decoration.
  • A transition is not appropriate for every property or every user.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Using media queries
  • MDN: prefers-reduced-motion

docs.title: HTML Audio and Video
docs.text: The native <audio> and <video> elements let browsers play media without requiring a custom player. Their controls, captions, and alternatives help people use the content across devices and abilities.

docs.title: Sources and playback attributes
docs.text:
Both elements can use a src attribute or one or more nested <source> elements.

Attribute Meaning controls Shows the browser's playback controls autoplay Requests automatic playback; browsers commonly restrict it muted Starts playback without sound; often required for autoplay eligibility loop Restarts playback when it ends preload Hint: none, metadata, or auto; the browser may choose differently poster Preview image for video before playback playsinline Allows inline playback on supported mobile browsers 
<video controls width="640" poster="/media/lesson-preview.jpg">
  <source src="/media/lesson.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="/media/lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="/media/lesson-en.vtt"
         srclang="en" label="English">
  Your browser does not support embedded video.
</video>

The browser can select a source format it supports. Fallback text is shown when the element itself is unsupported; it is not a substitute for captions.

docs.title: Captions and alternatives
docs.text:
<track> provides timed text. Use kind="captions" for captions that include relevant speech and sounds; use kind="subtitles" for translated dialogue. The src points to a WebVTT file, srclang identifies its language, and label gives the choice a readable name.

Provide a transcript or description when the media's information cannot be understood from its audio or video alone. Avoid unexpected autoplay, especially with sound.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: preload is a hint, not a promise. autoplay may be blocked by browser policy. Captions improve access but do not necessarily describe visual information; provide an appropriate audio description or transcript when needed.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <audio>
  • MDN: <video>
  • MDN: <track>

docs.title: HTML Document Structure
docs.text: HTML is a tree of nested elements. A well-formed document gives browsers a predictable starting point and makes content understandable to people and assistive technology.

docs.title: Why use a document structure?
docs.text: Browsers can recover from many markup mistakes, but relying on recovery can produce surprising results. A consistent structure also gives search engines, accessibility tools, and other developers clearer information.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• <!doctype html> selects modern HTML parsing behavior.
  • <html lang="en"> is the root and declares the document language.
  • <head> contains metadata and links to resources; it is not visible page content.
  • <body> contains the page's content and controls.
  • Elements nest to express relationships. An element should not be placed inside another element where HTML does not allow it.

docs.title: Important head elements
docs.text:
Element Purpose Common attributes <title> Browser-tab and document title Text content; one clear title per document <meta charset="utf-8"> Declares character encoding charset; place near the start of head <meta name="viewport"> Configures mobile viewport behavior name, content <meta name="description"> Summary that may be used in search snippets name, content <link rel="stylesheet"> Links an external stylesheet rel, href, optional media <link rel="icon"> Links a site icon rel, href, optional type, sizes <base> Sets base URL/target for relative links href, target; use carefully because it changes all relative URLs <script> Embeds or loads JavaScript src, type, defer, async, integrity, crossorigin

defer runs a classic external script after parsing while preserving script order. async runs it when available without preserving order. Module scripts have different default loading behavior. Use the strategy that matches dependencies and consult current browser documentation.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <meta name="description" content="Simple recipes and cooking notes.">
    <title>Recipe notes</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/site.css">
  </head>
  <body>
    <header><a href="/">Recipe notes</a></header>
    <main>
      <h1>Vegetable soup</h1>
      <p>A simple weeknight recipe.</p>
    </main>
  </body>
</html>

The viewport declaration helps a mobile browser use the device width when laying out the page. A meaningful title identifies the page in browser tabs, history, and search results.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use one clear page-level heading, meaningful section headings, and landmarks such as header, nav, main, and footer when they match the content. Element means a named part of the document; an attribute configures an element; the DOM is the browser's parsed, in-memory representation.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• HTML is not a visual layout language; use CSS for presentation.
  • Browsers accepting malformed markup does not mean the structure is correct.
  • head and header are different: one contains document metadata, the other is content within the page.
  • async and defer have different scheduling behavior; neither should be added blindly to a script that depends on parsing order.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Basic HTML syntax
  • WHATWG: HTML syntax

docs.title: HTML Elements and Global Attributes
docs.text: HTML is made from elements. An element can have a start tag, content, and an end tag; some elements are void and have no end tag or child content. An attribute adds configuration or information to an element.

docs.title: Element anatomy
docs.text:
<a href="/lessons" class="primary-link">Browse lessons</a>
  • a is the element name.
  • href and class are attributes.
  • The text is the element's content.

Attribute values should be quoted. HTML tag names and attribute names are case-insensitive in HTML documents, but lowercase is the conventional style. Void elements include img, br, hr, input, meta, link, source, track, and area; do not write closing tags for them in HTML.

docs.title: Global attributes
docs.text:
Global attributes can be used on most HTML elements, subject to the rules for each element.

Attribute Meaning Example id Unique identifier in the document <section id="pricing"> class One or more CSS/JS classification tokens <p class="lead muted"> title Advisory text, often shown as a tooltip <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> lang Language of the element's text <html lang="en"> dir Text direction: ltr, rtl, or auto <p dir="auto">...</p> hidden Indicates content is not currently relevant and should be hidden <div hidden>...</div> tabindex Controls focusability and sequential focus order <div tabindex="0">...</div> contenteditable Makes an element's content editable <p contenteditable="true">Draft</p> data-* Stores custom data for scripts <button data-product-id="p7">Add</button> style Inline CSS declarations <p style="color: navy">Text</p> spellcheck Requests spell checking for editable text <textarea spellcheck="true"></textarea> draggable Controls whether an element can be dragged <img draggable="false" ...> autofocus Requests initial focus when a page or dialog opens <input autofocus>; use sparingly inert Makes a subtree non-interactive and unavailable to assistive technology <div inert>...</div> popover Declares an element as a popover target <div popover id="help">...</div> translate Hints whether text should be translated <span translate="no">API</span> accesskey Defines a keyboard shortcut hint <button accesskey="s">Save</button>

aria-* attributes add accessibility semantics when native HTML is not sufficient. Use the correct native element first; ARIA does not add keyboard behavior or validation by itself. Avoid positive tabindex values such as tabindex="3" because they create a confusing focus order.

On inputs, inputmode hints which virtual keyboard to show and enterkeyhint hints the action label for the Enter key. These are hints and do not validate the entered value.

docs.title: Common attributes on important elements
docs.text:
Element Common attributes Purpose a href, target, rel, download Destination and navigation behavior img src, alt, width, height, loading, srcset, sizes Image source, alternative, dimensions, and responsive loading form action, method, enctype, autocomplete, novalidate Submission destination and behavior input type, name, value, required, placeholder, autocomplete, min, max, pattern Form field type, submitted value, and constraints script src, type, async, defer, integrity, crossorigin Script source, scheduling, and integrity link rel, href, media, hreflang Relationship to an external resource button type, disabled, name, value Button behavior and submitted value

Attributes are element-specific: for example, required applies to supported form controls but not to a heading. Check the element reference before using an attribute.

docs.title: Boolean and enumerated attributes
docs.text: Boolean attributes are true when present and false when absent. For example, <input required> means the control is required; required="false" is still present and therefore still true. Enumerated attributes accept one of a defined set of values, such as dir="ltr" or dir="rtl".

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Use semantic elements and valid attributes instead of encoding behavior in custom names. IDs should be unique within a document. The style attribute works, but reusable design belongs in CSS. data-* is for application data, not a replacement for accessible names or built-in semantics.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTML attributes reference
  • WHATWG: HTML syntax
  • MDN: ARIA

docs.title: HTML Embedded Content
docs.text: Embedded content places another resource inside a page. The common <iframe> element embeds a separate browsing context, often for a map, video, or another web document.

docs.title: The <iframe> element
docs.text:
Attribute Meaning src URL of the document to embed title Accessible name explaining the embedded content width, height Initial dimensions of the frame loading lazy can defer loading until the frame is near the viewport sandbox Applies restrictions to the embedded document allow Permissions policy features that may be available to the frame referrerpolicy Controls referrer information sent with the request 
<iframe
  src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
  title="Introduction to HTML forms"
  width="560"
  height="315"
  loading="lazy"
  referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
  allowfullscreen>
</iframe>

Provide a useful title; otherwise people using assistive technology may not know what the frame contains. Use a responsive wrapper or CSS sizing when a fixed width does not fit smaller screens.

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text: An iframe loads a separate document and can make network requests. Embed only trusted sources. The sandbox attribute can restrict capabilities; add only the permissions the content needs. Combining allow-scripts and allow-same-origin for same-origin untrusted content can undermine sandbox restrictions, so understand the trust boundary before using those tokens.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: An iframe title is not a caption for the content inside it; it identifies the frame. loading="lazy" is a loading hint and may not defer a frame in every situation. Embedding a page does not make its content part of the parent document's DOM.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <iframe>
  • MDN: iframe sandbox

docs.title: HTML Form Submission
docs.text: Form submission turns named control values into data and sends that data to a destination. Knowing the browser’s submission model helps developers choose appropriate methods and process requests safely.

docs.title: The <form> element
docs.text:
Attribute Purpose action URL that processes the submission; defaults to the current URL method get or post; controls how form data is sent enctype Encoding for the request body; use multipart/form-data for file uploads with POST autocomplete Hints whether browser autofill is appropriate novalidate Disables native constraint validation for this form target Browsing context where the response should be displayed

GET is suitable for safe retrieval such as search. Form values are encoded into the URL, making the result shareable and bookmarkable. Do not use GET for passwords or state-changing actions. POST sends form data in the request body, but HTTPS is still necessary to protect it in transit.

docs.title: How values are submitted
docs.text:
1. A user submits the form with a submit button or keyboard action.
  2. The browser checks applicable native constraints unless validation is disabled.
  3. Enabled controls with a name contribute name-value pairs.
  4. The browser encodes the values according to the method and encoding type.
  5. The browser sends the request to the form’s action.

Controls without a name are generally not included. Disabled controls are not successful controls and are omitted. The server must treat all received values as untrusted.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="search-query">Search lessons</label>
  <input id="search-query" name="q" type="search">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

A search for HTTP basics can produce a URL similar to /search?q=HTTP+basics, which can be revisited or shared.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Use a server route or application handler to validate and process submissions. method="post" does not encrypt data, and a hidden or disabled control is not a security boundary. Protect state-changing requests against cross-site request forgery where relevant to the application's authentication model.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <form>
  • MDN: Sending form data

docs.title: HTML Form Validation
docs.text: Form validation checks whether submitted values meet expected constraints. HTML provides useful browser-side checks, while the application server must validate every request independently.

docs.title: Native constraint attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Typical use required Require a value or selection type="email" / type="url" Check a browser-recognized value shape min / max / step Bound numeric or date/time values minlength / maxlength Set a text-length range pattern Match a supported text value against a regular expression novalidate Disable native checks for a form

These constraints help the user correct mistakes before submission. Browser messages and exact behavior may differ. A browser check does not prove that the value is true, safe, authorized, or even sent by the intended page.

docs.title: Label errors clearly
docs.text:
Associate visible labels with controls through matching for and id values, or by nesting the control inside its label. Explain what needs to change and keep the error close to the affected field. Do not communicate errors by color alone.

<label for="age">Age</label>
<input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="13" max="120" required>

For custom validation, use the browser Constraint Validation API where it fits, but ensure server responses also identify invalid fields in an accessible way.

docs.title: Server-side validation
docs.text: On the server, validate type, length, format, allowed values, and any business rule. Separately check authorization and ownership. Normalize or reject unexpected values before using them in database operations or other systems.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Client-side validation is a usability aid, not a security boundary.
  • pattern does not sanitize a value or prevent malicious requests.
  • An error should explain how to fix the problem, not only say “invalid.”
  • Validation does not replace output encoding or parameterized database operations.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Constraint validation
  • W3C WAI: Forms notifications

docs.title: HTML Forms
docs.text: Forms collect information from people and submit it for an application to process. A search box, account sign-in, checkout, and feedback form all use the same core HTML form model.

docs.title: Follow the form learning path
docs.text:
• Form submission: the <form> element, action, method, and how names become submitted data.
  • Input types and attributes: common <input> types, their behavior, and useful attributes.
  • Selects, checkboxes, and radios: choices and grouped controls.
  • Form validation: labels, browser constraints, error feedback, and server-side validation.

docs.title: A small example
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="query">Search lessons</label>
  <input id="query" name="q" type="search">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

The label gives the control an accessible name. The name determines the key included in submission. The form’s method and action determine how and where the browser sends the data.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Native controls provide keyboard interaction, mobile input hints, and baseline validation. They improve usability but do not replace server-side validation, authorization, or secure transport over HTTPS.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text: • MDN: Forms

docs.title: HTML Headings
docs.text: Headings label sections and communicate how the content is organized. Browsers display them prominently by default, but their most important job is to describe the document hierarchy.

docs.title: Heading levels
docs.text:
<h1> through <h6> represent six levels of section headings. A page usually has one clear main heading, followed by headings that introduce related sections.

<main>
  <h1>Learning web development</h1>
  <section>
    <h2>Start with HTML</h2>
    <h3>Build a document</h3>
  </section>
</main>

Choose a level based on the heading’s relationship to nearby sections. Do not skip levels simply to get a smaller font; style the heading with CSS. Modern HTML does not automatically reset heading levels inside nested <section> elements.

docs.title: Why hierarchy matters
docs.text: People often scan headings before reading a page. Screen-reader users may also navigate by heading level. A clear outline makes long content easier to understand and helps developers maintain the page.

docs.title: Developer checklist
docs.text:
• Write concise headings that accurately describe the section.
  • Keep sibling sections at the same level where appropriate.
  • Use CSS classes for visual differences rather than selecting a heading level for its default appearance.
  • Avoid using heading elements only to make text bold or large.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A heading level is not just a font-size choice.
  • A page is not required to contain all six heading levels.
  • Nesting a section does not automatically change the meaning of its heading level.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Headings
  • W3C WAI: Headings

docs.title: HTML Images
docs.text: Images communicate information, add illustration, or provide decoration. HTML gives the browser image sources and gives assistive technology a text alternative when appropriate.

docs.title: The <img> element
docs.text:
<img> is a void element. Its important attributes include:

Attribute Purpose src Image resource URL alt Text alternative; use alt="" for a decorative image width, height Intrinsic dimensions that help reserve layout space srcset Candidate images with width or density descriptors sizes Expected rendered width so the browser can select a candidate loading lazy can defer off-screen images; eager requests early loading decoding Hint about decoding behavior fetchpriority Priority hint for fetching; not a guarantee 
<img src="/images/city-800.jpg"
     srcset="/images/city-400.jpg 400w, /images/city-800.jpg 800w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 800px"
     width="800" height="500"
     alt="City skyline beside a river at sunset"
     loading="lazy">

srcset describes available image candidates. sizes describes how wide the image is expected to appear at different viewport sizes; the browser uses both to choose a suitable resource.

docs.title: Art direction with <picture>
docs.text:
<picture> provides alternate sources, such as a crop for a narrow screen or a supported image format. Put <source> elements before a fallback <img>.

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="/images/city-portrait.jpg">
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="/images/city.avif">
  <img src="/images/city.jpg" width="800" height="500"
       alt="City skyline beside a river at sunset">
</picture>

docs.title: Write useful alternatives
docs.text: Describe the relevant information, not every visual detail. For decorative images that add no information, use alt="" so assistive technology can skip them. If an image is the only content inside a link, its alternative should convey the link's purpose.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Set dimensions to reduce layout shifts. Lazy-load below-the-fold images where useful, but avoid delaying the main image visible immediately. alt text is not a caption, and loading="lazy" does not make an oversized image small.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Responsive images
  • MDN: <img>
  • W3C WAI: Images

docs.title: HTML Inline Text Semantics
docs.text: Inline elements describe the role or meaning of words within a line. Choose the element that matches the content, then use CSS if its default appearance needs to change.

docs.title: Common inline elements
docs.text:
Element Meaning <strong> Importance, seriousness, or urgency <em> Stress emphasis that can affect the sentence meaning <b> Draws attention without adding importance <i> Alternate voice, technical term, or idiomatic text <u> Non-textual annotation; use carefully because it resembles a link <s> Content that is no longer accurate or relevant <del> / <ins> Deleted / inserted changes; may include cite and datetime <sub> / <sup> Subscript / superscript <code> A fragment of computer code <span> Generic inline container when no semantic element applies

<br> creates a line break when the break is part of the content, such as in an address or poem. <hr> represents a thematic change between paragraphs or sections.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
<p>
  Use <strong>HTTPS</strong> for secure transport.
  The variable <code>userId</code> identifies the account.
</p>

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• <strong> and <b> are not interchangeable: one conveys importance, the other draws attention without that meaning.
  • <em> is not simply an italic style; it expresses stress emphasis.
  • Repeated <br> elements should not be used to create paragraph spacing.
  • <span> has no built-in meaning; do not use it when a semantic element fits.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Text-level semantics
  • MDN: <strong>
  • MDN: <code>

docs.title: HTML Input Types and Attributes
docs.text: <input> creates many kinds of form controls. Its type changes the expected value, browser interface, validation behavior, and sometimes the mobile keyboard.

docs.title: Common input types
docs.text: Type Typical purpose text, search General text or a search query email, url, tel Address/contact input with browser hints password Conceals entered characters visually; does not encrypt or store them securely number, range Numeric value or approximate slider selection date, time, datetime-local, month, week Date and time values; UI varies by browser checkbox, radio Independent choices or one choice from a named group file Select one or more files hidden Submit a non-visible value; not trusted for authorization submit, button, reset Button-like controls; a <button> is often more flexible color Choose a color value

docs.title: Useful attributes
docs.text: Attribute Meaning name Key used when the value is submitted value Initial or current value depending on the type and state required Requires a value before native validation succeeds placeholder Short hint; does not replace a visible label autocomplete Describes the expected value to support browser autofill min, max, step Constraints for supported numeric/date inputs minlength, maxlength Text length constraints pattern Regular-expression constraint for supported text inputs checked Initial checked state for a checkbox or radio multiple Allows multiple values or files for supported types accept Suggests file types in the picker; not a security validation disabled Prevents use and omits the control from submission readonly Prevents editing while generally including the value in submission

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
<label for="account-email">Email</label>
<input id="account-email" name="email" type="email"
       autocomplete="email" required>

The id connects the label to the control, while name supplies the submitted key. The browser can provide a suitable keyboard and basic validation for the email type.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Select types that fit the data rather than using text for every field. Use autocomplete tokens for common information. accept, pattern, and required improve the browser experience but do not replace validation on the server.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <input>
  • MDN: Input types

docs.title: HTML Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: Review these questions after the focused HTML lessons. Each answer highlights the practical meaning of the concept rather than relying on memorized definitions.

docs.title: 1. What is HTML?
docs.text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and meaning of web content. CSS controls presentation and JavaScript adds behavior.

docs.title: 2. What is the purpose of <!doctype html>?
docs.text: It tells browsers to use modern standards mode when parsing the document. It is a declaration, not an HTML element.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between an element and a tag?
docs.text: A tag is markup such as <p> or </p>. An element is the document construct represented by its start tag, content, and optional end tag. Some elements, such as <img>, are void and have no end tag.

docs.title: 4. What are HTML attributes?
docs.text: Attributes provide additional information or configuration on an element: <a href="/about">About</a> uses href to provide the link destination. Some attributes are global; others only apply to particular elements.

docs.title: 5. What is semantic HTML?
docs.text: Semantic HTML uses elements that describe the purpose of content, such as <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <button>. It helps browsers, assistive technology, and developers understand the document.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between <section> and <div>?
docs.text: <section> represents a thematic grouping of content, usually with a heading. <div> is a generic container with no built-in meaning. Use <div> when no more appropriate semantic element fits.

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between <article> and <section>?
docs.text: An <article> is self-contained content that can stand on its own, such as a post or comment. A <section> groups related content within a larger page or article.

docs.title: 8. Why should heading levels follow a logical hierarchy?
docs.text: Headings communicate the structure of a page and help people scan or navigate it. Choose a level based on section relationships, not its default font size; CSS controls appearance.

docs.title: 9. What is the difference between <strong> and <b>?
docs.text: <strong> conveys importance or urgency. <b> draws attention without adding that importance. Use CSS for visual styling alone.

docs.title: 10. When should you use <ol> instead of <ul>?
docs.text: Use <ol> when sequence or ranking matters, such as ordered instructions. Use <ul> when the items form a group but order is not meaningful.

docs.title: 11. What is the difference between a link and a button?
docs.text: An <a href="..."> navigates to a resource or location. A <button> performs an action, such as submitting a form or opening a dialog.

docs.title: 12. Why does an image need alt text?
docs.text: alt supplies a text alternative for users who cannot see the image and for cases where it cannot load. Use useful descriptive text for meaningful images and alt="" for decorative images.

docs.title: 13. What do srcset and sizes do?
docs.text: srcset lists image candidates. sizes tells the browser the expected rendered width at different viewport conditions, helping it choose a suitable candidate.

docs.title: 14. Why should a data table use <th> and <td> correctly?
docs.text: <th> identifies a header cell and <td> identifies a data cell. Appropriate headers and scope communicate row or column relationships to assistive technology.

docs.title: 15. Why should every form control have a label?
docs.text: A label gives a control an accessible name and often enlarges its clickable area. Connect a <label for="email"> to a control with id="email", or wrap the control in its label.

docs.title: 16. What is the difference between id and name on a form control?
docs.text: id identifies an element in the document and can connect it to a label. name supplies the key used when a successful control's value is submitted.

docs.title: 17. What is the difference between GET and POST in a form?
docs.text: GET generally places form data in the URL and suits safe retrieval such as search. POST sends data in the request body and is commonly used for state-changing operations. POST does not encrypt data; HTTPS is needed for transport confidentiality.

docs.title: 18. Does required replace server-side validation?
docs.text: No. Browser constraints improve feedback but can be bypassed. The server must validate input and enforce authorization independently.

docs.title: 19. What is the purpose of <fieldset> and <legend>?
docs.text: <fieldset> groups related controls, and <legend> gives that group a caption. They are especially useful for related radio buttons or checkboxes.

docs.title: 20. Does semantic HTML automatically make a page accessible?
docs.text: No. Semantics provide a strong foundation, but content, labels, keyboard behavior, focus, color contrast, alternatives, and testing also matter.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• HTML overview
  • MDN: HTML elements reference
  • WHATWG HTML Living Standard
  • W3C WAI: Tutorials

docs.title: HTML Links and Media
docs.text: Use HTML links to navigate and media elements to provide visual or audio content. Each has its own attributes and accessibility requirements.

docs.title: Focused lessons
docs.text:
• Links: destinations, fragments, email and phone links, and safe new-tab behavior.
  • Images: alternative text, responsive sources, and intrinsic dimensions.
  • Audio and video: sources, playback controls, captions, and accessible alternatives.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text: A link performs navigation; a button performs an action on the current interface. Media elements describe content that the browser can render or play. Choose descriptive names and alternatives so people using assistive technology can understand the purpose and meaning.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTML elements reference
  • W3C WAI: Images

docs.title: HTML Links
docs.text: Links connect one resource to another. They let people navigate to another page, jump to a section, start an email, or call a phone number.

docs.title: The <a> element and its attributes
docs.text:
An anchor becomes a link when it has an href.

Attribute Meaning href Destination URL, fragment, email address, or phone number target Browsing context; _blank requests another tab or window rel Describes the relationship to the destination; useful with _blank download Suggests downloading a permitted resource hreflang Language of the linked resource type Hint about the linked resource's media type 
<a href="/lessons/html/images/">Learn about HTML images</a>
<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/" target="_blank"
   rel="noopener noreferrer">Read MDN (opens in a new tab)</a>
<a href="#examples">Jump to examples</a>
<a href="mailto:hello@example.com">Email us</a>

For a new browsing context, rel="noopener" prevents the destination from controlling the opener page in supporting browsers; noreferrer also suppresses referrer information. Modern browsers generally imply noopener for _blank, but stating the relationship explicitly is clear.

docs.title: Choose links or buttons
docs.text: Use an anchor for navigation to a URL. Use a <button> for an action such as submitting a form, opening a dialog, or changing the current interface. Do not use href="#" as a substitute for a button.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common mistakes
docs.text: Write link text that makes sense out of context, such as “Read the HTML forms guide” rather than “click here.” Ensure keyboard focus is visible. Check that internal links still resolve after moving pages.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <a>
  • W3C WAI: Link purpose

docs.title: HTML Lists
docs.text: Lists group items that belong together. Select a list element based on whether item order matters or whether each item has a term and description.

docs.title: Unordered and ordered lists
Description lists
docs.text:
<dl> groups one or more terms and their descriptions. <dt> is a term or name; <dd> is its description or value.

<dl>
  <dt>HTTP</dt>
  <dd>A protocol for exchanging web messages.</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: Menu
docs.text: <menu> represents a list of commands or items. Its common browser presentation resembles a list, and it is not a replacement for navigation landmarks or buttons.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Use <ol> when sequence or ranking matters, such as numbered instructions. Use <ul> for a group such as a set of related features. Do not select list elements only because their default markers are convenient.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <ul>
  • MDN: <ol>
  • MDN: <dl>

docs.title: HTML Selects, Checkboxes, and Radio Buttons
docs.text: Choice controls let people select one or more values from a known set. Choose the control based on whether choices are independent, mutually exclusive, or presented as a menu.

docs.title: Select menus
docs.text:
<select> contains <option> elements. Each option’s value is the submitted value; its text is the label shown to the user. <optgroup> organizes related options using its label attribute.

<label for="topic">Topic</label>
<select id="topic" name="topic" required>
  <option value="">Choose a topic</option>
  <optgroup label="Frontend">
    <option value="html">HTML</option>
    <option value="css">CSS</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>

Useful <select> attributes include name, required, disabled, multiple, and size. Use multiple when selecting several values is appropriate and explain the interaction clearly.

docs.title: Checkboxes
docs.text:
Use checkboxes for independent on/off choices or when several options may be selected. Give related controls meaningful labels. A checked checkbox contributes its value; an unchecked checkbox is generally omitted.

<label>
  <input type="checkbox" name="topics" value="html">
  HTML
</label>

docs.title: Radio buttons
docs.text:
Use radio buttons when exactly one option should be selected from a group. Give options in the same group the same name and different value attributes. A <fieldset> and <legend> can provide a group label.

<fieldset>
  <legend>Preferred format</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="format" value="video"> Video</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="format" value="text"> Text</label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: Developer perspective and common mistakes
docs.text: Use a visible label for every choice and make groups understandable without relying only on visual placement. Do not treat a selected value as trusted: the server must validate that the value is allowed for the current user.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <select>
  • MDN: Checkbox inputs
  • MDN: Radio inputs

docs.title: Semantic HTML and Accessibility
docs.text: Semantic HTML gives content elements names that describe their purpose. It helps browsers, search engines, developers, and assistive technologies understand page structure and behavior.

docs.title: Semantic page structure elements
docs.text: Element Meaning and typical use Important notes <header> Introductory content for a page or section Can appear more than once for different sections <nav> A major group of navigation links Not every list of links needs a nav <main> The document's primary content Normally one visible main landmark per page <section> A thematic grouping, usually with a heading Do not use only as a generic styling wrapper <article> Self-contained content that can stand on its own Examples: post, comment, news story <aside> Complementary content related to surrounding content Examples: related links, callout <footer> Footer for a page or section May appear at page and article level <address> Contact information for the nearest article or page Not a general-purpose postal-address wrapper <search> A region containing search or filtering controls Use a form and labeled controls inside

docs.title: Text and content semantics
Interactive and disclosure semantics
docs.text:
• <button> performs an action; its type is button, submit, or reset. Inside a form, set the type intentionally.
  • <details> creates a disclosure widget; <summary> is its visible heading and must be its first child.
  • <dialog> represents a dialog; use the dialog APIs to manage modal behavior rather than simulating a dialog with a styled div.
  • <label> gives a form control an accessible name; see the dedicated forms lesson.

docs.title: Attributes and accessibility
docs.text: Global attributes such as id, lang, dir, and hidden may apply to semantic elements. Use aria-label only when visible text cannot provide the accessible name; prefer a visible <label> or button text. role can refine semantics when necessary, but an incorrect role can remove useful native behavior. See HTML elements and global attributes.

docs.title: Developer checklist
docs.text:
• Use headings in a logical hierarchy; do not choose a heading for its font size.
  • Use a link for navigation and a button for an action.
  • Ensure keyboard focus is visible and the page works without a mouse.
  • Provide useful image alternatives and captions where relevant.
  • Do not convey required, invalid, or selected state through color alone.
  • Test with keyboard and assistive technology where practical.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Semantic elements do not automatically make every page accessible; content and interaction still matter.
  • A <section> is not just a more meaningful-looking <div>; use it for a thematic section, usually with a heading.
  • ARIA adds semantics but generally does not implement interaction behavior.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: HTML elements reference
  • W3C WAI: Page structure
  • W3C WAI: Introduction to accessibility

docs.title: HTML Tables and Embedded Content
docs.text:
Tables represent relationships between row and column values. Embedded content places a separate resource, such as another document, inside the current page. Learn each separately:

  • Tables: captions, headers, rows, cells, and accessible relationships.
  • Embedded content: iframes, titles, permissions, and security considerations.

Use a table for data that has meaningful rows and columns, not to position the page layout. Embed another page only when it adds real value and can be used accessibly.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <table>
  • MDN: <iframe>

docs.title: HTML Tables
docs.text: Tables represent data with meaningful row and column relationships. They are useful for schedules, comparison data, and reports, but not for general page layout.

docs.title: Table elements
Developer perspective and common mistakes
docs.text: Tables should retain understandable headers on small screens; a wrapper with horizontal scrolling may be appropriate for wide data. Do not use tables to position unrelated interface regions. CSS Grid and Flexbox are layout tools.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <table>
  • W3C WAI: Tables

docs.title: HTML Text and Paragraphs
docs.text: HTML text elements structure prose and preserve the meaning of written content. Browsers and assistive technologies use this structure; CSS controls how it looks.

docs.title: Paragraphs
docs.text:
<p> represents a paragraph. Browsers add default spacing, but the element is not a generic spacing tool. Use CSS margins to adjust layout.

<p>HTML describes the structure and meaning of web content.</p>
<p>CSS controls how that content is presented.</p>

docs.title: Quotations
docs.text:
Use <blockquote> for a longer quotation taken from another source. Its optional cite attribute can store a source URL, but it is not shown as a visible citation. Use <q> for a short inline quotation; browsers may add quotation marks.

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/article">
  <p>Accessible structure helps more people use the web.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The guide calls this idea <q>inclusive design</q>.</p>

Provide a visible attribution in the surrounding content when readers need to know who said the quoted words.

docs.title: Preformatted text
docs.text:
<pre> preserves whitespace and line breaks. It is often paired with <code> for source code. Escape characters such as < and & when they should be displayed literally.

<pre><code>if (ready) {
  start();
}</code></pre>

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prose is ordinary written content. Preformatted text preserves spacing instead of being collapsed like regular HTML whitespace. Prefer meaningful elements over manually inserting spaces or repeated line breaks.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A <p> should not contain another <p> or other block-level sections.
  • <blockquote cite> does not by itself display a citation.
  • <pre> is not a general-purpose way to preserve page layout whitespace.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: <p>
  • MDN: <blockquote>
  • MDN: <pre>

docs.title: HTML Text, Headings, and Lists
docs.text: This overview links to focused lessons about the HTML elements used to structure written content. Choose elements for their meaning; use CSS for visual appearance.

docs.title: Learn these topics
docs.text:
• Text and paragraphs: paragraphs, quotations, and preformatted text.
  • Headings: heading levels and a clear document hierarchy.
  • Lists: ordered, unordered, and description lists.
  • Inline text semantics: emphasis, code, edits, and other meaning within a line.

docs.title: How they work together
docs.text: Headings introduce sections, paragraphs contain prose, lists group related items, and inline elements express meaning within text. For example, an instruction page can use an <h1> for its title, <h2> for each step, <p> for explanations, and <ol> when the order matters.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text: • MDN: Structuring content with HTML

docs.title: JavaScript Arrays and Array Methods
docs.text: Arrays store ordered values. JavaScript provides methods for searching, transforming, filtering, and combining array data. Many methods accept a callback that is called once for each visited element.

docs.title: Creating and reading arrays
docs.text:
const topics = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"];
console.log(topics[0]); // "HTML"
console.log(topics.length); // 3

Array indexes begin at zero. Arrays can contain different value types, but consistent item shapes are usually easier to reason about. A two-dimensional array is an array whose elements are themselves arrays:

const grid = [
  ["A1", "A2"],
  ["B1", "B2"],
];
console.log(grid[1][0]); // "B1"

docs.title: Core methods
Sorting
docs.text:
sort() mutates the array and sorts values as strings by default. Supply a comparator for numbers, and copy first if the original order must remain:

const scores = [30, 4, 100];
const ascending = [...scores].sort((a, b) => a - b);

The comparator should return a negative value, zero, or a positive value to order a before, equal to, or after b. For object records:

const byName = [...users].sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name));

docs.title: Random example: a dice roll
docs.text:
const roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;
console.log(`You rolled ${roll}`);

Math.random() is not suitable for security-sensitive randomness.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Methods such as map create a new outer array but do not deep-copy objects inside it. sort, splice, push, and pop mutate the array. Choose methods based on whether mutation is intended.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Indexed collections
  • MDN: Array.prototype.reduce
  • MDN: Array.prototype.sort

docs.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
docs.text: Asynchronous JavaScript lets a program start work that may take time—such as a network request—without blocking all other browser activity while waiting.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Waiting synchronously for a slow response would make a page feel frozen. Promises and async/await let code describe how to continue after work finishes and how to handle failure. For callback-based APIs and timers such as setTimeout, first see callbacks, timers, and callback hell.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A Promise represents a result that may be fulfilled or rejected later. async functions always return a Promise; await pauses that function until the awaited Promise settles, without blocking the browser's whole JavaScript thread. Browser tasks, promise callbacks, and rendering are scheduled by the event loop.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
async function loadProfile(userId) {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

loadProfile("42")
  .then((profile) => console.log(profile))
  .catch((error) => console.error("Could not load profile", error));

fetch does not reject solely because the server returned an HTTP error such as 404; check response.ok or the status.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Show loading, success, empty, and error states in the interface. Consider cancellation or stale responses when users can start a new request before an old one completes. Promise represents eventual completion; event loop coordinates queued work; race condition is behavior affected by the order in which operations complete.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• await does not make a network request instantaneous or block all browser work.
  • A rejected Promise should be handled at an appropriate boundary.
  • Promise.all rejects if one of its input Promises rejects; use other combinators when partial results are required.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Promises
  • MDN: Using fetch

docs.title: Browser APIs and Client-Side Storage
docs.text: The browser provides APIs that JavaScript can use for tasks such as network requests, navigation, timers, storage, and offline behavior. These APIs are host features; they are not all part of the JavaScript language itself.

docs.title: Fetching data
docs.text: fetch() sends an HTTP request and returns a Promise. Check the response status and validate data before relying on its shape. Handle network and parsing failures at a useful boundary. For detailed JSON parsing, request options, response handling, and safe rendering of API data, see JSON and Fetch API data. For cookies and the browser's window and document objects, see window, document, and cookies.

docs.title: Choosing browser storage
docs.text:
Mechanism Typical use Important limit localStorage Small string preferences that persist Synchronous; readable by same-origin JavaScript sessionStorage Short-lived per-tab state Usually removed when the page session ends IndexedDB Larger structured client-side data Async API with more involved data modeling Cookies Values sent with matching HTTP requests Must consider size, scope, expiry, and security attributes

Never store passwords, private keys, or sensitive bearer tokens in JavaScript-readable storage without a deliberate security design. Any same-origin script can access local and session storage.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
async function loadArticles() {
  const response = await fetch("/api/articles");
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
  }
  const data = await response.json();
  if (!Array.isArray(data)) {
    throw new Error("Unexpected articles response");
  }
  return data;
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use the smallest storage mechanism that fits the data and threat model. Origin scopes many browser capabilities; persistence describes how long data remains; same-origin script is JavaScript executing with the page's origin privileges.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• fetch does not throw just because the server returned a 404 or 500.
  • Local storage is not encrypted secret storage.
  • Browser APIs vary in availability and permission requirements.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Fetch API
  • MDN: Web Storage API
  • MDN: IndexedDB API

docs.title: JavaScript Browser Input, Output, and Debugging
docs.text: Browser JavaScript can gather simple input, update page content, and report diagnostic information. This lesson covers built-in dialogs and the console; real applications should usually use accessible HTML controls instead of blocking dialogs.

docs.title: Input dialogs
docs.text:
const answer = window.prompt("What is your name?");
if (answer !== null) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${answer}`);
}

prompt() returns a string or null if cancelled. confirm() returns a boolean. alert() displays a message. These dialogs are synchronous and block interaction with the page while open; they are mainly useful in small demos or experiments.

docs.title: Console API methods
docs.text: The Console API writes diagnostic information to the developer console. Browser presentation, filtering, and a few extensions can differ. These methods are useful during development, but production applications should use an intentional logging strategy.

docs.title: Logging levels
Inspect values and collections
Groups and counters
Timing and timestamps
Other useful behavior
docs.text:
console.clear() clears the visible console when allowed by the environment; DevTools may preserve messages or ignore clearing according to user settings. Console format strings commonly support substitutions such as %s (string), %d/%i (integer), %f (number), %o/%O (object inspection), and %c (CSS styling), with browser-specific details:

console.log("User %s has %d messages", "Mina", 3);
console.log("%cDevelopment only", "color: purple; font-weight: bold");

Do not use formatting as a way to insert untrusted content into page HTML; console output is diagnostic, not rendered page content.

For timing, use console.time(), console.timeLog(), and console.timeEnd() with the same label. These are useful quick checks, not a replacement for a browser Performance recording or a benchmark. Methods such as console.profile() are DevTools-specific and are intentionally not part of this core list.

docs.title: Display output to users
docs.text: The console is for developers, not page visitors. Use DOM text such as element.textContent = value for plain text. innerHTML parses markup and must not receive untrusted strings directly.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use browser DevTools breakpoints, the Console, and the Performance panel when debugging or profiling. Do not leave sensitive personal data in production logs. For output to the page, use semantic HTML, labels, and accessible status messages.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• console.log does not display text in the page UI.
  • prompt does not return a number; it returns text or null.
  • console.error logs a message; it does not throw an exception by itself.
  • console.assert logs when its condition fails; it is not an assertion that terminates the program.
  • console.time is not a substitute for a proper profiling workflow.
  • innerHTML parses markup and must not receive untrusted content directly.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
