• MDN: window.prompt
  • MDN: Console API
  • MDN: Console instance methods
  • MDN: Node.textContent

docs.title: JavaScript Callbacks and Timers
docs.text: A callback is a function passed to other code so that code can call it at the appropriate time. Callbacks are common in event listeners, array methods, timers, and many browser APIs.

docs.title: Callback example
docs.text:
function loadMessage(onSuccess) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    onSuccess("The message is ready");
  }, 500);
}

loadMessage((message) => console.log(message));

Callbacks can run immediately or later. Do not assume a callback is synchronous unless the API documents that behavior.

docs.title: Timers
Callback nesting and callback hell
docs.text:
Several dependent asynchronous operations can become deeply nested:

loadUser((user) => {
  loadOrders(user.id, (orders) => {
    loadRecommendations(orders, (items) => show(items));
  });
});

This is often called callback hell because nesting obscures control flow and error handling. Promises and async/await can express the same sequence more clearly; see Promises and async/await.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Callbacks are still useful and not inherently bad. Use them for event listeners and APIs designed around callbacks. Choose Promises for composable asynchronous results. A zero-delay timer still runs later, not immediately.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Functions as callbacks
  • MDN: setTimeout
  • MDN: setInterval

docs.title: JavaScript Closures and Classes
docs.text: A closure is a function together with access to the lexical environment where it was created. JavaScript classes provide syntax for constructing objects with shared methods, using the language's prototype system.

docs.title: Closures
docs.text:
function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return function increment() {
    count += 1;
    return count;
  };
}

const nextCount = createCounter();
nextCount(); // 1
nextCount(); // 2

The inner function keeps access to count after createCounter returns. Closures are useful for callbacks, event handlers, and encapsulating state—but captured values and retained objects can also keep memory alive.

docs.title: Classes and instances
docs.text:
class User {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }

  describe() {
    return `User: ${this.name}`;
  }
}

const learner = new User("Ari");

constructor initializes a new instance. Instance methods are typically shared through the prototype. extends establishes inheritance and super calls a parent constructor or method. A class body runs in strict mode.

docs.title: Static and private members
docs.text:
• static members belong to the class itself, not each instance.
  • Private fields/methods use #name syntax and are enforced by the language.
  • Getters and setters define property access behavior; use them only when their abstraction is useful.
class Temperature {
  #celsius;

  constructor(celsius) {
    this.#celsius = celsius;
  }

  get celsius() {
    return this.#celsius;
  }

  static fromFahrenheit(value) {
    return new Temperature((value - 32) * 5 / 9);
  }
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text:
Prefer simple functions and composition where they communicate intent more clearly than a class hierarchy. A class method's this depends on the call receiver; passing a detached method as a callback can lose that receiver. Closures share access to captured bindings, not snapshots of their values.

Lexical environment contains visible bindings; instance is an object created from a constructor/class; prototype provides shared behavior; encapsulation limits direct access to implementation details.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Closures
  • MDN: Classes

docs.title: JavaScript Control Flow and Collections
docs.text: Control flow determines which statements run and how often. Collections organize groups of data. Good choices make logic easier to read and reduce accidental mutation.

docs.title: Conditional execution
docs.text:
if (response.ok) {
  showResults();
} else if (response.status === 404) {
  showNotFound();
} else {
  showError();
}

Use switch when comparing one value with several cases. Use the conditional operator for a short expression, not a nested substitute for readable branches.

const label = isSaving ? "Saving…" : "Save";

&&, ||, and ?? short-circuit and return operand values. Do not assume they always return a boolean.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
for provides explicit iteration control; for...of iterates iterable values such as arrays and strings; for...in enumerates enumerable property keys and is usually not the right way to loop over array values.

for (const product of products) {
  console.log(product.name);
}

break exits a loop or switch; continue advances to the next iteration. Avoid loops whose exit conditions are difficult to understand.

docs.title: Arrays and common methods
Objects and collection types
docs.text:
• Object: named properties for record-like data; property keys are strings or symbols (numeric-looking keys are converted to strings).
  • Map: key/value collection where keys can be any value; preserves insertion order and provides get, set, has, delete, and size.
  • Set: unique values; provides add, has, delete, and size.
  • WeakMap / WeakSet: object-keyed collections that do not keep keys alive solely because they are entries; they are not enumerable.

Map is the built-in keyed collection sometimes called the Map object. It is different from the array .map() method: Map stores key/value pairs, while .map() transforms array elements.

const uniqueTags = new Set(["html", "css", "html"]);
const settings = new Map([["theme", "dark"]]);

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use a Map when keys are dynamic or not strings, a Set for uniqueness, and arrays for ordered lists. Predicate is a function that answers a condition; accumulator is the running value in reduce; mutation changes an existing object or collection.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• map() is for transforming and returning values; do not use it just for side effects.
  • sort() changes the array and sorts strings lexicographically by default.
  • Objects and arrays compare by reference, not by their contents.
  • for...in and for...of do different work.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Control flow and error handling
  • MDN: Indexed collections
  • MDN: Keyed collections

docs.title: JavaScript Dates and Internationalization
docs.text: JavaScript's Date object represents an instant in time as milliseconds from the Unix epoch. Formatting that instant for people is a separate task; the Intl APIs provide locale-aware formatting.

docs.title: Create and inspect dates
docs.text:
const now = new Date();
const launch = new Date("2026-11-06T09:00:00Z");

console.log(launch.getTime()); // milliseconds since the epoch
console.log(launch.toISOString()); // standardized UTC representation

Prefer ISO date-time strings with an explicit timezone when parsing. Date strings without timezone information can be interpreted as local time depending on their form; avoid ambiguous input. Date stores an instant, not a timezone or the user's calendar preferences.

docs.title: Locale-aware formatting
docs.text:
const formatted = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-IN", {
  dateStyle: "medium",
  timeStyle: "short",
  timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata",
}).format(launch);

toLocaleString() is a convenient instance method that also formats according to locale and options:

launch.toLocaleString("en-IN", {
  dateStyle: "long",
  timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata",
});

Available locale data and default locale vary by environment. Supply a locale and timezone when predictable user-facing output is important.

docs.title: Date arithmetic and common pitfalls
docs.text:
Date getters such as getFullYear() use local time; getUTCFullYear() uses UTC. Month indexes in several Date constructors and methods start at zero. Daylight-saving changes and timezone offsets make manual arithmetic in fixed numbers of milliseconds error-prone for calendar operations.

For complex calendar and timezone calculations, use a well-maintained date-time library or carefully scoped Intl APIs rather than assuming a date is just a formatted string.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text:
• A Date is not stored as a human-readable formatted string.
  • An ISO timestamp ending in Z is in UTC.
  • toLocaleString() output can differ by locale and runtime.
  • A date without timezone context can be interpreted differently than intended.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Date
  • MDN: Intl.DateTimeFormat
  • MDN: Date.prototype.toLocaleString

docs.title: The DOM and Browser Events
docs.text: The Document Object Model (DOM) is the browser's programmable representation of a page. JavaScript can read and update DOM nodes and respond to events such as clicks, keyboard input, and form submission.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: DOM APIs connect JavaScript with the document a user sees. Events let code react to actions without constantly checking whether something changed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The browser dispatches an event to a target element. Event listeners run registered callback functions. Events often travel through capture and bubble phases, so a listener on an ancestor may observe an event from a child. Calling preventDefault() cancels a default browser action when that is appropriate; it does not stop propagation.

docs.title: Common DOM methods and event properties
docs.text:
API/property Purpose document.querySelector(selector) Finds the first matching element, or null document.querySelectorAll(selector) Returns a static collection of matching elements element.textContent Reads or sets text without parsing HTML element.classList Adds, removes, toggles, or checks CSS classes element.addEventListener(type, handler, options) Registers an event listener event.target Element where the event originated event.currentTarget Element whose listener is currently running event.preventDefault() Cancels a cancelable default action event.stopPropagation() Stops further propagation through the event path

For selecting and traversing nodes, working with a NodeList, changing content, and using classList, continue to DOM navigation and updates. For keyboard events, checkbox checked state, event.target, and form submission, see event listeners and forms.

Use the capture, once, and signal listener options when their behavior is useful. Remove listeners or abort their controller when a component or view no longer needs them.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
<form id="search-form">
  <label for="query">Search</label>
  <input id="query" name="q">
  <button>Go</button>
</form>

const form = document.querySelector("#search-form");

if (form instanceof HTMLFormElement) {
  form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(form);
    console.log(data.get("q"));
  });
}

The submit event also works when a user activates the button with a keyboard. The instanceof guard confirms the queried element is a form before using form-specific APIs.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prefer semantic HTML controls and attach listeners to the appropriate elements. Event target is the element that originated an event; bubbling is an event phase where it travels from a target toward ancestors; event delegation handles events at a shared ancestor.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• querySelector can return null; check that an element exists before using it when the page structure may vary.
  • preventDefault() and stopPropagation() do different things.
  • Updating the DOM with user-provided HTML can create security risks; avoid inserting untrusted strings as markup.
  • querySelectorAll is static; it does not automatically include elements added later.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Introduction to events
  • MDN: Document Object Model

docs.title: JavaScript DOM Navigation and Updates
docs.text: The Document Object Model (DOM) is the browser's in-memory representation of a document. JavaScript can select nodes, move through relationships, create content, and update the page.

docs.title: Selecting elements
Navigate relationships
docs.text: Useful properties include parentElement, children, firstElementChild, lastElementChild, nextElementSibling, and previousElementSibling. Prefer element-specific relationships when text nodes and comments are not relevant.

docs.title: Change content and classes
docs.text:
const message = document.querySelector("#message");

if (message) {
  message.textContent = "Saved successfully";
  message.classList.add("is-success");
}

classList provides add, remove, toggle, contains, and replace. Use textContent for plain text. innerHTML parses markup and must not be populated with untrusted strings.

docs.title: Create and remove elements
docs.text:
const item = document.createElement("li");
item.textContent = "Practice JavaScript";
document.querySelector("#topics")?.append(item);

Other useful APIs include prepend, before, after, replaceWith, and remove. Build elements and assign text or safe attributes rather than concatenating untrusted data into HTML strings.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common mistakes
docs.text: Query results can be null or empty. Check for the expected element before using it. A static NodeList does not update when matching elements are added later. For interaction, prefer semantic buttons, links, and form controls over clickable generic containers.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Document Object Model
  • MDN: Element.classList
  • MDN: Document.querySelectorAll

docs.title: JavaScript Event Listeners and Forms
docs.text: Events notify code about user actions and browser activity. Event listeners connect an event type to a callback. Form and keyboard events let interfaces respond to input accessibly.

docs.title: Registering listeners
docs.text:
const button = document.querySelector("#save");

button?.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log(event.type, event.target);
});

event.target is where the event originated. event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently running. A child event can bubble to an ancestor, enabling event delegation.

Listener options include capture (listen during capture), once (remove after one call), and signal (remove when an AbortSignal is aborted). Use these or removeEventListener to avoid retaining unnecessary listeners.

docs.title: Keyboard events
docs.text: keydown fires when a key is pressed; keyup fires when it is released. For text entry, use input events on the relevant control rather than reconstructing text from key presses. Prefer semantic controls that already support keyboard behavior. If a custom shortcut is needed, consider event.key and avoid intercepting keys users need for assistive technology.

docs.title: Handle form submission
docs.text:
Listen for the form's submit event, not only a button click. This also supports Enter-key submission:

const form = document.querySelector("#search-form");

form?.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const formData = new FormData(form);
  console.log(formData.get("q"));
});

For checkboxes and radio inputs, the checked property reports the current selection state; it is a boolean. The HTML checked attribute describes the initial/default state, while the property reflects current interaction:

const newsletter = document.querySelector("#newsletter");
if (newsletter instanceof HTMLInputElement && newsletter.checked) {
  console.log("The current form selection is checked");
}

preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action when the event is cancelable. It does not stop propagation; stopPropagation() is separate. Validate on the server even when client-side checks are provided.

docs.title: Event phases and delegation
docs.text: Events can travel through capture, target, and bubble phases. Delegation places one listener on a parent and checks event.target or closest() for the relevant child. This is helpful for many similar or dynamically added controls.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• event.target and event.currentTarget can be different.
  • preventDefault() does not stop the event from bubbling.
  • A button click handler alone misses some form submission paths.
  • Client-side validation is not a security boundary.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Event reference
  • MDN: Event bubbling
  • MDN: Event.preventDefault

docs.title: JavaScript Event Loop and Concurrency
docs.text: The event loop coordinates JavaScript execution with queued work such as timers, user events, and completed network operations. It lets browser applications handle asynchronous activity without blocking on each result.

docs.title: A useful mental model
docs.text: JavaScript code runs to completion on an execution stack. The host environment (such as a browser) performs many operations outside that stack. When work is ready, callbacks are queued. Promise reactions use the microtask queue, which is generally processed before the browser moves to the next task and renders. Exact scheduling details depend on the host and specification.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("timer task"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise microtask"));
console.log("B");

The synchronous logs run first (A, then B); the Promise callback is normally processed before the timer callback. A zero-millisecond timer does not mean “run immediately.”

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Long synchronous work can block input and rendering. Break expensive tasks into manageable work or use a Web Worker for suitable CPU-heavy computation. Task is queued host work; microtask is a higher-priority queue used by Promise reactions; run to completion means the current JavaScript job finishes before another job starts on that thread.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• JavaScript being single-threaded in a given context does not mean browsers perform only one operation at a time.
  • setTimeout(fn, 0) does not guarantee immediate execution.
  • async/await changes how asynchronous code is written, not the underlying need to schedule completion.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: JavaScript event loop
  • HTML Standard: Event loops

docs.title: JavaScript Foundations: Values, Variables, and Functions
docs.text: JavaScript is a dynamically typed programming language standardized as ECMAScript. A browser supplies additional Web APIs—such as the DOM and fetch—that JavaScript programs can use.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
JavaScript's primitive types are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null. Objects, arrays, and functions are reference values.

const title = "Frontend";     // string
const lessonCount = 8;        // number
const published = true;       // boolean
const missingValue = null;    // deliberate absence
let notAssignedYet;           // undefined
const lessons = ["HTML", "CSS"]; // object (array)

typeof null returns "object" for historical reasons. Use explicit comparisons when checking for null. For more examples of string operations, escape sequences, and converting values from form input, see strings and type conversion.

docs.title: Variables and scope
docs.text:
• const prevents reassignment of the binding; an object stored in it can still be mutated.
  • let allows reassignment and is block-scoped.
  • var is function-scoped and has older hoisting behavior; prefer const and let in modern code.
const settings = { theme: "light" };
settings.theme = "dark"; // allowed: the object changed
// settings = {};        // TypeError: the const binding cannot be reassigned

docs.title: Operators and comparisons
docs.text:
Use === and !== to avoid implicit type conversion in comparisons. Logical operators &&, ||, and ! work with truthy/falsy values and return operands, not necessarily booleans. Nullish coalescing ?? uses a fallback only for null or undefined; unlike ||, it preserves values such as 0 and "".

const pageSize = requestedSize ?? 20;
const displayName = user.name || "Guest";
For arithmetic, logical, comparison, and conditional operators, plus if/switch and loop statements, see operators and control flow.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Functions can be declared, assigned to variables, passed as values, and returned from other functions.

function formatName(first, last = "") {
  return `${first} ${last}`.trim();
}

const double = (value) => value * 2;

An arrow function with an expression body returns that expression. Arrow functions do not create their own this; see objects, prototypes, and this.

docs.title: Objects and arrays
docs.text:
Objects organize named properties; arrays organize ordered values. Object and array assignment copies a reference, not a deep copy. Destructuring extracts properties; spread syntax creates a shallow copy.

const user = { id: "u1", name: "Ari" };
const { name } = user;
const renamed = { ...user, name: "Sam" };

Nested objects inside a spread result may still be shared references. The arrays and array methods lesson covers forEach, map, filter, reduce, sorting, and chained transformations. The objects, destructuring, and spread lesson covers nested data, rest parameters, and copying values in more detail.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
const cart = { items: 2, total: 18 };

function addItem(currentCart, price) {
  return {
    items: currentCart.items + 1,
    total: currentCart.total + price,
  };
}

const updatedCart = addItem(cart, 5);

Returning a new object avoids mutating cart, which is often helpful when reasoning about UI state.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Primitive: Immutable value such as a string or boolean.
  • Reference: A value that points to an object held elsewhere.
  • Scope: Where a binding can be accessed.
  • Hoisting: JavaScript's processing of declarations before execution; details vary by declaration type.
  • Closure: A function retaining access to its surrounding lexical scope.
  • Coercion: Conversion between types, sometimes implicit.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• const does not freeze objects.
  • JavaScript and Java are different languages.
  • null and undefined are different values.
  • TypeScript types do not change JavaScript's runtime type behavior.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: JavaScript Guide
  • MDN: Grammar and types
  • ECMAScript specification

docs.title: JavaScript Functions, Expressions, and Scope
docs.text: Functions package reusable behavior. A function can be declared, assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, or returned from another function. Scope determines where its bindings can be used.

docs.title: Function declarations and expressions
docs.text:
function formatName(first, last = "") {
  return `${first} ${last}`.trim();
}

const formatLabel = function (value) {
  return `Topic: ${value}`;
};

Function declarations are initialized before their containing scope runs (subject to module and block rules). Function expressions are values assigned where the expression executes. Prefer clear names and avoid relying on hoisting for readability.

docs.title: Arrow functions
docs.text:
const double = (number) => number * 2;
const logTopic = (topic) => {
  console.log(topic);
};

An expression body returns its expression implicitly; a block body needs return to return a value. Arrow functions do not have their own this or arguments; they capture this lexically from the surrounding scope.

docs.title: Parameters, return values, and callbacks
docs.text:
Parameters receive arguments. Default parameters apply when an argument is undefined, not whenever it is falsy. A callback is a function supplied to another function to be called later or during an operation.

function greet(name = "learner") {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

["HTML", "CSS"].forEach((topic) => console.log(topic));

Keep functions focused and return useful values rather than relying on unnecessary shared state.

docs.title: Scope and variable lifetime
docs.text:
• Global/module scope: bindings visible across a script or module's relevant top-level code.
  • Function scope: bindings local to a function.
  • Block scope: let and const bindings inside { ... }.
  • Lexical scope: visibility determined by where code is written.

var is function-scoped and has older hoisting behavior; prefer const unless reassignment is needed, then use let.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Passing a function does not call it: handler is a reference, while handler() invokes it. Closures let inner functions retain access to lexical bindings; see closures and classes.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Functions
  • MDN: Function expressions
  • MDN: Scope

docs.title: JavaScript Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: Use these questions to review JavaScript fundamentals, browser APIs, and common coding patterns. Answers are concise; follow the linked lessons for deeper explanations and practical examples.

docs.title: 1. What is JavaScript?
docs.text: JavaScript is a programming language standardized as ECMAScript. It runs in browsers and other environments such as Node.js. The environment supplies additional APIs: browsers provide the DOM and fetch, while Node.js provides server-side APIs.

docs.title: 2. What are var, let, and const?
docs.text:
• var is function-scoped (or global-scoped at script top level) and can be redeclared in the same scope. Its declaration is initialized to undefined when its scope is entered.
  • let is block-scoped and can be reassigned, but not redeclared in the same scope. It cannot be accessed before its declaration is initialized.
  • const is block-scoped and cannot be reassigned. If it holds an object, that object's properties may still be changed.

Prefer const by default, then use let when reassignment is needed.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between == and ===?
docs.text:
== allows type coercion before comparison. === compares without that coercion and is usually the clearer default:

5 == "5";  // true
5 === "5"; // false

docs.title: 4. What is a closure?
docs.text:
A closure is a function together with access to the lexical bindings around where it was created. Those bindings remain available even after the outer function returns:

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return () => ++count;
}

const counter = makeCounter();
counter(); // 1
counter(); // 2

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between null and undefined?
docs.text: undefined commonly means a value was not provided or assigned. null is an explicit value that represents an intentional absence. They are distinct values and are not strictly equal.

docs.title: 6. What is hoisting?
docs.text: Before execution, JavaScript establishes declarations according to their scope rules. Function declarations can generally be called before their textual position. var bindings exist as undefined before assignment. let and const bindings exist but cannot be accessed before initialization; that period is called the temporal dead zone. Hoisting does not move assignment expressions.

docs.title: 7. What are JavaScript's data types?
docs.text: The primitive types are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null. Other values are objects, including arrays and functions. typeof null returns "object" for historical reasons.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
docs.text:
A function declaration defines a function and is initialized according to declaration hoisting rules. A function expression creates a function value where the expression is evaluated; if assigned to const or let, that binding cannot be used before initialization.

function declared() {}
const expressed = function () {};

docs.title: 9. What does this mean?
docs.text: For an ordinary function, this is generally determined by how the function is called. In account.deposit(), it refers to account. In a plain function call it can be undefined in strict mode. Arrow functions do not create their own this; they capture it from the surrounding lexical context.

docs.title: 10. What is an arrow function?
docs.text:
An arrow function is a concise function expression using =>:

const add = (a, b) => a + b;

Arrow functions have no own this, arguments, or super, and cannot be used as constructors with new. They are useful for callbacks and functions that should use lexical this.

docs.title: 11. What is the event loop?
docs.text: The event loop coordinates JavaScript jobs with work performed by the host environment. Synchronous JavaScript runs to completion. Promise continuations use the microtask queue; timers and many events are scheduled as tasks. The host decides when queued work can run, and browser rendering is coordinated with that scheduling.

docs.title: 12. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?
docs.text: Synchronous code runs step by step and the current operation finishes before the next one begins. Asynchronous code arranges for later work to be handled when a result becomes available, allowing the main thread to do other work while waiting. It does not automatically make CPU-heavy synchronous code non-blocking.

docs.title: 13. What is a Promise?
docs.text:
A Promise represents the eventual fulfillment or rejection of an asynchronous operation. It begins pending, then settles as fulfilled or rejected:

const result = Promise.resolve("Done");
result.then((value) => console.log(value));

docs.title: 14. What are template literals?
docs.text:
Template literals use backticks and support interpolation with ${...} and multiline text:

const name = "Mina";
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`;

docs.title: 15. What is destructuring?
docs.text:
Destructuring extracts values from arrays or properties from objects into bindings:

const user = { name: "Mina", age: 24 };
const { name, age } = user;

docs.title: 16. What is a callback function?
docs.text: A callback is a function passed to other code so that code can invoke it. Callbacks may run immediately or later, depending on the API. Event listeners and array methods such as map use callbacks.

docs.title: 17. What is the difference between map() and forEach()?
docs.text: map() calls a callback for each visited element and returns a new array of the results. forEach() calls a callback for side effects and returns undefined.

docs.title: 18. What is spread syntax?
docs.text:
Spread syntax (...) expands iterable values or enumerable object properties in a context that accepts them:

const combined = [...[1, 2], 3];
const updated = { ...user, age: 25 };

These copies are shallow.

docs.title: 19. What is the difference between undefined and an undeclared variable?
docs.text: undefined is a JavaScript value. A declared binding can contain it. An undeclared identifier has no binding; reading it normally throws a ReferenceError.

docs.title: 20. What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
docs.text: A shallow copy copies the top-level structure but keeps references to nested objects. A deep copy recursively duplicates supported nested data. structuredClone() can deep-clone many built-in data types, but it does not support every value or every object behavior. Choose a clone strategy based on the data rather than assuming spread makes a deep copy.

docs.title: 21. What is the difference between primitive and object values?
docs.text: Primitive values such as numbers and strings are immutable values. Objects are mutable values that can be accessed through references. Assigning an object copies its reference value; it does not clone the object.

docs.title: 22. What is a higher-order function?
docs.text: A higher-order function accepts a function as an argument, returns a function, or both. map() is an example because it accepts a callback.

docs.title: 23. What is event delegation?
docs.text: Event delegation handles events from multiple descendant elements using a listener on a common ancestor. It often relies on event bubbling and is useful when child elements are added dynamically.

docs.title: 24. What do async and await do?
docs.text:
An async function always returns a Promise. await pauses that function's continuation until a Promise settles; it does not block the entire JavaScript thread:

async function getValue() {
  return await Promise.resolve(42);
}

docs.title: 25. What is a pure function?
docs.text: A pure function returns the same result for the same inputs and has no observable side effects, such as changing external state or performing network requests. Pure functions are usually easier to test and reason about.

docs.title: 26. What is memoization?
docs.text: Memoization caches results so a repeated call with the same inputs can reuse a previous result. It is useful when computation is expensive and inputs repeat, but cache size, invalidation, and memory use need consideration.

docs.title: 27. What does the typeof operator do?
docs.text:
typeof returns a string describing a value's primitive type or broad category:

typeof 123;        // "number"
typeof "hello";    // "string"
typeof undefined; // "undefined"

There are special cases: typeof null is "object", and arrays also report "object". Use Array.isArray() to identify arrays.

docs.title: 28. What is optional chaining (?.)?
docs.text:
Optional chaining stops property access or a call when the value to its left is null or undefined, returning undefined instead of throwing:

const city = user.address?.city;

It does not validate that a value has the correct shape.

docs.title: 29. What is nullish coalescing (??)?
docs.text:
?? uses its right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null or undefined:

const pageSize = suppliedSize ?? 20; // preserves 0

Unlike ||, it does not replace other falsy values such as 0 or "".

docs.title: 30. How does Object.is() differ from ===?
docs.text:
Both avoid ordinary type coercion, but Object.is() treats NaN as equal to itself and distinguishes positive zero from negative zero:

NaN === NaN;         // false
Object.is(NaN, NaN); // true
Object.is(+0, -0);   // false

docs.title: 31. What are JavaScript modules?
docs.text: Modules divide code into files with explicit imports and exports. ES modules use export and import, have their own scope, and help organize reusable code.

docs.title: 32. What is the difference between slice() and splice()?
docs.text: slice(start, end) returns a shallow copy of a selected range without changing the original array. splice(start, count, ...items) changes the original array by removing, replacing, or inserting elements.

docs.title: 33. What is event bubbling?
docs.text: Bubbling is an event propagation phase in which an event moves from its target through ancestor elements. Some events do not bubble. A listener can stop propagation with stopPropagation() when that behavior is appropriate.

docs.title: 34. What is a Promise chain?
docs.text: A Promise chain links asynchronous steps with .then(), .catch(), and .finally(). Each .then() returns a new Promise, so returned values and errors flow to the next step.

docs.title: 35. What is JSON?
docs.text: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for structured data. JSON.stringify() converts supported JavaScript data to JSON text; JSON.parse() parses JSON text and throws a SyntaxError if the text is invalid. Parsed data should still be checked against the shape the application expects.

docs.title: 36. What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
docs.text: for...in iterates enumerable property keys. for...of iterates values from an iterable such as an array or string. Use for...of for array values; use object-specific APIs when enumerating an object's own keys.

docs.title: 37. What does instanceof check?
docs.text: instanceof checks whether a constructor's prototype appears in an object's prototype chain. It is not a universal type check across realms such as separate windows, and it does not validate the object's data.

docs.title: 38. What is the DOM?
docs.text: The Document Object Model is the browser's object-based representation of a document. JavaScript can select, inspect, and update DOM nodes.

docs.title: 39. What are setTimeout() and setInterval()?
docs.text: setTimeout(callback, delay) schedules one callback after at least the requested delay. setInterval(callback, delay) repeatedly schedules a callback. Neither is an exact clock; the event loop and browser can delay execution. Cancel them with clearTimeout() and clearInterval().

docs.title: 40. How do localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies differ?
docs.text:
• localStorage stores string key/value pairs for an origin and generally persists until cleared.
  • sessionStorage stores string key/value pairs scoped to an origin and a page session, commonly a tab.
  • Cookies have scope and expiry rules, and matching cookies are sent with HTTP requests. Servers can set security attributes such as HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite.

Storage limits and session behavior vary by browser. JavaScript-readable storage is accessible to same-origin scripts and should not be treated as secret storage.

docs.title: 41. Does JavaScript pass objects by reference?
docs.text: JavaScript passes arguments by value. For an object, the copied value is a reference to the same object. A function can mutate that object, but reassigning its parameter does not reassign the caller's variable.

docs.title: 42. What are throttling and debouncing?
docs.text: Debouncing delays work until a period passes without a new call, useful for search input. Throttling limits how often work runs during repeated events, useful for scroll or resize handling.

docs.title: 43. What is a Symbol?
docs.text:
A Symbol is a primitive value that is unique, even when two Symbols have the same description. Symbols can be used as property keys to avoid collisions:

Symbol("id") === Symbol("id"); // false

docs.title: 44. What is the arguments object?
docs.text:
In a regular function, arguments is an array-like object containing arguments passed to that call. Arrow functions do not have their own arguments. Rest parameters are usually clearer:

function logAll(...values) {
  console.log(values);
}

docs.title: 45. What is the difference between rest and spread?
docs.text:
They share ... syntax but are used in different positions. Rest collects remaining values into an array or object; spread expands values or properties:

const [first, ...remaining] = [1, 2, 3]; // rest
const combined = [...remaining, 4];      // spread

docs.title: 46. What does eval() do, and why is it discouraged?
docs.text: eval() parses and executes a string as JavaScript. Avoid it: untrusted input can lead to code injection, and it makes code harder to analyze and optimize. Use structured data parsing or explicit functions instead.

docs.title: 47. What is the with statement?
docs.text: with adds an object's properties to the scope chain, making name lookup ambiguous. It is forbidden in strict mode and should not be used in modern JavaScript. ES modules are strict mode automatically.

docs.title: 48. What is a Proxy?
docs.text: A Proxy wraps an object and can intercept operations such as property reads and writes through a handler. Proxies enable metaprogramming but can make behavior harder to inspect and should be used deliberately.

docs.title: 49. What are microtasks and tasks?
docs.text: Promise reactions and queueMicrotask() schedule microtasks. Timers and many user events schedule tasks. After a JavaScript job completes, the host processes queued microtasks before moving on according to its event-loop rules. Avoid assuming that every browser renders at an identical point relative to every task.

docs.title: 50. What is the global object?
docs.text: The global object provides global environment properties. In browsers it is commonly accessible as window; in modern JavaScript the environment-neutral name is globalThis. Node.js has its own global environment. Global declarations do not all become properties in exactly the same way across scripts and modules.

docs.title: 51. What is function composition?
docs.text: Function composition combines functions so one function's output becomes another's input. It can build a larger transformation from small, reusable functions.

docs.title: 52. What are dynamic imports?
docs.text:
import() loads a module asynchronously and returns a Promise for its module namespace object. It can support conditional loading and code splitting:

const math = await import("./math.js");
console.log(math.add(2, 3));

docs.title: 53. How do default parameters work?
docs.text:
A default parameter value is used when the argument is omitted or is undefined, not whenever it is falsy:

function greet(name = "Guest") {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}
greet(""); // "Hello, "

docs.title: 54. What is method chaining?
docs.text: Method chaining calls a method on the value returned by a previous method. For example, filter(...).map(...) works because filter() returns an array. Not every method returns its receiver; forEach() returns undefined.

docs.title: 55. What is the difference between Object.freeze() and Object.seal()?
docs.text: Object.freeze() prevents adding, removing, or changing an object's own properties. Object.seal() prevents adding or removing properties but allows writes to existing writable properties. Both are shallow: nested objects are not automatically frozen or sealed.

docs.title: 56. What is the ternary operator?
docs.text:
The conditional (ternary) operator returns one of two expressions:

const label = isReady ? "Open" : "Wait";

Use it for short, readable choices; deeply nested ternaries are difficult to understand.

docs.title: 57. What is optional catch binding?
docs.text:
Optional catch binding allows omitting the error parameter when it is not needed:

try {
  runTask();
} catch {
  showGenericFailure();
}

docs.title: 58. Is {} different from new Object()?
docs.text: Both can create an ordinary object in common cases. {} is the object literal syntax and is the usual, concise choice. The Object constructor has special behavior for some inputs, so it is not a universal substitute for an object literal.

docs.title: 59. What is the difference between Math.floor(), Math.ceil(), and Math.round()?
docs.text: Math.floor() rounds toward negative infinity, Math.ceil() rounds toward positive infinity, and Math.round() rounds to the nearest integer using JavaScript's specified tie behavior. For negative values, floor is not the same as truncating toward zero.

docs.title: 60. Can function expressions be called before their line in the source?
docs.text: Function declarations are initialized according to their scope's hoisting rules. A function expression assigned to let or const cannot be used before that binding is initialized. A var binding exists earlier as undefined, so attempting to call it before assignment fails.

docs.title: 61. What are common pitfalls of typeof?
docs.text: typeof null is "object" and typeof [] is "object". Use value === null to check for null, Array.isArray(value) for arrays, and typeof for appropriate primitive-type checks.

docs.title: 62. What is type coercion?
docs.text: Type coercion is converting a value to another type. Explicit conversion uses functions such as Number() or String(). Implicit coercion happens as part of operations, such as string concatenation with +.

docs.title: 63. What is NaN?
docs.text: NaN means “Not a Number,” but its JavaScript type is number. It represents an invalid numeric result. Since NaN !== NaN, use Number.isNaN(value) to test for it.

docs.title: 64. How do for, while, and do...while differ?
docs.text: for combines initialization, a condition, and an update in one construct. while checks its condition before each iteration. do...while checks after its body, so it runs at least once.

docs.title: 65. What do &&, ||, and ! do?
docs.text: && and || short-circuit and return one of their operands. ! converts its operand to a boolean and negates it. They are logical operators, but && and || do not always return boolean values.

docs.title: 66. What are string escape sequences?
docs.text: Escape sequences use a backslash to represent special characters in a string, such as \n for a newline, \t for a horizontal tab, and \\ for a backslash. Quotes can also be escaped when needed.

docs.title: 67. What is short-circuit evaluation?
docs.text: Short-circuit evaluation stops evaluating an expression once its result is determined. For example, a && b does not evaluate b when a is falsy; a || b does not evaluate b when a is truthy. ?? similarly skips its right side when the left side is not nullish.

docs.title: 68. What is the difference between parseInt() and Number()?
docs.text:
parseInt() parses an integer prefix (provide radix 10 for ordinary decimal input); Number() converts the whole input:

parseInt("42px", 10); // 42
Number("42px");       // NaN
Number("42.5");       // 42.5

docs.title: 69. What are JavaScript's falsy values?
docs.text: The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, and NaN. All other values—including empty arrays and empty objects—are truthy.

docs.title: 70. What is the difference between innerText and textContent?
docs.text: textContent reads or sets text content without considering rendered appearance. innerText reflects rendered text and is affected by styling and layout. Use textContent for inserting plain text; avoid using innerHTML with untrusted strings.

docs.title: 71. How do arrow functions differ from regular functions?
docs.text: Arrow functions have lexical this, no own arguments, and cannot be constructors. Regular functions can have a call-dependent this and may be constructors when used appropriately. Choose based on behavior, not only shorter syntax.

docs.title: 72. What does fetch() return, and how should its response be checked?
docs.text: fetch() returns a Promise that fulfills with a Response when a response is received. HTTP statuses such as 404 and 500 do not normally reject that Promise; check response.ok or response.status before reading the body. Network errors and aborts can reject.

docs.title: 73. What is the difference between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
docs.text: preventDefault() cancels a cancelable event's browser default action, such as a form's normal navigation. stopPropagation() stops the event from continuing through the propagation path. They solve different problems.

docs.title: 74. What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
docs.text: event.target is the event's originating node. event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently executing. They can differ when an event bubbles.

docs.title: 75. What does the checked property represent?
docs.text: For a checkbox or radio input, checked is a boolean representing its current checked state. The HTML checked attribute describes the initial state; user interaction can change the property.

docs.title: 76. How should JavaScript errors be handled?
docs.text: Use try/catch for synchronous exceptions and awaited Promise failures. Catch an error where the code can respond meaningfully, such as displaying a retry option or reporting an operation failure. Avoid empty catches and do not expose sensitive internal details to users.

docs.title: 77. What is JSON parsing, and why validate the result?
docs.text: JSON.parse() converts valid JSON text into JavaScript values. Parsing only verifies JSON syntax; it does not ensure the result has the fields, types, or allowed values your application expects. Validate data at runtime before relying on it.

docs.title: 78. Why can assigning a value to innerHTML be risky?
docs.text: innerHTML parses its input as markup. If untrusted input is inserted, attackers may inject executable markup or otherwise alter the page. Use textContent for plain text and trusted, context-appropriate sanitization when HTML rendering is required.

docs.title: 79. How should dates be formatted for different locales?
docs.text: Use Intl.DateTimeFormat or Date.prototype.toLocaleString() with an explicit locale and, where needed, timezone. A Date represents an instant; formatting varies across locales and runtimes.

docs.title: JavaScript JSON and Fetch API Data
docs.text: JSON is a text format commonly used to exchange structured data. The Fetch API sends HTTP requests and exposes the response asynchronously through Promises.

docs.title: JSON conversion
docs.text:
JSON.stringify(value) converts compatible JavaScript values to JSON text. JSON.parse(text) parses JSON text into JavaScript values and throws a SyntaxError when the text is invalid.

const payload = JSON.stringify({ topic: "JavaScript", complete: true });
const value = JSON.parse(payload);

JSON does not represent every JavaScript value. For example, functions and undefined are not preserved as ordinary JSON values. Validate parsed data: valid JSON is not necessarily the shape or content your application expects.

docs.title: Fetch a response
docs.text:
async function loadTopics() {
  const response = await fetch("/api/topics");

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
  }

  const data = await response.json();
  if (!Array.isArray(data)) {
    throw new Error("Expected an array of topics");
  }
  return data;
}

fetch() resolves to a Response when an HTTP response arrives, including many error statuses such as 404 or 500. Check response.ok or status. Network failures and aborts reject. Reading a body with json() is also asynchronous and can fail if it is not valid JSON.

docs.title: Send JSON
docs.text:
const response = await fetch("/api/topics", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Learn fetch" }),
});

Choose the HTTP method and headers for the API contract. Handle errors, loading state, cancellation, and stale responses where needed. Never assume browser input is trusted; the server must validate and authorize requests.

docs.title: Display returned data safely
docs.text: Use DOM text APIs such as textContent for plain text. Do not insert untrusted API strings with innerHTML. Handle empty results and failures with useful, accessible interface states.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• response.json() does not return an already-parsed value synchronously.
  • A 404 response usually does not cause fetch() itself to reject.
  • Valid JSON does not guarantee valid application data.
  • CORS and authentication rules can affect whether a browser can read a response.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Fetch API
  • MDN: Using Fetch
  • MDN: JSON

docs.title: JavaScript Modules and Error Handling
docs.text: Modules divide JavaScript into files with explicit imports and exports. Error handling makes failures visible and gives an application a controlled way to respond.

docs.title: ES module exports and imports
docs.text:
// format.js
export function formatPrice(amount) {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {
    style: "currency",
    currency: "USD",
  }).format(amount);
}

export const currency = "USD";

import { currency, formatPrice } from "./format.js";
import defaultFormatter from "./default-formatter.js";

console.log(formatPrice(12.5), currency);

Named imports use the exported name, unless renamed with as. A module may also have one default export:

export default function formatDate(date) {
  return date.toLocaleDateString();
}

Modules have their own scope. In a browser without a bundler, load a module with <script type="module" src="/main.js"></script>. Modules are deferred by default and use strict mode.

docs.title: Dynamic imports
docs.text:
import() loads a module asynchronously and returns a Promise. It is often used to split code that is not needed immediately:

const button = document.querySelector("#edit");

if (button) {
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const { openEditor } = await import("./editor.js");
  openEditor();
});
}

docs.title: Exceptions and handling
docs.text:
Throw an Error for a failure that the current function cannot resolve. Catch errors where the application can respond meaningfully, such as a UI boundary or request handler. A finally block runs whether the operation succeeded or failed.

async function loadProfile() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch("/api/profile");
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
    }
    return await response.json();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Could not load profile", error);
    throw error;
  }
}

Logging and rethrowing is appropriate when adding context for a higher-level handler; avoid logging the same failure repeatedly at every layer.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Organize modules around cohesive responsibilities and keep imports explicit. Named export is imported by name; default export is the module's primary export; exception is an error value thrown during execution; dynamic import loads a module asynchronously.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Importing a module does not make its values global.
  • Catching an error and doing nothing hides failures.
  • A try block does not catch a rejected Promise unless the Promise is awaited there or has a rejection handler.
  • finally is not a place to return a second result that accidentally overrides the original return or exception.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: JavaScript modules
  • MDN: Control flow and error handling

docs.title: JavaScript Navigator and Device APIs
docs.text: navigator exposes information and capabilities provided by the current browser environment. It is not a reliable way to identify a person or device. Feature availability and permission behavior vary, so feature-detect APIs and handle denial or failure.

docs.title: Common navigator properties
docs.text:
Property Meaning and caution navigator.userAgent User-agent string; can be reduced, changed, or spoofed, so avoid browser detection when feature detection works navigator.language Preferred language reported by the browser navigator.onLine Best-effort online state; true does not prove a server is reachable

Some values may be reduced for privacy. Do not use these properties as authentication, authorization, or security signals.

docs.title: Capability APIs
docs.text:
API Typical use Important considerations navigator.geolocation Request device location Requires permission; can fail or be unavailable navigator.clipboard Read or write clipboard data Usually requires a secure context and user permission/activation navigator.mediaDevices Discover/request camera or microphone access Requires permission; handle device absence and denial navigator.serviceWorker Register or inspect service workers Requires secure context except local development exceptions navigator.sendBeacon() Send small analytics/diagnostic data during page lifecycle changes Not a general replacement for fetch; delivery is best effort navigator.share() Open the operating system's native share UI Requires support and usually transient user activation

Check for an API before using it, request permissions only when needed, explain why the capability is useful, and provide a fallback.

docs.title: Online/offline hints
docs.text:
window.addEventListener("online", () => updateConnectionHint(true));
window.addEventListener("offline", () => updateConnectionHint(false));

The offline event is a hint that the browser's network state changed. A real request can still fail while navigator.onLine is true.

docs.title: Feature detection
docs.text:
if ("geolocation" in navigator) {
  // Offer location access only when the user requests the feature.
}

Check for an API before using it. Permission-sensitive APIs should be invoked in response to an appropriate user action and failures should be handled explicitly.

docs.title: Developer perspective and security
docs.text: Device and browser information can contribute to fingerprinting. Collect only what the feature requires and disclose sensitive capability requests. Never trust client-reported platform, user-agent, online, or hardware information for security decisions.

  • MDN: Clipboard API
  • MDN: MediaDevices
  • MDN: Navigator online and offline events

docs.title: JavaScript Objects, Destructuring, Rest, and Spread
docs.text: Objects group values under property names. Destructuring extracts values; rest collects remaining values; spread expands iterable values or copies own enumerable object properties into a new object.

docs.title: Nested objects
docs.text:
const user = {
  name: "Ravi",
  address: {
    city: "Chennai",
    country: "India",
  },
};

console.log(user.address.city);
console.log(user.preferences?.theme ?? "light");

Optional chaining (?.) stops access when the left side is null or undefined. It is not a substitute for validating required data.

docs.title: Destructuring
docs.text:
const { name, address: { city } } = user;
const [firstTopic, secondTopic] = ["HTML", "CSS"];

Object patterns match property names; array patterns match positions. Aliases and default values are supported:

const { name: displayName = "Guest" } = user;

docs.title: Rest parameters and rest properties
docs.text:
A rest parameter gathers remaining function arguments into an array:

function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((total, number) => total + number, 0);
}

In destructuring, ...rest gathers remaining properties or elements:

const { name: ignored, ...publicDetails } = user;

docs.title: Spread syntax
docs.text:
Spread expands an iterable into values or copies enumerable object properties:

const original = ["HTML", "CSS"];
const allTopics = [...original, "JavaScript"];

const updatedUser = { ...user, name: "Anika" };

These are shallow copies. Nested objects remain shared references unless they are copied separately.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Destructuring and spread can make updates clear, but deeply nested patterns can hide assumptions about input shape. Spread is not a deep clone, and rest parameters are not the same feature as spread despite sharing ....

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Destructuring
  • MDN: Rest parameters
  • MDN: Spread syntax

docs.title: JavaScript Objects, Prototypes, and this
docs.text: Objects group properties and methods. JavaScript uses prototypes to provide shared behavior, and the meaning of this depends on how a function is called.

docs.title: Objects and prototypes
docs.text: An object can have another object as its prototype. Property lookup checks the object first, then follows the prototype chain. JavaScript classes provide syntax over this prototype-based behavior; they do not create a separate classical object model.

docs.title: this
docs.text: In a method call such as account.deposit(), this refers to the receiver object for that call. Arrow functions do not create their own this; they capture it lexically from the surrounding scope. Detached callbacks can lose the expected receiver if they are ordinary functions.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
const account = {
  balance: 10,
  deposit(amount) {
    this.balance += amount;
    return this.balance;
  },
};

account.deposit(5);

For callback code, use an arrow function when lexical this is intended, or explicitly bind/pass the needed value.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prefer composition and straightforward object data over deep prototype hierarchies. Prototype chain is the sequence checked during property lookup; method receiver is the object to the left of the method call; lexical this is captured from the surrounding scope.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• this is not always the object where a function was written.
  • Arrow functions do not have their own this or arguments.
  • JavaScript class syntax still uses prototypes for instance methods.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Working with objects
  • MDN: this

docs.title: JavaScript Operators and Control Flow
docs.text: Operators combine or compare values. Control-flow statements choose which code runs and how often. They are the building blocks for validation, business rules, and user-interface behavior.

docs.title: Common operator groups
docs.text:
Group Examples Purpose Arithmetic +, -, *, /, %, ** Numeric calculations; + also concatenates strings Assignment =, +=, ??= Assign or update a binding/property Comparison ===, !==, <, >= Compare values; strict equality avoids coercion Logical &&, ||, ! Combine conditions and short-circuit Nullish ??, ?. Fallback for nullish values; safely access optional paths Conditional condition ? a : b Select one expression for a short branch Type-related typeof, instanceof Inspect a value's runtime category or prototype relationship

&&, ||, and ?? return an operand, not necessarily a boolean. || uses a fallback for every falsy value; ?? only falls back for null or undefined.

docs.title: Conditionals and switch
docs.text:
if (response.ok) {
  showResults();
} else if (response.status === 404) {
  showNotFound();
} else {
  showError();
}

Use switch when one value is compared against several cases. Cases fall through unless break, return, or another control transfer exits:

switch (status) {
  case "ready":
    start();
    break;
  case "paused":
    showPaused();
    break;
  default:
    showUnknown();
}

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
• for offers explicit initialization, condition, and update.
  • while repeats while a condition remains true.
  • do...while runs its body at least once.
  • for...of iterates values from iterables such as arrays and strings.
  • for...in enumerates enumerable property keys and is usually unsuitable for array values.

break exits a loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration. Ensure loop conditions eventually become false.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
const scores = [80, 55, 92];
let passed = 0;

for (const score of scores) {
  if (score >= 60) passed += 1;
}

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• = assigns; === compares.
  • switch does not automatically stop after a matching case.
  • && and || do not always return true or false.
  • for...in does not provide array values in the same way for...of does.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Expressions and operators
  • MDN: Control flow

docs.title: JavaScript Strings and Type Conversion
docs.text: Strings represent text. JavaScript also converts values between types, either explicitly through code or implicitly through coercion. Understanding both helps avoid surprising comparisons, formatting bugs, and invalid input.

docs.title: Creating strings
docs.text:
Single quotes, double quotes, and backticks create strings. Template literals use backticks and can include expressions with ${...}:

const name = "Mina";
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`;
const multiline = `First line
Second line`;

Quoted strings can use escape sequences when a literal character would otherwise end the string or be difficult to type:

Escape Meaning \n New line \t Horizontal tab \\ Backslash \' / \" Quote characters \` Backtick inside a template literal 
const report = "Name:\tMina\nStatus:\tReady";

Strings are immutable: methods return new strings rather than changing the original value.

docs.title: Useful string operations
Explicit conversion
docs.text:
Use conversion functions when the expected type is known:

const quantity = Number("12");    // 12
const invalid = Number("twelve"); // NaN
const label = String(12);          // "12"
const enabled = Boolean("");       // false

parseInt and parseFloat parse a numeric prefix, and parseInt should usually be given a radix such as 10. Use Number.isNaN(value) to test for the NaN value.

docs.title: Coercion and common pitfalls
docs.text:
The + operator can add numbers or concatenate strings. Loose equality (==) converts values in ways that can be surprising; strict equality (===) avoids most implicit conversion.

"5" + 1;   // "51"
"5" - 1;   // 4
Number(""); // 0
Boolean("false"); // true: non-empty strings are truthy

Convert form values deliberately: input values are usually strings even when the control looks numeric. Validate the result and handle NaN.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: String conversion is not HTML escaping, URL encoding, or input validation. Use context-appropriate APIs when inserting data into HTML, URLs, or SQL.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Text formatting
  • MDN: Type conversion
  • ECMAScript: Abstract operations

docs.title: JavaScript window, document, and Cookies
docs.text: The browser exposes objects that connect scripts to a page and its browsing context. window represents the current browser window/global context; document represents the loaded page. Cookies are small values associated with web requests and have important security rules.

docs.title: window and globalThis
docs.text:
In a browser page, window represents the browsing context and is also the traditional global object. globalThis is the environment-neutral way to refer to the global object. Some browser globals, such as document, can also be accessed as window.document.

The Window interface is large and browser-dependent. These are the important APIs commonly used in frontend development, not every property.

API/property Common use window.location Read the current URL; set href to navigate window.history Navigate history or manage same-document URLs with pushState() and replaceState() window.document Access the current page DOM window.navigator Access browser capabilities; see Navigator and device APIs window.addEventListener() Listen for events such as resize, online, or offline window.setTimeout() / clearTimeout() Schedule or cancel a delayed callback window.setInterval() / clearInterval() Schedule or cancel repeated callbacks window.requestAnimationFrame() Schedule visual work before a repaint window.fetch() Make an HTTP request window.localStorage / sessionStorage Store same-origin string data window.innerWidth / innerHeight Read viewport dimensions in CSS pixels window.scrollTo() / scrollBy() Change the document scroll position window.matchMedia() Check a media query or user preference window.alert() / confirm() / prompt() Show simple blocking dialogs, mainly for demos

pushState() changes the URL and history entry without loading a new document; the application must render matching content and handle back/forward navigation. Use CSS media queries for layout breakpoints, and use requestAnimationFrame() for visual updates. Timers are not precise clocks. Browser globals are not available in every JavaScript runtime.

docs.title: document
docs.text:
document provides access to the page and its DOM, including document.title, document.body, document.forms, and selectors such as document.querySelector(). Common properties and methods include:

API/property Common use document.documentElement, document.head, document.body Access root, head, and body elements document.title Read or set the page title document.forms, document.images Access collections of document elements getElementById(), querySelector(), querySelectorAll() Find elements createElement() Create a DOM element visibilityState, visibilitychange Detect when the page is visible cookie Read/write cookies available to JavaScript; see cookie security below

document.write() is a legacy API that can replace or interfere with a document during parsing; do not use it for ordinary DOM updates. Use DOM APIs instead. See DOM navigation and updates.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Cookies are set by servers with the Set-Cookie response header and sent back by browsers when their scope and request rules match. A page may read and write some cookies through document.cookie, but this interface is a string containing visible cookie pairs, not a normal object.

Security-relevant cookie attributes include:

  • HttpOnly: prevents JavaScript access through document.cookie.
  • Secure: sends the cookie only over HTTPS.
  • SameSite: controls cross-site sending behavior.
  • Path, Domain, and expiry/Max-Age: scope and lifetime controls.

JavaScript cannot set HttpOnly; configure it in the server's Set-Cookie response. Session identifiers should generally be protected with appropriate server-set attributes and server-side authorization.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Do not store secrets in browser-readable cookies or local storage without understanding the threat model. HttpOnly reduces script access to a cookie but does not stop all request forgery or fix XSS. Cookie rules, SameSite defaults, and partitioning behavior vary with browsers and deployment; follow current standards and security guidance.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• MDN: Window
  • MDN: Document
  • MDN: Using HTTP cookies
  • OWASP: Session Management Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Next.js Route Groups and Advanced Routing
docs.text: The App Router has conventions that organize routes without necessarily adding URL segments, and advanced patterns for composing multiple route views. Learn static and dynamic routes first; advanced patterns add navigation and fallback complexity.

docs.title: Route groups
docs.text:
Parentheses create a route group whose name is omitted from the URL:

app/
  (marketing)/
    about/
      page.tsx             /about
  (account)/
    settings/
      page.tsx             /settings

Groups help organize teams or attach different layouts to parts of an application. Avoid creating conflicting routes with the same resulting URL.

docs.title: Private folders
docs.text: An underscore-prefixed folder, such as _components/, is used for implementation organization rather than a route segment. Keep route conventions and reusable UI easy to distinguish.

docs.title: Parallel routes
docs.text: Named slots such as @modal let a layout render multiple route branches in parallel. A dashboard can use slots for a main view and an independent overlay. Provide appropriate default or fallback behavior for navigation states.

docs.title: Intercepting routes
docs.text: Conventions such as (.), (..), (...), and (..)(..) can display a route in the current layout context, often to support modal navigation while preserving a direct URL for the full page. Exact route matching follows the framework's documented segment rules.

docs.title: Developer perspective and trade-offs
docs.text: These patterns can make rich interfaces feel natural, but add route state, fallback, and testing requirements. Use them only when their UI behavior benefits from the added complexity.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Route groups
  • Next.js: Parallel routes
  • Next.js: Intercepting routes

docs.title: Next.js App Router
docs.text: The App Router is Next.js's file-system-based application router. It uses folders and convention-named files to define URL segments, page UI, layouts, loading states, errors, and HTTP handlers.

docs.title: Follow the routing lessons
docs.text:
• File-system routing: static and nested routes, route files, and how folders map to URLs.
  • Dynamic and catch-all routes: URL parameters and routes that match variable segments.
  • Route groups and advanced routing: organize routes without changing URLs and learn parallel or intercepted route patterns.

docs.title: A minimal route tree
docs.text:
app/
  layout.tsx
  page.tsx
  about/
    page.tsx

In this example, app/page.tsx provides /, while app/about/page.tsx provides /about. A route becomes renderable through the appropriate special file; a folder alone is not necessarily a public route.

docs.title: App Router and Pages Router
docs.text: Next.js also supports the older Pages Router in many projects. The App Router uses app/, page.tsx, and route.ts; the Pages Router uses pages/, page files, and pages/api/ for API Routes. Their data-fetching and rendering APIs differ. Identify the router used by a route before following a tutorial.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Route parameters are untrusted input. Validate them before using them in queries, file access, or authorization decisions. A route handler is an HTTP endpoint, not a React page.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Getting started
  • Next.js: Project structure

docs.title: Authentication and Security in Next.js
docs.text: Authentication establishes who a user is. Authorization decides what that user is allowed to do. A Next.js application often combines browser UI, server-rendered routes, and server-side handlers, so security checks must be made at the data and action boundaries.

docs.title: Secure application flow
docs.text:
1. Authenticate a user through a well-reviewed identity solution.
  2. Store and manage session credentials using an appropriate secure design.
  3. On each protected server operation, verify the session.
  4. Check whether the user is authorized for the specific resource and action.
  5. Return only the data that the user is allowed to receive.

Middleware or layout redirects can improve navigation, but should not be the only protection. Route Handlers, Server Actions, and data access code must enforce authorization too.

docs.title: Security practices
docs.text:
• Keep private keys and server-only credentials out of client bundles.
  • Validate all inputs on the server and encode output for its context.
  • Use framework and library guidance for session and cookie attributes.
  • Protect state-changing requests against relevant CSRF risks.
  • Avoid exposing detailed internal errors to users.
  • Keep dependencies and framework versions maintained.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Authentication verifies identity; authorization decides permissions; session represents authenticated state across requests; CSRF tricks a browser into making an unwanted authenticated request.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Hiding a link or button is not access control.
  • A client component is not a place to keep secrets.
  • Middleware checks do not replace checks at the protected operation.
  • A successful login does not mean every resource is accessible.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Authentication
  • OWASP: Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • OWASP: Authorization Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Client-Side Rendering in Next.js
docs.text: Client-side rendering (CSR) means browser JavaScript creates or updates part of the interface after the document is delivered. In Next.js, Client Components enable browser interactions, but the framework may also produce initial HTML for them depending on the rendering mode.

docs.title: Typical lifecycle
docs.text:
1. The browser requests a route.
  2. The server or platform returns HTML and JavaScript resources.
  3. The browser loads and executes JavaScript.
  4. React attaches behavior and updates interactive parts as data or user input changes.

The exact sequence depends on the route and framework configuration. Client-side rendering is often useful for highly interactive controls, browser-only APIs, or data that changes frequently after page load.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Count: {count}</button>;
}

The "use client" directive marks a Client Component boundary; it does not mean that the component can never contribute to initial server-generated HTML. Browser-only APIs should be used in effects or event handlers, not during server rendering.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: CSR supports rich interaction but can add JavaScript work, delay useful content when data is fetched only after startup, and require careful loading and error states. It does not automatically make content invisible to search engines; indexing depends on the actual output and crawler behavior.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Use the smallest practical client boundary. Do not move an entire route to the browser just to implement one interactive widget. Keep secrets and privileged data operations on trusted server code.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Client Components
  • Next.js: Server and Client Components

docs.title: Cookies and Sessions in Next.js
docs.text: A cookie is a small value the browser stores and may send with matching requests. A session is server-managed authenticated state associated with a user. Cookies often carry an opaque session identifier, while the actual session data remains on the server.

docs.title: Cookie attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Purpose HttpOnly Prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie through document.cookie Secure Sends the cookie only over HTTPS, except local development behavior may differ SameSite Controls cross-site sending behavior: Strict, Lax, or None Path Limits which URL paths receive the cookie Domain Controls eligible hosts; omit it when host-only behavior is desired Max-Age Lifetime in seconds Expires Absolute expiry date

SameSite=None generally requires Secure. Cookie rules and browser privacy behavior can change; use HTTPS in production and test the actual browsers.

docs.title: Reading and writing cookies
docs.text:
In Next.js 15 and later, cookies() is asynchronous. Reading cookies is request-specific and may affect whether a route can be statically rendered. Cookie writes are allowed in supported mutation contexts such as a Server Action or Route Handler, not during ordinary Server Component rendering.

import { cookies } from "next/headers";

export async function GET() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const theme = cookieStore.get("theme")?.value ?? "system";
  return Response.json({ theme });
}

In a Server Action or Route Handler, a cookie can be set using the API supported by the installed version:

const cookieStore = await cookies();
cookieStore.set("session", sessionId, {
  httpOnly: true,
  secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
  sameSite: "lax",
  path: "/",
  maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24,
});

This illustrates attributes, not a complete authentication implementation. Do not generate session IDs with weak randomness or store sensitive identity data directly in a client-readable cookie.

In Next.js 14 and earlier, cookies() was synchronous. Next.js 15 provided a synchronous compatibility path during migration, but current code should use await cookies() and follow the installed version's API documentation. With newer Cache Components configurations, reading request-time cookies can also require a Suspense boundary or a different rendering design.

docs.title: Session security
docs.text:
• Use a maintained authentication/session library where appropriate.
  • Use unpredictable session identifiers and rotate or invalidate them when security-sensitive events occur.
  • Check authentication and authorization on every protected server action and data access.
  • Use HttpOnly, Secure, and a deliberate SameSite policy for session cookies.
  • Consider CSRF protections for state-changing requests.
