  • Never treat a client-provided user ID or hidden form value as proof of identity.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Cookie is browser-managed request state; session is authenticated state associated with the user; session fixation is an attack involving reuse of a known session identifier; CSRF induces a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• HttpOnly reduces script access but does not stop all XSS consequences.
  • Secure does not encrypt data at rest in browser storage.
  • Cookies are sent automatically under matching rules, so cookie-based authentication needs CSRF-aware design.
  • cookies() usage can make output depend on each request.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: cookies
  • MDN: HTTP cookies
  • OWASP: Session Management Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Next.js Data Fetching and Caching
docs.text: Data fetching loads information for a route or component. Caching reuses results so the application can avoid repeated work. Next.js caching defaults and APIs have changed across releases and differ when Cache Components are enabled, so first identify the project's version and configuration.

docs.title: Server-side fetching in the App Router
docs.text:
Server Components can call asynchronous functions directly. A fetch can call an external API; a server-only data-access function can call a database. Keep credentials and database clients out of Client Components.

type Post = { id: string; title: string };

async function getPosts(): Promise<Post[]> {
  const response = await fetch("https://example.com/api/posts");
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Could not load posts: ${response.status}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

export default async function PostsPage() {
  const posts = await getPosts();
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map((post) => <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}

In real code, validate the response shape at runtime; a TypeScript return type does not check remote JSON.

docs.title: Parallel and sequential work
docs.text:
If requests do not depend on one another, start them together:

const [profile, recommendations] = await Promise.all([
  getProfile(userId),
  getRecommendations(userId),
]);

Sequential awaits are appropriate when the second request needs the first result. They add latency if used unnecessarily. Consider how errors should be handled when one of several parallel requests fails.

docs.title: Client-side fetching
docs.text: Use a Client Component when fetching depends on browser interaction, such as search-as-you-type or refreshing a live panel. Model loading, empty, success, and error states. Handle cancellation or stale responses where users can change requests quickly. For larger apps, a data-fetching library may offer deduplication, retries, and cache coordination.

docs.title: Caching concepts
docs.text:
• Request memoization/deduplication: avoids repeating equivalent work during one render/request under supported conditions.
  • Data cache: reuses fetched or computed data across requests when configured.
  • Full route/output cache: reuses rendered route output where eligible.
  • Browser or CDN cache: controlled by HTTP caching headers and hosting.
  • Revalidation: marks data or output as needing refresh by time or event.

These are different caches with different lifetimes. Invalidating one does not automatically clear every browser, CDN, or external cache.

docs.title: Version-sensitive fetch example
docs.text:
In the traditional App Router caching model, a fetch can specify a revalidation interval:

const response = await fetch("https://example.com/api/posts", {
  next: { revalidate: 3600 },
});

The exact meaning and defaults depend on Next.js version. Some newer configurations use explicit cache directives such as 'use cache' and cacheLife; do not combine configurations without checking the current caching guide.

docs.title: Private and personalized data
docs.text: Before caching a result, decide whether different users may receive the same value. Account details, permissions, billing data, and private messages must not be accidentally served from a shared cache. Authenticate and authorize on the server, and use request-specific/dynamic handling where required.

docs.title: Error, loading, and streaming behavior
docs.text: Use route loading.tsx, Suspense boundaries, and error boundaries to present useful intermediate and recovery UI. A boundary affects presentation; it does not make the underlying fetch reliable or eliminate the need to handle expected errors.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Cache key identifies which result is reused; stale data may no longer reflect the source; deduplication avoids repeated equivalent work; revalidation refreshes cached data or output.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A successful HTTP status does not guarantee response JSON has the expected shape.
  • fetch behavior is not identical in browser and Next.js server contexts.
  • Caching is not automatically safe for per-user data.
  • ISR does not mean every cached page refreshes at an exact scheduled second.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Fetching data
  • Next.js: Caching
  • Next.js: Revalidating data

docs.title: Next.js Deployment and Production
docs.text: Deployment makes a built application available to users. Next.js can be deployed to supported managed platforms or to infrastructure that runs its server features, depending on the project configuration.

docs.title: Build and run locally
docs.text:
npm run build
npm run start

The build command checks and prepares production output. The start command runs the production server for projects configured with the standard scripts. Always inspect the scripts in package.json; starter options and deployment targets may differ.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Set environment variables in the deployment platform; do not commit secrets.
  • Confirm the selected host supports the features used by the app, including any server runtime or image optimization requirements.
  • Test production builds, route behavior, forms, and error states.
  • Configure domains and HTTPS at the hosting layer.
  • Review logs and monitoring after release.
  • Confirm caching does not mix data across users.

Static export can be appropriate for a site that can run entirely as static files, but it does not support every server feature. Choose it only after checking the current export limitations.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Build artifact is output prepared for deployment. Environment variable is configuration provided outside source code. Runtime is the environment that executes application code after deployment. Keep local, preview, and production settings distinct.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A successful development server does not prove a production build will succeed.
  • Hosting choices can limit or change supported framework features.
  • Public environment variables are not secrets; client-exposed values can be read by users.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Deploying
  • Next.js: Environment variables

docs.title: Next.js Dynamic and Catch-All Routes
docs.text: Dynamic segments let one route file handle many URLs. The URL provides parameters such as a product identifier or article slug; these values are input and must be validated before use.

docs.title: Dynamic segments
docs.text:
Square brackets define one variable path segment:

app/
  products/
    [productId]/
      page.tsx

This route can match /products/42. In a current App Router setup where params is asynchronous, a page can read it like this:

type Props = { params: Promise<{ productId: string }> };

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: Props) {
  const { productId } = await params;
  return <h1>Product {productId}</h1>;
}

params typing and behavior are version-sensitive. Use the generated types and documentation for the version installed in the project.

docs.title: Catch-all patterns
docs.text:
Folder Matches [...slug] One or more remaining path segments [[...slug]] Zero or more remaining path segments, including the base route

For example, app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx can match /docs/setup/linux; the parameter represents multiple segments. Use a catch-all for hierarchical content such as documentation, not as a shortcut for validating arbitrary paths.

docs.title: Static parameters
docs.text: generateStaticParams can return known parameter values for routes that can be prepared ahead of time. This can improve reuse for public content, but enumerating a very large or private data set may be inappropriate.

docs.title: Security and developer perspective
docs.text: Treat every route parameter as untrusted. Validate its format, confirm the requested record exists, and check authorization before returning protected data. Escaping or type-checking a parameter alone does not grant access.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Dynamic segments
  • Next.js: generateStaticParams

docs.title: Next.js Error and Not-Found UI
docs.text: The App Router provides special files for unexpected rendering errors and missing resources. Clear boundaries let an application show a useful recovery path without exposing internal details.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text:
error.tsx creates an error boundary for a route segment and must be a Client Component. It receives an error and a reset function in current App Router conventions:

"use client";

export default function ProductsError({
  reset,
}: {
  error: Error & { digest?: string };
  reset: () => void;
}) {
  return (
    <section>
      <h2>Products could not be loaded.</h2>
      <button onClick={() => reset()}>Try again</button>
    </section>
  );
}

reset() retries the boundary's rendering attempt; it cannot guarantee an underlying service has recovered. A segment's boundary generally does not catch errors from its own parent layout. global-error.tsx handles root level failures and must provide document tags because it replaces the root layout.

docs.title: Missing-resource UI
docs.text: not-found.tsx defines UI for a missing route or resource. Application code can call notFound() when a requested record does not exist. A not-found screen is not an authorization mechanism; protect private records before rendering them.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Model expected outcomes—such as invalid input, no matching record, or permission denied—deliberately. Log unexpected failures through a safe server-side observability path and do not display sensitive stack traces or internal service details.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• An error boundary does not catch every failure in the entire application.
  • A retry button does not ensure the failed service is healthy.
  • A not-found page does not protect a private URL.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Error handling
  • Next.js: notFound

docs.title: Next.js File-System Routing
docs.text: In the App Router, folders under app/ describe URL segments and page.tsx supplies the UI for a route. Special files such as layout.tsx and route.ts provide other route behavior.

docs.title: Static and nested routes
docs.text:
app/
  page.tsx                 /
  about/
    page.tsx               /about
  products/
    page.tsx               /products
    reviews/
      page.tsx             /products/reviews

A folder name becomes a path segment. A route is made public by the appropriate special file, usually page.tsx; a helper component can live in the folder without becoming a route by itself.

docs.title: Common special files
docs.text:
File Purpose page.tsx UI for a route segment layout.tsx Shared UI around child segments template.tsx Shared wrapper that remounts on navigation loading.tsx Loading fallback for the segment error.tsx Error boundary UI not-found.tsx Missing-resource UI route.ts HTTP method handlers, not a rendered React page

Use the convention appropriate to the feature; consult the installed Next.js version because exact behavior evolves.

docs.title: Practical route example
docs.text:
// app/about/page.tsx
export default function AboutPage() {
  return <main><h1>About these notes</h1></main>;
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Organize route files around URLs and shared boundaries. Do not assume a component folder is routable or that route.ts renders page UI. Pages Router conventions such as pages/about.tsx are a different routing system.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Defining routes
  • Next.js: Project structure

docs.title: Next.js Forms and Server Actions
docs.text: Forms submit user input to the application. In the App Router, Server Actions can run server-side functions in response to supported form submissions, reducing the need to manually build a client request for some workflows.

docs.title: The important security rule
docs.text: Treat every submitted value as untrusted. A Server Action is reachable through an application request and must validate input, verify the current user, and authorize the requested operation. Hiding a button in the UI does not protect the operation.

docs.title: A simple form pattern
docs.text:
async function createNote(formData: FormData) {
  "use server";
  const title = formData.get("title");
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim().length === 0) {
    throw new Error("A title is required");
  }
  // Authenticate, authorize, then persist validated data.
}

export default function NewNotePage() {
  return (
    <form action={createNote}>
      <label htmlFor="title">Title</label>
      <input id="title" name="title" required />
      <button type="submit">Create note</button>
    </form>
  );
}

This example shows the shape only. Real applications should return user-friendly validation state, avoid exposing internal exceptions, and follow the framework version's action conventions.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use native form semantics, validate on the server, and provide pending, success, and error feedback. FormData represents submitted key/value fields; Server Action is a server-executed function invoked through framework handling; authorization checks whether the authenticated user may perform the requested action.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Server Actions are not automatically authorized.
  • Browser validation is useful feedback, not trusted enforcement.
  • A hidden form field is user-controlled input.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Updating data
  • Next.js: Forms

docs.title: Getting Started and Project Structure
docs.text: The Next.js starter creates a React application with the framework's routing, development server, and build tooling already connected.

docs.title: Create and run a project
docs.text:
npx create-next-app@latest
cd my-app
npm run dev

The setup prompts vary by release and selected options. The development server normally opens at http://localhost:3000. To use another port with the standard npm script, run npm run dev -- --port 3001. A command such as npx create-next-app@13.4.12 intentionally selects an older release; use it only when reproducing a project that requires that exact version.

docs.title: Common App Router files
docs.text:
File or folder Typical role app/ App Router routes and shared UI app/page.tsx Page for the root URL / app/layout.tsx Shared layout around routes in its segment app/globals.css Global CSS imported by the root layout app/favicon.ico Site icon public/ Public static files, referenced from the site root package.json Scripts and dependency declarations next.config.ts, .js, or .mjs Optional framework configuration tsconfig.json TypeScript compiler and project settings, when using TypeScript eslint.config.* Lint configuration, depending on starter version next-env.d.ts Framework TypeScript declarations, normally generated

Generated files differ according to Next.js version and starter choices. The pages/ directory belongs to the older Pages Router when used for routes; the App Router uses app/.

docs.title: A route segment's special files
docs.text:
app/
  layout.tsx       shared UI for this segment and descendants
  template.tsx     remounted shared UI when navigation requires a fresh instance
  page.tsx         route's user-facing page
  loading.tsx      loading fallback for eligible work
  error.tsx        segment error boundary (Client Component)
  not-found.tsx    not-found UI for the segment
  route.ts         HTTP handler; cannot coexist with page.tsx at same segment

These files are conventions, not mandatory files for every folder. route.ts handles requests and is not the page rendering file.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
// app/page.tsx
export default function HomePage() {
  return <main><h1>My learning site</h1></main>;
}

This file defines the root route in the App Router.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Run the development server while editing, then run a production build before deployment. Development server provides local iteration; production build creates deployable output; static asset is a file served without being generated by a page component.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• public/logo.svg is normally referenced as /logo.svg, not /public/logo.svg.
  • A folder does not become a visible route unless it contains the appropriate route file.
  • route.ts is not a synonym for page.tsx; it defines an HTTP handler.
  • Starter defaults can change; check the files created by your installed version.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Installation
  • Next.js: Project structure

docs.title: Next.js Hydration Errors and Troubleshooting
docs.text: Hydration is the process where React in the browser attaches behavior to HTML that was rendered on the server. A hydration mismatch happens when the initial browser render does not match the HTML the server produced.

docs.title: Common causes
docs.text:
• Rendering different values on server and browser, such as Date.now(), random numbers, or locale-dependent formatting.
  • Reading window, localStorage, or browser-only state during the initial render.
  • Invalid HTML nesting that the browser repairs before React hydrates it.
  • Data changing between server rendering and the first browser render.
  • Browser extensions modifying the page before hydration.
  • Using a component or library that assumes it only runs in a browser.

docs.title: Debugging workflow
docs.text:
1. Read the mismatch message and identify the component and element.
  2. Compare server-generated markup with the first client render.
  3. Check invalid nesting and values that vary by time, randomness, locale, or environment.
  4. Move genuinely browser-only work to an effect that runs after hydration, or use an intentional client-only rendering boundary when appropriate.
  5. Ensure server and client start with the same data and deterministic markup.
  6. Re-test with extensions disabled only when needed to rule out extension interference.

docs.title: Avoid masking the cause
docs.text: suppressHydrationWarning is an escape hatch for a narrow, intentional text/attribute difference; it does not fix a mismatched component tree. Disabling SSR for a component can be appropriate for a browser-only widget, but can affect initial content and performance. Prefer deterministic initial rendering where possible.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
This is risky during initial rendering because time may differ:

function Clock() {
  return <time>{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}</time>;
}

For a live client clock, render a deterministic placeholder first and update after mounting, or format a server-provided timestamp consistently.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Hydration attaches client-side React behavior to server output. Mismatch means the expected initial client tree differs from the server HTML. Deterministic rendering produces the same initial result for the same inputs and environment.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Hydration errors are not always caused by Next.js itself.
  • useEffect can avoid an initial mismatch for browser-only values, but using it for every piece of data can cause flicker and delayed content.
  • suppressHydrationWarning should not be applied broadly.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: React hydration error
  • React: hydrateRoot

docs.title: Next.js Image Component
docs.text: Image from next/image extends the browser image element with layout and optimization features. It can help deliver appropriately sized images, but developers still need good source assets, alternatives, and responsive layout choices.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
import Image from "next/image";

export function TrailImage() {
  return (
    <Image
      src="/trail.jpg"
      alt="A marked trail through a forest"
      width={1200}
      height={800}
      sizes="(max-width: 700px) 100vw, 700px"
    />
  );
}

docs.title: Important props
docs.text:
Prop Meaning src Local public path, static import, or allowed remote source alt Text alternative; use an empty string only for decorative images width, height Intrinsic dimensions used to determine aspect ratio fill Fills a positioned parent; the parent must provide suitable layout sizes Describes rendered width for responsive source selection quality Image quality hint within the supported optimizer range preload Preloads an important above-the-fold image in supported versions placeholder Optional loading placeholder behavior unoptimized Skips built-in optimization when appropriate

Props and preload guidance can change across Next.js versions. Follow the documentation for the version installed; older projects may use a priority prop where newer versions provide preload.

docs.title: Remote images and layout
docs.text: Configure allowed remote sources in next.config rather than accepting arbitrary image URLs. When using fill, position the parent and give it a meaningful size or aspect ratio. The default loader does not forward request headers to the remote source, so authenticated remote images need an intentional design.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Optimization does not fix a huge source image or poor sizes value. Always provide an appropriate alt value; do not lazy-load the main image visible immediately without a reason. Availability of the default optimizer depends on the deployment platform.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Image
  • Next.js: Image optimization

docs.title: Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)
docs.text:
Incremental Static Regeneration is a way to reuse statically generated route output while allowing it to be refreshed without rebuilding the entire site. It is useful for public pages that need both fast cached delivery and eventual freshness.

This lesson describes the App Router ISR model without Cache Components. Projects using the cacheComponents option follow a different caching model and should use the current ISR with Cache Components guide.

docs.title: The basic lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Next.js generates or caches a route's output.
  2. Requests receive the cached result while it is valid.
  3. A time-based policy or an explicit invalidation marks data or route output for refresh.
  4. Regeneration happens according to the framework's cache strategy.
  5. A subsequent response can use the refreshed result.

Do not assume the first request after a timer always waits for regeneration. Stale-while-revalidate behavior, errors, and cache coordination vary by version and hosting platform.

docs.title: Time-based revalidation
docs.text:
With the traditional App Router data-cache model, a fetch can specify a revalidation interval in seconds:

const response = await fetch("https://example.com/api/articles", {
  next: { revalidate: 3600 },
});

In route-segment configurations supported by the project version, a route can also declare an interval:

export const revalidate = 3600;

An interval is a freshness threshold, not a precise scheduled timer that rebuilds output when no one is requesting it. Confirm the current caching model and whether the selected deployment adapter supports the configuration. Some newer Next.js modes use explicit cache directives or different revalidation APIs.

docs.title: Event-based or on-demand revalidation
docs.text:
When content changes—for example, a CMS publishes an article—the application can invalidate a matching route or cache tag from a trusted server-side workflow. In the App Router, APIs such as revalidatePath and revalidateTag are used for this purpose; signatures and semantics can vary between framework releases.

async function getArticles() {
  const response = await fetch("https://example.com/api/articles", {
    next: { tags: ["articles"] },
  });
  return response.json();
}

The tag must be attached to cached data before it can be invalidated. For cached functions in configurations that support Cache Components, follow the current cacheTag and 'use cache' documentation instead of assuming fetch tags apply unchanged.

// Illustrative Route Handler: verify the webhook before invalidating.
import { revalidatePath, revalidateTag } from "next/cache";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  // Verify a trusted webhook signature and validate its payload first.
  revalidatePath("/articles");
  revalidateTag("articles", "max");
  return Response.json({ revalidated: true });
}

This is deliberately incomplete as a webhook implementation: do not expose an unauthenticated endpoint that lets anyone trigger work or influence content. Use the version's official API signature and an actual signature verification mechanism. In current APIs, revalidateTag(tag, "max") marks tagged cached data stale using stale-while-revalidate semantics: a request can receive stale content while fresh data is generated. It does not eagerly regenerate every matching page at the moment the webhook arrives. In current releases, updateTag is intended for read-your-own-writes flows from Server Actions; confirm its availability and semantics in the installed version. Do not select an immediate-expiration policy without understanding the latency and stale-data trade-off.

docs.title: Common patterns
docs.text:
• Time-based: refresh when data becomes old enough under the configured cache rules.
  • Event-based: refresh after a trusted event such as a CMS publish.
  • Path-based: invalidate a route or route subtree.
  • Tag-based: associate cached data with a tag and invalidate related cached entries.

These patterns may be combined. Do not mix examples from older Pages Router ISR APIs with App Router cache APIs without checking the version.

The Pages Router uses a different model, commonly getStaticProps with its revalidate return value and res.revalidate(path) for on-demand ISR. Pages Router examples do not belong in an App Router route without translation.

docs.title: When ISR is a good fit
docs.text: Use it for public product catalogs, articles, documentation, or other content that can be shared and may tolerate a defined freshness window. It is usually not the right approach for personalized dashboards or data that must be immediately consistent for every user.

docs.title: Important caveats
docs.text:
• Static output must not leak user-specific information.
  • A webhook must be authenticated and its input validated.
  • Revalidation can fail; decide how the site and monitoring should handle it.
  • Cache invalidation does not automatically clear every browser, CDN, or external cache.
  • Static export does not support all server-backed ISR behaviors.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Revalidating data
  • Next.js: revalidatePath
  • Next.js: revalidateTag
  • Next.js: ISR guide

docs.title: Next.js Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review Next.js routing, rendering, server/client boundaries, and production concerns. Framework APIs change over time; verify version-specific behavior against the documentation for your project.

docs.title: 1. What is Next.js?
docs.text: Next.js is a React framework that provides application conventions and features such as routing, rendering options, server-side capabilities, and production build tooling.

docs.title: 2. What is the App Router?
docs.text: The App Router uses the app/ directory and special file conventions. Folders represent route segments, page.tsx provides route UI, and other files define layouts, loading UI, errors, or route handlers.

docs.title: 3. What is a dynamic route?
docs.text: A dynamic route uses a bracketed segment, such as app/products/[id]/page.tsx, to match variable path values. Treat route parameters as untrusted input and validate and authorize before returning data.

docs.title: 4. What is a route group?
docs.text: A folder such as (marketing) organizes routes or layouts without adding the group name to the URL.

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between page.tsx and route.ts?
docs.text: page.tsx defines rendered route UI. route.ts defines HTTP method handlers for an endpoint; it is not a React page.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between SSR, static rendering, and CSR?
docs.text: SSR creates output on the server for a request. Static rendering prepares reusable output ahead of requests under the route's supported configuration. CSR builds or updates UI in the browser. A Next.js route can combine these approaches; exact behavior depends on framework version and route setup.

docs.title: 7. What is ISR?
docs.text: Incremental Static Regeneration reuses static output while allowing it to be refreshed through supported time-based or on-demand revalidation mechanisms. It is not necessarily a scheduled rebuild at an exact time.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between Server and Client Components?
docs.text: Server Components execute as part of server rendering and can keep server-only code out of the browser bundle. Client Components enable interactivity and browser APIs. The "use client" directive marks a client boundary; it does not make secrets safe to expose in props or bundled code.

docs.title: 9. What is hydration?
docs.text: Hydration attaches client-side React behavior to server-rendered HTML for interactive components. A hydration error can occur when the initial client render does not match the server-rendered markup.

docs.title: 10. What are layout.tsx and loading.tsx?
docs.text: layout.tsx provides shared UI around a route segment and its descendants. loading.tsx provides a loading fallback for eligible work within a segment, often through a Suspense boundary.

docs.title: 11. What is the purpose of error.tsx?
docs.text: error.tsx defines a segment-level error boundary UI. In the App Router it must be a Client Component. It should provide safe recovery UI and must not expose sensitive server details.

docs.title: 12. How does a Next.js Route Handler differ from a Server Action?
docs.text: A Route Handler implements HTTP methods at a route. A Server Action is a server-side function invoked through supported React/Next.js mechanisms, often for mutations. Both require validation and authorization.

docs.title: 13. How should cookies be used for sessions?
docs.text: Session cookies should be issued and configured server-side with appropriate attributes such as HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite. Authentication must also validate the session and authorize each protected operation.

docs.title: 14. What does the Next.js Link component do?
docs.text: Link provides framework-aware navigation between application routes and renders an anchor so browser navigation, keyboard use, and link semantics remain available.

docs.title: 15. What does the Next.js Image component provide?
docs.text: Image adds image layout and optimization features. It still needs appropriate alternative text, dimensions or layout, responsive sizes, and deliberate configuration for remote images.

docs.title: 16. Does metadata guarantee good SEO?
docs.text: No. Metadata helps describe pages, but useful content, crawlability, performance, accessibility, and correct indexing behavior also matter. Metadata does not enforce access control.

docs.title: 17. How should Next.js API input be secured?
docs.text: Validate all input on the server, authenticate and authorize the caller, avoid exposing secrets to Client Components, and use safe database and output-handling practices. A hidden button or client-side check is not authorization.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js overview
  • Next.js documentation
  • Next.js App Router

docs.title: Next.js Layouts, Loading UI, and Error UI
docs.text:
The App Router uses special files to share page structure, show a pending state, and handle errors or missing resources. Each behavior has its own boundary and is explained in a focused lesson:

  • Layouts: root and nested shared UI, templates, and route structure.
  • Loading UI: loading.tsx, Suspense boundaries, and streaming.
  • Error and not-found UI: error.tsx, global-error.tsx, and not-found.tsx.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text: These files improve structure and recovery; they do not replace validation, authorization, or monitoring. Handle expected outcomes such as invalid input and missing records deliberately, and avoid displaying sensitive server details to users.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Routing
  • Next.js: Error handling

docs.title: Next.js Layouts
docs.text: A layout is shared UI around a route segment and its descendants. It is useful for persistent elements such as site navigation, section menus, and common page structure.

docs.title: Root and nested layouts
docs.text:
The root app/layout.tsx is required in the App Router and must provide the document's <html> and <body> elements. Nested layouts wrap pages beneath their folder.

// app/layout.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <header>Learning notes</header>
        {children}
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Layouts can preserve shared UI during client navigation. A template.tsx is similar but creates a new instance on navigation where remount behavior is desired.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Keep shared structure in the closest appropriate layout. Avoid putting request-specific secrets or user data into a shared cacheable layout without understanding its rendering and caching behavior. Route groups can organize distinct layouts without adding URL segments.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A layout does not create a page route by itself.
  • A nested layout wraps its descendants, not unrelated routes.
  • A layout and a template have different lifecycle behavior.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Layouts and pages
  • Next.js: Route groups

docs.title: Next.js Link and Image Components
docs.text:
Next.js provides React components for application navigation and image delivery. They build on browser features and add framework-specific behavior.

  • Link: internal navigation and prefetching.
  • Image: responsive image dimensions and optimization.

These components still require familiar web fundamentals: semantic navigation, descriptive link text, appropriate alternative text, and responsive layouts.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Link
  • Next.js: Image

docs.title: Next.js Link Component
docs.text: Link from next/link is the primary way to navigate between internal routes in a Next.js application. It renders an anchor, preserving browser features such as opening a link in a new tab, copying its destination, and keyboard navigation.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
import Link from "next/link";

export function LessonLink() {
  return <Link href="/frontend/html">Learn HTML</Link>;
}

docs.title: Common props
docs.text:
Prop Meaning href Destination URL or route object prefetch Controls prefetch behavior where supported; defaults and production behavior are version-sensitive replace Replaces the current history entry instead of pushing one scroll Controls scroll restoration behavior for navigation target, rel Standard anchor behavior for opening external destinations

Use a regular anchor for external links or downloads when framework navigation is not useful. For _blank, include an appropriate rel, such as noopener noreferrer. Never nest a button or another interactive control inside a link.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Use descriptive link text that explains the destination. Link does not replace accessibility or remove browser history; it enhances internal route navigation. Do not enable prefetch indiscriminately without considering the installed version and network cost.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text: • Next.js: Link

docs.title: Next.js Loading UI
docs.text: loading.tsx provides a loading fallback for a route segment while eligible server work is pending. It can make navigation feel responsive by showing useful structure before slower work finishes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// app/products/loading.tsx
export default function LoadingProducts() {
  return <p role="status">Loading products…</p>;
}

The file creates a loading boundary associated with the route segment. Streaming may allow ready portions of a page to appear while slower portions continue. Exact behavior depends on route structure, data work, and framework version.

docs.title: Design useful loading states
docs.text:
• Describe what is loading when that context helps.
  • Keep the layout close to the final content to reduce visual movement.
  • Use skeletons for stable content regions and role="status" for helpful status text when appropriate.
  • Avoid indefinite spinners without explanation or recovery.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: A loading fallback does not mean every task can be cancelled or retried. It also does not replace explicit error handling. Use smaller boundaries when parts of a page can load independently.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text: • Next.js: Loading UI and streaming

docs.title: Next.js Metadata, SEO, and Social Previews
docs.text: Metadata describes a page to browsers, search engines, and link-preview systems. Search engine optimization (SEO) also depends on useful content, accessibility, performance, links, and correct indexing behavior; metadata alone does not guarantee ranking.

docs.title: Metadata API
docs.text:
In the App Router, export a metadata object for static values or implement generateMetadata when values depend on route data. Metadata exports belong in Server Components; Client Components cannot export them.

import type { Metadata } from "next";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "HTML Forms | Full Stack Notes",
  description: "Learn form elements, attributes, validation, and accessible labels.",
  alternates: {
    canonical: "https://notes.example.com/frontend/html/forms/",
  },
  openGraph: {
    title: "HTML Forms",
    description: "A practical guide to HTML forms.",
    images: ["/images/forms-preview.png"],
  },
};

For dynamic pages, generateMetadata can use validated route parameters and the same trusted data source as the page. Avoid exposing private data in metadata, which is sent to browsers and crawlers.

docs.title: Important metadata concepts
docs.text:
• Title: unique and descriptive page title; layouts can provide a template for child pages.
  • Description: concise summary; search engines may choose other snippets.
  • Canonical URL: preferred URL when equivalent content is reachable at multiple URLs.
  • Open Graph / social metadata: controls previews on platforms that support it.
  • Robots directives: guide indexing/crawling; they do not enforce access control or protect private pages.
  • metadataBase: base URL used when resolving relative metadata URLs; configure a production origin deliberately.

docs.title: Practical dynamic metadata example
docs.text:
import type { Metadata } from "next";

type Props = { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> };

export async function generateMetadata({ params }: Props): Promise<Metadata> {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const article = await getPublicArticle(slug);
  return {
    title: `${article.title} | Learning Notes`,
    description: article.summary,
  };
}

getPublicArticle is illustrative. Handle missing content and authorization according to the route's requirements. params typing and behavior depend on the Next.js release.

docs.title: Images and SEO
docs.text: Use descriptive image alt text, appropriate dimensions, and optimized formats. Include structured data only when it accurately describes visible page content and conforms to the relevant search documentation. Never use hidden or misleading metadata to claim content that users cannot see.

docs.title: Developer checklist
docs.text:
• Give important pages distinct titles and accurate summaries.
  • Set a correct production base URL and canonical URL strategy.
  • Do not put secrets or private user details in metadata.
  • Ensure pages intended to be private are protected by server-side authorization, not merely noindex.
  • Test rendered head output, social previews, and mobile layouts.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A meta description is not a guaranteed search-result snippet.
  • noindex does not prevent someone from directly visiting a URL.
  • Server rendering and metadata do not guarantee search ranking.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Metadata and OG images
  • Google Search Central: SEO starter guide
  • Open Graph protocol

docs.title: Next.js Rendering Strategies
docs.text: Rendering describes when and where page output is produced. Next.js can combine browser rendering, static output, server rendering, cached data, and interactive Client Components. A route's behavior depends on its code, configuration, framework version, and hosting platform.

docs.title: Choose a focused lesson
docs.text:
• Client-side rendering: build or update UI in the browser.
  • Static rendering: prepare shareable output before visitors request it.
  • Server-side rendering: produce output on the server for a request.
  • Incremental Static Regeneration: refresh cached output using time-based or event-based revalidation.

docs.title: These strategies can be combined
docs.text: A page can contain server-produced HTML, cached public data, and interactive client-side controls. Server Components describe where component code runs; SSR, static rendering, and revalidation describe when or how output is produced. They are related but are not interchangeable terms.

docs.title: Questions to guide a choice
docs.text:
1. Is the content public or specific to one signed-in user?
  2. How quickly must updates appear?
  3. Can the output be reused safely for many visitors?
  4. Does the deployment platform support the required server and cache behavior?

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Server rendering does not guarantee a fixed speed increase or search ranking.
  • Static output must not contain private, user-specific information.
  • Hydration is not the same thing as rendering.
  • ISR is not necessarily a scheduled rebuild at an exact wall-clock time.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Rendering
  • Next.js: Caching

docs.title: Next.js API Routes and Route Handlers
docs.text: Next.js has two API conventions because it has two routers. The App Router uses route.ts; the Pages Router uses files under pages/api/. They both create server-side HTTP endpoints, but their APIs and project conventions differ.

docs.title: App Router: app/api/.../route.ts
docs.text:
app/
  api/
    health/
      route.ts       -> /api/health

Export functions named for HTTP methods. Standard Request and Response work for basic handlers; Next.js also provides request/response helpers.

// app/api/health/route.ts
export function GET() {
  return Response.json({ status: "ok" });
}

A dynamic handler can read a path parameter and validate it. Parameter typing is version-sensitive in current Next.js releases.

// app/api/products/[id]/route.ts
export async function GET(
  request: Request,
  context: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }
) {
  const { id } = await context.params;
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/i.test(id)) {
    return Response.json({ error: "Invalid product id" }, { status: 400 });
  }
  return Response.json({ id });
}

The example validates only a simple identifier format; production code must load the resource and apply authorization before returning protected data.

docs.title: Pages Router: pages/api/...
docs.text:
pages/
  api/
    health.ts       -> /api/health

Pages Router API routes commonly use a default handler receiving request and response objects, then branch on the HTTP method. This differs from App Router named method exports. Do not mix the two handler signatures.

docs.title: HTTP methods and status codes
docs.text:
Method Common use GET Read a resource; should not change server state POST Create or submit an operation PUT Replace a resource representation PATCH Partially update a resource DELETE Remove a resource

Return appropriate status codes, validate content type and body size, and handle unsupported methods. Do not expose stack traces or sensitive server details in responses.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• Authenticate the caller and authorize the requested resource/action.
  • Validate and constrain path parameters, query values, headers, and body.
  • Treat webhook requests as untrusted until their signatures are verified.
  • Consider CSRF for cookie-authenticated state-changing requests.
  • Configure CORS only when browser cross-origin access is needed.
  • Rate limit or otherwise protect expensive/public operations where needed.
  • Avoid logging passwords, tokens, or unnecessary personal data.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: An API endpoint is a contract, not just a function. Request body carries submitted data; status code communicates broad outcome; webhook is a request from another system; authorization checks permission after identity is established.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• route.ts is an HTTP handler; page.tsx is a UI route.
  • An API route is not protected automatically.
  • CORS is not authentication and does not prevent non-browser clients from calling an endpoint.
  • HTTP method names do not enforce that a handler is safe; the code must implement the intended semantics.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Route Handlers
  • Next.js: Pages Router API Routes
  • MDN: HTTP request methods

docs.title: Server and Client Components
docs.text: The App Router uses React Server Components by default. Client Components are used when a component needs browser-side interactivity or APIs.

docs.title: Why separate components?
docs.text: Code that only prepares or displays data does not always need to be sent to the browser. Interactive controls, however, need browser JavaScript. Keeping the boundary intentional can reduce client work and clarify where code runs.

docs.title: How the boundary works
docs.text: A file beginning with the "use client" directive becomes a Client Component entry point. Its imported component subtree is included in the client boundary. Server Components can access server-side resources, but cannot use browser-only APIs or client hooks. Props crossing the boundary need to be serializable; functions and many server-only values cannot be passed directly.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
// app/components/counter.tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Count: {count}</button>;
}

A page can render this small interactive control alongside server-rendered content. Add "use client" only where browser behavior is required.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep database access, secrets, and server-only work on the server. Keep interactive state near the controls that use it. Server Component runs within the server-oriented rendering model; Client Component participates in browser-side React behavior; hydration attaches client behavior to server-rendered UI when needed.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• "use client" does not mean “render only in the browser”; a client component may also contribute to initial server-generated HTML.
  • Server Components are not a security boundary by themselves; do not expose sensitive values in rendered output.
  • Adding "use client" to the root unnecessarily can increase client-side JavaScript.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Server and Client Components
  • Next.js: Client Components

docs.title: Server-Side Rendering in Next.js
docs.text: Server-side rendering (SSR) produces HTML on the server in response to a request. It can use request-specific information, but the browser may still need JavaScript to make interactive components usable.

docs.title: Request lifecycle
docs.text:
1. A browser requests a route.
  2. The server executes the route's required rendering and data work.
  3. HTML is returned to the browser.
  4. The browser displays the document and loads the client JavaScript needed for interactive components.

This is a simplified model. Streaming can send portions progressively, and Next.js may combine server output, cached data, and Client Components.

docs.title: When it can help
docs.text: SSR can be useful when output depends on request context or must reflect fresh server-side data. It can provide meaningful HTML before client JavaScript finishes, but the full response still depends on server work, database latency, network transfer, and browser processing.

docs.title: Trade-offs and safe data access
docs.text: Per-request work can increase server load and response latency. Keep secrets on the server, validate request data, and authorize access before returning user-specific content. Do not put private values in metadata or shared caches.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text:
• SSR does not guarantee faster interaction; hydration and JavaScript may still be required.
  • SSR does not guarantee a search ranking or indexing outcome.
  • Server-rendering a page does not mean all its components are Server Components.
  • Rendering does not replace access control.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Server rendering
  • Next.js: Caching

docs.title: Static Rendering in Next.js
docs.text: Static rendering prepares a route's output so it can be reused for later visitors rather than generating the entire response separately for each request. It is well suited to public content that can safely be shared.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The framework renders a route during a build or another supported prerendering process.
  2. The resulting output can be served from a cache or content delivery network.
  3. Each visitor receives reusable output until the framework's cache rules require an update.

In the App Router, whether a route can be statically rendered depends on its data access, request-specific APIs, configuration, and Next.js version. Use official docs for the project version rather than assuming every route is static by default.

docs.title: Example: known public content
docs.text: A public article or documentation page can be prepared from known content. For dynamic paths, generateStaticParams can list identifiers to prepare ahead of time. A large or unbounded set may be better handled with another strategy.

docs.title: Benefits and trade-offs
docs.text: Static output is reusable and can be served efficiently. It is not suitable for embedding private per-user data in a shared response, and content may become stale until revalidated or rebuilt.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Static rendering is different from static export: a static export has additional deployment constraints and does not support every server-dependent Next.js feature. Static does not mean “no JavaScript”; client-side interaction can still be added.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Next.js: Static exports
  • Next.js: generateStaticParams

docs.title: React Components, JSX, and Props
docs.text: React components are reusable descriptions of interface parts. JSX is syntax commonly used to describe the elements a component returns, and props pass information from a parent component to a child.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Breaking a page into focused components makes repeated UI easier to reuse and helps keep each piece of behavior understandable. Props make the data flow explicit.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A function component receives props and returns React elements. JSX resembles HTML but is JavaScript syntax with React-specific rules. JavaScript expressions can be inserted with braces. Components should be named with an uppercase first letter when used in JSX.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
function ProductCard({ name, price }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>${price.toFixed(2)}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

function Catalog() {
  return <ProductCard name="Notebook" price={4.5} />;
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep a component responsible for a clear UI concept. Props are read-only inputs from a parent; JSX is syntax transformed by tooling; component tree is the nested arrangement of components in a rendered UI. With TypeScript, props can have an explicit type.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• JSX is not directly understood by browsers without a build or transform step.
  • Props should not be mutated by the receiving component.
  • A component is not required for every single HTML element; use components where they clarify reuse or responsibility.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Your first component
  • React Learn: Passing props to a component

docs.title: React Context and State Sharing
docs.text: Context lets a component make a value available to descendants without passing it through every intermediate component. It is useful for data such as the current theme or locale that many components need.

docs.title: When to use context
docs.text: If only a few nearby components need state, keep it in their closest shared parent and pass props. Context can reduce repetitive prop passing across deep trees, but a frequently changing context value can cause many consumers to update.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { createContext, useContext } from "react";

const ThemeContext = createContext("light");

function Page() {
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">
      <Toolbar />
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

function Toolbar() {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <p>Current theme: {theme}</p>;
}

In modern React, provider syntax and conventions may vary by React version; follow the version used by the project.

docs.title: State ownership
docs.text: “Lifting state up” means moving shared state to the nearest common ancestor that needs to coordinate it. Context distributes a value; it does not automatically provide a complete state-management architecture.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep context values focused and stable. Provider supplies a context value; consumer reads it; lifting state up moves ownership to a shared parent. For complex shared client state, choose a dedicated store only when the application has a need for its capabilities.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Context is not automatically faster or simpler than props.
  • Context does not replace server data fetching or persistence.
  • Any component reading a changed context value may need to render again.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Passing data deeply with context
  • React reference: useContext

docs.title: React Custom Hooks
docs.text: A custom Hook is a JavaScript function whose name begins with use and that calls React Hooks. It lets components reuse stateful logic without sharing the same state instance.

docs.title: Why use a custom Hook?
docs.text: If multiple components need the same subscription or interaction logic, a custom Hook can keep that behavior in one place. Each component calling the Hook still gets its own Hook state unless the Hook connects to shared state or an external store.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    const update = () => setOnline(navigator.onLine);
    update();
    window.addEventListener("online", update);
    window.addEventListener("offline", update);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener("online", update);
      window.removeEventListener("offline", update);
    };
  }, []);

  return online;
}

function StatusMessage() {
  const online = useOnlineStatus();
  return <p>{online ? "Online" : "Offline"}</p>;
}

In server-rendered applications, use a stable initial value that matches between server and client, then synchronize with the browser after mounting. Libraries may provide external-store APIs for this use case.

docs.title: Rules of Hooks
docs.text:
• Call Hooks at the top level of a function component or another custom Hook.
  • Do not call Hooks inside conditions, loops, nested functions, or event handlers.
  • Call Hooks in the same order on every render.
  • Use the use prefix for custom Hooks so lint tooling can identify Hook rules.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Extract a Hook when it gives behavior a meaningful name or removes real duplication. Do not create a custom Hook only to hide a few lines of markup. Custom Hooks share logic, not automatically shared state.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Reusing logic with custom Hooks
  • React reference: Rules of Hooks

docs.title: React Hooks and Effects
docs.text: Hooks are functions that let function components use React features such as state and context. Effects synchronize a component with systems outside React, such as subscriptions or browser APIs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Hooks support reusable stateful logic without class components. Effects are useful when rendering must connect to an external system, but using them for ordinary calculations can make code harder to follow.

docs.title: How effects work
docs.text: useEffect runs after React commits a render. Its dependency list tells React which reactive values the effect uses. A cleanup function can unsubscribe or release resources before the effect runs again or the component is removed. Development Strict Mode may run setup and cleanup an extra time to reveal unsafe effects.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function OnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    const update = () => setOnline(navigator.onLine);
    update();
    window.addEventListener("online", update);
    window.addEventListener("offline", update);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener("online", update);
      window.removeEventListener("offline", update);
    };
  }, []);

  return <p>{online ? "Online" : "Offline"}</p>;
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Follow the Rules of Hooks: call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook, not conditionally or inside loops. Dependency array lists reactive values used by an effect; cleanup reverses external setup; custom hook reuses stateful logic between components.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• An effect is not the normal place to derive one value from another; compute derived values during rendering when possible.
  • An empty dependency array does not mean “run once in every environment”; development behavior and component remounts matter.
  • Effects do not run during server rendering.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Synchronizing with Effects
  • React reference: useEffect

docs.title: React Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review React's component model, state, rendering, and common application patterns.

docs.title: 1. What is React?
docs.text: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. It describes UI based on data and updates the rendered interface when relevant state changes.

docs.title: 2. What is a React component?
docs.text: A component is a reusable unit of UI, commonly a JavaScript function that returns React elements. Components can receive props and use state and other React features.

docs.title: 3. What are props?
docs.text: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child. A component should treat its props as read-only and ask the owner to change data through callbacks or shared state.

docs.title: 4. What is state?
docs.text: State is data managed by a component or React store that can change over time. Updating state requests a render; it does not directly mutate the already-rendered UI.

docs.title: 5. Why should state not be mutated directly?
docs.text: React relies on update patterns and identity to reason about changes. Mutating existing state can make updates hard to detect and reason about. Create updated arrays or objects and pass them through the state setter.

docs.title: 6. What are Hooks?
docs.text: Hooks are functions such as useState and useEffect that let function components use React features. Call Hooks at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not conditionally or inside loops.

docs.title: 7. What is useEffect for?
docs.text: useEffect synchronizes a component with an external system after rendering, such as a subscription or browser API. It is not needed for every calculation or for deriving values that can be computed during render.

docs.title: 8. Why do list items need keys?
docs.text: Keys help React match items between renders so it can update the correct elements. Use a stable identifier from the data; array indexes can cause incorrect state association when items are inserted, removed, or reordered.

docs.title: 9. What is reconciliation?
docs.text: Reconciliation is React's process for comparing the new element description with the previous one and determining updates to apply. It is an implementation concept, not a guarantee that every update has a particular performance cost.

docs.title: 10. What is a controlled input?
docs.text: A controlled input gets its current value from React state and updates that state through an event handler. An uncontrolled input keeps its current value in the DOM and can be read with a ref or form APIs.

docs.title: 11. What is Context used for?
docs.text: Context makes a value available to descendants without passing it through every intermediate component's props. It is useful for shared values such as theme or locale, but frequent broad updates may cause unnecessary rendering.

docs.title: 12. What is a ref?
docs.text: A ref stores a mutable value that persists between renders without itself triggering a render. Refs can also reference DOM elements for focus or measurement when appropriate.

docs.title: 13. What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
docs.text: useMemo caches a computed value between renders when dependencies are unchanged. useCallback caches a function identity. They are performance tools, not correctness fixes, and should be used when measurement or component behavior justifies them.

docs.title: 14. What is an Error Boundary?
docs.text: An Error Boundary catches certain rendering errors in its descendant component tree and displays fallback UI. It does not catch every error, such as most event-handler errors or arbitrary asynchronous failures.

docs.title: 15. What is Suspense used for?
docs.text: Suspense displays a fallback while a supported child operation is pending, such as certain code-loading or data integrations. It only handles work integrated with Suspense; it does not automatically track every Promise.

docs.title: 16. How should a React component be tested?
docs.text: Test observable behavior: render the component, interact as a user would, and assert visible results or accessible state. Keep tests focused and avoid depending unnecessarily on private implementation details.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React overview
  • React documentation
  • React: Rules of Hooks

docs.title: React Lists, Forms, and UI States
docs.text: Lists, forms, and request states are common building blocks in React applications. Model them explicitly so the interface remains understandable for loading, empty, success, and error situations.

docs.title: Rendering lists and keys
docs.text:
Use map() to return UI for each item. A key helps React match items between renders and should come from stable data such as a database ID.

function TaskList({ tasks }) {
  if (tasks.length === 0) return <p>No tasks yet.</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {tasks.map((task) => (
        <li key={task.id}>{task.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Keys are only required among siblings and are not passed to the component as a normal prop. Array indexes can cause incorrect associations when items are inserted, deleted, or reordered; use them only when the list is static and never changes order.

docs.title: Controlled form fields
docs.text:
A controlled input gets its value from React state. Its onChange handler updates that state:

import { useState } from "react";

function SearchForm() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  function submit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    console.log("Search:", query);
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={submit}>
      <label htmlFor="query">Search</label>
      <input
        id="query"
        value={query}
        onChange={(event) => setQuery(event.target.value)}
      />
      <button type="submit">Search</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Controlled fields are useful when the UI must respond to each edit, validate as the user types, or coordinate multiple fields.

docs.title: Uncontrolled form fields
docs.text: An uncontrolled input keeps its current value in the DOM. Use defaultValue for its initial value, and read the submitted data through FormData or a ref. This can be simpler for a basic form. Do not mix value and defaultValue for the same field.

docs.title: Request and form states
docs.text:
Represent state explicitly:

type RequestState<T> =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; data: T }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

A discriminated union prevents impossible combinations such as loading and error being true at the same time. Show validation errors next to fields, announce status changes appropriately, and prevent accidental duplicate submissions when needed.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use semantic labels and native form controls. A controlled input's state should update synchronously in its change handler. Controlled input gets its value from React; uncontrolled input holds its value in the DOM; discriminated union represents mutually exclusive state cases.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A key is used by React for matching and is not automatically a component prop.
  • An array index is not always a safe key.
  • Client-side validation improves UX but does not replace server validation.
  • A disabled button alone may not explain why submission is unavailable.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Rendering lists
  • React Learn: Reacting to input with state
  • React Learn: Sharing state between components

docs.title: React Refs and Performance
docs.text: A ref stores a value that persists between renders without causing a render when it changes. Refs can also provide access to a DOM node for tasks such as focusing an input.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useRef } from "react";

function SearchBox() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  return (
    <>
      <input ref={inputRef} aria-label="Search" />
      <button onClick={() => inputRef.current?.focus()}>Focus search</button>
    </>
  );
}

Ref values are mutable and are not reactive state. If a changed value must be shown in the UI, use state instead.

docs.title: Measuring performance
docs.text:
Start by identifying a real user-visible problem. Use browser Performance tools and React profiling tools where available. Avoid adding memoization (memo, useMemo, useCallback) without evidence that repeated rendering or calculation is a bottleneck.

Ref is a mutable container associated with a component; memoization caches a result or component work under specified conditions; profiling measures where time is spent.

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text: Do not use refs as a second state system or to bypass React for routine UI updates. Direct DOM manipulation may conflict with React's own updates. A component re-render is not automatically a performance problem; optimize measured expensive work.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Referencing values with refs
  • React Learn: Manipulating the DOM with refs
  • React Developer Tools

docs.title: React Rendering and Reconciliation
docs.text: Rendering is React calling components to calculate the UI for current props and state. Reconciliation is how React compares the new description with the previous one and decides what changes are needed in the host environment.

docs.title: What triggers a render?
docs.text: A component may render when its state changes, its parent renders and passes new props, or a context value it reads changes. Rendering calculates a description; it does not mean React replaces the whole DOM tree.

docs.title: Render and commit
docs.text: React's render work calculates the next UI. The commit phase applies required changes to the DOM and runs relevant effects. React may skip work or render again before committing; components should therefore remain pure and avoid side effects during render.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep rendering deterministic: the same props and state should describe the same UI. Give list items stable keys so React can match them across updates. Reconciliation compares element trees; commit applies changes; pure component render avoids changing external state while calculating UI.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Every render does not mean every DOM node is recreated.
  • A component function may run more than once in development.
  • Do not perform network requests or mutate global values during render.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: Render and commit
  • React Learn: Keeping components pure

docs.title: React State and Events
docs.text: State is data that changes over time and affects what a component displays. Event handlers connect user actions—such as clicks and form input—to updates.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Interactive interfaces need a reliable source of truth. React state lets a component describe the UI for the current data rather than manually editing DOM nodes after every action.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: useState returns a current value and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a render using the updated value. When a new value depends on the previous one, use the functional update form to avoid stale values.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount((current) => current + 1)}>
      Count: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

The state setter requests a render; it does not directly edit the DOM.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Keep state as close as practical to the components that need it. State is component data that can change; event handler is a function run in response to an event; render calculates the UI for current props and state.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Do not mutate arrays or objects stored in state; create updated values.
  • A state update may be batched and is not an immediate variable assignment.
  • Props and state have different owners: a component receives props and owns its local state.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Learn: State — a component's memory
  • React Learn: Responding to events

docs.title: React Suspense and Error Boundaries
docs.text: Suspense lets a part of a React tree display a fallback while a supported child is not ready. Error boundaries display fallback UI when descendant rendering throws an error.

docs.title: Suspense
docs.text:
import { Suspense, lazy } from "react";

const HelpPanel = lazy(() => import("./HelpPanel"));

function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading help…</p>}>
      <HelpPanel />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

lazy defers loading a component's code until it is rendered. Suspense behavior for data sources depends on the library or framework providing that integration; wrapping an arbitrary Promise does not automatically make it Suspense-enabled.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text: An error boundary catches errors thrown while rendering descendants and shows fallback UI. In React's core API, error boundaries are traditionally implemented with a class component or supplied by a framework/library. They do not automatically catch errors in event handlers, arbitrary asynchronous callbacks, or server requests; handle those at their proper boundary.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Place boundaries around areas that can fail or load independently. A useful fallback should preserve context, explain what happened, and offer a next step when possible. Log unexpected failures without exposing sensitive details.

Fallback is temporary or recovery UI; code splitting loads code in separate chunks; error boundary catches descendant render/lifecycle errors within its supported scope.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Suspense does not automatically fetch data from any Promise.
  • A React error boundary does not catch every JavaScript error.
  • A loading fallback should not be the only feedback for a failed operation.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React reference: Suspense
  • React reference: lazy
  • React: Error Boundary

docs.title: Testing React Interfaces
docs.text: React interface tests verify behavior a user or another component depends on. They help catch regressions when props, state, forms, and async UI change.

docs.title: What to test
docs.text:
• A component shows the expected content for its inputs.
  • User actions produce visible, correct results.
  • Loading, success, empty, and error states are understandable.
  • Important keyboard and form behavior works.

Prefer queries based on accessible roles and labels where possible. Tests should check observable behavior rather than private implementation details such as internal hook call counts.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: With a testing library installed and configured, a test might render a button and assert that activating it changes the visible count. Keep setup specific to the project's chosen test runner; React itself does not prescribe one universal test stack.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Use unit tests for small logic, component tests for UI behavior, and end-to-end tests for important user journeys across the app. Assertion checks an expected result; mock replaces a dependency for a test; test double is a controlled substitute such as a fake or stub.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A test that passes does not prove every real-world browser case works.
  • Snapshot output alone may not explain whether behavior is correct.
  • Tests tied to implementation details can break during harmless refactoring.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React Testing Library
  • Vitest documentation

docs.title: Advanced and Utility Types
docs.text: TypeScript includes features for deriving, combining, and transforming types. These tools help model real application data without duplicating every definition.

docs.title: Unions and intersections
docs.text: A union such as A | B represents a value that may be either type. An intersection such as A & B combines requirements from both types. Use discriminated unions for variants that need different fields or behavior.

docs.title: Useful built-in utility types
docs.text:
• Partial<T> makes properties optional.
  • Pick<T, K> selects a subset of properties.
  • Omit<T, K> removes selected properties.
  • Record<K, V> describes an object keyed by K with values of type V.
  • Readonly<T> prevents reassignment of properties in checked code.
  • ReturnType<F> derives a function's return type.
type Account = { id: string; name: string; active: boolean };
type AccountUpdate = Partial<Pick<Account, "name" | "active">>;
type AccountById = Record<string, Account>;

These are compile-time descriptions. Readonly does not freeze an object at runtime, and Partial does not validate incoming JSON.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prefer types that make valid states clear and remain easy to understand. Mapped type transforms properties of another type; conditional type selects a type based on a type relationship; utility type is a reusable built-in type transformation.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A complex type is not automatically more precise or safer.
  • Readonly<T> is generally shallow unless nested values are also readonly.
  • Utility types do not change runtime objects.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: Utility Types
  • TypeScript Handbook: Creating types from types

docs.title: TypeScript Compiler and Project Configuration
docs.text: The TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks TypeScript source and can emit JavaScript. A project configuration describes which files and language features the compiler should use.

docs.title: tsconfig.json
docs.text: tsconfig.json marks a TypeScript project and configures compiler behavior. Options such as strict, target, module, and moduleResolution affect checking or output. Frontend frameworks often provide recommended defaults; understand and extend those defaults instead of copying an unrelated setup.

docs.title: Type checking and emitting
docs.text: Some tools transpile TypeScript without performing full type checking. Therefore a project may need a separate tsc --noEmit check in addition to its bundler or framework build.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext"
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

This illustrates options only; actual projects should use compatible settings for their runtime, module system, and build tool.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
