docs.text: Keep the compiler version and configuration under version control so local and CI checks agree. Type checking analyzes type compatibility; emit writes output files; module resolution determines how imports map to files or packages.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Successful transpilation does not necessarily mean type checking passed.
  • strict affects multiple checks and may reveal existing issues when enabled.
  • A tsconfig option copied from another framework may conflict with the project's build system.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: TSConfig
  • TypeScript: Compiler options

docs.title: TypeScript Functions, Objects, and Generics
docs.text: TypeScript describes function inputs and outputs, object shapes, and relationships between reusable values. These types help callers understand contracts and help the checker catch mismatches.

docs.title: Object types
docs.text:
type User = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  nickname?: string;
  readonly createdAt: Date;
};
  • ? marks a property optional; reading it may produce undefined.
  • readonly prevents reassignment through that type in checked code; it does not freeze the object at runtime.
  • Types are generally structural: compatible property shapes can be assignable even when type names differ.

interface and type can both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be declaration-merged and extended; type aliases can represent unions, tuples, and other type expressions. Choose a consistent project convention.

docs.title: Function types and overloads
docs.text:
type Formatter = (value: number, currency?: string) => string;

const formatPrice: Formatter = (value, currency = "USD") =>
  new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency }).format(value);

Function types can describe parameters, optional/rest parameters, and return values. Use overload signatures only when callers truly get different type-level behavior from different argument shapes; avoid overloads that obscure a simple union.

docs.title: Generics
docs.text:
A generic type parameter preserves a relationship between types:

function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

const firstName = first(["Ari", "Sam"]); // string | undefined

Constraints narrow which types are accepted:

function getId<T extends { id: string }>(value: T): string {
  return value.id;
}

Generic defaults and multiple type parameters can model more complex relationships, but use the simplest type that communicates the contract.

docs.title: keyof, indexed access, and typeof
docs.text:
type Product = { id: string; price: number; title: string };
type ProductKey = keyof Product; // "id" | "price" | "title"
type ProductPrice = Product["price"]; // number

const defaults = { pageSize: 20, compact: false };
type Defaults = typeof defaults;

These operators derive types from existing structures and reduce duplication.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type ApiResult<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

type Book = { id: string; title: string };
const result: ApiResult<Book[]> = {
  ok: true,
  data: [{ id: "b1", title: "Web Basics" }],
};

docs.title: Developer perspective and misconceptions
docs.text:
Use generics when the input/output relationship matters, not simply to make a function look reusable. Use readonly arrays and properties when mutation should be discouraged. Types do not validate runtime API data; validate external boundaries.

  • Structural typing checks compatible members, not just declared names.
  • readonly is a compile-time restriction and is often shallow.
  • T extends U constrains T; it does not mean T is exactly U.
  • Avoid defaulting to any for convenience.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: Object types
  • TypeScript Handbook: Functions
  • TypeScript Handbook: Generics
  • TypeScript Handbook: keyof

docs.title: TypeScript Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: Review these questions after learning the TypeScript lessons. TypeScript checks source code before runtime; it does not replace runtime validation.

docs.title: 1. What is TypeScript?
docs.text: TypeScript is a programming language that builds on JavaScript with a static type system. It is typically checked and transformed into JavaScript for execution; browsers do not execute TypeScript types.

docs.title: 2. What is type inference?
docs.text: Type inference is the compiler deriving a type from a value or context, so developers do not need to annotate every variable.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between any and unknown?
docs.text: any disables many type checks for a value. unknown can hold any value, but code must narrow or validate it before using it as a specific type. Prefer unknown at untrusted boundaries.

docs.title: 4. What is never used for?
docs.text: never represents a value that cannot occur, such as a function that always throws or an impossible branch after exhaustive narrowing.

docs.title: 5. What are union types?
docs.text: A union such as string | number says a value can be one of several types. The program must narrow the value before using operations that only apply to one member.

docs.title: 6. What is type narrowing?
docs.text:
Narrowing uses control flow or type guards to refine a broader type into a more specific one:

function show(value: string | number) {
  if (typeof value === "string") return value.toUpperCase();
  return value.toFixed(2);
}

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between interface and type?
docs.text: Both can describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended and declaration-merged; type aliases can express unions, intersections, and other type expressions. Choose the form that best communicates the model and follow project conventions.

docs.title: 8. What are generics?
docs.text:
Generics let code express relationships between input and output types without choosing one concrete type in advance:

function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

docs.title: 9. What is a type assertion?
docs.text: A type assertion tells the compiler how the programmer wants a value treated. It is removed at runtime and does not check or convert the value. Use it only when the program has information the compiler cannot infer.

docs.title: 10. What are utility types?
docs.text: Utility types transform existing types. Examples include Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, and Readonly<T>. They affect compile-time checking and do not enforce runtime behavior.

docs.title: 11. What is a discriminated union?
docs.text: A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a property whose literal value identifies the variant. Checking that property lets TypeScript narrow the object safely.

docs.title: 12. What is the difference between optional and nullable properties?
docs.text: An optional property may be absent. A nullable property is present with a value that may be null. These states are distinct and should be modeled according to the data contract.

docs.title: 13. Do TypeScript types validate API responses at runtime?
docs.text: No. Type annotations and assertions are erased from emitted JavaScript. Validate untrusted responses at runtime with checks or a schema-validation library before relying on them.

docs.title: 14. What does strict do in tsconfig.json?
docs.text: The strict option enables a family of stronger type-checking options. It helps catch issues such as implicit any and possible null access. Individual flags and project settings can further change the checks.

docs.title: 15. What is the difference between tsc and a runtime?
docs.text: tsc type-checks and can emit JavaScript. A JavaScript runtime such as a browser or Node.js executes JavaScript. Build tools may combine or replace these steps, but type checking and execution remain different concerns.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript overview
  • TypeScript Handbook
  • TypeScript: tsconfig.json

docs.title: Runtime Validation of Data
docs.text: TypeScript checks code during development and build time, but external data arrives while an application is running. Runtime validation checks that data actually has the expected shape before code relies on it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Network responses, browser storage, user input, and environment values are not made trustworthy by adding a TypeScript annotation. A malformed response can still cause a runtime failure or an incorrect decision.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Treat data from outside the typed program as unknown. Check its structure and values, then convert it to a trusted application representation. Larger projects often use a schema-validation library; small boundaries can use careful explicit checks.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type Profile = { id: string; displayName: string };

function parseProfile(value: unknown): Profile {
  if (
    typeof value === "object" &&
    value !== null &&
    "id" in value &&
    "displayName" in value &&
    typeof value.id === "string" &&
    typeof value.displayName === "string"
  ) {
    return { id: value.id, displayName: value.displayName };
  }
  throw new Error("Invalid profile response");
}

This is a small example; production schemas may need limits, nested checks, and useful error reporting.

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Validate at trust boundaries, especially before using values for access control, database writes, or rendering. Trust boundary is where data enters from a source not controlled by the current code. Parsing turns input into a structured representation; validation verifies constraints.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• const profile: Profile = await response.json() does not inspect the JSON.
  • A successful HTTP status does not guarantee a response has the expected content.
  • Validation improves correctness but does not replace authorization or output encoding.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: unknown
  • MDN: Working with JSON

docs.title: TypeScript Types and Narrowing
docs.text: TypeScript's type system describes the values a program expects. Type narrowing uses checks and control flow to refine a broad type to a more specific one.

docs.title: Everyday type forms
docs.text: Type form Example Meaning Primitive string, number, boolean Common basic values Array string[], Array<number> Ordered values of one element type Object { id: string; active: boolean } Named properties with declared types Optional property { nickname?: string } Property can be absent or undefined Union string \| number Value can be one of several types Literal "idle" \| "loading" Value must match listed values Tuple [string, number] Ordered positions with known types unknown unknown Must be checked before being used as a specific type never never No possible value; useful for exhaustive branches

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Types help editors explain how code is used and help catch mismatches before execution. Narrowing is especially useful when a value may be absent or may have one of several shapes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: TypeScript infers many types from assigned values. An annotation can make a public contract clearer. Union types represent alternatives; checks such as typeof, in, and equality comparisons can narrow those alternatives inside a branch.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
type Result =
  | { ok: true; value: string }
  | { ok: false; message: string };

function showResult(result: Result): string {
  if (result.ok) {
    return result.value;
  }
  return result.message;
}

Checking the discriminant ok allows TypeScript to know which properties exist in each branch.

docs.title: Common narrowing checks
docs.text:
function describe(value: string | number | null): string {
  if (value === null) return "No value";
  if (typeof value === "number") return value.toFixed(2);
  return value.toUpperCase();
}

Other narrowing tools include in for object properties, instanceof for class instances, equality checks, and user-defined type guards. Prefer checks that prove the value's shape rather than assertions that merely tell the compiler to trust you.

docs.title: Exhaustiveness checks
docs.text:
When handling a union, a never assignment can help identify a new case that was not handled:

type Theme = "light" | "dark";

function labelTheme(theme: Theme): string {
  switch (theme) {
    case "light": return "Light";
    case "dark": return "Dark";
    default: {
      const exhaustive: never = theme;
      return exhaustive;
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Developer perspective and terminology
docs.text: Prefer precise types over any, which disables many useful checks. Use unknown for data whose shape has not yet been verified. A union allows one of several types; a discriminated union shares a property whose value identifies each case; narrowing reduces possible types after a check.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Type annotations are removed from emitted JavaScript and do not validate data at runtime.
  • A type assertion changes the checker's view; it does not convert or verify the value.
  • any can hide errors rather than solve them.
  • An optional property may be missing; reading it can produce undefined.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• TypeScript Handbook: Everyday types
  • TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing

docs.title: TypeScript with React
docs.text: TypeScript can describe React component props, event handlers, state, and children. It helps document component contracts and catch incompatible values while editing.

docs.title: Typing component props
docs.text:
type GreetingProps = {
  name: string;
  formal?: boolean;
};

function Greeting({ name, formal = false }: GreetingProps) {
  return <p>{formal ? `Good day, ${name}` : `Hi, ${name}`}</p>;
}

TypeScript can infer many event types from JSX context. Add annotations when they clarify an API or when inference cannot identify the intended type.

docs.title: State and events
docs.text: Use useState with a clear initial value when inference is sufficient. When state may have multiple forms, use a union type. Prefer native DOM event types provided by React's type definitions rather than broad any.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Avoid typing every component as a generic React component type unless a real API requires it. Type the data the component accepts and returns, and keep runtime validation at external boundaries.

Props type describes a component's input contract; event type describes the event value provided to a handler; inference derives types from the surrounding JSX and values.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• TypeScript does not validate props received from arbitrary runtime JavaScript automatically.
  • React.FC is not required for every function component.
  • A type assertion cannot repair an incorrectly shaped response.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• React TypeScript Cheatsheet
  • TypeScript Handbook: JSX

docs.title: Backend Development
docs.text:
This section follows the server side of an application: receiving requests, running application logic, and returning useful and reliable responses.

Begin with backend fundamentals, then learn how Node.js and Express provide a practical server runtime and framework. Continue with REST APIs, and see how middleware, authentication and authorization, and error handling support dependable services.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the responsibilities of a backend service.
  • Explore Node.js, Express, and REST API concepts.
  • Learn how middleware, authentication, and error handling fit into a server.
  • Trace a request through a server and identify where common backend concerns belong.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Backend Fundamentals
  • Node.js
  • Express
  • REST APIs
  • Authentication and Authorization
  • Middleware
  • Error Handling

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Authentication asks, “Who are you?” Authorization asks, “What are you allowed to do?” An application identifies a user and checks permissions before exposing or changing data.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Authentication establishes identity or a session; authorization applies rules to the identity and requested action. Without authorization, a signed-in user might access someone else's records.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A user may authenticate with a password, passkey, or identity provider. The application maintains proof of sign-in, often with a session cookie or token. For protected requests, the backend validates it and checks permission. Passwords require a dedicated password hashing scheme, never plain text.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A task application can let users view their own tasks. Authentication identifies the user; authorization checks task ownership. A successful login does not permit access to every task.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Enforce access on the server, deny by default, and check resource ownership. Protect credentials and plan for session expiration and revocation. REST APIs should not leak private details in errors.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Query a record using both its ID and the current user's ID:

SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?;

This does not treat a user-supplied ID as proof of permission.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Identity: The person or service represented by a request.
  • Authentication: Establishing or verifying identity.
  • Authorization: Deciding whether an identity may perform an action.
  • Session: Server-recognized state associated with a client.
  • Credential: Evidence used to authenticate, such as a password or token.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Separate identity and permission checks to keep rules clear. Credentials can be stolen and overly broad permissions can expose data. Use established protocols and libraries rather than inventing schemes.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Being authenticated does not mean a user is authorized for every action.
  • Hiding a button in the frontend is not an access-control check.
  • Encoding a token does not necessarily encrypt it or make it trustworthy.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Reference: MDN: HTTP authentication explains HTTP authentication mechanisms and challenges.
  • Official standard: RFC 6749: OAuth 2.0 specifies an authorization framework for delegated access; it is not itself a user-login protocol.
  • Third-party security guidance: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet offers practical recommendations for authentication design.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Backend development builds an application's server-side parts. A backend receives requests, applies business rules, accesses data, and returns responses. It may integrate with email, payment, or search services.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Some responsibilities cannot safely live only in a browser. A server can enforce access rules, coordinate shared data, protect credentials, and serve multiple clients.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A client sends an HTTP request. The server routes it to logic that can validate input, check permissions, and access a database. It returns a status, headers, and possibly a body. REST APIs are one common interface style.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: For a task list, the backend authenticates a user, retrieves only their tasks, and returns a structured response. A database preserves tasks across devices.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Keep responsibilities clear: routing receives requests, business logic applies rules, and persistence code handles storage. Validate input, limit data access, and return predictable failures. The Node.js and Express lessons show one JavaScript server stack.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: A conceptual endpoint might respond to GET /tasks with status 200 and a JSON array of tasks. For a request to create a task, the backend should check that the title is valid and that the caller is allowed to create it before storing anything.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: A program that initiates a request, such as a browser.
  • Server: A program that receives and responds to requests.
  • Business logic: Rules describing what the application should do.
  • Persistence: Keeping data beyond the lifetime of a single request.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Backend services centralize data and rules for multiple clients. They require deployment, monitoring, and careful handling of failures, security, and scaling.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Backend code is not automatically secure just because it runs on a server.
  • A database is not the whole backend; validation and application rules matter.
  • A successful HTTP response does not prove that the result is correct.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Reference: MDN: Introduction to the server side explains server-side responsibilities and request processing.
  • Reference: MDN: Client-server overview introduces clients, servers, and HTTP communication.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Error handling detects failures and responds in a controlled way. A backend may encounter invalid input, missing records, unavailable dependencies, or programming mistakes. Clear responses help clients and developers.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Failures are normal in networked systems. Without a strategy, an application may crash, expose internal details, or return inconsistent responses. Good handling gives clients an outcome and preserves diagnostics for operators.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Code detects an error, logs relevant details, and maps it to a response. HTTP status codes communicate outcomes; a body can provide a stable code and safe explanation. Express passes errors to centralized middleware; see middleware.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: If a task does not exist, return 404 Not Found. If a database is unavailable, return 503 Service Unavailable without exposing a connection string or stack trace. Operators can investigate logs.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Distinguish expected errors from unexpected faults. Return consistent responses, log useful context without secrets, and ensure each request gets a response or reaches an error handler. Check Express's version-specific async error behavior.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
app.use((error, request, response, next) => {
  console.error(error);
  response.status(500).json({ error: "Internal server error" });
});

This sends a generic message while recording a server-side diagnostic. Configure production logs to protect private information.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Operational error: An expected failure condition, such as a missing record.
  • Programmer error: A defect in the code that should be investigated.
  • Error middleware: Express middleware dedicated to handling errors.
  • Status code: HTTP response value describing the general result.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Centralized handling supports predictable responses and monitoring. Generic errors can hide distinctions; overly detailed responses can leak information.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Returning status 200 with an error message does not communicate failure clearly.
  • A try/catch block does not automatically handle every asynchronous error.
  • Logging an error is not the same as recovering from it or notifying the client.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official guide: Express error handling explains how errors are passed through Express and handled.
  • Official API docs: Node.js errors describes error objects and conventions used by Node.js APIs.
  • Official standard: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics defines HTTP status code classes and their meaning.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Express is a web framework for Node.js. It provides a small set of tools for handling HTTP requests and responses, defining routes, and composing middleware. Developers can use it to create APIs and web servers without manually managing every low-level HTTP detail.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Node.js includes built-in networking APIs, but an application still needs an organized way to match URLs and methods to behavior. Express supplies a minimal routing and middleware model that developers can extend with additional libraries.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: An Express application registers middleware and route handlers. For each request, Express runs applicable middleware in order, then finds a matching route. A handler can send a response, modify the request/response context, or pass control onward. A request must eventually receive a response or be handed to another handler.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A task API can use GET /tasks to list items and POST /tasks to create one. A logging middleware can run for both routes, while an authentication middleware can protect only routes that require a signed-in user. See REST APIs for method and resource conventions.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Register middleware in the intended order, keep route handlers focused, and handle errors centrally. Express does not automatically validate every input or define an authentication system; add these deliberately with middleware and appropriate application logic. For authentication concepts, see authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.get("/health", (request, response) => {
  response.json({ status: "ok" });
});

app.listen(3000);

The JSON middleware parses JSON request bodies; the route returns a JSON health response. Production applications should configure listening and errors for their environment.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Application: The Express instance that configures a server.
  • Route: A method and path associated with request-handling code.
  • Handler: A function that processes a request or passes it onward.
  • Router: A modular set of route and middleware definitions.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Express is lightweight, flexible, and supported by a large ecosystem. That flexibility means applications must choose their own conventions for validation, structure, security, and many other concerns.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Express is not part of Node.js; it is a separate framework package.
  • Registering a route does not automatically validate its request data.
  • Middleware order can change application behavior.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official guide: Express routing explains route methods, paths, and handlers.
  • Official guide: Express middleware describes middleware behavior and registration.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Middleware is reusable request-processing code that runs between receiving a request and sending a response. In Express, middleware can inspect or update the request, perform a task such as logging, end the response, or pass control to another middleware or route handler.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Many routes need the same cross-cutting behavior: parsing request bodies, recording request details, checking authentication, or setting security headers. Middleware helps share that behavior rather than duplicating it in every route.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Express executes middleware in registration order. A middleware function typically receives request, response, and next. Calling next() passes control onward; ending the response completes the request. If middleware neither calls next() nor sends a response, the request can remain unfinished. Errors can be passed to the error-handling flow.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A logging middleware can record the request method and path before a route runs. Authentication middleware can check a session and reject a request before it reaches a private endpoint. The concepts apply to routes in Express, including those that implement a REST API.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Keep middleware focused and predictable. Place parsing and logging where needed, and put access checks before protected route behavior. Avoid logging passwords, tokens, or other sensitive values. Centralized error handling is described in error handling.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
function requestLogger(request, response, next) {
  console.log(`${request.method} ${request.path}`);
  next();
}

app.use(requestLogger);

This logger runs for requests after it is registered. A production logger should use an appropriate logging system and avoid recording private data.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Middleware function: Code invoked during the request-response cycle.
  • next(): Express callback used to pass control to the next handler.
  • Application middleware: Middleware registered for an app or router.
  • Error-handling middleware: A handler with a four-argument signature that processes errors.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Middleware encourages reuse and makes shared request behavior easier to compose. Too many layers or unclear ordering can obscure what a route does, and a middleware that forgets to continue or respond can stall a request.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Middleware does not always modify a request; it can also log, check, or respond.
  • Calling next() does not mean a response has been sent.
  • Authentication middleware should not be confused with authorization policy.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official guide: Express: Using middleware explains application, router, and error middleware.
  • Official API reference: Express application API documents app.use() and middleware registration.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Node.js is an open-source JavaScript runtime outside the browser. It runs server programs, command-line tools, and automation, with APIs for files and network communication.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Node.js made JavaScript practical for servers and general-purpose tools. Using one language across an application can simplify code sharing, though browser and server APIs differ.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Node.js runs JavaScript with V8 and provides an event-driven runtime. Many I/O operations are asynchronous, so a program can continue while waiting. The event loop coordinates queued work; CPU-heavy synchronous work can block it.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A Node.js server can accept HTTP requests and return JSON. A service may use Express for routes and middleware for shared request processing.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use asynchronous APIs appropriately, handle errors, and keep secrets out of source control. Choose dependencies carefully. Node.js APIs differ from browser APIs described in JavaScript.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  response.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/plain" });
  response.end("Hello from Node.js\n");
});

server.listen(3000);

This listens on port 3000 and sends plain text. A service also needs configuration, graceful shutdown, and failure handling.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Runtime: The environment that executes a program and supplies APIs.
  • Event loop: Mechanism that coordinates queued callbacks and asynchronous work.
  • Non-blocking I/O: Starting I/O without waiting synchronously for it to finish.
  • Package: Reusable code distributed for use by a project.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Node.js handles I/O-heavy workloads well. Synchronous work can block the event loop, and its package ecosystem requires dependency management.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Asynchronous I/O does not make CPU-bound work automatically fast.
  • Node.js is not a browser and does not provide browser-only APIs such as document.
  • Node.js can serve HTTP without Express, though a framework may add useful structure.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official docs: Node.js: Introduction to Node.js explains the runtime and common uses.
  • Official API docs: Node.js HTTP API documents the built-in HTTP server and client interfaces.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: An API (Application Programming Interface) defines how software systems communicate. REST is an architectural style. In common web APIs, URLs identify resources and HTTP methods request or change them.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: An API lets browsers, mobile applications, and services use a backend through a defined interface. Resource URLs and standard HTTP semantics help clients integrate with it.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A client sends an HTTP method, URL, headers, and sometimes a body. The server returns a status, headers, and often JSON. GET retrieves, POST commonly creates or processes, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes a resource. The API contract defines exact behavior.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A task service might use GET /tasks/42 to retrieve task 42 and PATCH /tasks/42 to change its title. It can return 200 for success and 404 for a missing task. See Express for route implementation.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use consistent resource names, validate request bodies, return meaningful status codes, and document response shapes. Plan pagination, errors, and version changes. See authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
GET /api/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":42,"title":"Read the API lesson","completed":false}

An API should document its exact schema and error responses.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Resource: A concept or item exposed by an API.
  • Endpoint: A reachable API location, often described by method and path.
  • HTTP method: A standardized action such as GET or POST.
  • Status code: A number that communicates the result of an HTTP request.
  • Idempotent: Repeating an operation has the same intended effect as doing it once.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: REST-style APIs use familiar web infrastructure and serve many clients. Design still requires decisions about schemas, compatibility, security, and failures; REST does not prescribe one universal URL or JSON format.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• REST is not synonymous with JSON; REST is an architectural style, while JSON is one possible representation format.
  • A URL alone does not define the operation; method semantics matter.
  • Every successful request does not need to use status 200; for example, resource creation can use 201.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official standard: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics defines HTTP methods, status codes, and message semantics.
  • Reference: MDN: REST provides a concise explanation of REST and its constraints.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text: This section explores how applications store, retrieve, organize, and optimize data using database concepts and selected database systems.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand core database concepts and the trade-offs behind data models.
  • Build familiarity with MongoDB and PostgreSQL.
  • Connect database choices and operations to application needs.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Database Fundamentals
  • MongoDB
  • PostgreSQL

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A database is an organized system for storing information so software can find and change it reliably. Applications use databases for user profiles, orders, messages, and product catalogs. The MongoDB learning path and PostgreSQL learning path show two approaches.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Keeping application data only in a program's memory loses it when the program stops and makes it hard to share. A database persists data, provides ways to search it, and coordinates simultaneous changes.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
The application sends a request using a database language or client library. The database locates or changes records, applies consistency rules, and returns a result. Relational databases organize values into tables; document databases store structured documents. Indexes speed up selected lookups at the cost of storage and write work.

Transactions group operations so they succeed or fail together. Backups and replication help with recovery and availability.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A shop might store customers, products, and orders. Staff can look up an order by number or total sales by date.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Choose a database based on data shape, query patterns, consistency needs, and operational constraints—not popularity alone. Define what each record means before optimizing. Use parameters, validate input, and keep credentials out of source code.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
This local-only SQL example illustrates a table and a read; it assumes a practice database and creates no external connection:

CREATE TABLE demo_notes (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO demo_notes (id, title) VALUES (1, 'Database basics');
SELECT title FROM demo_notes WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Schema: rules describing data structure.
  • Query: a request to read or change data.
  • Index: structure that helps locate records faster.
  • Transaction: a group of database operations treated as one unit.
  • Persistence: retaining data beyond a program's lifetime.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Databases make durable, shared, searchable data practical and can enforce constraints. They also add setup and maintenance. No one data model is best for every workload.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A database is not automatically a backup. Adding indexes to every field can slow writes and consume space. “NoSQL” does not mean “no structure”; document data still benefits from clear rules.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official PostgreSQL documentation — Getting Started: a guided introduction to relational database concepts and SQL.
  • Official MongoDB documentation — Documents: explains MongoDB's basic unit of stored data.

docs.title: MongoDB
docs.text: MongoDB stores BSON documents in collections. This module is a focused learning path through its data model, query language, development tools, performance, consistency, security, and operations. It is divided into short lessons so each subject can be studied on its own.

docs.title: Suggested learning path
docs.text:
1. Start with databases and collections, BSON documents and types, and ObjectIds.
  2. Practice query operators, projection and pagination, inserts, updates, upserts, and deletes.
  3. Learn data modeling, schema validation, index design, and query plans.
  4. Study aggregation pipelines, then work through the dedicated lessons on stages, expressions, joins, facets, and output.
  5. Use Atlas, Compass, mongosh, and driver connections to practice with a development deployment.
  6. Finish with consistency, transactions, replication, sharding, change streams, security, networking, backup, and operations.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text: Use the MongoDB questions and answers lesson to review the module and identify topics to revisit.

docs.title: Topics beyond the core path
docs.text:
The navigation also covers collation, geospatial queries, views, time-series collections, TTL indexes, capped collections, GridFS, MongoDB Search and Vector Search, storage engines, journaling, import/export, and migration.

Start with Database Fundamentals and compare this document model with PostgreSQL. Choose designs from workload and consistency needs; flexible schema still benefits from deliberate contracts and indexes.

docs.title: Official documentation
docs.text:
• MongoDB Manual
  • Atlas documentation
  • Compass documentation
  • mongosh documentation
  • MongoDB drivers

Use documentation for the server and tool versions you deploy because features and behavior evolve.

docs.title: Aggregation Expressions and Accumulators
docs.text:
Expressions compute values in stages such as $project, $set, and $group. A field path such as "$price" reads a field; $$ROOT refers to the current root document, while variables such as $$NOW expose server values in supported contexts.

Arithmetic operators include $add, $subtract, $multiply, and $divide. Conditional operators include $cond, $ifNull, and $switch. Comparison and boolean expressions can build derived flags. Array, string, date, and type operators support transformations without application-side loops.

Accumulators summarize a group or window: $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $first, $last, $push, and $addToSet. In $group, _id is the grouping key and each accumulator computes a value for that group. $first and $last depend on input order; sort explicitly if order matters.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $set: { lineTotal: { $multiply: ["$quantity", "$unitPrice"] } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$customerId",
      revenue: { $sum: "$lineTotal" },
      average: { $avg: "$lineTotal" },
      products: { $addToSet: "$sku" }
  } }
])

Null, missing, and type conversions can produce subtle results. Use $ifNull, $convert, or explicit type checks where inputs vary, and test edge cases. See aggregation expressions and accumulators.

docs.title: Aggregation Joins, Facets, and Windows
docs.text:
$lookup performs a left outer join from the current collection to a foreign collection and places matching documents in an array. Equality joins use localField and foreignField; pipeline form supports more complex matching. Index the foreign join field and bound the result where possible.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer"
  } },
  { $unwind: { path: "$customer", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } }
])

$unwind turns array elements into separate pipeline documents. preserveNullAndEmptyArrays keeps documents with a missing or empty array. This option changes whether a join behaves like an inner or left join after unwind.

$facet runs multiple branches over a common input, often for a page plus facets or counts. $setWindowFields calculates over partitions and sort order, such as rankings or running totals, without collapsing every partition into one document. These stages can require substantial memory and sort work; inspect plans and pipeline limits. See lookup, unwind, and setWindowFields.

docs.title: Aggregation Output and Materialized Results
docs.text:
Most aggregation pipelines return a cursor. $merge and $out write pipeline output to a collection and must be the final stage. They are useful for batch summaries, precomputed reports, or materialized views.

$merge can insert new output and merge, replace, keep, or fail on matching target documents according to its options. Choose a stable on-field and unique index so reruns have predictable behavior. $out replaces a target collection with pipeline results and has restrictions on target namespace and deployment. Neither stage should be treated as a casual substitute for an application write.

Design refresh schedules and failure behavior: Is the result stale while recomputing? Can consumers read the old result until the new one is ready? What happens if the job stops midway? Restrict privileges on output collections and avoid targeting live collections unintentionally.

Use a non-production target while learning. Check server-version and sharded-cluster restrictions before deployment. See $merge and $out.

docs.title: Aggregation Patterns and Tuning
docs.text:
Aggregation is a staged transformation. A common reporting flow matches a bounded time range, unwinds line items, joins dimensions, computes values, groups results, sorts, and limits output. Stage order affects both meaning and cost.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { state: "paid" } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $set: { lineTotal: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$customerId",
      spend: { $sum: "$lineTotal" },
      products: { $addToSet: "$items.sku" }
  } },
  { $sort: { spend: -1, _id: 1 } },
  { $limit: 20 }
])

Use $facet to run multiple branches over one input, such as a page and count summary. $bucket and $bucketAuto group values into ranges. $setWindowFields calculates over ordered partitions, for example a running total. $unionWith combines another collection's pipeline output. $replaceRoot and $replaceWith change the current document shape.

$merge writes results to a target collection and supports merge/replace strategies; $out writes pipeline output as a collection under its documented restrictions. Both are terminal write stages. Check deployed-version rules before using them.

Filter early where semantics allow, bound arrays before $unwind, and use indexes for initial matching and sorting. Large $group and sort stages can consume substantial memory. Inspect explain output and intermediate result sizes with representative data. See pipeline stages and pipeline limits.

docs.title: Aggregation Stages
docs.text:
A pipeline applies stages in sequence. Each stage receives the prior stage's documents, so placing a stage changes both output and cost.

  • $match filters by query predicates and can use an index when placed early.
  • $project selects or computes output fields; $set/$addFields adds or replaces fields.
  • $unwind emits one document per array element.
  • $group combines documents by a key and uses accumulators.
  • $sort orders output; $skip and $limit control result windows.
  • $lookup joins another collection into an array; $unionWith combines another pipeline's output.
  • $facet runs independent subpipelines over the same input.
  • $bucket and $bucketAuto group values into ranges; $setWindowFields computes over ordered partitions.
  • $replaceRoot/$replaceWith changes the current document shape.
  • $count returns a count of pipeline documents.

Use $match early to reduce work, but preserve semantics when moving stages. Put a limit before expensive work only when it does not change the intended result. See aggregation pipeline stages.

docs.title: Aggregation Pipelines
docs.text: An aggregation pipeline transforms documents through an ordered list of stages. Each stage receives the previous stage's output. Stages filter, reshape, split arrays, group, join, sort, paginate, or write results. Expressions compute values within stages.

docs.title: Example: category revenue
docs.text:
Assume each order has a status, date, and items array with productId, quantity, and unitPrice. Products contain a category.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "paid", createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2026-01-01") } } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "products",
      localField: "items.productId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "product"
    }
  },
  { $unwind: "$product" },
  {
    $project: {
      category: "$product.category",
      lineTotal: { $multiply: ["$items.quantity", "$items.unitPrice"] }
    }
  },
  {
    $group: {
      _id: "$category",
      revenue: { $sum: "$lineTotal" },
      lineCount: { $sum: 1 },
      averageLine: { $avg: "$lineTotal" }
    }
  },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

The initial $match reduces input and may use an index. $unwind emits one pipeline document per array element. $lookup matches another collection and adds an array of results; the second $unwind turns each matched product into a document. $project keeps or computes fields, and $group groups by its _id expression.

docs.title: Common stages
docs.text:
• $match: keep documents matching a query predicate.
  • $project: include, exclude, rename, or compute fields.
  • $group: group documents and calculate accumulators.
  • $unwind: expand array elements into separate documents.
  • $lookup: join a foreign collection into an array field.
  • $sort, $skip, and $limit: order and paginate results. Large offsets with $skip require walking past skipped results; range pagination can scale better.
  • $facet: run multiple subpipelines over the same input, for example a result page and summary counts.
  • $merge: write pipeline output into a collection, merging with or replacing matching documents according to its options.
  • $out: write results to a collection by replacing it; it has restrictions, so check the server-version documentation before using it.

$merge and $out are terminal write stages and are useful for batch summaries or materialized views. Treat their target collections and rerun behavior as part of the job design.

docs.title: Expressions and accumulators
docs.text:
Expressions include field paths such as "$price"; arithmetic such as $add and $multiply; conditionals such as $cond and $ifNull; comparisons; and array, string, and date operations. For instance, { $cond: [{ $gte: ["$qty", 10] }, "bulk", "single"] } classifies a quantity.

Accumulators operate within $group or selected other stages: $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $first, $last, $push, and $addToSet. Sort before $first or $last when a specific ordering is required.

Stage order changes both meaning and cost. Filter early, keep only useful fields where appropriate, and measure large groups and sorts. See aggregation pipeline stages and aggregation expressions.

docs.title: Arrays and Embedded Values
docs.text:
Arrays are useful for bounded, related values such as tags or order line items. They support atomic updates alongside the parent document. Unbounded arrays can grow documents, increase write cost, and complicate pagination.

A filter such as { tags: "sale" } matches an array containing that value. Use $all when every listed value must exist, $size for exact length, and $elemMatch when multiple predicates must match one array element.

db.orders.find({
  items: { $elemMatch: { sku: "p-100", quantity: { $gte: 2 } } }
})

Array updates include $push (append), $addToSet (append only when absent), $pull (remove matches), and $pop (remove an endpoint). The positional $ operator updates the first matched element; $[] updates all elements; $[name] updates elements matching arrayFilters.

db.orders.updateOne(
  { _id: orderId },
  { $set: { "items.$[line].quantity": 3 } },
  { arrayFilters: [{ "line.sku": "p-100" }] }
)

Array fields create multikey indexes; compound multikey indexes have restrictions. If a child list can grow without a practical bound, consider a separate collection with a reference to its parent. See array query operators and array update operators.

docs.title: MongoDB Atlas
docs.text: Atlas is MongoDB's managed database platform. Its hierarchy includes organizations, projects, database deployments, Atlas users, and database users. Atlas users sign in to manage cloud resources; database users authenticate applications and tools to database data. These identities are separate and have separate privileges.

docs.title: Create a learning deployment
docs.text:
Create a project and development deployment, create a narrowly privileged database user, add the client network to the project's IP access list, then connect using the Atlas connection dialog. A database deployment is not reachable merely because it exists: network access and database authentication both need configuration.

Atlas tiers, regions, backup features, and network options vary. Review current availability and pricing before choosing a production design. Clean up test users, access-list entries, and unused deployments when finished. Store connection URIs as secrets; never commit them to source control.

Atlas provides managed infrastructure features, but application teams still own data modeling, indexes, authorization, retention, recovery objectives, cost controls, and safe query behavior. See the official Atlas documentation and connect guide.

docs.title: Backup and Restore
docs.text:
Define recovery point objective (acceptable data loss) and recovery time objective (time to restore) before selecting a backup method. Replication is not backup: accidental updates and deletes replicate.

Atlas backup capabilities and retention vary by deployment configuration. Self-managed options include storage snapshots and logical dumps using mongodump/mongorestore. Database Tools are useful for logical exports and smaller deployments but can add performance load; sharded deployments need a coordinated backup approach.

mongodump --uri="$MONGODB_URI" --archive=backup.archive --gzip
mongorestore --uri="$RESTORE_URI" --archive=backup.archive --gzip

Keep backups encrypted, access-controlled, and outside the database failure domain. Protect credentials and avoid putting them in shell history. Schedule restore drills: verify target cluster, collections, indexes, user/role requirements, application compatibility, and recovery time. Document point-in-time recovery steps if the selected service supports them.

A backup job that reports success is not proof that recovery will work. Regularly test restoration against the stated RPO/RTO. See backup and restore tools, mongodump, and Atlas backup.

docs.title: BSON Documents and Types
docs.text:
A BSON document is an ordered set of fields and values. MongoDB stores documents in collections; each document has a unique _id field. Nested documents model structured values, while arrays model ordered lists. BSON supports strings, booleans, null, dates, binary data, ObjectIds, Decimal128, and multiple integer and floating-point types.

Use BSON Date for timestamps rather than strings so range queries and date operators behave correctly. For money, use Decimal128 or integer minor units instead of binary floating point when exact decimal arithmetic matters. Choose one consistent identifier type for related documents. Field names and types should be stable even though MongoDB permits variation.

JSON tools may not preserve BSON distinctions. Extended JSON represents BSON-only types when exporting or transmitting documents through JSON-oriented systems. Documents are limited in size; large content can use GridFS or object storage.

See BSON types, documents, and Extended JSON.

docs.title: Bulk Writes
docs.text:
bulkWrite() sends multiple insert, update, replace, and delete operations together. It reduces round trips and can improve throughput for imports or synchronization, but it does not make a whole arbitrary batch one atomic transaction.

db.inventory.bulkWrite([
  { updateOne: { filter: { sku: "p-100" }, update: { $inc: { stock: -1 } } } },
  { updateMany: { filter: { discontinued: true }, update: { $set: { available: false } } } },
  { insertOne: { document: { sku: "p-200", stock: 20 } } },
  { deleteOne: { filter: { sku: "retired" } } }
], { ordered: false })

Ordered writes execute in sequence and stop on an error. Unordered writes continue where possible and may execute operations in parallel. Results can contain partial success and per-operation errors. Bound batch sizes, use stable identifiers, and make retries idempotent.

Drivers generally expose bulkWrite at collection level. Newer server/driver versions may support cross-namespace operations; verify compatibility before using them. On sharded collections, unordered writes may distribute more efficiently, but shard-key choice still matters. See bulk write operations.

docs.title: Capped Collections
docs.text:
A capped collection is a fixed-size collection that preserves insertion order and overwrites the oldest documents when it reaches its configured size. It can support bounded rolling logs or event buffers when overwrite semantics are acceptable.

Capped collections have behavioral restrictions compared with ordinary collections: documents cannot be deleted individually, and update operations cannot increase document size. They do not provide general retention guarantees based on event time. For time-based expiration, consider a TTL index; for high-volume time-stamped measurements, consider a time-series collection.

db.createCollection("recentEvents", {
  capped: true,
  size: 10485760,
  max: 100000
})

Choose size and max-document limits from expected event size and retention rate. Capped collections preserve insertion order, but they are not a replacement for a durable event log or backup. See capped collections.

docs.title: Change Streams
docs.text:
Change streams let applications subscribe to majority-committed changes on a collection, database, or deployment. They use aggregation pipelines to filter and reshape event notifications and require a replica set or sharded cluster. Common uses include cache invalidation, event-driven integration, and synchronizing a search index.

const stream = db.orders.watch([
  { $match: { "fullDocument.state": "paid" } }
])
while (stream.hasNext()) {
  const event = stream.next()
  printjson(event)
}

Production applications should use the official driver stream API and close cursors during shutdown. Every event includes an _id resume token. Persist a token only after its event has been processed durably; after a crash, processing can repeat, so consumers should be idempotent. Resume requires that the oplog still contains the needed history. Handle network interruption, elections, invalidation, and expired tokens.

Pre- and post-images can be enabled for collections when the application needs document state before or after updates and deletes. They add storage and retention considerations. Do not remove or alter the event _id in the pipeline. See change streams.

docs.title: Collation and String Comparison
docs.text:
Collation defines language-aware string comparison rules, including case and accent handling. Without an explicit collation, MongoDB uses simple binary comparison. Collation can be specified on a collection or on supported operations and indexes.

db.users.createIndex(
  { displayName: 1 },
  { collation: { locale: "en", strength: 2 } }
)
db.users.find({ displayName: "ada" })
  .collation({ locale: "en", strength: 2 })

An operation's collation must be compatible with an index for the index to support string comparisons. A collection default collation can affect operations that do not specify one. Collation is not equivalent to normalizing stored strings; consider product requirements around case folding, accents, and locale sorting.

Use consistent collation across index creation and query execution. Test with representative Unicode values and check explain output. See collation.

docs.title: MongoDB Compass
docs.text: Compass is MongoDB's graphical interface for connecting to deployments, exploring documents, building filters and aggregation pipelines, inspecting schemas, and managing indexes.

docs.title: Everyday workflow
docs.text:
Connect with a local or Atlas URI, select the intended database and collection, and use the Documents tab to filter, sort, project, and inspect records. The query filter uses MongoDB Query Language, for example: { status: "paid", total: { $gte: 50 } }. The Schema tab samples documents to summarize field types and values; sampling is useful for discovery but does not prove that every document follows the same shape.

The Aggregations tab helps construct stages and examine intermediate results. The Indexes tab shows existing indexes and may provide index management actions, depending on Compass edition, connected server, and privileges. Explain plans help investigate query behavior.

Treat Compass edits as real database writes. Confirm the selected environment before deleting or changing data, use least-privilege credentials, and practice against a development deployment. Turn exploratory work into reviewed scripts or migrations so it can be repeated. See Compass documentation, view documents, and analyze a schema.

docs.title: Connection Strings and Drivers
docs.text:
Use an official MongoDB driver for application access. Drivers handle connection pools, BSON conversion, topology discovery, sessions, and supported retry behavior. Select a version compatible with both the application runtime and server deployment.

A standard URI can list hosts, while an Atlas SRV URI uses DNS to discover hosts. URIs can also define a default database, authentication source, TLS, and timeouts. Atlas supplies a URI through its connect workflow. Do not commit credentials in connection strings; reserved characters in credentials may need percent encoding. Keep secrets in environment-specific secret storage and prevent them from appearing in logs.

Create one long-lived client per application process so requests can reuse its connection pool. Close it during orderly shutdown. Tune pool sizes and timeouts from measured concurrency and failure behavior. Let the driver implement retryable operations where supported; for application retries, ensure the operation is idempotent or protected by an idempotency key.

A connection failure can arise from DNS/SRV lookup, firewall routes, TLS verification, the Atlas IP access list, authentication, or database roles. Diagnose the failing layer without disabling certificate checks or broadening network access unnecessarily. See the connection string reference and official drivers.

docs.title: Cursors and Read Methods
docs.text:
find() returns a cursor, which retrieves result batches instead of materializing every document at once. Drivers expose cursor iteration APIs; consume results incrementally and close cursors when finished. Avoid converting unbounded result sets into arrays in application memory.

findOne() returns one matching document or null. Without sort, it does not mean newest or otherwise preferred. countDocuments(filter) counts matching documents; estimatedDocumentCount() uses collection metadata and cannot apply a filter. distinct(field, filter) returns distinct values but can be expensive for high-cardinality fields.

const cursor = db.orders.find({ state: "open" }).sort({ createdAt: 1 })
while (await cursor.hasNext()) {
  const order = await cursor.next()
  // process a bounded unit of work
}

Cursors use batches and can expire when idle or when the session ends. Configure batch size based on payload and memory needs, not as a substitute for limits. Keyset pagination is usually preferable to a long-lived cursor for user-facing page navigation. See cursor behavior and find.

docs.title: Data Modeling and Validation
docs.text: Design a MongoDB schema from the operations the application needs: list important reads and writes, their filters and sort order, and the expected data growth. Data accessed and updated together is often a useful modeling clue.

docs.title: Embed or reference
docs.text:
Embed bounded data that is commonly read with its parent, such as a shipping address snapshot inside an order. This can reduce round trips and lets a single-document update preserve an invariant atomically. Reference data that is shared, independently queried, or grows without a practical bound, such as a customer's orders. References require additional queries or an aggregation join such as $lookup.

Embedding duplicates values when useful, but duplicated values need an update policy. Avoid unbounded arrays: large arrays can grow documents and make writes increasingly expensive. MongoDB supports relational patterns; a document model does not mean every relationship should be embedded.

docs.title: Enforce useful shape
docs.text:
Collections have flexible schemas by default. Add validation when a collection needs a reliable contract. This example requires a nonnegative numeric price:

db.createCollection("products", {
  validator: {
    $jsonSchema: {
      bsonType: "object",
      required: ["sku", "price"],
      properties: {
        sku: { bsonType: "string" },
        price: { bsonType: ["int", "long", "double", "decimal"], minimum: 0 }
      }
    }
  },
  validationLevel: "strict",
  validationAction: "error"
})

Validation is evaluated on writes and can reject invalid documents; it complements application validation and domain rules. Choose validation behavior deliberately when rolling out schema changes to existing data.

docs.title: Design workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the workload and high-value queries.
  2. Map relationships and decide what to embed or reference.
  3. Choose document shapes that support those operations.
  4. Add validation for invariants and indexes for query patterns.
  5. Revisit the model as measurements and access patterns change.

See MongoDB's data modeling guide and schema validation reference.

docs.title: Databases and Collections
docs.text:
A database is a namespace for collections. A collection stores documents and has collection-level options such as validation, default collation, capped behavior, or time-series configuration. Databases and collections are often created implicitly by first write, but explicit creation is useful when configuring validation, capped size, time-series options, or other collection settings.

use shop
db.createCollection("products")
show dbs
show collections

An empty database may not appear in listings until it contains data. Collection names should be stable and avoid reserved system namespaces. Collections can have indexes and validators; those properties are part of the data contract and should be managed deliberately.

Use separate databases when access boundaries, deployment ownership, or lifecycle needs differ. Use collections to group documents with related query and validation behavior. Splitting collections solely because fields differ is often unnecessary; polymorphic documents can share a collection when queries and indexes remain clear.

See databases and collections and create collections.

docs.title: Delete and Bulk Operations
docs.text:
deleteOne(filter) removes at most one match; deleteMany(filter) removes all matches. An empty filter matches every document. Before deletion, run find(filter) with a projection and a small limit to confirm the target. A TTL index can suit automatic expiry when the retention rule is based on a date.

db.sessions.deleteMany({ expiresAt: { $lt: new Date() } })

bulkWrite() combines inserts, updates, replacements, and deletes in fewer round trips. Ordered batches stop on an error; unordered batches continue where possible. Use bounded batch sizes, account for partial failures, and ensure retries cannot create duplicate business effects.

db.inventory.bulkWrite([
  { updateOne: { filter: { sku: "p-100" }, update: { $inc: { stock: -1 } } } },
  { insertOne: { document: { sku: "p-101", stock: 20 } } }
], { ordered: false })

Deletion is not reversible without a backup or another recovery path. Use transactions only when deletion must coordinate atomically with other writes. Grant application roles only the write actions they need. See delete methods and bulk write operations.

docs.title: Delete Operations
docs.text:
deleteOne(filter) removes at most one document matching a filter. deleteMany(filter) removes every match. A filter of {} matches all documents, so never use an empty filter unless removing the full collection contents is deliberate.

const target = { state: "expired", expiresAt: { $lt: new Date() } }
db.sessions.find(target, { _id: 1, expiresAt: 1 }).limit(20)
db.sessions.deleteMany(target)

Preview a destructive filter with find(), countDocuments(), and a narrow projection before issuing the delete. Check deletedCount and log enough operational context to audit the action without logging secrets or sensitive document contents.

Deletion is not automatically reversible. Backups or point-in-time recovery may be needed. TTL indexes can expire documents asynchronously based on a BSON Date; use them for retention, not exact-time deletion. A multi-document delete is not a single-document atomic operation. See delete methods.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A single-document write is atomic, including changes to nested fields and arrays in that document. Prefer a model that keeps common invariants within one document when that is natural. Use a multi-document transaction when a business operation must commit or roll back changes across documents. Transactions have coordination and performance costs and are supported on replica sets and sharded clusters, not standalone deployments.

In a driver, start a session, run the related operations in a transaction, then commit; abort on failure. Design for transient transaction errors and retries using the driver's documented transaction API. Choose read concern, write concern, and read preference to match the consistency and durability contract. See transactions.

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
A replica set is a group of MongoDB processes that maintain the same data set. The primary accepts writes and records operations in its oplog; secondaries replicate those operations. If the primary becomes unavailable, eligible members can elect a replacement. Replication improves availability and can support reads from secondaries, but secondary reads may lag behind writes.

Write concern controls acknowledgment requirements. A majority write concern waits for acknowledgment from a majority of voting members, subject to deployment configuration. Replication is not a backup: accidental updates and deletions replicate too. Maintain backups and test restores. See replica set architecture.

docs.title: Sharding
docs.text:
Sharding distributes collection data across shards, coordinated by query routers and configuration servers. A shard key controls how documents are partitioned and where operations are routed. A good key offers sufficient cardinality and distributes writes and storage while supporting common query targeting.

A monotonically increasing key can concentrate new writes on one range. Hashed keys can spread writes but make range queries less targeted. Poor shard-key choices are expensive to correct, so understand workload, distribution, and growth before sharding. Queries that include the shard key can often target fewer shards; scatter-gather queries consult more of the cluster. Sharding adds operational complexity and should be driven by measured capacity or throughput needs. See sharding.

docs.title: Documents and CRUD
docs.text: MongoDB organizes data as databases, collections, and BSON documents. BSON is a binary representation with types such as dates, ObjectIds, and 64-bit integers. Documents have an _id key, generated as an ObjectId when omitted; nested objects and arrays express related values naturally.

docs.title: Create and read
docs.text:
In mongosh, select a database and insert a document:

use shop
db.products.insertOne({
  sku: "p-100",
  name: "Notebook",
  price: 8.5,
  tags: ["paper", "stationery"],
  createdAt: new Date()
})

Find matching documents with a filter. The second argument is a projection; inclusion projections can include _id unless explicitly excluded.

db.products.find(
  { price: { $gte: 5 }, tags: "paper" },
  { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 }
).sort({ price: 1 }).limit(20)

Filters support comparison operators such as $gt, $in, and $ne, logical operators such as $and and $or, and array matching. Use a field path such as "address.city" to match a nested field. Treat request input as data and validate it; do not accept arbitrary client-supplied query operators.

docs.title: Update and delete
docs.text:
Use update operators to change selected fields without replacing the full document:

db.products.updateOne(
  { sku: "p-100" },
  { $set: { price: 9 }, $inc: { stock: 1 } }
)

Other common operators include $unset, $min, $max, and array operators such as $push and $addToSet. A replacement update replaces the document contents except for its identity. Use it only when replacement is intended. An upsert inserts when no document matches; choose its filter and update carefully to avoid accidental duplicates.

db.products.deleteOne({ sku: "p-100" })

Check acknowledged results and matched/modified/deleted counts. A write to one document is atomic. Multi-document operations can partially succeed unless enclosed in a transaction. See the official CRUD guide.

docs.title: Encryption and Data Protection
docs.text:
TLS protects network traffic between MongoDB and clients. Configure certificate verification and hostname validation; do not disable them to bypass a connection error. Atlas configures transport encryption for its service, while self-managed deployments require server and client TLS configuration.

Encryption at rest protects stored files and snapshots. Atlas and self-managed offerings differ in key-management options. Customer-managed keys can give an organization more control but create responsibilities for availability, access, rotation, and recovery. Keep keys separate from encrypted backups and rehearse rotation.

Client-side field-level encryption encrypts selected values before sending them to the database, reducing what database infrastructure can read. Queryable Encryption and related capabilities have driver, server, and workload constraints. Encryption does not hide all metadata and does not replace authorization, secure logs, data minimization, or backup protection.

Classify data and keep secrets out of logs and exports. Review TLS configuration and encryption.

docs.title: Geospatial Queries
docs.text:
MongoDB supports geospatial data using GeoJSON objects and legacy coordinate pairs. GeoJSON uses longitude before latitude and stores geometry in a field such as location.

db.places.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" })
db.places.find({
  location: {
    $near: {
      $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [77.5946, 12.9716] },
      $maxDistance: 5000
    }
  }
})

A 2dsphere index supports spherical geometry operations and GeoJSON. A 2d index supports legacy planar coordinate pairs. Operators include $near, $geoWithin, and $geoIntersects, with behavior depending on index type and geometry.

Validate coordinate order, coordinate ranges, and geometry shape at the application boundary. Geospatial queries can be expensive if the search region is broad; constrain them with additional predicates and limits when appropriate. See geospatial queries and 2dsphere indexes.

docs.title: GridFS and Large Files
docs.text:
BSON documents have a 16 MiB size limit. GridFS stores a file as metadata and chunks in collections, allowing a driver to stream content larger than one document. Drivers provide upload and download APIs.

GridFS can fit applications that need file metadata queries or want content managed through MongoDB's access model. Object storage is often a better choice for large media delivery, lifecycle management, and cost. Compare network, backup, and operational costs before choosing.

A file spans multiple documents, so it does not behave as one atomic document update. Failed uploads can leave partial chunks that need cleanup. Define versioning and deletion rules, and store metadata such as owner, content type, size, and checksum deliberately. Never trust user-supplied filenames or MIME types for access control or content safety.

See the GridFS manual.

docs.title: Import, Export, and Data Migration
docs.text:
MongoDB Database Tools include mongoimport and mongoexport for JSON/CSV-oriented exchange, and mongodump/mongorestore for BSON database dumps. These tools serve different purposes: JSON/CSV are useful for interchange, while BSON dumps preserve MongoDB-specific types better.

mongoimport --uri="$MONGODB_URI" --db=shop --collection=products --file=products.json
mongoexport --uri="$MONGODB_URI" --db=shop --collection=products --out=products.json

Test imports on a disposable database. Decide whether the target collection should be dropped, merged, or appended; validate field types, duplicate keys, encoding, and row counts. Large imports should use bounded batches and report rejected records. Avoid putting credentials in command history.

For production migration, plan source/target compatibility, indexes, validation, change capture or write downtime, cutover, rollback, and data verification. Atlas migration tools and cloud provider features vary. See mongoimport, mongoexport, and migration guidance.

docs.title: Index Types
docs.text:
An index supports particular query patterns. MongoDB creates the _id index automatically; other indexes should be justified by filters, sorts, uniqueness rules, or specialized workloads.

  • Single-field and compound indexes support equality/range predicates and sorts. Compound field order is significant and can support leading prefixes.
  • Multikey indexes index array values. Compound multikey indexes have restrictions when multiple indexed fields are arrays.
  • Unique indexes enforce uniqueness; creating one fails if existing values conflict.
  • Partial indexes include only documents matching a filter and can reduce size for a subset workload.
  • Sparse indexes omit documents without the indexed field. Understand how this differs from partial filters.
  • TTL indexes expire documents asynchronously based on dates; they are not exact timers.
  • Text and geospatial indexes serve specialized search patterns. Wildcard indexes can support queries over unknown fields but are not a substitute for schema and query design.
  • Hidden indexes let you evaluate planner impact without serving queries, where supported.

Indexes improve reads but consume disk and memory and increase write work. Avoid redundant indexes and measure usage. See index types and index properties.

docs.title: Indexes and Query Performance
docs.text:
An index stores an ordered representation of selected fields so MongoDB can locate and order matching documents without scanning the whole collection. The _id index is created automatically; other indexes should support measured query patterns.

db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 })
db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })

The compound index supports equality on customerId followed by a recent-first order on createdAt. Field order matters: a compound index can support its leading prefixes, but not every permutation. Unique indexes enforce a data rule as well as speeding lookups; resolve existing duplicates before creating one.

Indexes consume storage and memory and add work to inserts, updates, and deletes. Avoid indexing every field. For each important query, inspect the plan:

db.orders.find({ customerId: "c-42" })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .explain("executionStats")

Compare documents and keys examined with documents returned, and check whether the plan uses the intended index. A covered query can return from index keys alone when the filter and projection are supported by that index. Use representative data and production-like cardinalities; a query that is fast on a tiny collection may behave differently at scale.
