Other index types support specific workloads, including text, geospatial, and TTL expiration. TTL indexes remove eligible documents asynchronously and are not an exact timer. Review index types and index properties.

docs.title: Insert and Read Operations
docs.text:
insertOne() inserts one document and returns its _id. insertMany() inserts a batch; by default an error can stop ordered inserts, while unordered inserts continue where possible and report failures. Unique indexes can reject duplicates, so bulk imports need error reporting and a safe restart strategy.

db.products.insertOne({
  sku: "p-100", name: "Notebook", price: 8.5,
  tags: ["paper"], createdAt: new Date()
})

find() returns a cursor. Iterate it or use a limit rather than reading an unbounded collection into application memory. findOne() returns one match or null. Without an explicit sort, the selected matching document is not guaranteed to be the newest or otherwise meaningful first result.

db.products.find({ price: { $lt: 10 } }, { name: 1, price: 1 })
  .sort({ price: 1, _id: 1 }).limit(50)
db.products.countDocuments({ tags: "paper" })

countDocuments(filter) counts matching documents. estimatedDocumentCount() uses collection metadata and cannot filter; it is intended as a faster estimate. Write concern controls acknowledgment and durability expectations; choose it with the deployment and application requirements in mind. See insert methods and find methods.

docs.title: Insert Operations
docs.text:
insertOne() writes one document. If _id is omitted, MongoDB generates an ObjectId. insertMany() writes a list of documents and reports inserted identifiers and errors. Ordered inserts stop at the first error by default; unordered inserts continue where possible and may improve throughput for independent records.

db.products.insertMany([
  { sku: "p-100", name: "Notebook", price: 8.5 },
  { sku: "p-101", name: "Pen", price: 1.25 }
], { ordered: false })

A unique-index conflict or schema validation failure can make an insert fail. For unordered batches, account for partial success and retry only records that did not succeed. Design imports to be idempotent, often with stable keys and upserts rather than assuming a batch runs once.

Single-document inserts are atomic. Bulk writes can mix insert, update, replace, and delete operations; see bulk writes. See official insert methods and insert documents.

docs.title: mongosh
docs.text: mongosh is MongoDB's interactive JavaScript shell. It connects to local, self-managed, or Atlas deployments and is useful for learning, inspecting data, running administrative commands, and executing scripts. It is the current shell; old tutorials may refer to the legacy mongo shell.

docs.title: Connect and inspect
docs.text:
mongosh "mongodb://localhost:27017"
mongosh "mongodb+srv://user@cluster.example.mongodb.net/app"

Avoid placing passwords directly in shell commands, shell history, or logs. Use a secure prompt or secret handling appropriate to the environment.

show dbs
use app
show collections
db.products.find({ active: true }).limit(10)
db.products.getIndexes()
db.products.countDocuments({ active: true })

The db helper refers to the selected database. Collection methods issue database operations. Use help, db.help(), and db.collection.help() for shell guidance. Scripts can be loaded and run from mongosh; scope them to an explicit database and make them safe to rerun.

Before destructive work, print the current database and deployment, inspect the filter with find(), and use a disposable collection for practice. Install and connection details are in the mongosh documentation.

docs.title: Atlas Network Access and IP Allowlisting
docs.text:
An Atlas project IP access list restricts which client source addresses can connect to its database deployments. Add the public egress IP used by the application or workstation, or a carefully controlled CIDR range. Private networking options such as VPC/VNet peering and private endpoints may be preferable for production environments.

Atlas requires both network permission and a valid database user. An allowed IP without credentials cannot authenticate; valid credentials from an unlisted IP cannot connect. Home and office public addresses can change, causing previously working clients to fail. Some access-list entries can be temporary for short-lived administration.

Do not add 0.0.0.0/0 for convenience. It allows connection attempts from anywhere and increases exposure. Use the narrowest viable range, strong authentication, TLS, and least-privilege roles. Removing an entry may not close already established sessions immediately.

Client firewalls may also need documented outbound TCP access to Atlas hosts and ports. Check DNS/SRV resolution, outbound routing, TLS verification, Atlas allowlist entries, database credentials, then roles when diagnosing a connection failure. See Atlas IP access lists and Atlas connection requirements.

docs.title: ObjectIds and Identifier Design
docs.text:
MongoDB requires each document to have a unique _id within its collection. If the client omits it, MongoDB drivers commonly generate an ObjectId. ObjectIds are 12-byte BSON values that include a timestamp component and additional bytes designed to make collisions very unlikely across processes.

The timestamp can help roughly order creation, but ObjectIds are not a strict global clock, sequence, or reliable business timestamp. Client clocks can differ and values can be generated before insertion. Store a separate BSON Date for event or creation time when that meaning matters.

Applications can use UUIDs, strings, or other supported BSON values as _id. Choose one stable type and format across references; type mismatches affect equality matching and index behavior. If an identifier is supplied by the client, validate its format and uniqueness. A unique index can enforce other business identifiers such as email or external order number.

See BSON ObjectId and document structure.

docs.title: MongoDB Operations
docs.text: Operations includes routine health checks, capacity planning, incident response, upgrades, backup verification, and query troubleshooting. Managed Atlas automates parts of infrastructure operation; application teams still own access policy, data lifecycle, recovery requirements, query quality, and cost.

docs.title: Monitor
docs.text: Track availability, latency percentiles, request throughput, errors, connections, CPU, memory, disk space and latency, storage growth, replication lag, and backup status. Use alerts tied to user impact and document the response steps. For self-managed deployments, collect server metrics and logs and protect administrative interfaces.

docs.title: Troubleshoot slow queries
docs.text: Capture the filter, sort, projection, result count, and realistic values. Use explain("executionStats") and compare keys/documents examined with documents returned. Check collection scans, blocking sorts, low selectivity, and oversized results. Profiler output can help find slow operations but adds overhead; enable it deliberately and manage sensitive query data in logs.

docs.title: Operate safely
docs.text: Reuse driver clients and connection pools. Bound query results and batches. Keep supported server versions, review upgrade compatibility, and rehearse upgrades with representative data. Plan disk space for data, indexes, journal, oplog, temporary aggregation work, and backups. Test recovery procedures and certificate rotation before an incident. See the operations checklist and Atlas monitoring.

docs.title: Projection, Sorting, and Pagination
docs.text:
A projection controls which fields a read returns. Inclusion projections specify fields to keep; exclusion projections specify fields to omit. They generally cannot be mixed, except that _id can be excluded from an inclusion projection. Smaller results reduce network transfer and application memory.

db.orders.find(
  { status: "paid" },
  { customerId: 1, total: 1, createdAt: 1, _id: 0 }
).sort({ createdAt: -1, _id: -1 }).limit(25)

Sort order can use ascending 1 or descending -1. Include a unique tie-breaker such as _id so results with equal sort keys have deterministic order. A matching compound index may support both filter and sort.

Large skip offsets can be slow because the server must advance past skipped results. Range pagination uses the last seen sort key as the next query boundary. For example, for descending createdAt plus _id, request values lower than the last returned pair, then limit the next page. Ensure the range predicate and sort use compatible indexed fields. See project fields and sort query results.

docs.title: Query Filters and Projections
docs.text:
A filter selects matching documents. Equality can be written as { status: "open" }. Common comparison operators include $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $ne, and $in. Logical operators include $and, $or, $nor, and $not. Multiple fields in a filter are implicitly combined with AND.

db.orders.find(
  { status: { $in: ["paid", "shipped"] }, total: { $gte: 25 }, "shipping.country": "IN" },
  { customerId: 1, total: 1, status: 1, _id: 0 }
).sort({ total: -1 }).limit(25)

The second find argument is a projection. Inclusion and exclusion projections generally cannot be mixed, except that _id can be excluded from an inclusion projection. Array matching has special semantics: a simple equality can match an array element; use $elemMatch when multiple conditions must match the same embedded array element.

Sorting should be deterministic for pagination; include a unique tie-breaker such as _id. Large skip offsets can become expensive, so range pagination is often better at scale. Always bound results.

Do not accept arbitrary client-built filter objects. Map allowed API fields to server-created filters, validate types, and cap ranges and result sizes. See query documents and query operators.

docs.title: Query Operators
docs.text:
Query predicates select documents by matching field values. Equality uses concise syntax; comparison operators include $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $ne, and $in. Logical operators include $and, $or, $nor, and $not. Multiple field predicates are ANDed by default.

db.orders.find({
  status: { $in: ["paid", "shipped"] },
  total: { $gte: 25, $lt: 500 },
  $or: [{ region: "west" }, { priority: true }]
})

For arrays, a simple equality can match an element. Use $all to require several values and $elemMatch when multiple predicates must match the same embedded element. For nested documents, dot notation addresses a path such as customer.address.city. Exact embedded-document equality is sensitive to the document shape and field order; dot-notation predicates are usually more flexible.

Use $exists to distinguish an absent field from present values, and type-aware comparisons where values may have mixed BSON types. Do not accept raw client-supplied filter documents; validate allowed fields, operators, values, and complexity. See query operators and query documents.

docs.title: Query Plans and Explain
docs.text:
MongoDB chooses a query plan from the filter, sort, projection, collation, and available indexes. A plan may use an index scan, fetch matching documents, sort in memory, or scan the full collection. Similar query shapes can use different plans as data distribution changes.

db.orders.find({ customerId: "c-42" })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1, _id: -1 })
  .explain("executionStats")

Inspect the winning plan, execution time, nReturned, totalKeysExamined, and totalDocsExamined. A high examined-to-returned ratio can signal a weak index or low-selectivity predicate. A COLLSCAN may be correct for a small collection or a query returning much of the data; do not add indexes solely to eliminate every collection scan.

Use realistic data volumes and parameter distributions. Compare plans before and after index changes, and account for write cost. The profiler and slow-query logs help identify workload patterns in production; enable profiling deliberately because it adds overhead and can capture sensitive query values. See query plans, explain, and query performance.

docs.title: MongoDB Questions and Answers
docs.text: Use these questions to review MongoDB concepts, application usage, data modeling, performance, and operations. The answers are concise; follow the linked lessons for detailed explanations and examples.

docs.title: 1. What is MongoDB?
docs.text: MongoDB is a document database. It stores BSON documents in collections and provides query, aggregation, indexing, replication, and sharding features.

docs.title: 2. How are databases, collections, and documents related?
docs.text: A deployment contains databases. A database contains collections, and collections contain documents. Documents in one collection can differ in shape, but a consistent model makes application queries and validation easier.

docs.title: 3. What is BSON?
docs.text: BSON is MongoDB's binary document format. It supports JSON-like objects and arrays plus types such as ObjectId, Date, Decimal128, binary values, and distinct integer types.

docs.title: 4. What is the purpose of the _id field?
docs.text: Each document has a unique _id within its collection. If omitted, a driver or MongoDB generates an ObjectId. Applications can choose other supported BSON values when they need a different identifier scheme.

docs.title: 5. Is an ObjectId a timestamp or a sequential number?
docs.text: No. It contains a timestamp component and other bytes that make collisions very unlikely, but it is not a strict global clock or sequence. Store a BSON Date separately when creation or event time matters.

docs.title: 6. Is MongoDB schema-less?
docs.text: No. MongoDB permits flexible document shapes, but applications still need a deliberate schema. Teams can enforce required fields and BSON types with collection validation.

docs.title: 7. What does single-document atomicity mean?
docs.text: A write affecting one document is applied atomically: other operations do not observe a partially updated document. Embedding values that change together can use this property to protect invariants.

docs.title: 8. When should data be embedded or referenced?
docs.text: Embed bounded data commonly read and updated with its parent. Reference shared, independently queried, or unbounded data. Choose from access patterns and growth rather than a rule that all relationships must use one approach.

docs.title: 9. What do CRUD operations stand for?
docs.text: Create, read, update, and delete. MongoDB provides methods such as insertOne(), find(), updateOne(), and deleteOne(), with corresponding batch methods for many documents.

docs.title: 10. What is the difference between insertOne() and insertMany()?
docs.text: insertOne() writes one document. insertMany() submits a batch; ordered batches stop on an error by default, while unordered batches continue where possible and may partially succeed.

docs.title: 11. What does find() return?
docs.text: find() returns a cursor, not a fully materialized array. Cursors retrieve results in batches, so applications should iterate and bound results rather than loading an unbounded collection into memory.

docs.title: 12. How does findOne() choose a document?
docs.text: It returns one document matching the filter. Without an explicit sort, the selected document is not guaranteed to be the newest or otherwise meaningful first match.

docs.title: 13. How are multiple fields in a query filter combined?
docs.text: Predicates on separate fields are combined with AND by default. Use operators such as $or, $and, and $nor when the query needs explicit logical alternatives.

docs.title: 14. What is the difference between $in and $all?
docs.text: $in matches when a field equals any listed value; for an array field it can match an element. $all requires an array to contain every specified value.

docs.title: 15. When should $elemMatch be used?
docs.text: Use $elemMatch when multiple conditions must match the same element of an array. Without it, separate predicates may be satisfied by different array elements.

docs.title: 16. What is a projection?
docs.text: A projection controls which fields a read returns. It reduces response size and can support covered queries when the filter and returned fields are available in an index.

docs.title: 17. Why include a tie-breaker in a sort?
docs.text: Documents can have equal values for the chosen sort key. Adding a unique field such as _id makes the order deterministic and supports stable pagination.

docs.title: 18. Why can large skip values be slow?
docs.text: The server still has to advance past skipped results. Range pagination based on the last seen sort key often scales better for deep pages.

docs.title: 19. What does updateOne() do?
docs.text: It updates at most one document matching a filter, even if several documents match. Use a selective filter and inspect matchedCount and modifiedCount in the result.

docs.title: 20. What is the difference between $set and $unset?
docs.text: $set creates or replaces specified fields, including nested fields addressed with dot notation. $unset removes specified fields from the document.

docs.title: 21. What does $inc do?
docs.text: $inc adds a numeric amount to a field and creates the field if it does not exist. It is useful for atomic counters and inventory changes, but the application must still define how negative values are prevented when required.

docs.title: 22. How is updateMany() different from updateOne()?
docs.text: updateMany() applies the update to every document matching the filter. It is not one atomic operation across the whole matched set; individual document writes are atomic.

docs.title: 23. What is the difference between an update and a replacement?
docs.text: An update document changes fields specified by operators and preserves other fields. replaceOne() replaces the document contents, so omitted fields are removed (subject to _id rules).

docs.title: 24. What is an upsert?
docs.text: An upsert updates a matching document or inserts one if no match exists. Use a stable key and a unique index when an upsert represents one logical entity; otherwise concurrent operations can create duplicates.

docs.title: 25. What is the difference between deleteOne() and deleteMany()?
docs.text: deleteOne() removes at most one match; deleteMany() removes every match. An empty filter matches the full collection, so inspect destructive filters before running them.

docs.title: 26. What is bulkWrite() used for?
docs.text: bulkWrite() batches insert, update, replace, and delete operations to reduce round trips. It can partially succeed; ordered mode stops on errors, while unordered mode continues where possible.

docs.title: 27. How do common array update operators differ?
docs.text: $push appends a value, $addToSet appends only if the value is not already present, $pull removes matching values, and $pop removes an endpoint element. Use array filters when updates should target particular embedded elements.

docs.title: 28. What is an unbounded array, and why is it risky?
docs.text: It is an array that can grow without a practical limit. It can make documents large, increase write costs, and complicate pagination; move independently growing children to another collection when appropriate.

docs.title: 29. What does schema validation enforce?
docs.text: A validator can require fields and constrain BSON types, ranges, or allowed values. It protects writes at the collection boundary but does not replace application-level business validation.

docs.title: 30. How can a schema change be deployed safely?
docs.text: Make readers tolerate old and new shapes, introduce and backfill fields, update writers, then tighten validation after old data and clients are migrated. Test the migration on representative data.

docs.title: 31. What is an index?
docs.text: An index is an ordered data structure that helps MongoDB find or sort matching documents without scanning the entire collection. Indexes speed some reads but require storage and extra work on writes.

docs.title: 32. Why does field order matter in a compound index?
docs.text: A compound index is ordered by its fields and can generally support queries on leading prefixes. Choose field order from equality filters, sort order, and range predicates in real query patterns.

docs.title: 33. What does a unique index do?
docs.text: It enforces that indexed key values are unique, in addition to supporting lookup. Existing duplicates must be corrected before the index can be created.

docs.title: 34. What is a multikey index?
docs.text: It indexes values from an array field. It supports array queries, but compound multikey indexes have restrictions, particularly when more than one indexed field is an array.

docs.title: 35. What is a TTL index?
docs.text: A TTL index removes eligible documents after a configured duration or expiration date. Cleanup is asynchronous, so TTL is useful for retention but not precise real-time deletion.

docs.title: 36. What does explain("executionStats") show?
docs.text: It reports the selected query plan and execution statistics, including keys and documents examined and results returned. Use it to understand collection scans, index effectiveness, and expensive sorts.

docs.title: 37. What is collation?
docs.text: Collation defines language-aware string comparison, including case and accent rules. Queries and indexes need compatible collation settings for the index to support those string comparisons.

docs.title: 38. What is a geospatial index used for?
docs.text: A 2dsphere index supports queries over GeoJSON geometries on a spherical model. A 2d index supports legacy planar coordinate pairs; choose based on the stored representation and query semantics.

docs.title: 39. What is an aggregation pipeline?
docs.text: It is an ordered sequence of stages that filters, reshapes, groups, joins, or writes documents. Each stage receives the output of the previous stage.

docs.title: 40. Why put $match early in a pipeline?
docs.text: An early $match reduces the number of documents passed to later stages and may use an index. Only move filters when doing so preserves the intended result.

docs.title: 41. What does $unwind do?
docs.text: $unwind emits a separate pipeline document for each element in an array. Its preserveNullAndEmptyArrays option controls whether documents with missing or empty arrays remain.

docs.title: 42. How does $lookup work?
docs.text: $lookup performs a left outer join to another collection and adds the matches as an array. Index the foreign join field and account for the size of the joined results.

docs.title: 43. What does $group do?
docs.text: $group combines documents that share a key in its _id expression. Accumulators such as $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $push, and $addToSet compute group results.

docs.title: 44. What is the difference between $project and $set?
docs.text: $project selects, excludes, renames, or computes fields in the output shape. $set adds or replaces fields while retaining other fields; it is an alias of $addFields in aggregation.

docs.title: 45. What is $facet used for?
docs.text: $facet runs multiple subpipelines over the same input, such as calculating a page of results and summary counts. It can reduce repeated source work but may need substantial memory.

docs.title: 46. What are $merge and $out used for?
docs.text: They are terminal pipeline stages that write aggregation results to a collection. Their replacement and merge behavior differs; use them deliberately for batch outputs or materialized results.

docs.title: 47. How should an aggregation be tuned?
docs.text: Filter early, keep intermediate documents small, bound array expansion, use indexes for initial matches and sorts, and measure with representative data. Large groups and blocking sorts can consume substantial memory.

docs.title: 48. When is a multi-document transaction needed?
docs.text: Use one when a business invariant must atomically span multiple documents. Prefer a single-document model when natural; transactions add coordination and latency.

docs.title: 49. What deployments support transactions?
docs.text: Multi-document transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster. A standalone mongod does not support them.

docs.title: 50. What are read concern and write concern?
docs.text: Read concern controls the consistency level of data returned by a read. Write concern controls the acknowledgment requested for a write. Choose both from the application's durability and latency requirements.

docs.title: 51. What does majority write concern mean?
docs.text: It requests acknowledgment from a majority of voting members, subject to deployment configuration. It is commonly used when writes need stronger durability than a single-member acknowledgment.

docs.title: 52. What is a replica set?
docs.text: A replica set is a group of mongod processes that maintain the same data. One primary accepts writes while secondaries replicate the operation log; eligible members can elect a new primary after failure.

docs.title: 53. Does replication replace backups?
docs.text: No. Replication copies changes, including accidental deletes and harmful updates. Backups provide a separate recovery path and should be restored in regular drills.

docs.title: 54. What is sharding?
docs.text: Sharding partitions collection data across multiple shards to distribute storage and workload. It introduces routing and operational complexity, so use it when measured scale requires it.

docs.title: 55. Why is shard-key selection important?
docs.text: The shard key determines document distribution and how queries target shards. Evaluate cardinality, write distribution, growth, and common query filters; a poor key can create hot spots or scatter-gather queries.

docs.title: 56. What are change streams?
docs.text: Change streams let applications subscribe to majority-committed changes on a collection, database, or deployment. They require a replica set or sharded cluster and are consumed through a cursor or driver API.

docs.title: 57. How does a change-stream resume token work?
docs.text: The event _id is a resume token that identifies progress in the stream. Persist it after processing an event durably; consumers should be idempotent because events may be delivered again after a restart.

docs.title: 58. What do sessions provide?
docs.text: Sessions group operations and support transactions, retryable writes, and causal consistency. Use driver-managed sessions and end them when work is complete.

docs.title: 59. How are Atlas users different from database users?
docs.text: Atlas users manage cloud resources and project settings. Database users authenticate to the data deployment and receive database roles. Permission in one system does not automatically grant permission in the other.

docs.title: 60. What is an Atlas IP access list?
docs.text: It restricts which client source IP addresses or CIDR ranges may connect to a project deployment. Network access and database authentication are both required; avoid broad entries such as 0.0.0.0/0.

docs.title: 61. What is MongoDB Compass useful for?
docs.text: Compass is a graphical tool for browsing documents, testing filters, inspecting sampled schema, building aggregation pipelines, and viewing indexes. Its schema view is based on sampling and does not prove every document has the same shape.

docs.title: 62. What is mongosh?
docs.text: mongosh is MongoDB's interactive JavaScript shell. It is useful for exploration and administration; production applications should use an official language driver with a reused connection pool.

docs.title: 63. Why should credentials not be embedded in a connection URI in source code?
docs.text: Source code can be copied, committed, or logged. Store credentials in a secret manager or protected environment configuration, and prevent them from appearing in process logs and shell history.

docs.title: 64. What does TLS protect?
docs.text: TLS protects network traffic and verifies the server identity when certificate validation is enabled. It complements authentication and authorization; it does not encrypt every stored field from database administrators.

docs.title: 65. What should be monitored in production?
docs.text: Track latency, errors, throughput, connections, CPU, memory, disk space and latency, storage growth, replication lag, and backup status. Use explain and slow-query profiling to investigate performance, with awareness that profiling adds overhead.

docs.title: 66. Why should backups be restore-tested?
docs.text: A successful backup job does not prove that data can be restored within recovery time objectives. Restore tests reveal missing data, incompatible versions, access gaps, or incomplete runbooks.

docs.title: 67. What is the difference between a standard view and a materialized result?
docs.text: A standard view is a read-only virtual collection whose pipeline runs when queried. A materialized result stores computed documents, often using $merge or $out, and needs a refresh and staleness policy.

docs.title: 68. What are time-series collections for?
docs.text: They optimize storage and queries for measurements recorded over time. Choose a BSON Date time field and suitable metadata; check feature limitations before using one instead of a regular collection.

docs.title: 69. What is GridFS?
docs.text: GridFS stores large files as metadata and chunks across collections so drivers can stream files larger than the 16 MiB BSON document limit. Object storage may be preferable for many media-delivery workloads.

docs.title: 70. What is a capped collection?
docs.text: It is a fixed-size collection that preserves insertion order and overwrites old records when full. It has update and delete restrictions and is suited only when those overwrite semantics are acceptable.

docs.title: 71. What is MongoDB Search?
docs.text: MongoDB Search provides indexed full-text search with analyzers and relevance features. Search availability and deployment requirements depend on the MongoDB product and version; check the current documentation.

docs.title: 72. What is Vector Search?
docs.text: Vector Search retrieves documents by similarity to embeddings and can combine semantic relevance with filters or text search. The application must generate compatible embeddings and evaluate result quality for its use case.

docs.title: Read Concern, Write Concern, and Read Preference
docs.text:
Read concern controls which data state a read may observe. Write concern controls the acknowledgment a write waits for. Read preference chooses which replica-set members can serve a read. These are distinct controls and should match the application's consistency and availability needs.

A majority write concern requests acknowledgment by a majority of voting members. A majority read concern returns data acknowledged by a majority. Local reads can observe data that may later roll back. Reading from secondaries can be stale even with a chosen read preference. Linearizable reads provide stronger real-time guarantees in supported contexts, with latency and availability costs.

db.orders.find({ state: "open" }).readConcern("majority")
db.orders.insertOne(
  { orderId: "o-42", state: "created" },
  { writeConcern: { w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000 } }
)

Driver APIs and shell helper syntax vary; use the driver documentation for application code. Transactions specify concerns at the transaction level. Avoid selecting strong settings by habit: write down the required guarantee, failure behavior, and latency budget. See read concern, write concern, and read preference.

docs.title: Replication and Replica Sets
docs.text:
A replica set is a group of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. The primary accepts writes and records them in its oplog; secondaries replicate oplog entries. If the primary becomes unavailable, eligible voting members can elect a replacement.

A majority of voting members is needed to elect and maintain a primary. Plan members across failure domains, and understand votes, priority, hidden members, delayed members, and maintenance procedures. Secondaries may serve reads, but their data can lag. Read preference chooses eligible nodes; it does not alone guarantee freshness.

Write concern controls the acknowledgment requested for writes. A majority write concern waits for acknowledgment from a majority of voting members, subject to configuration. Read concern controls visibility guarantees. These settings trade latency and availability for consistency and durability behavior; select them from the application's contract.

Monitor member health, elections, replication lag, and oplog window. Replication improves availability but is not a backup: accidental writes propagate. Maintain independent backups and test recovery. See replication and read and write concerns.

docs.title: Schema Validation and Evolution
docs.text:
MongoDB permits flexible document shapes, but collection validators can enforce required fields, BSON types, ranges, and allowed values. Validation is checked on inserts and updates. Invalid writes may be rejected or logged according to validationAction.

db.createCollection("products", {
  validator: {
    $jsonSchema: {
      bsonType: "object",
      required: ["sku", "price"],
      properties: {
        sku: { bsonType: "string" },
        price: { bsonType: ["int", "long", "double", "decimal"], minimum: 0 },
        status: { enum: ["draft", "active", "retired"] }
      }
    }
  },
  validationLevel: "strict",
  validationAction: "error"
})

strict checks every insert and update. moderate has different behavior for existing invalid records. error rejects invalid writes; warn records validation failures but allows the write. Understand these settings before changing production rules.

Evolve schemas compatibly: make readers tolerate old and new forms, introduce and backfill new fields, migrate writers, then tighten validation after old records and clients are handled. Use collMod to change a validator. Validation complements application and domain rules; it does not prove business correctness. See schema validation and JSON Schema query operator.

docs.title: MongoDB Search and Vector Search
docs.text:
MongoDB Search provides indexed full-text retrieval with analyzers, relevance scoring, facets, autocomplete, and other search operators. Search queries are expressed through aggregation stages and rely on a dedicated search index. It is distinct from ordinary B-tree indexes and the legacy $text operator.

Vector Search retrieves documents by similarity to an embedding. It supports approximate or exact nearest-neighbor modes depending on deployment and version. Hybrid retrieval combines lexical search, vector relevance, and metadata filters. Embeddings must be generated and versioned consistently with the model that produced them.

Design indexes for the fields and analyzers used by the search workload. Evaluate relevance with representative queries and data; do not assume vector similarity alone produces useful results. Search features, availability, and syntax vary between Atlas and self-managed releases, so check current deployment requirements.

See MongoDB Search and Vector Search.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Enable authentication and grant users only the roles their work requires.
  • Restrict network exposure; use TLS for connections and protect credentials in a secret manager.
  • Apply encryption for storage and backups according to the deployment's requirements.
  • Validate application input and construct filters from known fields and typed values. Do not pass untrusted objects directly as query documents.
  • Keep database credentials out of source control and client-side code. Rotate secrets and review access regularly.

Use the MongoDB security checklist for deployment-specific controls.

docs.title: Operational practices
docs.text:
Monitor query latency, slow operations, connection usage, disk space, memory pressure, replication lag, and storage growth. Use explain("executionStats") and representative workload measurements to investigate slow queries. Applications should reuse driver clients and their connection pools rather than opening a connection for each request.

Take backups and periodically test restoring them. Replication does not protect against logical mistakes or destructive writes. Plan upgrades against the deployed release's compatibility notes, and rehearse changes in a representative environment. Define alert thresholds and capacity plans before an incident.

See MongoDB's operations checklist and backup methods.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Authentication establishes who a user or service is. Authorization determines its permitted database actions. Atlas console users and database users are different identities: a person who can manage a project does not automatically need application data privileges.

Enable access control on self-managed deployments. Give applications the narrowest role and database scope that supports their work. Built-in roles cover common tasks; custom roles can grant a specific action set. Avoid application use of root or cluster-wide administrator roles.

Use strong, unique credentials or supported enterprise identity integrations. Rotate credentials, remove stale accounts, audit privilege changes, and keep secrets out of source control and client bundles. Authentication does not replace TLS, IP restrictions, or safe application query construction.

See authorization, built-in roles, and Atlas database users.

docs.title: Self-Managed Operations
docs.text:
Self-managed MongoDB requires ownership of installation, configuration, upgrades, storage, networking, security, monitoring, backups, recovery, and incident response. Follow official instructions for the operating system and exact server version.

Keep deployments on supported versions. Plan upgrades with server compatibility, feature compatibility version, drivers, and rollback constraints in mind. Test against representative data and workload, and automate consistent configuration across members. Protect configuration files and credentials.

Plan disk capacity for data, indexes, journal, oplog, temporary aggregation work, and backups. Monitor disk latency and free space as well as CPU and memory. Configure replica members across suitable failure domains. Document maintenance for index builds, certificate rotation, member replacement, and restore.

Restrict operating-system access and network paths. Prepare alerts and runbooks before incidents. Atlas shifts some infrastructure work to MongoDB but does not transfer responsibility for application access policy, schema, retention, query quality, and recovery objectives. See operations checklist and installation.

docs.title: Sessions and Causal Consistency
docs.text:
A session groups related operations and carries logical session metadata. Drivers use sessions for transactions, retryable writes, and causal consistency. Create sessions through the driver and pass them to operations that belong to the session.

Causal consistency lets a session observe its own causally prior writes and reads when used with the required concerns. This is useful when a user writes data and then reads it through a deployment that may route reads to different replica-set members. It does not make unrelated operations globally serializable.

Sessions have lifetimes and must be ended. Do not share one session concurrently across independent operations unless the driver explicitly supports that usage. Transactions run within a session and require sequential handling according to driver rules.

const session = client.startSession()
try {
  // pass { session } to related driver operations
} finally {
  await session.endSession()
}

Use the official driver API for the language in use; shell examples are not a substitute for application session handling. See sessions and causal consistency.

docs.title: Sharding
docs.text:
Sharding distributes collection data across multiple shards. A sharded deployment includes shards, mongos query routers, and config servers. Applications connect through mongos, which uses shard-key values and cluster metadata to target operations.

Shard-key choice strongly affects distribution and query efficiency. Evaluate cardinality, write patterns, range queries, common filters, and growth. A monotonically increasing key can concentrate new writes on one range. A hashed key can distribute writes but make range queries less targeted. Compound keys can balance access patterns when selected from measured workload.

Queries containing shard-key predicates can target a subset of shards. Queries without them may scatter across many shards. Balancing and chunk migration move data but do not fix a hot key or poor targeting. Unique indexes and shard-key rules constrain choices; plan carefully because changing a key can be costly.

Do not shard by default. First confirm that data modeling, indexes, and a replica set cannot meet measured capacity or throughput needs. Sharding adds operational complexity. See sharding and choose a shard key.

docs.title: Storage Engines and Journaling
docs.text:
A storage engine manages how MongoDB stores data in memory and on disk. WiredTiger is the default engine for current self-managed deployments. It provides document-level concurrency, compression, checkpoints, and journaling. Storage engine selection affects performance, durability, and operational behavior.

Journaling is write-ahead logging used to recover writes after an unexpected shutdown between checkpoints. Checkpoints create consistent on-disk snapshots; the journal records later operations needed for recovery. Current MongoDB versions enable journaling by default and remove older controls, so follow documentation for the deployed release.

Storage-engine concepts inform disk capacity, cache pressure, checkpoints, compression, and recovery time. Do not manually edit data files while mongod is running. Use supported backup and maintenance procedures. Atlas manages underlying storage configuration differently from self-managed deployments.

See storage engines and journaling.

docs.title: Time Series and TTL
docs.text:
Time-series collections are optimized for measurements recorded over time, such as telemetry and sensor readings. Choose a BSON Date timeField and a stable metaField that groups measurements by source or device. Set granularity based on event frequency and expected query windows. Time-series collections have feature and update limitations compared with regular collections, so check compatibility with the operations your application needs.

db.createCollection("readings", {
  timeseries: {
    timeField: "timestamp",
    metaField: "device",
    granularity: "minutes"
  }
})

A TTL index removes eligible documents after a configured duration. For example, an index on expiresAt with expireAfterSeconds set to zero expires documents at their stored timestamp. TTL cleanup is asynchronous, not an exact timer. Use BSON dates and do not rely on TTL for immediate deletion or precise scheduling.

Retention choices affect storage, compliance, and query history. Validate the actual behavior with the deployed server version. See time-series collections and TTL indexes.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A write to one document is atomic. Prefer a document model that keeps common invariants together. Use a multi-document transaction when a business operation must commit or roll back changes across multiple documents, such as transferring value between two accounts.

Transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster, not a standalone server. They add coordination and latency, so they should solve a real cross-document requirement rather than compensate for every modeling choice. Keep them short and avoid waiting on user input or unrelated external services inside a transaction.

In a driver, start a session and use the driver's transaction helper. It handles transaction labels and retry rules according to that driver. Operations in a transaction must use the session. Do not perform non-idempotent external side effects in a callback that may be retried. Use idempotency keys or an outbox pattern when a committed database change must trigger an external action.

Choose transaction read concern and write concern according to consistency requirements and deployment support. Test transient errors and uncertain commit results. See transactions and production considerations.

docs.title: Field Update Operators
docs.text:
Update operators change selected fields while preserving unspecified fields. updateOne() changes at most one match; updateMany() changes all matches. Always scope the filter deliberately and inspect matchedCount and modifiedCount.

db.inventory.updateOne(
  { sku: "p-100" },
  {
    $set: { price: 9.25, "details.color": "blue" },
    $unset: { legacyCode: "" },
    $inc: { stock: -1 },
    $currentDate: { updatedAt: true }
  }
)

$set creates or replaces fields, including dotted nested paths. $unset removes a field. $inc adds a numeric value, useful for counters when the update must be atomic. $min and $max only replace a value when the new value is lower or higher. $mul multiplies a numeric field; $rename changes a field name; $setOnInsert applies only when an upsert inserts.

Do not confuse update operators with aggregation pipeline stages that share names. In an update pipeline, $set computes an expression from the existing document. For array element updates, see array operators. See update operators.

docs.title: Update Operations and Operators
docs.text:
updateOne(filter, update) changes at most one matching document; updateMany() changes every match. A selective filter matters: an empty filter can update the entire collection. Inspect matchedCount and modifiedCount. Set upsert: true only when inserting a new document on no match is intended.

db.inventory.updateOne(
  { sku: "p-100" },
  { $set: { price: 9.25 }, $inc: { stock: -1 }, $currentDate: { updatedAt: true } }
)

Common update operators:

  • $set assigns fields, including dotted nested paths such as "profile.city".
  • $unset removes a field; its operand value is ignored.
  • $inc adds or subtracts a number.
  • $mul, $min, $max, and $rename update numeric values or field names.
  • $currentDate writes the current date or timestamp.
  • $setOnInsert runs only when an upsert inserts.
  • $push, $addToSet, $pull, $pullAll, and $pop modify arrays.

replaceOne() replaces the document, removing fields not in the replacement (subject to _id rules); it is not the same as $set. findOneAndUpdate() atomically updates and can return the before or after document. Array filters target matching embedded elements. Update pipelines can compute values from the old document; in a pipeline, $set and $unset are aggregation stages rather than update modifier operators.

See update methods and update operators.

docs.title: Upserts, Replacements, and Find-and-Modify
docs.text:
An upsert inserts a document when an update matches nothing. It is useful for idempotent synchronization when the filter identifies a stable business key and a unique index enforces that key.

db.settings.updateOne(
  { name: "theme" },
  { $set: { value: "dark" }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date() } },
  { upsert: true }
)

An upsert can construct inserted fields from equality predicates in the filter plus update operators. Design the filter carefully; a broad filter can create surprising records or duplicate logical entities. A unique index protects against concurrent duplicate upserts.

replaceOne() replaces the matched document contents, removing omitted fields while preserving _id constraints. Use it only when full replacement is intended. findOneAndUpdate() and findOneAndReplace() atomically modify one matching document and return a before or after image according to options. They are useful when the caller needs the changed record in the same round trip.

See upsert behavior and findOneAndUpdate.

docs.title: Views and On-Demand Materialized Views
docs.text:
A standard view is a read-only virtual collection defined by an aggregation pipeline. It does not store results; MongoDB runs the view pipeline when it is queried. Views can present a stable or restricted shape without duplicating source documents.

db.createView(
  "activeCustomers",
  "customers",
  [{ $match: { active: true } }, { $project: { name: 1, region: 1 } }]
)

Views are useful for reusable transformations and exposing only selected fields to a read role. They have restrictions on updates and pipeline stages; avoid assuming a view behaves like a writable collection.

An on-demand materialized view stores computed results in a collection, commonly using $merge or $out from an aggregation. It can make expensive reads faster but requires refresh, staleness, and failure policies. Index the stored results according to consumer queries.

See views and on-demand materialized views.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database. It stores data in tables with defined columns and supports SQL for querying and changing that data. Relationships and constraints help represent rules explicitly; PostgreSQL also supports additional data types and capabilities as application needs grow.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Describe tables, rows, columns, keys, and relationships.
  • Read a simple SQL query and understand its result.
  • Explain how constraints and indexes help protect and retrieve data.
  • Recognize the benefits and costs of a relational model.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text: Start with Database Fundamentals, then follow the diagram from an application query to related PostgreSQL tables.

docs.title: Relevant resources
docs.text:
• Official PostgreSQL documentation — Tutorial: introduces PostgreSQL and fundamental SQL operations.
  • Official PostgreSQL documentation — Data Definition: explains creating tables, constraints, and related structures.
  • Official PostgreSQL documentation — Queries: covers retrieving and combining data.
  • Official PostgreSQL documentation — Indexes: describes index behavior and trade-offs.

Compare this relational model with MongoDB and review shared concepts in Database Fundamentals.

docs.title: Application Architecture
docs.text: This section examines how application components fit together and how systems can remain responsive and dependable as their needs grow.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Recognize common architectural concerns and trade-offs.
  • Understand caching, Redis, and message queues at a system level.
  • Develop a foundation for reasoning about scalability and system design.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Software Architecture
  • Caching
  • Redis
  • Message Queues
  • Scalability
  • System Design

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A cache keeps a temporary copy of data so a later request can be served faster. Caches appear in browsers, content delivery networks, and applications. Redis is one common caching service.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Repeatedly fetching the same information adds latency and consumes capacity. Caching is most useful when reads repeat and the source is slower than the cache.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: An application checks the cache for a key. On a hit, it uses the cached value; on a miss, it reads the source, returns the result, and may store a copy with an expiration time. When source data changes, cached values can become stale. Developers choose expiration, invalidation, or refresh strategies based on how fresh the data must be.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A public catalog page may be requested many times per minute. Caching its rendered content near readers reduces repeated application and database work. Private account data, by contrast, must not be shared across users through an incorrectly scoped cache key.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Treat the source as authoritative unless the design says otherwise. Choose safe values, keys, and expiration times. Measure hit rate and latency, and plan for cache outages.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
This local pseudocode demonstrates a cache-aside lookup; cache and load_from_source are placeholders, not remote services:

value = cache.get("catalog:demo")
if value is missing:
    value = load_from_source("demo catalog")
    cache.set("catalog:demo", value, expires_in=60 seconds)
return value

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cache hit/miss: whether a requested key was found.
  • TTL: time to live; how long an entry may remain cached.
  • Invalidation: removing or refreshing data that may be stale.
  • Cache-aside: the application checks the cache and loads misses from the source.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Caching can lower response times and source-system load. It adds memory use, operational complexity, and a risk of stale or incorrectly shared data. Cache behavior should be an optimization, not an undocumented source of truth.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A cache does not make data permanently available or automatically consistent. A high hit rate is not proof of correctness; a longer TTL can delay visible changes.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Third-party explanation — Cloudflare: What is caching?: introduces caching and explains how it helps deliver content.
  • Official Redis documentation — Key expiration: documents a concrete way to set a key's lifetime in Redis.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A message queue lets one part of a system hand work to another without requiring both to finish at the same moment. A producer sends a message; a consumer processes it. This suits asynchronous work such as sending a receipt.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Some tasks take longer than a user-facing request should wait or depend on a temporarily unavailable service. A queue buffers work, smooths bursts, and separates responsibilities.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A producer submits a task or event message to a broker. A consumer reads and processes it, then acknowledges success. Unacknowledged messages may be delivered again, so consumers should tolerate duplicates. Repeated failures need bounded retries and a review path.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: An online shop can record an order first and place a “send confirmation” message on a queue. A separate worker sends the email. If the mail provider is briefly unavailable, the worker can retry without holding the customer's checkout request open.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Define message format, retry policy, and failure handling. Make side effects idempotent where possible: processing a message twice should not repeat an action. Monitor queue depth and age.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Safe local-only pseudocode illustrates the flow:

queue = LocalDemoQueue()
queue.publish({"type": "welcome-email", "user_id": 42})

message = queue.receive()
if message is not None:
    print("Would prepare email for demo user", message["user_id"])
    queue.acknowledge(message)

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Producer/consumer: sends messages / processes messages.
  • Broker: service that stores, routes, or delivers messages.
  • Acknowledgment: confirmation that a message was handled.
  • Dead-letter queue: holding place for messages that cannot be processed normally.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Queues absorb spikes and reduce timing dependencies. They add moving parts and delays; ordering and delivery guarantees vary by product.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A queue does not guarantee exactly-once side effects. Acknowledgment does not prove business logic was correct, and a queue cannot fix a consumer that cannot keep up.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation — Amazon SQS Developer Guide: explains a managed queue service, its concepts, and usage.
  • Official AWS documentation — Queue-based load leveling pattern: describes how a queue can separate producers from slower consumers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Redis is an in-memory data store commonly used for caching and short-lived state. It supports strings, hashes, lists, and sets. Redis is related to, but not identical with, caching.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Applications sometimes need quick access to shared state without repeatedly querying a primary database. Whether data belongs in Redis depends on persistence and recovery requirements.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A client sends commands for keys and values. A string can store a counter, a set can represent unique members, and a list can model ordered items. Keys can expire. Redis persistence and recovery depend on its configuration.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A learning application might keep a temporary count of page views for a demo lesson. The application increments a Redis counter and lets it expire later, while durable course records remain in a primary database.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Select structures that match access patterns, use clear key names, and expire temporary data. Handle Redis unavailability gracefully; a cache outage should not overload the primary database.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
On a locally installed Redis server used only for practice, these commands set and retrieve a harmless demo value:

SET lesson:demo "hello" EX 60
GET lesson:demo

The expiration limits the example value's lifetime. Do not run these commands against a production endpoint.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Key: name used to address a stored value.
  • Data structure: supported value shape, such as string, hash, or set.
  • Expiration: automatic removal after a configured lifetime.
  • Persistence: saving in-memory data to durable storage for recovery.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Redis provides fast access and useful data structures. Memory is limited and can be costly; persistence and failover require deliberate configuration. It may not fit data that must never be lost unless durability is designed.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Redis is not only a cache, but using it does not automatically make data durable. “In memory” does not mean unlimited capacity or zero latency.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Redis documentation — Data types: introduces Redis structures and their core use cases.
  • Official Redis documentation — EXPIRE command: explains setting a key's expiration period.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Scalability is a system's ability to handle growth in users, requests, or data while meeting its responsiveness goals. Growth may require changing how work is performed or stored. System design provides a broader view.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: A design that works for a demo may become slow under higher load. Planning helps identify bottlenecks, but scaling before measuring can waste money and add complexity.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Vertical scaling adds resources to one machine; horizontal scaling adds instances and distributes requests. Horizontal approaches may require load balancing, shared state, and safe concurrent work. Caching, queues, and indexes can reduce repeated work.

A system may be limited by its database, network, or an external service. Metrics and load tests help find the constraint.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A registration service gets a burst when enrollment opens. A load balancer can distribute requests and a queue defer confirmation emails. Adding web instances alone may increase database pressure.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Identify workload and service goals, then measure latency, throughput, errors, and resource use. Scale the bottleneck, check costs, and test failure behavior.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a local demo, record response duration while repeating a harmless request to a local endpoint. Compare a small and larger sample, then inspect logs and resource use. This is an observation exercise, not a production load test; avoid sending generated traffic to systems you do not own.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Vertical scaling: increasing resources on one machine.
  • Horizontal scaling: adding machines or service instances.
  • Throughput: work completed per unit of time.
  • Latency: time taken for one operation.
  • Bottleneck: constrained component limiting overall performance.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Scaling can improve capacity but raises cost and complexity. Horizontal scaling exposes state-sharing challenges; scaling blindly may only move a bottleneck.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: More servers do not guarantee faster responses or reliability. “Scale later” works best when architecture preserves a path to evolve.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation — Reliability Pillar: Design Principles: discusses resilient workload design, including scaling and recovery principles.
  • Official AWS documentation — Elastic Load Balancing: explains distributing traffic across targets.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Software architecture describes a system's important structures and the decisions shaping how its parts work together. It includes components, responsibilities, communication, and constraints—not just a diagram.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: As an application grows, one feature change can affect many areas. Clear boundaries help teams see responsibilities and trade-offs.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
A team identifies goals such as security or maintainability, then chooses structures that support them. A monolith packages capabilities in one application; a service-oriented design separates them into communicating processes. Either can work well.

Teams document high-impact decisions and revisit them when constraints change.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A course platform may begin as one application with modules for accounts, lessons, and progress. Distinct modules clarify responsibility without requiring separate deployments.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Understand the responsibilities and interfaces of the component you change. Prefer explicit contracts and avoid distributed services unless they solve a real problem.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a local design exercise, sketch a browser, application, and database. Label each arrow with the request or data being exchanged. Then ask which component validates input, owns the data, and handles failure. This diagram is a discussion aid, not a deployment prescription.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Component: a system part with a defined responsibility.
  • Boundary: a separation of responsibility or change ownership.
  • Quality attribute: a non-functional goal, such as reliability or maintainability.
  • Trade-off: a benefit gained at the cost of another property.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Good architecture clarifies responsibilities. Unhelpful abstraction becomes overhead; distributed designs add network failures and operations work.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: There is no universally best architecture, and microservices are not automatically more scalable. A useful design is one a team can operate and change.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation — AWS Well-Architected Framework: provides a structured set of questions and pillars for evaluating cloud workloads.
  • Third-party explanation — Martin Fowler: Microservices: explains the microservices style and the organizational and technical trade-offs involved.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: System design turns requirements into a plan for a system's components, data, interfaces, and operating behavior. A good design fits the expected workload and quality goals without unnecessary complexity.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Before implementation, a team should agree on what the system must do and how well. Design exposes questions about traffic, security, failure, cost, and future changes.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Start with functional requirements (what users can do) and non-functional requirements (performance, availability, or security goals). Estimate workload, define APIs and data models, and sketch components and failure paths. Compare approaches and validate uncertain areas.

System design overlaps with software architecture, while concerns such as caching, queues, and scalability are techniques to consider—not default requirements.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: For a photo-sharing demo, requirements might include uploading, viewing, and restricting images to their owner. Decide where image data lives, how access is checked, and what happens if storage is unavailable.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Clarify requirements before choosing technologies. Include security and failure handling, keep the first version proportional to need, and measure its results.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a local-only exercise, write three requirements for a notes app, draw a browser-to-application-to-database flow, and annotate where identity is checked and where notes are stored. Discuss a database timeout without connecting to any external service.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Functional requirement: behavior the system must provide.
  • Non-functional requirement: quality target or constraint.
  • Workload: expected pattern and volume of system activity.
  • Failure mode: way a component or interaction can stop working.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Designing early can reveal risks, but capacity estimates are uncertain. Too much design before feedback slows learning; update plans as evidence changes.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: System design is not a choice of fashionable tools. A simple system can be well designed; unneeded redundancy or caching may add failure modes.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation — AWS Well-Architected Framework: offers questions for reviewing operational, security, reliability, and performance decisions.
  • Official AWS documentation — Architecture Center: provides reference architectures and design material for common workloads.

docs.title: Servers and Infrastructure
docs.text: This section introduces the infrastructure that makes applications reachable and available in production, including domains, servers, and delivery services.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand how domains and DNS configuration connect users to services.
  • Learn the roles of servers, Nginx, reverse proxies, and load balancers.
  • Become familiar with cloud infrastructure and content delivery networks.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Domains and DNS Configuration
  • Servers
  • Nginx
  • Reverse Proxy
  • Load Balancing
  • AWS
  • CDN

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a cloud platform offering computing, storage, databases, and networking. Instead of maintaining physical machines, a team can rent resources and manage them through a console, command-line tools, or APIs.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Organizations need infrastructure that can be provisioned and resized quickly. Cloud services let teams start small and pay for measured usage, but do not remove the need to secure and monitor infrastructure.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: AWS divides its infrastructure into geographic Regions and Availability Zones. Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, S3 stores objects, and Route 53 offers DNS. Teams combine services and configure access permissions. Costs depend on service and usage.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A small web application might run its API on EC2, save images in S3, and use Route 53 for its domain. More instances can later sit behind a load balancer. This is only one possible design.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Developers should understand service dependencies, data location, and who can access resources. Keep configuration repeatable, use least-privilege permissions, and review costs and backups. See servers, load balancing, and CDNs.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Before deploying, list application, storage, and DNS needs. Choose services, set a spending alert, and test a small deployment. Never place credentials in source code.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cloud computing: on-demand access to computing resources over a network.
  • Region: a geographic AWS area.
  • Availability Zone: an isolated location within a Region.
  • EC2 instance: a virtual server.
  • IAM: AWS identity and access management.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: AWS offers broad choices and global infrastructure. Its breadth can make selection difficult, and unmonitored usage can create unexpected bills. Cloud hosting does not automatically make an application reliable.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Cloud resources are not free or maintenance-free. AWS manages underlying facilities, but customers remain responsible for application behavior, data protection, access rules, and many configuration choices.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon EC2? introduces virtual server concepts and EC2 terminology.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon S3? explains object storage and buckets.
  • Third-party explainer: Cloudflare: What is cloud computing? gives a vendor-neutral introduction to cloud concepts.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A content delivery network (CDN) is a distributed group of servers that delivers content closer to users. CDNs commonly cache public assets such as images, stylesheets, and scripts.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: When every request travels to one distant server, network delay and origin workload can rise. A CDN can serve cached content from a nearby point of presence, reducing repeated trips to the origin.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A site's configuration sends requests through the CDN. On a cache hit, it returns the stored response; on a miss, it fetches from the origin and may cache the response. Cache headers, time-to-live settings, and invalidation control freshness.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A user opening a product page may download the same images as other visitors. A CDN can return cached images without asking the web server each time. Personalized account details should not be cached publicly.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Decide which paths are safe to cache and for how long. Version static filenames, such as app.a81f.js, or arrange invalidation. Test cache hits and misses. Related: DNS and reverse proxies.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For /images/logo.svg, configure a suitable cache lifetime. A new versioned filename lets browsers and CDN edges retain the old image safely.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Origin: the source server or storage for content.
  • Edge/point of presence: a CDN location serving nearby users.
  • Cache hit/miss: whether the requested response was already cached.
  • TTL: how long a cached item may remain fresh.
  • Purge/invalidation: removing cached content before expiry.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: CDNs can reduce latency and origin traffic. They add configuration complexity; stale content and extra costs are possible. Dynamic or private responses may not benefit.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A CDN does not automatically speed every page: cacheability and origin response time matter. It does not replace secure application code.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Cloudflare documentation: What is a CDN? explains CDN locations, caching, and delivery.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon CloudFront? describes AWS CDN distributions, origins, and caching.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A domain name, such as example.com, is a human-readable name used to reach internet services. The Domain Name System (DNS) lets software look up records associated with a domain, such as addresses or mail servers.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Names are easier to remember than numeric IP addresses. DNS lets an organization change hosting addresses without changing the domain name. Cached answers mean updates may take time to appear.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A registrar manages a domain's registration. Its delegation points resolvers to authoritative nameservers, which publish records. A recursive resolver looks up an answer and may cache it for its time to live. Common records include A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), and TXT (verification or policy text).

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: For www.example.com, an A record can point to a web server's IPv4 address, or a CNAME can point a subdomain to a provider hostname. Email uses MX records.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Resolvers cache DNS answers, so changes may not be immediate. Confirm the record type, hostname, destination, and TTL before changing production DNS. DNS directs clients to a service; the service decides its response. See servers, CDN, and SSL certificates.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: To direct api.example.com, get the exact target and record type from the hosting provider. Add it in the DNS control panel and verify with a DNS lookup tool.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Registrar: company through which a domain is registered.
  • Authoritative nameserver: source of published DNS records.
  • Resolver: service that looks up DNS on a client's behalf.
  • TTL: time a DNS answer can be cached.
  • Propagation: informal term for caches updating after a change.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Buying a domain does not create a website or mailbox. DNS helps clients find a service; it does not store a web page. Lowering a TTL does not instantly clear existing caches.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Internet standard: RFC 1034: Domain Names—Concepts and Facilities describes DNS architecture and concepts.
  • Official Cloudflare learning resource: What is DNS? provides a beginner-friendly lookup walkthrough and record overview.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon Route 53? explains hosted zones, records, and AWS DNS routing.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Load balancing distributes requests across backend servers or application instances. A load balancer sits between clients and backends and chooses where requests go.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: A single server can become overloaded or unavailable. Sharing work across healthy instances increases capacity and reduces the effect of one failure. Other parts of the system must also be designed for failure.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Clients connect to the balancer, which selects a backend using a policy such as round robin or least connections. Health checks help it avoid unresponsive instances. Some balancers understand HTTP hostnames and paths. Session affinity keeps a client on one backend but may limit flexibility.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: An online store has three web instances. The balancer sends requests to available instances and avoids one that fails its health check.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Applications should avoid relying on local memory or disk for shared user state. Store durable data in a shared service and make health checks reflect readiness. Understand forwarded headers, TLS termination, and timeouts. Related: servers, Nginx, and reverse proxies.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Start with two instances and a /health endpoint. Route traffic only to healthy instances, then stop one in a test environment and confirm requests still succeed.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Backend/target: a server receiving forwarded requests.
  • Health check: a test used to decide whether a target is usable.
  • Algorithm: rule for choosing a target.
  • Failover: directing traffic away from an unavailable component.
  • Session affinity: repeatedly choosing the same backend for a client.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Load balancing spreads load and can help with maintenance or failure recovery. It adds a component to monitor and does not fix slow code or an overloaded database.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Adding instances does not always make an application scale: shared dependencies may still limit it. A passing health check does not prove every feature works.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Nginx documentation: HTTP load balancing explains upstream servers and balancing methods.
  • Official AWS documentation: Elastic Load Balancing describes load balancers, targets, and health checks.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Nginx (pronounced “engine-x”) is web-server software used to serve files and handle HTTP traffic. It can also act as a reverse proxy, TLS endpoint, or load balancer.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Web applications need to accept requests, serve static content, and route requests to application processes. Nginx can sit in front of an application server, separating public traffic entry from application execution.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Nginx reads configuration blocks describing listeners, hostnames, and actions. A server block can match a hostname; a location block serves a file or proxies to an upstream application. Configuration changes should be syntax-tested before reload.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A Node.js app listens on a private port while Nginx listens on port 443. Nginx serves /assets/ and forwards /api/ to the app.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Included files can affect the effective configuration. Restrict public access to upstream applications when appropriate, preserve needed headers, and configure timeouts. Related: reverse proxies and load balancing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Configure a development host to proxy an API path to a local service. Run nginx -t before reloading. If it fails, inspect the error log and confirm the upstream is listening.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Directive: a configuration instruction.
  • Server block: virtual host configuration for a listener and host.
  • Location: rule matching a request URI.
  • Upstream: one or more proxy backend servers.
  • TLS termination: decrypting HTTPS at a front-end component.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Nginx is flexible, widely deployed, and can efficiently serve static files or proxy traffic. Its configuration language has details that take time to learn; mistakes in headers, paths, or access rules can cause outages or expose unintended content.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
