docs.text: Nginx is not a programming language or a replacement for an application's business logic. It can be a web server and proxy at once, but those roles are distinct and independently configured.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Nginx documentation: Beginner’s Guide introduces configuration structure and common tasks.
  • Official Nginx documentation: Reverse proxy module documents proxy directives and behavior.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A reverse proxy accepts client requests and forwards them to backend services. To a visitor, it appears to be the site's server, though the application may run elsewhere.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: A reverse proxy provides a front door for application servers. It can route by hostname or path, terminate HTTPS, serve static files, and distribute traffic. With suitable network rules, it can keep backends off the public network.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: The proxy evaluates routing rules, forwards a request to an upstream, then returns its response. It may add headers such as X-Forwarded-For. Applications should trust these only from known proxies; a client could otherwise forge them.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: Route example.com/api/ to an API and example.com/ to a frontend. Both can stay private while the proxy exposes intended routes.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: When debugging, identify whether a response came from the proxy or application. Check path rewriting, forwarded headers, TLS settings, and timeouts. See Nginx and load balancing.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Configure a development proxy to forward /api/ to a local API. Compare proxied and direct requests to identify routing problems.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: program or user making the request.
  • Upstream/backend: service receiving a forwarded request.
  • Forwarded header: metadata about the original client or connection.
  • TLS termination: ending the encrypted connection at the proxy.
  • Path rewriting: changing a URI before forwarding it.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: A reverse proxy centralizes routing and can simplify TLS and traffic management. It adds a network hop and can become a bottleneck or single point of failure.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A reverse proxy is not automatically a firewall or authentication system. Backends still need access controls and secure application logic.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Nginx documentation: Reverse proxy module explains proxying requests and related directives.
  • Official Cloudflare learning resource: What is a reverse proxy? gives a visual overview and compares proxy roles.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A server is a computer or software process that provides a service to clients. A web server receives HTTP requests and returns pages or data. “Server” describes a role, not necessarily hardware.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Applications need a place to run and respond to requests. A server can provide a website, API, or database. It may be physical hardware, a virtual machine, or a managed platform.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A server process listens on an address and port. A client connects and sends a request using an agreed protocol; the server returns a response. Operating systems, networking rules, and software affect whether it works. Public servers need updates and access control.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a browser requests https://example.com, DNS helps find the service address and web software handles the request. The server may return a file or call an application and database.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Know what listens on each port, how to view logs, and how services restart. Keep private services private and apply updates. Applications must handle timeouts and unavailable dependencies. Related: DNS, Nginx, and AWS.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Run a local development server and open its address in a browser. If it fails, check the process, port, and firewall or container mapping. Do not expose development servers publicly without understanding their protections.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Client: requester of a service.
  • Host: a network-connected computer.
  • Port: number identifying a service endpoint on a host.
  • Process: running program managed by an operating system.
  • Virtual machine: software-defined computer with its own operating environment.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Servers give teams control over software and runtime settings. They require planning, patching, backups, and monitoring. Managed hosting reduces some work but not application responsibilities.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A server need not be a large physical computer. One host can run several services, and one service can span hosts. “Always on” does not mean “always available.”

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation: Amazon EC2 concepts introduces virtual servers and their lifecycle.
  • Third-party tutorial: DigitalOcean: What Is a Server? explains the client-server model in plain language.

docs.title: DevOps and Deployment
docs.text: This section covers the practices and tools used to build, test, deploy, and maintain applications throughout their lifecycle.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Understand source control and automated build-and-release workflows.
  • Learn the purpose of containers and environment-specific configuration.
  • Explore certificates, operational visibility, and data backups.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Git and GitHub
  • Docker
  • CI/CD
  • Environment Variables
  • SSL Certificates
  • Monitoring and Logging
  • Backups

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A backup is a recoverable copy of data or configuration. It protects against accidental deletion, bugs, device failure, and some security incidents. It is useful only if it can be restored in time.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Production data can be lost or corrupted. Replication may keep a service running but also copy accidental deletion. A backup provides a point-in-time recovery option.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A backup process copies selected data to another location on a schedule or continuously. A retention policy defines how long copies are kept. Protect copies and test that they can be restored.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A shop keeps a month's worth of nightly database backups. If a migration corrupts records, the team can restore a clean copy.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Identify what to back up: databases, uploaded files, and configuration may need different schedules. RPO is acceptable recent data loss; RTO is target restore time. Practice restoring safely. See servers, Docker, and monitoring.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Schedule database exports to protected storage and periodically restore one into a test database. Never overwrite the only live copy during a test.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Snapshot: point-in-time representation of data or a volume.
  • Retention: how long backup versions are kept.
  • Restore: recovering data from a backup.
  • RPO: acceptable data-loss interval.
  • RTO: target recovery duration.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Backups enable recovery but consume storage and require maintenance. Replicas alone are not a complete backup plan.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A successful backup job does not prove a restore will work. A backup on the same machine may be lost with the original.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation: What is AWS Backup? describes managed backup and recovery concepts.
  • Official AWS documentation: What is AWS Backup? explains managed backup plans, recovery points, and supported AWS resources.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) automate software checks and releases. A pipeline runs repeatable steps when code changes, helping teams find problems early.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Manual build and release steps can be inconsistent. Automation makes checks predictable and records what was tested. CI/CD does not guarantee a change is correct.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A repository event starts a workflow. Jobs install dependencies, test, lint, and build. A delivery pipeline may publish an artifact; continuous deployment can release automatically after checks pass. Scope secrets and permissions carefully.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A pull request starts tests and a build. After review and merge, a workflow publishes the artifact to staging; production can require approval.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use familiar local commands, clear failures, and deterministic tests. Review workflow permissions and actions; do not expose secrets to untrusted pull-request code. See Git and GitHub, Docker, and environment variables.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Create a workflow that tests each pull request. Run the command locally, then confirm the workflow reports success and failure accurately.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Pipeline/workflow: automated sequence of jobs.
  • Job/step: grouped work and an individual command or action.
  • Artifact: output retained or passed between jobs.
  • Continuous delivery: changes are kept ready for release.
  • Continuous deployment: qualifying changes are released automatically.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: CI/CD reduces repetitive work and catches defects earlier. Pipelines need maintenance and secure credentials. A green check means configured checks passed, not that software is defect-free.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: CI/CD does not mean deploying every commit to production. Teams can automate tests and require production approval.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official GitHub documentation: Understanding GitHub Actions explains workflows, jobs, events, and runners.
  • Official GitHub documentation: Building and testing your code provides examples for configuring automated checks.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Docker builds and runs containers. A container packages an application with user-space dependencies for a more consistent environment across development and deployment.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Applications can behave differently across libraries and runtime versions. A container image records much of the runtime environment, but does not erase differences in hardware, networking, or external services.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A Dockerfile describes how to build an image. The Docker engine runs containers from images. Containers are isolated processes; data that must outlive one belongs in a volume or external service. Images are often published to a registry.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A team builds an API image with declared dependencies and a start command. Teammates and CI run the same setup, connected to a development database.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Avoid embedding credentials and use a non-root user when practical. Understand copied files, exposed ports, and where state is stored. See CI/CD, environment variables, and backups.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Build an image for a small app, start a container, and map a local port. Store persistent test data in a volume instead of assuming it survives container removal.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Image: packaged, read-only template used to create containers.
  • Container: running instance of an image.
  • Dockerfile: instructions for building an image.
  • Registry: service for storing and distributing images.
  • Volume: managed persistent storage attached to containers.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Containers improve consistency and repeatability. They add networking and storage concepts and are not automatically secure. Handle persistent data and secrets deliberately.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A container is not a full virtual machine; it may share the host kernel. Configuration and external services can still differ in production.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Docker documentation: Docker overview introduces images, containers, and the engine.
  • Official Docker documentation: Dockerfile reference explains Dockerfile instructions and syntax.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Environment variables are named values supplied to a running process. Applications use them for deployment settings such as a port, feature mode, or external service.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: The same code may run on a laptop, test system, and production server with different settings. Environment variables supply those values without changing source code. They are not a complete secrets-management system.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: An operating system, shell, container, or platform sets variables before starting a process. The application reads and validates them. Values are usually strings, so parse numbers and booleans carefully. Protect secret values and do not print them in logs.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: An application might read PORT and DATABASE_URL. Development and production can receive different database addresses.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Document required names and safe defaults; never commit passwords or tokens. Exclude local .env files from version control and provide a placeholder .env.example. Use an appropriate secret store for production. See Docker and CI/CD.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Validate PORT on startup and show a useful error if it is missing or invalid. Put placeholders in .env.example; keep local values separately.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Configuration: values that control application behavior.
  • Environment variable: name/value supplied to a process.
  • Secret: sensitive value such as a token or password.
  • .env file: local text file commonly used by tooling to set variables.
  • Validation: checking that a value exists and has an acceptable form.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Environment variables separate settings from code and are widely supported. They can leak through logs or diagnostics and are not encrypted automatically.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: Environment variables are not automatically secret or shared across processes. A .env file is a convention that requires tool or shell support.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Node.js documentation: process.env describes how Node.js applications access environment variables.
  • Official Docker documentation: Environment variables explains environment configuration in Docker Compose.
  • Third-party security guidance: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet discusses safe handling and lifecycle management for secrets.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Git is a distributed version control system that records file changes. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features such as pull requests. Git works without GitHub.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Version control gives developers a history, supports parallel work, and helps review or restore changes. Hosting helps a team exchange and discuss work.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Git records snapshots in commits. Developers edit files, stage selected changes, then commit locally. They can push to a remote and fetch others' work. A GitHub pull request proposes changes for review; it is not a Git command.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A developer creates a branch, commits a search form, then pushes it. A pull request lets teammates review it before merging.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Make understandable commits and review diffs. Do not commit credentials or unrelated edits. Resolve conflicts by understanding both changes. Related: CI/CD runs checks on pull requests.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Inspect git status, create a branch, stage a file, and review git diff --staged before committing. Push the branch and open a pull request.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Repository: project files plus version history.
  • Commit: recorded change with an identifier and metadata.
  • Branch: named pointer to a line of commits.
  • Remote: another copy of a repository, often hosted online.
  • Pull request: proposal and discussion for integrating changes.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Git supports history, offline work, and collaboration. Merges and rebases require care. Hosted services add features but introduce access and availability considerations.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: GitHub is not Git, and local commits are not automatically published. Deleting a file does not erase it from repository history.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Git documentation: About Version Control introduces version-control ideas and Git's model.
  • Official GitHub documentation: About Git explains Git and its use on GitHub.
  • Third-party explainer: Atlassian Git tutorials provides diagrams and practical workflow explanations.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Monitoring collects signals about a system. Logging records events and messages. Together they help teams detect failures and investigate behavior.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Without operational information, a developer may know only that a user reported a problem. Metrics show trends, alerts notify a team, and logs provide details. They do not repair a system automatically.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Applications and infrastructure emit signals. Metrics are numeric measurements over time, such as request duration. Logs are timestamped events; traces follow a request across components. Dashboards visualize signals, while alert rules notify people when a threshold is met. Correlation IDs connect logs for one request.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: After a release, a dashboard shows rising API errors. Request logs with a correlation ID reveal that an endpoint fails when a dependency times out.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use structured logs, but do not record passwords, tokens, or unnecessary personal data. Track latency and errors; set actionable alerts. Related: servers, CI/CD, and backups.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: Add a request ID to each request and include it in logs. Track successes, failures, and latency. Generate a test error and confirm it appears without private data.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Metric: numeric measurement over time.
  • Log: record of an event or message.
  • Trace: connected view of work across services.
  • Alert: notification triggered by a rule.
  • Observability: ability to infer system behavior from its outputs.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Monitoring shortens diagnosis and reveals trends. It needs storage and access controls; excessive logging creates cost and privacy risks.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: More logs do not automatically ease debugging. An alert is not a diagnosis, and dashboards cannot show uncollected data.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official AWS documentation: What is Amazon CloudWatch? describes metrics, logs, alarms, and monitoring.
  • Official OpenTelemetry documentation: What is OpenTelemetry? introduces vendor-neutral instrumentation for traces, metrics, and logs.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: TLS certificates help a browser verify a website's identity and establish an encrypted HTTPS connection. “SSL certificate” is a common older name; modern web encryption uses TLS.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Without HTTPS, traffic could be read or changed in transit. TLS protects confidentiality and integrity and helps authenticate a domain when the certificate is correctly checked.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: A certificate binds a public key to a domain and is signed by a trusted certificate authority. During a TLS handshake, the server presents it and proves possession of the private key. The browser checks the chain, domain, and validity period. Certificates expire; protect private keys.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When a user visits https://shop.example, the server presents a certificate for that hostname. An expired or mismatched certificate triggers a browser warning.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use HTTPS throughout the site and renew certificates before expiry. Protect private keys; never put them in source control. Related: reverse proxies and DNS.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a test domain, use a tool such as Certbot with a compatible web server. Confirm the hostname and test automatic renewal.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• TLS: protocol for securing communication over a network.
  • Certificate authority (CA): organization that issues certificates.
  • Public/private key pair: cryptographic keys used for authentication and secure exchanges.
  • Certificate chain: links from a site certificate to a trusted root.
  • Renewal: replacing a certificate before expiration.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: TLS protects data in transit. Certificate renewal requires care, and HTTPS does not prove a site is honest or encrypt data after it reaches the server.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: A certificate does not guarantee an application is safe or prevent phishing. It is not an endorsement of the site's content.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official Let’s Encrypt documentation: Getting started explains free automated certificates and how to begin.
  • Official Cloudflare learning resource: What is an SSL certificate? explains certificates, HTTPS, and validation in accessible terms.
  • Internet standard: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3 specifies TLS 1.3 for readers seeking the protocol details.

docs.title: Operating Systems and Linux
docs.text:
This section introduces the software that manages computer resources and the Linux tools developers use to work with those resources.

An operating system coordinates programs, memory, files, and devices. Linux gives developers a practical environment for observing those resources using small command-line tools.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Explain how operating systems coordinate programs and hardware.
  • Distinguish processes, threads, and the memory they use.
  • Understand files, permissions, and essential Linux concepts.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Operating System Fundamentals
  • Processes and Threads
  • Memory Management
  • File Systems
  • Linux Fundamentals

Start with operating-system fundamentals, then explore processes and threads, memory management, and file systems. The Linux fundamentals lesson ties these ideas to everyday diagnostic commands.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A file system organizes data and metadata on storage. Programs can create, find, and manage files without knowing how a drive stores bits.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Storage devices provide blocks; a file system tracks names, directories, ownership, permissions, and content locations. File systems vary in features and supported devices.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Linux exposes files in one tree rooted at /. Directories map names to entries. On Unix-like systems, an inode stores file metadata and points to data; a filename is a directory entry, so hard links can give data multiple names.

Mounting attaches another file system at a directory called a mount point. Permissions and ownership help control access but are not a complete security model.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: Saving /home/lee/project/app.py asks the OS to write through the mounted file system. Opening it later looks up the path and reads the contents.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use file APIs rather than assuming a disk layout. Handle missing files, permissions, full storage, and partial failures. File extensions do not prove file contents.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Linux, ls -l displays permissions and sizes, stat file.txt shows metadata, and df -h reports file-system space. These are read-only.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Directory: collection of named entries.
  • Metadata: information about a file beyond its content.
  • Mount point: directory where a file system is attached.
  • Inode: Unix-like file metadata object, distinct from its filename.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: File systems organize persistent data and access. Hardware faults or software errors can damage them, so backups remain necessary; formats are not universally compatible.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: • A directory is not necessarily a physical folder, and deleting a name does not ensure that its data is unrecoverable.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — Linux man-pages project: inode(7) explains Unix inode metadata and directory entries.
  • Official documentation — GNU: GNU Coreutils manual documents standard file and directory inspection utilities.
  • Third-party explanation — DigitalOcean: An Introduction to Linux Permissions explains common owner, group, and permission concepts.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Linux is an open-source kernel used across many kinds of devices. A Linux distribution combines it with utilities, libraries, package management, and applications. The command line helps inspect and manage a system.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Distributions provide flexible environments used on developer computers, containers, and servers. Core conventions make troubleshooting easier across interfaces.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
A shell reads commands and starts programs. Pipes connect one program's output to another's input. The file tree starts at /; /home commonly contains user files. Absolute paths start with /; relative paths use the current directory.

Permissions control file access. PATH helps the shell find programs. Distributions differ in package managers, shells, and service tools.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A developer may inspect logs, processes, and disk space to diagnose a server without changing its configuration.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Read manual pages before using unfamiliar commands. Be careful with commands that delete, change ownership, or require administrator privileges.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: pwd, ls -la, whoami, and uname -a inspect directory, files, account, and system details. man ls opens documentation where available; press q to exit.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Distribution (distro): packaged Linux system built around the kernel.
  • Shell: command interpreter, such as Bash.
  • Root directory: top of the file-system tree, written /.
  • Package manager: tool for installing and tracking software packages.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Linux supports automation and configurable systems, but distribution differences and command-line complexity can challenge beginners.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: • Linux is not one distribution. A terminal hosts a shell, and diagnostic output alone does not guarantee system health.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — Linux man-pages project: Linux manual page index provides searchable references for Linux commands, system calls, and interfaces.
  • Official documentation — GNU: Bash Reference Manual explains Bash syntax, commands, and shell behavior.
  • Third-party explanation — DigitalOcean: An Introduction to Linux Basics gives new Linux users a guided overview of the command line.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Memory management assigns and protects working memory. Programs use virtual addresses, which the OS and hardware map to physical memory.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: RAM is limited and shared. Virtual memory gives each process an address space and helps prevent unintended access to another process's memory.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Hardware translates virtual addresses through page tables. Memory uses fixed-size pages and frames; the OS controls their mappings and permissions. Under pressure, it can reclaim caches or move pages to swap. Swap is much slower than RAM and does not replace sufficient memory.

Processes have separate virtual spaces, while shared libraries and mappings can share memory. When memory is exhausted, an allocation may fail or a process may be terminated.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: The OS tracks memory used by browser tabs and can reclaim unused caches to support active work.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Watch for leaks and invalid access. Cached memory may be reclaimable, and virtual size is not the same as resident physical memory.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Linux, free -h summarizes memory and vmstat 1 3 samples activity. These commands are read-only; interpret results alongside application measurements.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Virtual memory: per-process address-space abstraction.
  • Page: fixed-size block used for memory mapping.
  • Swap: disk-backed space that may hold less-active memory pages.
  • Resident memory: process memory currently held in physical RAM.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Virtual memory enables isolation and sharing. Translation and page faults have costs; heavy swapping can make a system slow.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: • High memory use may include reclaimable caches; virtual memory is not identical to swap.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — Linux man-pages project: mmap(2) documents mapping files or anonymous regions into a process address space.
  • Third-party explanation — DigitalOcean: How To Add Swap Space on Ubuntu 20.04 explains what swap is and its trade-offs. The commands in that tutorial change a system; this lesson's practical commands remain read-only.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: An operating system (OS) coordinates hardware and provides common services to programs. Examples include Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Without an OS, each program would need to manage hardware itself. The OS offers shared interfaces and coordinates competing requests.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Programs have limited privileges. To read a file or create a process, they request a system call. The kernel performs permitted operations; drivers help it communicate with hardware.

The OS schedules tasks, manages memory and files, handles input/output, and enforces isolation. Operating systems expose different interfaces and policies.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: When an editor opens a document, the OS checks permissions and provides the file data without exposing the device's physical layout.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Applications rely on OS APIs and may behave differently across platforms. Diagnose whether a problem belongs to the application, OS configuration, resource pressure, or hardware.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Linux, uname -a reports kernel and machine information and ps -ef shows processes. Both are read-only; the kernel version does not identify every OS component.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Kernel: privileged core managing hardware and system resources.
  • System call: controlled request from a program to the kernel.
  • Driver: software that helps an OS communicate with a device.
  • User space: environment where ordinary applications run.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: An OS makes hardware easier to share, but adds complexity and can contain bugs or security weaknesses. Maintenance and limited permissions matter.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: • The kernel is not the whole OS, and an OS does not guarantee applications are safe. A Linux distribution adds utilities and applications.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — Linux man-pages project: syscalls(2) describes the Linux system-call interface and points to individual calls.
  • Third-party explanation — DigitalOcean: An Introduction to Linux Basics introduces Linux concepts and common command-line practices.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A process is a running program with execution state and resources. A thread is an execution path within a process. The OS schedules many tasks across available processor cores.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Processes isolate programs. Threads let one program perform activities such as handling input while working in the background. The OS creates and schedules them.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
A process has an address space and resources such as open files. Threads typically share memory but have their own execution state and stack. Uncoordinated access to shared data can cause race conditions.

The scheduler selects runnable work; switching has a cost, and busy tasks compete for CPU time. Linux tasks have identifiers and states.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A web server may use processes or threads for multiple clients. Shared state must be managed carefully when using threads.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Threads share data but require synchronization. Processes offer more isolation but need communication mechanisms. Consider failures and cleanup, not only speed.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: On Linux, ps -ef lists processes and ps -eLf includes threads. They inspect state; output varies by system. Exit live top with q.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• PID: process identifier.
  • Thread: scheduled execution path within a process.
  • Scheduler: OS component choosing runnable work.
  • Race condition: outcome depends on timing of concurrent operations.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Concurrency can improve responsiveness, but races, deadlocks, and oversubscription make programs harder to test.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text: • A process is a running instance, threads sharing a process are not isolated, and adding threads does not guarantee speed.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation — Linux man-pages project: clone(2) documents the Linux interface used to create tasks with selected sharing behavior.
  • Third-party explanation — Wikipedia: Process (computing) describes processes and their relationship to programs and threads.

docs.title: Security and Testing
docs.text: This section introduces methods for checking application behavior, protecting systems and data, and evaluating reliability and performance.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Build a foundation in web and API security concepts.
  • Understand authentication security and the OWASP project.
  • Learn testing fundamentals and performance testing concepts.
  • Apply security checks throughout design, implementation, and operation.
  • Use testing to produce evidence about behavior, reliability, and performance.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Web Security Fundamentals
  • OWASP
  • Authentication Security
  • API Security
  • Testing Fundamentals
  • Performance Testing

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: An application programming interface (API) lets software exchange data and request actions. API security designs interfaces so only intended users and services can perform permitted actions and data stays protected. See Web Security Fundamentals for related ideas.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: APIs often expose private records or powerful operations. A hidden button is not a security control: anyone who can send a request may try it directly. API security limits risks from mistakes, stolen credentials, and unexpected inputs.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Use HTTPS, authenticate each caller, and authorize every action against its specific resource. Validate input, limit request sizes and rates, and return only needed fields. Keep secrets out of URLs and logs; use safe errors and retire old API versions deliberately.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A note-taking API may allow a signed-in user to list notes. The server must also check that each requested note belongs to that user; knowing a note ID must not grant access. This is object-level authorization, a frequent API design concern.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Treat every request as untrusted, including those from your frontend. Document authorization rules and expected inputs, and test allowed and denied cases. Rate limits and monitoring help, but do not replace authorization.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For GET /notes/42, authenticate the caller, load the note, and check its owner before returning it. For creation, accept documented fields such as title and body, not privileged fields such as ownerId or isAdmin. Test access denial for another user's note.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Authentication: establishing who or what is making a request.
  • Authorization: deciding what that identity may do.
  • Object-level authorization: checking access to the particular record named by a request.
  • Rate limiting: restricting request volume over time.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Explicit API controls reduce accidental data exposure and make behavior testable. They take ongoing effort: rules must evolve with features, versions, and data models. Overly broad permissions are unsafe; overly narrow or inconsistent rules can break legitimate clients.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• CORS is not authentication; it mainly controls browser cross-origin access.
  • An unguessable identifier does not replace an ownership check.
  • A valid token does not automatically authorize every operation.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official standard/project: OWASP API Security Project describes common API risks and defensive guidance.
  • OWASP guidance: REST Security Cheat Sheet provides practical controls for REST APIs.
  • Continue with Authentication Security and Testing Fundamentals.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Authentication checks that a person, device, or service is the identity it claims to be. Authorization determines what that identity may do. Secure authentication protects accounts, private data, and administrative actions.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Applications need to distinguish one user's data and actions from another's. Weak passwords, stolen sessions, and unsafe recovery flows can enable account takeover. Strong checks lower these risks without making legitimate access unnecessarily difficult.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Users present authenticators such as a password, device-bound credential, or one-time code. The service verifies proof, then creates a session or token. Store passwords with a dedicated, slow hashing function and unique salt, never as plaintext or reversible encryption. Sessions need unpredictable identifiers, secure cookie settings, expiration, and revocation. Protect recovery and enrollment as carefully as sign-in.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A banking service may ask for a password and a hardware-backed passkey. The password alone is not enough to complete sign-in when stronger verification is required. After success, a short-lived session cookie lets the browser make later requests without resending the password.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Choose a mature identity library or provider. Protect login and recovery against guessing, use generic failure messages where appropriate, and revoke sessions after password changes or suspected compromise. MFA reduces some takeover risks but does not make phishing impossible.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: In a browser app, issue a session cookie with HttpOnly, Secure, and an appropriate SameSite value. Rotate its identifier after login or privilege changes. On logout, invalidate the session and expire the cookie. Never put session tokens in URLs.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Authenticator: something used to prove an identity.
  • MFA: verification using more than one type of factor.
  • Session: server-recognized state associated with a signed-in client.
  • Password hashing: one-way transformation designed to protect stored password verifiers.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Passkeys and MFA reduce takeover risk, while sessions add convenience. Added steps complicate recovery, so design for usability and recovery abuse.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A login form is not secure just because it uses HTTPS.
  • Encoding or encrypting passwords is not a substitute for password hashing.
  • MFA is valuable, but does not prevent every phishing or session theft scenario.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• OWASP guidance: Authentication Cheat Sheet covers defensive implementation and verification practices.
  • Official standard: W3C Web Authentication (WebAuthn) Level 3 specifies browser and authenticator interactions for public-key authentication.
  • Continue with API Security and Web Security Fundamentals.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a nonprofit community creating open software security resources. Projects include risk lists, verification standards, testing guidance, and cheat sheets. OWASP provides guidance, not a product that automatically secures applications.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Application security can feel broad. OWASP helps developers, testers, and organizations share vocabulary and identify common risks. Its materials are starting points for training, design reviews, and security requirements.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: OWASP projects serve different purposes. The Top 10 summarizes major web application risk categories for awareness. The Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) offers testable requirements, while cheat sheets provide focused implementation advice. Check each resource's version and scope.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A team planning a new account feature can use the Top 10 to prompt threat discussions, consult the Authentication Cheat Sheet for implementation considerations, and translate applicable ASVS requirements into review and test criteria.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use OWASP materials to ask better questions, then adapt controls to the application's architecture and threats. A list is not a complete audit, and a passing checklist does not prove safety. Revisit assumptions when the product changes.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For file uploads, consider unauthorized access, unsafe handling, and resource exhaustion. Write requirements such as checking ownership, limiting size, validating formats, and storing uploads outside executable paths. Link each requirement to a test.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• OWASP Top 10: an awareness resource describing prevalent web application risk areas.
  • ASVS: a framework of security verification requirements.
  • Cheat sheet: concise, topic-specific implementation guidance.
  • Risk: a combination of potential impact and likelihood in a given context.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: OWASP provides accessible, widely used references and a shared vocabulary. Lists can be misused as checkboxes, and generic guidance cannot replace threat modeling or expert review. Always select the resource appropriate to the question.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• OWASP is not a certification that an application is safe.
  • The Top 10 is not an exhaustive catalog or a step-by-step secure coding standard.
  • A control copied from guidance still needs testing in its real environment.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• OWASP project: OWASP Top 10 introduces major web application risk categories for awareness.
  • OWASP standard: Application Security Verification Standard provides structured, testable security requirements.
  • OWASP guidance: Cheat Sheet Series offers focused defensive implementation advice across many topics.
  • Continue with Web Security Fundamentals and API Security.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Performance testing measures application behavior under workloads. It helps teams understand response time, throughput, resource use, and stability, find bottlenecks, and verify service expectations.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: An application may slow down or fail when many people use it at once. Slow pages frustrate users; overloaded services affect reliability and costs. Testing helps detect regressions.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Start with a question and representative actions, data sizes, arrival rates, and duration. Measure a baseline, then vary load while observing latency percentiles, throughput, errors, CPU, memory, and dependencies. A load test checks expected demand; a stress test explores limits; a soak test looks for problems over time. Test only in an authorized environment.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A team expects a ticketing site to handle a launch-day surge. It models browsing, search, and checkout. Results may show that search queries dominate database time, suggesting indexing or caching work.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Define success criteria, such as a p95 response-time limit at a request rate and an acceptable error rate. Document test data and conditions. Repeat tests and account for network noise, caches, and shared infrastructure.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a local service, use a load-testing tool to send a modest, gradually increasing set of requests to a test endpoint. Record p50 and p95 latency plus status codes, then compare with a baseline commit. Stop if the test causes unexpected load or errors in shared services.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Latency: time taken for a request to complete.
  • Throughput: completed work per unit of time.
  • Percentile: a value below which a stated fraction of observations fall; p95 covers 95%.
  • Load, stress, soak: tests of expected demand, capacity limits, and sustained operation.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Performance tests provide evidence for capacity and can expose bottlenecks early. Real systems are complex, and simulated workloads may not match production. Testing consumes resources and can disturb shared environments, so scope and authorization matter.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Average latency can hide slow experiences; inspect percentiles and errors.
  • More virtual users do not automatically mean a more realistic test.
  • A passing result today does not guarantee future capacity.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: Grafana k6 documentation explains load-test scripts, execution, and performance metrics.
  • Third-party explanation: Google web.dev: Web Vitals explains user-facing web performance measurements and their thresholds.
  • Continue with Testing Fundamentals.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Software testing checks whether a program behaves as intended and reveals defects before users encounter them. Tests can be automated or manual. Testing gives evidence about behavior under selected conditions; it does not prove software is perfect.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Small code changes can affect other parts of an application. Tests make expected behavior visible, support refactoring, and catch regressions. They document decisions about edge cases and errors.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Start from requirements. A unit test checks a small piece; an integration test checks component interactions; an end-to-end test exercises a user journey. Good suites balance speed, confidence, and maintenance. Tests should be repeatable and have clear assertions.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: For a shopping cart, unit tests can verify quantity calculations, integration tests can check that orders are saved correctly, and an end-to-end test can verify a customer can add an item and see the updated total.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Test normal cases, boundaries, and expected failures. Use descriptive names and make each test explain a behavior. When fixing a bug, add a test that would have caught it. A green suite covers only the scenarios it checks.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a function that computes a discount, check a normal eligible purchase, a purchase below the minimum, and an invalid negative amount. Assert the exact results and error behavior. Run the focused tests while iterating, then run the wider suite before sharing the change.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Assertion: a condition a test expects to be true.
  • Regression: a previously working behavior that breaks after a change.
  • Fixture: prepared state or data used by a test.
  • Coverage: a measure of which code or behavior tests exercise; it is not a measure of correctness.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Tests can catch regressions early and make refactoring less risky. They cost time to create and maintain, and brittle tests can slow teams without adding confidence. Prefer meaningful behavior checks over maximizing line coverage alone.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A passing test does not guarantee absence of bugs.
  • High code coverage does not guarantee useful assertions.
  • Manual testing and automated testing complement one another.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: pytest documentation explains Python test discovery, assertions, fixtures, and running tests.
  • Third-party explanation: Martin Fowler: Test Pyramid discusses balancing test levels and feedback speed.
  • Continue with Performance Testing and OWASP.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Web security protects websites, browsers, servers, and exchanged data. Secure applications use multiple controls because no single technique prevents every attack. See API Security and Authentication Security for related topics.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Web applications handle personal information, payments, and business operations. A weakness can expose data, alter records, or disrupt a service. Security protects users and supports reliable operation.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Identify valuable data and likely threats. Use HTTPS, validate input, encode output for its context, enforce server-side authorization, and store secrets safely. Limit privileges and data collection. Security headers, updates, logging, tests, backups, and incident plans add layers.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A comment feature should treat submitted text as untrusted. The server validates length and format, stores it safely, and the page encodes it as text rather than interpreting it as markup. The server also checks that the current user is allowed to create or remove the comment.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Security is a lifecycle activity. Include it in design, review, deployment, and maintenance. Use least privilege and threat modeling. Log important events without recording passwords, session secrets, or unnecessary personal data.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: For a profile update endpoint, verify the session and edit permission, validate fields, and update only allowed properties. Use parameterized queries, return safe errors, and test permitted and denied updates.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Threat: a possible cause of harm to a system or its data.
  • Vulnerability: a weakness that could be misused.
  • Least privilege: granting only the access needed for a task.
  • Defense in depth: using multiple complementary controls.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Layered security reduces reliance on any one control and limits the impact of mistakes. More controls can add complexity and operational work; select them according to risks and test that they do not create unsafe workarounds.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• HTTPS protects communication in transit, not every stored value or authorization decision.
  • Input validation does not replace output encoding or access control.
  • Security is not finished when an application launches.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• OWASP project: OWASP Top 10 is an awareness overview of common web application risks.
  • OWASP guidance: Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet explains how CSP can add a browser-enforced layer against some content injection risks.
  • Official documentation: MDN: Transport Layer Security explains how TLS protects web communications.

docs.title: Rust and Systems Programming
docs.text: This section explores systems programming with Rust, including memory, concurrency, operating-system interaction, and the Tauri application framework.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Learn core Rust concepts and how ownership and borrowing work.
  • Understand memory and concurrency topics in systems software.
  • Explore how Rust programs interact with operating systems and Tauri.
  • Practice Rust's core types and error handling through small examples.
  • Understand how ownership supports safe memory use and concurrency.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Rust Fundamentals
  • Ownership and Borrowing
  • Concurrency
  • Memory Management
  • Operating System Interaction
  • Tauri

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Concurrency makes progress on multiple tasks during overlapping periods. Parallelism executes tasks at the same instant on different processing units. Rust supports both and prevents many data races in safe code.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Applications need to handle network requests, background work, or independent calculations without blocking. Concurrency can improve responsiveness and use processor cores, but introduces coordination challenges.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Rust threads may communicate through channels or shared state. Start one with std::thread::spawn; moving owned data transfers it safely. Channels send values without shared mutable access. Shared state can use Mutex<T> and Arc<T>: a mutex allows one holder at a time, while Arc shares ownership but does not itself make mutation safe.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A command-line tool can download files on worker threads and send results to a coordinator, which reports progress and handles errors.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Prefer message passing or ownership transfer when practical. Shared mutable state requires careful locking and can lead to deadlocks, contention, or difficult-to-reproduce bugs. Choose the simplest model that meets the application's needs and handle thread panics and task failures deliberately.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
use std::thread;

let worker = thread::spawn(|| {
    2 + 2
});
let answer = worker.join().expect("worker panicked");
assert_eq!(answer, 4);

join waits for the worker and returns its result. Real programs should also consider cancellation, work limits, and graceful shutdown.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Thread: an execution path managed by the operating system.
  • Data race: unsynchronized conflicting memory access, including a write.
  • Mutex: a lock that gives one thread at a time access to protected data.
  • Channel: a communication path for sending values between tasks.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Concurrency can keep applications responsive and increase throughput. It adds coordination costs and can create nondeterministic behavior. More threads are not always faster, especially when work is small or contends for the same resource.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Concurrency and parallelism are related but not identical.
  • Arc<T> provides shared ownership, not automatic thread-safe mutation.
  • Rust's safety guarantees do not prevent deadlocks or incorrect business logic.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: The Rust Book, Fearless Concurrency introduces threads, message passing, and shared state.
  • Official standard library documentation: std::sync documents synchronization primitives including mutexes and atomic reference counting.
  • Continue with Ownership and Borrowing.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Memory management is how a program obtains, uses, and releases memory. Rust combines ownership rules with types such as Box, Vec, and String to make common errors difficult to express in safe code without a tracing garbage collector.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Programs need memory for values and collections. Incorrect lifetime handling can cause leaks, invalid references, or double frees. Rust helps manage resource lifetimes with predictable runtime costs.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Each value has an owner. When it leaves scope, Rust drops it and releases its resources. Moving transfers ownership; borrowing gives temporary access. Stack-local values are typically released at scope end, while growable data commonly uses the heap. Types can implement Drop for cleanup. The borrow checker ensures references do not outlive their data.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A Vec<String> owns a growable list of strings. When the vector is dropped, it drops its strings, which in turn release their allocations. The developer can pass a reference to inspect the list without copying ownership.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Prefer standard library types: Box<T> for a heap allocation, Vec<T> for growable sequences, and String for owned UTF-8 text. Unsafe code shifts proof obligations to the programmer; keep it small and carefully reviewed.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
fn first_length(words: &[String]) -> Option<usize> {
    words.first().map(String::len)
}

The slice borrow lets the function inspect strings without taking ownership of the vector. The returned length is an owned integer, so it remains valid after the borrow ends.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Stack: common storage for scoped values with known layout.
  • Heap: storage used for values whose size or lifetime needs dynamic allocation.
  • Drop: cleanup behavior run when an owned value is released.
  • Leak: memory that remains allocated when no longer useful; Rust memory safety does not guarantee that programs never leak.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Ownership provides predictable cleanup and prevents many memory errors in safe code. Lifetimes and shared access take practice. Reference counting and interior mutability add runtime costs or complexity.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Rust does not put every value on the stack; containers commonly own heap allocations.
  • Borrowing does not duplicate the owned value.
  • Memory safety does not prevent all leaks or excessive memory use.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: The Rust Book, Understanding Ownership explains moves, references, and lifetimes.
  • Official standard library documentation: std::boxed::Box documents owned heap allocation.
  • Continue with Ownership and Borrowing and Rust Fundamentals.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Operating-system interaction is how a program uses host services such as files, processes, environment variables, and networking. Rust's standard library provides common interfaces; lower-level APIs may vary by platform.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Programs need to read input, save data, or launch work. Operating systems control these resources, so code must handle missing files, denied permissions, and unavailable devices.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Rust's std::fs provides filesystem APIs, std::process supports child processes, and std::env exposes arguments and environment variables. These APIs return Result<T, E> because operations can fail. Handle or propagate errors; platform-specific APIs may need conditional compilation or a crate.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A configuration utility reads a file from a user-selected path. It should report a useful error if the file is absent or unreadable, validate its contents, and avoid writing outside the intended location. The OS enforces permissions, but application policy still matters.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Treat paths, environment values, and arguments as inputs. Use least privilege, avoid shell commands built from untrusted strings, and pass process arguments directly. Consider encoding and platform differences.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
use std::fs;

fn read_config(path: &str) -> Result<String, std::io::Error> {
    fs::read_to_string(path)
}

The function returns the I/O error to its caller, which can decide how to display or recover from it. Production code may use Path and add context to errors.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• System call: a controlled request from a program to the operating system.
  • I/O: input and output, such as reading a file or writing to a socket.
  • Permission: an operating-system rule governing resource access.
  • Portability: the ability to build and behave correctly across environments.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Standard library interfaces make common tasks clear and portable. Operating-system behavior can still differ by platform, and I/O is fallible and often slower than in-memory work. Avoid assuming that a path, permission, or process behaves identically everywhere.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Rust's type safety does not guarantee that a file exists or access is allowed.
  • Checking a path and using it later can have race conditions; design sensitive file operations carefully.
  • A command string should not be assembled from untrusted input and passed through a shell.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: The Rust Book, I/O Project demonstrates reading input, structuring errors, and building a small command-line program.
  • Official standard library documentation: std::fs describes Rust's filesystem operations.
  • Continue with Rust Fundamentals and Tauri.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Ownership decides which part of a program is responsible for a value. Borrowing gives temporary reference-based access. These rules prevent dangling references and unsafe shared mutation in safe Rust.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Systems programs need resource control and predictable cleanup. Memory errors can happen when data is freed too early or twice, or changed while another part of a program assumes it is stable. Rust checks many such constraints at compile time.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Each value has one owner. Assigning many non-Copy values moves ownership, so the old binding cannot be used. A reference borrows a value. You may have multiple immutable references or one mutable reference at a time. Lifetimes describe how long references remain valid; the compiler often infers them.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A function can borrow a string to count its characters without consuming it. The caller keeps ownership and can use the string after the call. If the function needs to return newly created text, it can return an owned String.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: When the compiler reports a borrow error, consider borrowing, moving, or cloning. Cloning may copy more data than needed. First clarify ownership intent rather than using unsafe code to silence an error.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
fn byte_count(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

let message = String::from("hello");
let count = byte_count(&message);
println!("{message}: {count}");

The function receives a shared borrow. It does not own or modify the string, so the caller can still use it afterward.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Move: transfer of ownership from one binding to another.
  • Borrow: temporary access through a reference.
  • Immutable reference (&T): read-only access.
  • Mutable reference (&mut T): exclusive mutable access while the borrow is active.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Ownership enables automatic cleanup without a garbage collector. Its rules can be unfamiliar when sharing data, but clear ownership can simplify architecture.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Borrowing is not the same as copying.
  • A reference cannot safely outlive the value it refers to.
  • &mut means exclusive access, not simply a preference to mutate.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: The Rust Book, References and Borrowing gives examples of borrowing rules.
  • Official documentation: The Rust Book, Ownership explains scope, moves, and cleanup.
  • Continue with Memory Management and Concurrency.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Rust is a systems programming language designed for performance and reliability. It offers low-level control, compile-time memory-safety checks, and strong types. It is used for tools, servers, embedded software, and libraries.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Software close to hardware needs performance and resource control, but memory errors can be easy to introduce. Rust prevents many common errors in safe code before a program runs.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: Rust code uses crates and modules. The compiler checks types and ownership; Cargo manages builds, dependencies, and tests. match handles enums such as Option<T> and Result<T, E>, making missing values and errors explicit.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A command-line utility can accept a filename, read it, and report a clear error if it does not exist. Rust's standard library provides file access, and Result lets the program decide whether to retry, display a message, or return an error status.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Use Cargo to build and test, keep dependencies intentional, and read compiler diagnostics carefully. Favor clear code over premature optimization. Use unsafe only when needed and document its safety requirements.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
fn greeting(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", greeting("Rust"));
}

The function borrows its input and returns a newly owned string. Save the example in a Cargo project and run it with cargo run.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Crate: a Rust compilation unit and package.
  • Cargo: Rust's build and package manager.
  • Enum: a type that can represent one of several named variants.
  • Result<T, E>: a value representing success (Ok) or failure (Err).

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Rust combines performance with strong compile-time guarantees and a productive package toolchain. Its ownership model and compiler messages can take time to learn. Not every task requires low-level control, and Rust's ecosystem or build times may not suit every project.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Rust is not automatically faster than every other language in every workload.
  • A successful compile does not prove program logic is correct.
  • Safe Rust greatly reduces certain memory risks but does not remove all security or reliability concerns.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: The Rust Programming Language is the primary guided introduction to Rust.
  • Official documentation: The Rust standard library documents built-in types and APIs.
  • Continue with Ownership and Borrowing and Memory Management.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Tauri builds desktop applications with a web-based interface and Rust application layer. The frontend runs in the platform's webview, while Rust commands provide native capabilities.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text: Tauri lets teams reuse web skills for desktop applications and use Rust for native operations. The result still depends on a webview and operating-system behavior.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: The frontend calls registered Rust commands through Tauri's IPC mechanism. Rust performs approved work and returns results. Capabilities govern access to features. A secure app exposes only needed commands, validates inputs, and treats frontend data as untrusted.

docs.title: Real-world example
docs.text: A notes app might use a web interface for editing and a Rust command to save data to a selected local file. The command should validate the request and apply a clear file-access policy instead of granting broad filesystem access to every frontend component.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Treat the UI-to-Rust boundary as an API. A hidden button does not prevent a command call. Keep secrets out of frontend code, minimize permissions, validate commands, and test on supported systems.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text: A command can be registered in the Rust application and invoked from the frontend using Tauri's documented API. In a real project, configure the command and capability according to the installed Tauri version, handle errors in both layers, and avoid giving a demo command access to sensitive files.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Webview: a platform component that renders web content inside a desktop application.
  • IPC: inter-process or component communication used to pass requests and results.
  • Command: a Rust function exposed to the frontend.
  • Capability: a policy describing which application components may access particular permissions.

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages
docs.text: Tauri reuses web UI skills and invokes native Rust code. Behavior can differ among webviews, and developers must secure both the frontend and native boundary.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Rust commands should not trust data just because it came from the app's own UI.
  • A desktop app is not automatically safe from web-style injection.
  • Tauri's permission model still requires careful configuration.

docs.title: Further Learning & References
docs.text:
• Official documentation: Tauri documentation explains setup, application architecture, commands, and security concepts for Tauri 2.
  • Official documentation: Tauri security documentation describes security practices and the permission model.
  • Continue with Operating System Interaction and Web Security Fundamentals.
